20019-lectures-on-landscape-delivered-at:
John Ruskin delivered his Lectures on Landscape at Oxford in Lent term 1871. He compares two Turner paintings by their harmony of color. One is a harmony of cool color, the other of hot. Both are exquisitely designed in ornamental lines, he grants. But they were not painted for those qualities, he insists. One scene is full of delight to men; the other, of pain and danger. Turner's object is the human meaning of landscape.

Ruskin was Oxford's first Slade Professor of Fine Art. His lectures drew crowds and set Victorian taste. Landscape here means truth to nature, morally read. These talks teach students how to see before judging. Turner stands as prophet of that seeing throughout. The lectures remain a gateway into Ruskin's mind.
20765-diary-of-anna-green-winslow-a-bost:
Alice Morse Earle edited the diary of Anna Green Winslow, a Boston schoolgirl of 1771. Anna was sent from Nova Scotia to Boston, her parents' birthplace, to be finished at good schools. She wrote with care, both for her parents' joy and for practice in fine handwriting.

Daily life in colonial Boston fills the small pages: lessons, calls, dress, and church. A girl's eye catches what grand histories miss. The diary shows the prim, narrow round of a town on the edge of revolt. Few sources let young readers hear the past in a voice so close to their own age.
9896-my-days-of-adventure-the-fall-of-fr:
Ernest Alfred Vizetelly, who had already written of the Tuileries court, published this memoir of the Franco-German War in London in 1914. He was in France when war broke out, and he stayed through revolution, siege, and defeat.

Chapters carry him from Paris under siege to Versailles, then to Brittany with its army, and on to Le Mans and the bitter end. Vizetelly reports what he saw, not what generals later claimed: hunger, rumor, flight, and stubborn hope. The book is a firsthand record of France's fall, vivid and unromantic.
arxiv-2509-00271:
Yishu Li, Xinyi Mao, Ying Yuan, Kyutae Sim, Ben Eisner, and David Held present HAVE in 2025, a history-aware verifier that helps robots pick actions under ambiguity. Robots often face objects whose handling outcome is unclear until touched. Generative models can propose actions, but even with action history they tend to choose poorly in ambiguous cases.

HAVE splits action generation from verification. A diffusion-based generator proposes many candidate actions with no conditions. The verifier then picks the most promising one by reasoning over past interactions with the object. Theory shows a verifier lifts expected action quality. Tests in simulated and real settings back the gain, with analysis of where history helps most.
arxiv-2509-00471:
A D Grinenko and one co-author, D A Kovaleva, track how often open star clusters, loose groups of stars born together, pass close to each other. They follow cluster centers over sixty-four million years, using the galpy package to move orbits through the pull of the Galaxy.

Near the Sun, they find pairs meet at distances near their own sizes about thirty-five to forty times per million years. Meetings between clusters of very unlike ages happen about fifteen times per million years. They also flag one likely bound pair, HSC 1428 and Gulliver 22, and list expected close passes for many pairs, showing such meetings may shape star groups more than once thought.
arxiv-2509-00671:
Siavash Jafarizadeh, writing alone, studies ribbon concordance for periodic links. A periodic link sits in three-dimensional space and has rotational symmetry. The symmetry acts around a fixed unknot. He uses a version of Khovanov homology, an algebraic tool for links. This version is built to respect the link's symmetry.

Jafarizadeh proves the tool behaves well under surfaces that link one link to another. Such surfaces must respect the symmetry too. He also shows ribbon concordances act as split injections on the groups. A split injection is an embedding that another map can undo. These facts give a new obstruction test for the field. The test can rule out some concordances outright.
arxiv-2509-00971:
Jay Vaghasiya leads a team of five authors on CoreThink, a symbolic reasoning layer for large language models. CoreThink targets long horizon tasks. Its method is called General Symbolics. The approach diverges from test-time scaling and fine-tuning routes. It also diverges from reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards.

Their General Symbolic Reasoner focuses on three use cases. They are tool-calling, code generation, and planning. It reports leading scores across seven benchmarks in those areas. Benchmarks include LiveCodeBench, instruction-following evals, and ARC-AGI-2. An agentic coding environment built on the same principles scores strongly on SWE-Bench Lite. The gains come without any fine-tuning or training costs. The layer is designed never to hurt a model's accuracy.
arxiv-2509-01071:
Images of tissue under a microscope often suffer noise, blur, and low detail, which can slow or skew diagnosis. Ziyi Liu, with nine co-authors, builds a single foundation model to fix many such flaws at once. Earlier methods each handled one flaw only, such as removing noise or sharpening an image.

Their model restores images through tasks such as super-resolution, deblurring, and denoising, and it can also do virtual staining, where stain colors are added by software instead of chemicals. A contrast-based training step helps one design serve all these jobs. Liu and the team present it as the first unified low-level model of its kind for pathology, aiming for faster and more consistent lab work.
arxiv-2509-01171:
Plasma etching carves tiny features into chips, and the energy of ions striking the surface decides how clean and selective that carving is. Jonas Giesekus, with five co-authors, studies a tailored bias waveform applied to the substrate in an industrial etching reactor. They track how the shaped voltage affects ion energy, electron density, and etch rates.

Using several diagnostic tools, the team found the waveform barely changed electron behavior above the substrate, yet it shaped ion flow at high source power. They achieved narrow ion energy spreads, under ten electron volts wide, with mean energies from twenty to one hundred. With those beams they measured the sputter threshold energies of two silicon materials, guiding finer control of nanoscale plasma processes.
arxiv-2509-01471:
Motion captioning turns recorded movement into a sentence, but training data rarely pair motions with both broad and detailed labels. Clayton Leite and Yu Xiao propose a two-step hierarchical method to enrich such captions. Existing data sets give high-level captions, such as a person doing jumping jacks, without the low-level detail of how limbs move.

First, large language models expand each high-level caption into a detailed description of the motion, and motion-to-text models are retrained on those refined annotations to produce richer captions. Second, a retrieval mechanism aligns the detailed captions with candidate high-level captions drawn from extra text sources, joining them with motion features. Leite and Xiao aim for captions that state both what a movement is and how it is performed, without new rounds of human annotation.
arxiv-2509-01971: Vassily Olegovich Manturov discusses a way to extend Vassiliev knot invariants and their weight systems to framed chord diagrams with framings zero and one. Vassiliev invariants are numeric measures that distinguish knots, and chord diagrams encode their combinatorial data. The short paper focuses on maps from knots to two-links and on how the framing values enter the diagrams.
arxiv-2509-02171:
Yevhen Havrylenko, Meelis Kaarik, and Artur Tuttar weigh fake data ways for insurance price work, with a stress on fill in based builds. Price work needs good data, yet cost and privacy rules cut the flow of fresh data. Fake data can fill the gap if it keeps the shape and links of real data. Their fill in route builds on chained rules that fill one field at a time from the rest.

Tests pit fill in builds next to autoencoders and foe nets that make fake tables. Checks span field shapes, field links, and price model fit on real versus fake training. Rows of fake data are mixed with real rows to test claim count models too. Fill in ways give high truth tables with less build pain than deep nets. Ease of use counts a lot in day to day price work.
arxiv-2509-02771:
Nirmalya Mallick Thakur, Jia Qi Yip, and Eng Siong Chng wrote a 2025 speech technology paper measuring how audio compression affects speaker verification, the task of confirming who is speaking. Neural audio codecs are entering many pipelines, yet their distortions may erase voice identity cues.

Three leading verification models were tested on the VoxCeleb1 dataset after speech passed through traditional and neural codecs at varied bitrates. Performance fell for every model and codec as bitrate dropped. Neural codecs did not break verification: they beat the Opus codec clearly at low bitrates and trailed only slightly at high ones. The authors blame the small high-bitrate gap on perceptual tuning that discards speaker details, and they suggest speaker-aware codec design as the fix.
arxiv-2509-03271:
Sylvie Delacroix and 14 co-authors argued in 2025 that professional AI systems must express uncertainty in richer ways than percentages. Large language models now help doctors, teachers, and lawyers make consequential calls. Research often asks such systems to attach a probability to each answer, as if confidence were a single number.

Many professional doubts resist that treatment. A physician weighing whether to document possible domestic abuse, or a teacher judging cultural sensitivity, faces uncertainty about framing and values, not just facts. The authors propose participatory refinement: professional communities jointly shape how different kinds of uncertainty get communicated. Expressing doubt well is part of how professionals make sense of their work, they argue. It should be developed collectively rather than left to an algorithm to optimize.
arxiv-2509-03571:
Amy Secunda and five co-authors ask a direct question in a 2025 research paper: do little red dots vary in brightness? Little red dots are compact, red, distant objects found by the James Webb Space Telescope, with V-shaped spectra. Many researchers suspect they are active galactic nuclei, bright centres powered by growing black holes.

Ordinary active nuclei flicker, yet these objects show little variability and weak X-ray emission, casting doubt on that picture. The authors simulate light curves under two models: traditional slower accretion, and faster super-Eddington accretion drawn from radiation simulations. Traditional models predict far more flickering than observations show, even with few visits per object. Super-Eddington models match the quiet behaviour well. Upcoming high-cadence campaigns should test the difference, and broad emission lines may still vary under either model.
arxiv-2509-03771:
Brennen Hill devotes a 2025 research paper to growing training curricula for multi-agent reinforcement learning through adversarial co-evolution. Agents are only as good as the environments they train in, and hand-built environments are finite and biased. Scaling environment complexity, diversity, and interactivity remains a bottleneck for building general, robust agents.

Hill frames environment generation as an adversarial game between two learning sides. A team of cooperative defenders learns to survive, while a procedural attacker learns to generate ever harder layouts of enemy units. Each new world is tailored to the defenders' current weaknesses, so challenge scales by itself. The defenders answer by building cooperative strategies against the fresh threats. With minimal training, complex behaviour already emerges: attackers flank and shield, while defenders focus fire and spread out. The author argues this co-evolution can supply an endless stream of relevant training data, driving strategic depth.
arxiv-2509-03871:
In a 2025 survey paper, Yanbo Wang and three co-authors ask whether chain-of-thought reasoning makes large language models more trustworthy, or quietly less so. Writing out intermediate steps has raised performance on understanding tasks, hard problems, and code generation. What that reasoning style does to trust has lacked a comprehensive account.

Five dimensions structure the review: truthfulness, safety, fairness, robustness, and privacy. Studies of reasoning models and chain-of-thought methods are surveyed for each, arranged chronologically, with methods, findings, and limitations dissected. A double-edged picture emerges. Reasoning helps on several fronts, reducing hallucination, catching harmful content, and improving robustness in places. Yet the strongest reasoning models frequently match or exceed plainer systems in their safety, robustness, and privacy weaknesses. Synthesising that tension is the survey's contribution: a timely map, aimed at the AI safety community, of where reasoning earns trust and where it spends it.
arxiv-2509-04371:
P T Rahna and thirty-one co-authors announce a giant glowing gas cloud around two quasars in the early universe in a 2025 astrophysics paper. Early survey data from J-PAS, a sky survey, revealed the nebula, nicknamed RaJav, shining in Lyman-alpha light from hydrogen. It surrounds a bright known quasar and a fainter newly found one, separated by a wide gap. The cloud stretches enormous distances and ranks among the largest of its kind, classed as an enormous Lyman-alpha nebula.

Its glow traces a dense region of quasars that may grow into a massive galaxy cluster. Carbon emission shows the surrounding gas already holds heavy elements, not pristine material. Shocks and quasar light likely power the shine, with fresh stars forming nearby.
arxiv-2509-04571:
Pujita Das and three co-authors work out which superconducting patterns emerge inside kagomé metals with intertwined orders in a 2025 physics paper. Kagomé lattices, woven triangle patterns, host materials where charge order coexists with loop currents that break time-reversal symmetry. Self-consistent Bogoliubov-de Gennes calculations, a standard superconducting framework, explore local and neighbor attractive interactions under mean-field approximations.

Plain s-wave pairing, uniform and round, morphs when charge order appears into a pair density wave repeating every two-by-two cells. Adding loop currents twists it into a chiral d-wave version. Thin films lacking inversion symmetry gain an extra triplet p-wave channel through Rashba spin-orbit coupling. Scanning tunneling microscopy fingerprints for each pattern are discussed, relevant to a real material family.
arxiv-2509-04771:
Repeated small magnetic reconnection events may slowly cut a solar filament loose. Song Tan, lead author with nine co-authors, report that picture from Solar Orbiter observations in a 2025 solar physics paper. They study a medium-scale filament eruption that ultimately failed, using sharp ultraviolet and magnetic tools.

The data show such events between the filament and the fields around it, more often and in more forms than earlier work found. Those events shook its stability and produced a chain of coronal jets before the failed eruption. The authors propose persistent magnetic cutting as a concept: many small events add up to reshape a filament's fate as it evolves.
arxiv-2509-04971:
Letting a computational mesh move with the damage it simulates can sharpen fracture predictions. Nicolas Moës, lead author with three co-authors, test that idea in a one-dimensional study in a 2025 mechanics paper. They compare phase-field and lip-field approaches to fracture, optimising the incremental potential over displacement, damage, and the mesh node positions themselves.

As damage reaches its maximum, the optimisation shrinks the most damaged element toward zero size. That element then represents the displacement jump of a broken bar precisely. The overall solution is much more accurate than a fixed mesh solution, supporting the extreme mesh programme.
arxiv-2509-05071:
Motion during an MRI scan blurs images, and artificial intelligence is increasingly used to spot and fix those artifacts. Mojtaba Safari, lead author with five co-authors, systematically review and meta-analyse that literature in a 2025 paper. Their review focuses on deep learning approaches, especially generative models, for detecting and correcting motion artifacts.

The authors find such methods reduce artifacts and improve image quality, with generative models showing particular promise. Key limits remain: weak generalisation, reliance on paired training data, and risk of visual distortion. They call for standardised public datasets and reporting of artifact levels, plus methods needing less paired data.
arxiv-2509-05171:
Collisions of oxygen and neon nuclei at the Large Hadron Collider show flow patterns that reveal the shapes of those nuclei. The ATLAS Collaboration report the first such measurements in a 2025 particle physics paper, using data recorded that year. They measure azimuthal anisotropy coefficients, which describe how particle emission varies with direction, for several orders.

Two methods, pair correlations and multi-particle cumulants, give complementary views that suppress background effects. The coefficients follow a clear ordering and peak at a modest transverse momentum. Central neon collisions show stronger second-order flow than oxygen, matching predictions from the prolate deformation of neon nuclei.
arxiv-2509-05371:
Materials designed to bend how fluids, sound, and vibration interact are surveyed by Francesco Avallone and twenty-two co-authors in a 2025 review paper. Metamaterials are composites whose inner structure gives properties their ingredients lack, opening new ways to shape flow around solid objects.

Fuel use, renewable energy capture, noise, and structural fatigue all depend on these coupled interactions. The review organises theory and recent work into flow with structure, sound with structure, and exotic material ideas that may affect both. It covers regimes from smooth laminar flow to turbulent and separated flow. Open challenges and future directions close the survey, aimed at fields from aerospace to biomedical devices.
arxiv-2509-05471:
Harmful requests dressed in harmless wording are benchmarked by Youjia Zheng, Mohammad Zandsalimy, and Shanu Sushmita in a 2025 paper on language model safety. These camouflaged jailbreaks hide intent inside polite or ambiguous language, slipping past keyword-based defences that look for obvious danger signs.

The authors built a dataset of five hundred curated prompts, most harmful and a smaller set benign, designed to stress-test safety systems. Their scoring framework rates responses on seven dimensions, from safety awareness to compliance. Models behaved well on plainly benign inputs but dropped sharply in safety and quality against camouflaged attacks. The gap shows why defences need finer reading of context.
arxiv-2509-05571:
Two faces of quantum behaviour trade off in exact relations: seeing interference fringes, and knowing which path a particle took. Yue Sun, Ming-Jing Zhao, and Peng-Tong Li derive those relations in a 2025 quantum physics paper. Their setting is a multi-path interferometer fitted with detectors and a quantum memory.

The input states may be mixed rather than pure. The authors establish a duality between fringe visibility and path distinguishability, then derive two three-way relations. One links those quantities with mixedness, the other with entanglement, so entanglement's role in the interferometer is measured quantitatively. For the two-path case all the relations are complete, leaving no slack.
arxiv-2509-05671:
Recognising human activity from several body-worn and ambient sensors, without centralising private data, is the aim of Labani Halder, Tanmay Sen, and Sarbani Palit in a 2025 paper. Labels are scarce, sensors are noisy or incomplete, and pooling raw data raises privacy problems.

Their framework models each sensor stream, from pressure mats to depth cameras and accelerometers, as its own graph. Residual graph networks process the streams, and an attention step fuses them by importance rather than simple joining. Training is federated with differential privacy, so only protected updates are shared. The graph model beat a feed-forward baseline modestly without privacy noise and by wide margins under privacy budgets.
arxiv-2509-05771:
Fair classification that stays reliable when training data are noisy or scarce is the goal of a 2025 paper by Darinka Dentcheva and Xiangyu Tian. Their framework builds on coherent risk measures, tools that score bad-tail losses rather than averages alone. It targets problems with several classes and labels that may sometimes be wrong.

The authors lay foundations for linear and kernel-based versions, then extend the idea with nonlinear aggregation that leads to a two-stage stochastic program, a plan optimized under uncertainty in steps. A decomposition method solves it, and tests against a popular benchmark show stronger results on unseen data than error-minimizing rivals. Because the risk view spreads errors more evenly, it also supports fairness across groups, and the gains grow as the number of classes rises.
arxiv-2509-06171:
More light escapes an OLED screen when a nanorod array funnels it out, show Khondokar Zahin and four co-authors in a 2025 paper. Much of an OLED's light stays trapped in the substrate, wasting efficiency. Their array stacks metal, insulator, and semiconductor-oxide layers into rods on the display's bottom surface, guiding surface plasmon-coupled emission outward.

An inverse design search, run by particle swarm optimization, tunes the rod geometry for chosen colors. Extraction improves by roughly thirty to fifty percent at blue and green wavelengths over conventional OLEDs, with high luminous efficiency, reduced ultraviolet leakage, and uniform emission direction. The authors present the simple periodic design as a practical upgrade path for display technology.
arxiv-2509-06371:
An Android safety service can be disarmed by extracting its on-device AI model, demonstrate Victor Guyomard and two co-authors in a 2025 paper. On-device deployment improves privacy and latency but creates security risks unlike traditional software. Their case study is SafetyCore, Google's system service that detects sensitive images on the phone itself.

The authors show how the model can be pulled from the device and manipulated until detection is bypassed, rendering the protection ineffective. The analysis generalizes: models shipped to hostile hardware can be inspected and subverted by their owners or attackers. The paper is a practical warning for designers of on-device safety systems.
arxiv-2509-06571:
Stealing data out of a company network is cast as a simple strategic game by Tristan Caulfield in a 2025 paper. Firms face real costs when confidential data leaks, and extortion can follow. A stripped-down model helps clarify what each side is choosing and why.

In the model, an attacker picks a route out of the network and a speed for sending data. The defender sets monitoring thresholds that decide when traffic looks unusual enough to trigger an alert. The attacker gains from data taken out, while the defender weighs the cost of losing data against the cost of responding to alerts. Even in this simple form, the game frames the basic trade-off behind exfiltration defense: watch too loosely and data slips away, watch too tightly and staff drown in alarms.
arxiv-2509-06671:
Proving that certain wave equations have no lasting solutions at all is the work of Luis Gustavo Longen in a solo 2025 analysis paper. The equation mixes wave and plate behavior, with rotational inertia, fractional damping, and a memory term, where past states feed into the present. A companion study by other means asks which exponent values allow small starting disturbances to survive for all time.

Longen takes the non-existence side. A modified test function argument shows that for exponent values below the critical one, even arbitrarily small initial data cannot produce a global solution. In the critical case itself, he also rules out global solutions when the memory exponent passes a threshold tied to the space dimension. Results like these bracket the true critical exponent from both sides, sharpening the map of when such equations settle or blow up.
arxiv-2509-06871:
Open quantum systems spread across space are learned by a neural network in a 2025 quantum information paper by Dounan Du and one co-author. Simulating such systems means integrating coupled master and field equations, which is slow and blocks real-time control and network-scale studies. A fast surrogate is needed.

Their regional-attention transformer learns the space-time dynamics directly. Built-in translational invariance, the idea that physical laws do not depend on position, keeps the model's complexity scalable, and it can condition on time-dependent global control settings. Two test systems are learned well: a driven, dissipative single qubit and an electromagnetically induced transparency quantum memory. Predictions stay accurate even for control protocols outside the training data, and the model runs up to a thousand times faster than numerical solvers, suiting quantum network design and device modeling.
arxiv-2509-06971:
Designing a part's inner structure on a graphics card, forty times faster, is shown by Mingyuan Yang and two co-authors in a 2025 engineering paper. Topology optimization decides where material should go inside a part. Their approach, PeTTO, rewrites the constrained problem using phase field methods as time-based partial differential equations, which suit pseudo-transient solvers.

Sensitivities to the design are computed by automatic differentiation, avoiding tedious and error-prone hand derivations. A hybrid of pseudo-transient and sped-up pseudo-transient methods balances convergence speed against stability. Examples cover mechanical and thermal problems, single and multiple materials, in two and three dimensions. Running the same code on one graphics chip instead of desktop chips gave speedups of roughly forty to fifty times, a step toward interactive design tools.
arxiv-2509-07071:
CP violation in decays that produce neutral kaons is the subject of a 2025 paper by Yuval Grossman and 4 co-authors. CP violation means that matter and antimatter do not behave in quite the same way. Here the effect appears when particles decay into final states that contain neutral kaons, which are short-lived particles made of quarks.

The authors show that an efficiency function, which reflects the setup of a given experiment, splits into two parts. One part is the energy spectrum of the kaons, and the other is a factor that depends only on the detector. They also show that matter effects on kaon oscillations can change CP asymmetries in a clear way. Estimates for a Belle II type experiment show what sizes of effect such a machine could expect to see.
arxiv-2509-07171:
František Bartoš and 1 co-author propose the z-curve plot in 2025, a picture-based check for publication bias in meta-analysis. Meta-analysis combines results from many studies, but journals favor studies with clear positive results, which skews the pool. A z-statistic measures how far a result sits from no effect, and its pattern across studies can reveal that skew.

The plot overlays the distribution of z-values a model predicts on the distribution actually observed. A good fit shows little gap between the two, while jumps at key thresholds expose bias. Models that account for bias should track those jumps closely. The authors demonstrate the plot with several Bayesian models on simulated and real data. The tool ships in the RoBMA software package, so researchers can add it to routine checks.
arxiv-2509-07571:
Xiyu Guo's team of 9 authors tackles a routing problem for AI services in 2025: which model or agent should answer each user query? Queries span many domains and task types, while the ecosystem of large language models and specialized agents keeps growing. Sending every query to the biggest model wastes money, and sending hard queries to weak models hurts quality.

Their framework, MoMA, mixes model routing and agent routing in one system. A training dataset profiles what each model does well under different routing structures. At run time, intent recognition and adaptive strategies send each query to the unit with the best cost-performance balance. An efficient agent selection strategy handles the agent side. The design targets services that must answer varied questions quickly without paying top-model prices for easy ones.
arxiv-2509-07871:
Extended reality, brain-computer interfaces, and AI assistants all raise a basic question: when do users feel in control? Angjelin Hila develops an enactivist framework for human-computer interaction in a 2025 research paper written alone. Enactivism treats people as self-organizing systems that build their world through action. That view clashes with the standard comparator model of agency used in interface research.

Hila proposes feelings of agency as a richer target than the usual sense of agency. The concept has two parts: emotional engagement and willed attention. Both can be tracked through brain signals combined with first-person reports. The framework builds on an existing multifactor model of agency feelings. Hila argues these neurophenomenological measures give designers more useful guidance. Interfaces for immersive and AI-driven settings could then protect, rather than quietly erode, human autonomy.
arxiv-2509-08071:
Learning the equations behind data without opening the simulator is the goal of a 2025 paper by Engin Danis and 3 co-authors. Operator inference builds discrete operators from snapshot data and uses them to predict how physical systems evolve. Real datasets, though, can be enormous, and standard methods strain under their size.

A tensor-train format compresses the snapshots, or builds them by cross interpolation, so the learning stays cheap. Three variants cover full-order models, a quantised version for even bigger data, and a reduced-order version for speed. Nonintrusive learning matters wherever experiments or legacy codes produce data but no handy equations, from fluids to structures, and compression decides whether the approach scales at all.
arxiv-2509-08571:
Bayu Adhi Tama and 5 co-authors present GraphTopoNet in a 2025 paper on mapping the bed under Greenland's ice. Radar soundings there are sparse and uneven, yet bed maps guide sea level forecasts. Their graph learning method also tracks its own uncertainty.

Graphs built from surface height, ice speed, and mass balance gain extra features for local and broad patterns. A mixed loss function weights trusted radar data and fills gaps with care. On three Greenland regions, error falls by up to sixty percent against older methods. Better maps support climate modeling and public planning.
arxiv-2509-08771:
M. Rothman and 4 co-authors introduce NuLattice, a Python package for nuclear calculations on lattices, in a 2025 paper. Ab initio means starting from basic interactions rather than fitted shortcuts. The package places atomic nuclei on a grid and solves for their states.

Tools include Hartree-Fock, coupled cluster, and other many-body methods named in the paper. Interactions come from pion-less effective field theory at leading order, with two-body and three-body contact terms. Results cover light nuclei from deuterium to oxygen. Algorithms use sparsity and locality of the grid, so computations can run on laptops. That ease may widen access to nuclear theory.
arxiv-2509-08971:
Julien Loiseau and 9 co-authors present HARD, a performance portable radiation hydrodynamics code, in a 2025 paper. The code simulates compressible fluid flow coupled with radiation diffusion. It is built on the FleCSI framework for high performance computing.

Work is expressed as tasks that can run under several back ends, including Legion, MPI, and HPX. Node level parallelism uses Kokkos, so one code base runs from laptops to supercomputers. A regression suite checks classic shock tube and blast wave problems against known answers. The project is open source with build scripts and continuous integration, aiming at sustainable community use.
arxiv-2509-09071:
Crystal Qian and 6 co-authors study strategic tradeoffs between humans and AI in multi-agent bargaining in a 2025 paper. Markets increasingly use language models as autonomous decision makers. How they bargain compared with humans and statistical agents is poorly known.

Over two hundred humans, several frontier models, and custom Bayesian agents play the same dynamic bargaining games. Bayesian agents gain the most surplus with aggressive offers that are often rejected. Humans and models gain similar totals but act differently. Models favor cautious, concessionary offers, while humans follow fairness norms and face more rejection. Equal scores can hide deep procedural differences.
arxiv-2509-09371:
Zitao Wang and 2 co-authors make robust optimization aware of representations in a 2025 paper. Robust methods guard a model by planning for the worst shift in its data. Standard forms spread that guard evenly over all features, which can waste effort and lose accuracy.

Often the true signal sits in a low dimensional representation of the features, learned from past tasks. Their READ method charges more for shifts that move those representation axes, steering the guard where it counts. Shifts off those axes stay guarded too. Theory covers confidence regions and transfer to future groups from the same model. A single cell multi-omics test shows transfer gains.
arxiv-2509-09471: The Schwarz lemma bounds how fast a holomorphic map can grow. David Kalaj extends a boundary version of it in a 2025 research paper. He first proves a boundary Schwarz lemma for holomorphic disks mapped into the unit ball in complex space of any dimension. He then proves the matching statement for minimal conformal disks, the surfaces of least area in their class. That proof builds on a recent Schwarz-Pick result for harmonic maps conformal at a point.
arxiv-2509-09571:
Raphael M. Tromer and 5 co-authors examine tubulanes, networks of cross-linked carbon nanotubes, in a 2025 materials paper covering six structures. Diamond is famously hard and behaves much the same in every direction. Tubulanes behave differently: their stiffness depends strongly on the direction of the push, which opens room for tuning a material to a task.

One structure beat diamond's Young's modulus along its vertical axis, while values across directions varied by more than a factor of two. Poisson ratios were also uneven, nearly vanishing along at least one direction. All six structures had indirect band gaps below diamond's, set mostly by carbon 2p states. The narrowest gap, in the 16-tetra-22 structure, may suit electronic uses.
arxiv-2509-09871:
Bastián González-Bustamante and 2 co-authors test whether language models can fake a national opinion survey in a 2025 proof-of-concept study from Chile. Synthetic respondents could ease the cost and coverage problems of real polling, but they might also echo stereotypes baked into training data. The team compares machine answers against a genuine probabilistic survey of Chilean public opinion, question by question.

Across 128 prompt, model, and question combinations they generated nearly one hundred ninety thousand fake profiles. Trust questions were mimicked superbly, with top accuracy marks above nine tenths. Two commercial models and one open model performed about equally well overall. Pooling every result in a meta-analysis exposes where alignment with human answers holds and where social patterns bend it.
arxiv-2509-10071:
Zeya Mi and 1 co-author exhibit robust dynamical systems whose long-run statistics come in a fixed, countable set in a 2025 paper on partially hyperbolic dynamics. Their systems split motion into stable, unstable, and several one-dimensional centre directions at once. The question is how many physical measures, the statistics a typical starting point actually settles into, such a system can carry, and whether that number can wobble under small changes.

Two carefully built examples answer firmly: every Gibbs u-state is hyperbolic, and the count of physical measures stays pinned. In the second example the measures carry different unstable dimensions, and some can be parked onto a non-uniformly hyperbolic region using tools from the first. Earlier studies had to assume the very hyperbolicity these examples now display openly.
arxiv-2509-10171: Filippus S. Roux derived evolution equations in a 2025 optics paper for the statistical moments of a light state crossing turbulent air. Rather than track the full quantum state, which the atmosphere scrambles beyond recognition, Roux starts from an equation for the state's characteristic functional covering every spatial and temporal degree of freedom. Moments then follow directly, and everyday measured quantities such as intensity and photon counts can be rebuilt from those moments alone. A simple coherent starting state is carried through as the worked example.
arxiv-2509-10371:
Training giant language models across many graphics processors burns power and generates heat, and Seokjin Go with seven co-authors measure that process end to end in this 2025 systems paper. They run varied real workloads on NVIDIA H100 and H200 cards and AMD MI250 units, testing dense and sparse models under tensor, pipeline, data, and expert parallelism.

The lessons are practical. Fewer, memory-rich processors can beat larger fleets when communication dominates, but only with careful tuning. Some parallelism pairings waste bandwidth through poor data chunking, and oversized microbatches cause bursty running, power spikes, and heat throttling. Tricks like recomputing activations and overlapping communication help unevenly. The authors distill design advice for building training systems that scale without cooking themselves.
arxiv-2509-10971:
Bhoomit Vasani and three co-authors extract lightweight adapters from fully fine-tuned models in this 2025 paper. Low-rank adapters, LoRA modules, are the cheap, swappable way to specialize a model. Normally they must be trained as adapters from the start. PHLoRA, pronounced flora, works after the fact. It decomposes the difference in weights, separating a base model from its fine-tuned counterpart. Put that difference in low-rank form, and an adapter falls out.

No training data are needed. No gradients are needed, either. Adapters can be harvested even from third-party checkpoints. The modules merge back into models. They route dynamically. They serve on industrial platforms. Tests covered text, image, and video benchmarks on Amazon's Nova family. Extracted adapters preserved most of the weight change's energy. They pruned safely. Re-merged, they cost negligible task performance. The practical promise: every existing full model becomes adapter-ready.
arxiv-2509-11071:
Jinghan Peng and 3 co-authors describe their winning entry to a driving-with-language contest in this 2025 report. The contest was part of the CVPR 2024 Autonomous Grand Challenge. It asks vision-language systems to answer questions about driving scenes. The items mix choice questions and yes-or-no items. Some are open questions about what a car sees and should do.

The CPS team built on the LLaVA model family. They fine-tuned it with two light methods, LoRA and DoRA. Training used only the DriveLM-nuScenes data set. Depth estimates from open models enriched both training and use. For choice questions they used step-by-step reasoning at test time. The approach took first place on the validation board, with the top score.
arxiv-2509-11371:
Ewelina Gajewska tests machine creativity with a twist on the Turing test in this 2025 cognitive science paper, naming it after Ada Lovelace. Judges with training in cognitive science and computing were asked to sort paintings into AI-made and human-made, and to rate how good each piece looked.

Two formats were tried: side-by-side paired comparisons and a spoken viva voce examination. Under some conditions the judges did no better than chance at telling machine work from human work. Just as strikingly, the AI-generated pieces were rated as aesthetically equal to the human-made ones. Gajewska reads the results as a challenge to the assumption that creativity is uniquely human, and as rare evidence gathered from expert judges rather than laypeople or working artists.
arxiv-2509-11771:
Nazar Budaiev and eleven co-authors give the James Webb Space Telescope its first look at Sagittarius B2. This 2025 astronomy paper treats the Galaxy's wildest star-forming cloud. It sits near the Galactic center. Webb's near- and mid-infrared cameras imaged it in fourteen filters.

The images reveal a multilayered cloud. An exposed population of massive stars appears. A hidden one lies buried in dust. Candidate ionized regions were found around massive stars. Radio telescopes had missed them. Radiation escapes along outflow cavities from the forming cluster Sagittarius B2 North. Light finds exits even in the densest regions. A sharp, straight eastern edge marks the cloud's asymmetry. No wide population of young stellar objects appeared. Star formation there may have only just begun.
arxiv-2509-12371:
Fables end with a moral, but pulling that moral out of a story is a test of abstract reading, not keyword matching. Matteo Marcuzzo and four co-authors build MORABLES in 2025, a human-checked benchmark of fables and short tales from older literature, with multiple-choice questions aimed at the moral of each story.

Tricky wrong answers force models past surface cues, and adversarial rewrites expose shortcuts and contamination effects. Bigger models score better yet still contradict their own answers in about a fifth of cases when the framing shifts. Models tuned for reasoning did no better, suggesting raw scale, not reasoning style, drives the score.
arxiv-2509-13171:
Luca Lunati, Enrico Pierobon and five co-authors design in 2025 a hybrid simulator for galactic cosmic rays at GSI in Europe. Ion beams have long stood in for space radiation in life studies and gear tests. Single-energy beams miss the mixed field of deep space.

Active and passive parts are joined for a truer mix. The design serves Moon and Mars mission prep. A tuned particle source for the Geant4 toolkit ships with the work. Outside users can plan studies with the same source. Bench tests in software back the layout and its tuned settings before hardware runs.
arxiv-2509-13471:
Sina Gogani-Khiabani, Ashutosh Trivedi and two co-authors build legal-critical software in 2025 with LLM agents, tested on United States tax preparation. Statutes in plain words must become executable logic, yet ambiguity and hallucination threaten trust. Test oracles are the core snag.

Higher-order metamorphic relations compare outputs across structured shifts among similar persons. Authoring those relations by hand is tedious, so role-based LLM agents automate generation and code synthesis. A testing agent hunts counterexamples in loop. A smaller model in the agentic frame beats frontier solo models on complex tax tasks by large pass gaps. Agents offer a path to trustworthy statute code.
arxiv-2509-13571:
Robert Jarolim and 10 co-authors present SuNeRF-CME in a 2025 paper on mapping huge eruptions of plasma from the Sun in three dimensions. Telescopes that block the Sun's disk can watch these eruptions, called coronal mass ejections, by the light that free electrons scatter. But the plasma is thin, so a flat image does not give its true 3D layout in a direct way.

Their method uses neural radiance fields, nets that learn a 3D scene from images, with ray tracing that copies how the scattered light forms. The net is fit step by step to images taken over time from more than one viewpoint. Rules from physics, on flow, path, and speed, help fill the gaps left by the few viewpoints. Tests on fake data from a sim let the team score how well each viewpoint setup works.
arxiv-2509-13671:
Tobias M. Weinberg, Ricardo E. Gonzalez Penuela, Stephanie Valencia, and Thijs Roumen report an autoethnographic study in a 2025 paper on ultra-personalized AI for augmentative and alternative communication. People who cannot speak rely on such devices to compose messages, and generic autocomplete often misses their personal voice, forcing heavy editing.

Over seven months the lead author logged all of his communication device data, fine-tuned a model on it, then used its suggestions daily for three months. Logging itself reshaped his sense of agency, training amplified some parts of his identity and muted others, and suggestions sometimes resurfaced private details in new contexts. The authors draw design lessons for keeping personalized communication tools expressive and authentic.
arxiv-2509-13771:
Mengzhu Li and three co-authors present CDFlow in a 2025 robotics paper, a new way to build configuration-space distance fields. Planners use these fields to know, for every joint configuration of a robot arm, how far it is from collision. Older fields return only one nearest collision point and rely on sparse samples, so their gradients can mislead high-degree-of-freedom robots.

CDFlow instead models the whole distribution of nearest collision configurations, since several can tie. A neural ordinary differential equation learns a continuous flow in configuration space that represents that distribution, trained on data from an adaptive sampling strategy. Its gradient, an expected direction to safety, stays smooth and sharp, and planning tests showed better efficiency, path quality, and robustness.
arxiv-2509-13871:
Dror Fried and Gad E. Yaron revisit Toda's theorem in a 2025 complexity theory paper. The theorem is a landmark result whose proof reduces quantified Boolean formulas, statements with a fixed number of alternating quantifiers, to counting satisfying assignments. With model counting tools now practical, the authors ask whether that elegant reduction could power a real QBF solver.

They turn the reduction into a concrete probabilistic solver that calls a model counter as an oracle. A naive version explodes in formula size, so they isolate three factors driving the blow-up. Some factors admit workarounds; the dominant one, a union bound factor the literature had largely overlooked, is sometimes unavoidable, though special cases escape it. A prototype solver gives preliminary results.
arxiv-2509-14271:
Gustavo Sandoval, Denys Fenchenko and Junyao Chen look back in 2025 at defence work from 2022. The threat is prompt injection, where hidden text tries to hijack a language model. A related attack, goal hijacking, tries to swap the model task for the attacker task.

The team built both attacks, tested them on models of the time, and measured how often they worked. On GPT-3 models the attacks succeeded in about a third of trials with no defence. Their proposed defence, adversarial fine tuning, cut success to near zero for the smaller GPT-3 variants. Later work has found limits to fine tuning defences, which the authors note. Flexible models also proved easier to hijack, a pattern still relevant to current systems.
arxiv-2509-14871:
Leolin Nkuete, Antigona Pajaziti, Hamide Suluyer, and Rabia Gülşah Uysal study maximal curves of genus five over finite fields in a 2025 algebra paper. A maximal curve has as many points as the Hasse-Weil-Serre bound allows, the highest count theory permits. The team focuses on fields whose discriminant, a number built from the field size, equals negative nineteen.

Using knowledge of the automorphism group, the group of symmetries of such a curve, they prove no maximal genus-five curve exists for several residue classes of the field size modulo five. For the class congruent to one modulo five, they give explicit models of the potential curve. For fields whose size is a power of five, existence survives only for one specific large case. The results narrow where searchers should look.
arxiv-2509-14971:
Logan Harris and Patrick Breheny build error ranges for the lasso that stay centered on the lasso's own point values, in a 2025 paper. The lasso is a key tool for fitting models with many inputs. Classic ranges demand exact hit rates for each input on its own. That demand forces a debiasing step and cuts the link between the ranges and the values users report.

Past work by the same authors let ranges be biased on purpose, under a weaker average hit-rate rule. Those ranges could still miss the point values. The new ranges use fresh ways to approximate the full high-input likelihood. They stay centered on the lasso values and still hold the average hit rate. The paper backs biased ranges as a sound, useful tool.
arxiv-2509-15071:
Haechan Pyon and Gyunghoon Park design safe stabilizing controllers for nonlinear systems whose constraints react slowly, in a 2025 control theory paper. Control Lyapunov-barrier functions merge stability and safety into one certificate, but constraints with relative degree two or more resist that construction. Simply adding a barrier function to a Lyapunov function may fail because a suitable barrier might not exist.

Their key move is scaling: multiply the Lyapunov function's value on the unsafe set by a sigmoid-based factor, reshaping it into a valid combined certificate. A systematic design procedure comes with explicit conditions on the sigmoid's parameters. The method is then applied to task-space control of a planar robot arm, where a feedback linearization controller guarantees both stability and safety. The scaling trick widens the class of systems with provable safe control.
arxiv-2509-15271:
Sebastian Ray Mason and four co-authors test whether large vision models can mentally rotate objects in a 2025 cognitive AI paper. Mental rotation, imagining a shape turned in space, is a classic probe of human spatial reasoning. Whether vision Transformers develop anything similar was unclear despite their success at recognition.

The evaluation covers the classic block structures used in human studies, more complex block figures, rotated text in three forms, and photo-realistic objects. Probing layer by layer shows where rotation skill lives inside the networks. Self-supervised models capture geometric structure better than supervised ones, and intermediate layers outperform final layers. Difficulty grows with rotation complexity and occlusion in a pattern echoing human reaction times, hinting that the models face some of the same constraints people do.
arxiv-2509-15371:
Jeffrey Roskes writes about a gap in how medical studies show survival curves. These curves, named for Kaplan and Meier, track how long patients live or stay well. They are often drawn with no error bands at all. When bands appear, they show only the doubt that comes from having few patients, not the doubt in the measures themselves.

Roskes presents a software tool called KoMbine, built on methods from particle physics. It is the first tool that carries both kinds of doubt through the curve, step by step. As patient data sets grow, the second kind of doubt matters more. The tool gives medical teams a fuller, more honest picture of their results.
arxiv-2509-15571:
Karthik Elamvazhuthi and Sachin Shivakumar sample the full reach of a moving system more evenly. The reachable set holds all states a system can reach with bounded controls. Plain random sampling bunches paths near strong attractors, leaving much of the set bare. The pair wanted samples that spread across the whole set.

They frame the task with optimal transport, which steers a system so its final spread matches a target spread. Since the true set is unknown, an exact match is out of reach. They soften the goal with a penalty that still pushes for even spread. The soft form turns into a finite control problem solved with particles. Tests show far more even coverage than random controls.
arxiv-2509-15871:
Liwei Liao leads a team that finds objects in 3D scenes from text prompts, with no task training. A scene built as 3D Gaussians stores its look in a spread out, implicit way. Past finders needed training for each scene and large labeled sets. Their frame turns the 3D search into a 2D retrieval problem across views.

For each view of the scene, they retrieve object level clues that match the prompt. Pooling clues across views pins the object in 3D. No per scene training and no 3D annotation are needed. Tests reach top scores among rivals while skipping that training. The work lays a base for zero shot 3D grounding. Video demos are shared online.
arxiv-2509-15971:
Owen Truong leads a team that builds a tool to catch data leakage in machine learning notebooks. Leakage means test data sneak into training, which inflates scores and misleads builders. It takes three main forms: overlap, preprocessing leaks, and repeated test use. Their tool is an editor extension for the VS Code platform.

The extension scans Jupyter notebooks for these leak types as the user writes. Beyond flagging, it offers two fixes. A quick fix applies a standard manual repair. A language model guide instead walks the developer toward best practice for the pipeline. The aim is cleaner code and honest scores. The paper presents version two of the tool.
arxiv-2509-16071:
Early galaxies shine with a puzzling mix of oxygen and carbon light, with far more oxygen glow than nearby dwarf galaxies show. Hiddo Algera and twenty-eight co-authors present new radio telescope data for eight distant galaxies first seen through their carbon lines. All eight also glow in oxygen, at rates that match a known link with star birth in nearby dwarfs.

Adding data for eleven more early galaxies, the team finds the high ratio holds at fixed metal mix. The main driver seems to be burst-like star birth, which dims the carbon glow. Oxygen light thus stays a strong tracer of gas in the first galaxies.
arxiv-2509-16171:
Counting holes in a shape built from simple blocks is a basic task in data analysis, and a classic random method can estimate that count. Julien Sorci takes a fresh look at how many samples that method needs to be trusted. The spread of its estimates turns out to depend on the block structure of the shape at hand.

That insight leads to an improved method that needs fewer samples when the spread is small. Tests on random graph models show both easy and hard cases for the two methods. In some ranges the cost still grows at an exponential rate, which marks the limit of the classic route.
arxiv-2509-16871:
Yitian Shi and co-authors teach robots grasps from human hands in a 2025 paper. A single photo of a hand holding an object can show how to grasp it. Their method turns that cue into grasps for a two-finger robot gripper. It needs no exact shape model of the target object.

Three cues guide the synthesis: image features, hand-object contact, and a taxonomy of grasp types. A flow-based generator then proposes grip poses. Real-world tests topped a high success rate on varied objects. Object-agnostic grasps could help warehouse and home robots handle new items without a fresh scan each time. Code is shared in public.
arxiv-2509-17671:
Selva Taş and four co-authors built the first hallucination detectors tuned for Turkish retrieval systems. Their 2025 arXiv paper notes that language models invent facts with ease, and retrieval grounding only partly cures that. Turkish makes detection harder: it is morphologically complex and low-resource, so tools trained on English transfer poorly.

The suite, Turk-LettuceDetect, grows from the LettuceDetect framework and treats detection as token-level classification. Three encoder designs were fine-tuned: a Turkish ModernBERT, a Turkish embedding model, and the multilingual EuroBERT. Training used the RAGTruth benchmark in machine-translated form, with tens of thousands of cases across question answering, data-to-text, and summarization. The ModernBERT variant led the pack on the full test set. The authors offer the suite as a guardrail for Turkish RAG products.
arxiv-2509-17871:
Samuel Breckenridge and 6 co-authors rethink privacy for votes where each vote counts by wealth held. Their 2025 paper deals with token-weighted votes, now common in crypto groups. With secret ballots, raw tallies can still leak who voted how when one holder is huge.

Their new scale, B-privacy, rests on the cost to bribe voters from what tallies reveal. They add noise to tallies to raise that cost, and bound the loss in tally truth. Across thousands of real group votes, huge holders limit any such fix. Where five or more voters must flip to change a result, the noise helps a lot.
arxiv-2509-18071:
Lorenzo Rosasco gives a course-style tour of learning with kernels. His 2025 article is teaching material from a summer school on machine learning and maths. Kernel spaces let a learner work with functions by their pair-wise scores, a neat trick for many tasks.

The tour starts with plain value learning in those spaces. It then widens to learning operators, which map one function to a second. Last, it casts learning of moving systems as an operator task, via Koopman theory. The piece aims to give students the full frame in one place, with the maths that backs it.
arxiv-2509-18471:
Search systems store items as long number lists called embedding vectors, and those lists are costly to keep and fetch. Mariano Tepper and Ted Willke present NVQ, a compression method for such vectors in this 2025 paper. Search quality depends on keeping the vectors accurate, which is called the high-fidelity regime. Most shrink methods lose ground exactly there.

NVQ builds a non-uniform quantizer, a rounding scheme with uneven steps, for each vector on its own. New compact nonlinear functions make those quantizers cheap to build and store. Learning them per vector, rather than sharing one scheme, is the core idea. In tests, NVQ beat the current best methods on accuracy. The gain came with minimal extra computing cost. The authors aim the method at large search indexes where memory and speed both bite. Smaller footprints mean faster, cheaper semantic search.
arxiv-2509-18571:
Watching live video for threats means spotting danger fast and explaining the call. Yuhan Wang, Cheng Liu, Zihan Zhao, and Weichao Wu present Live-E2T, a framework that tries to do both at once. Their 2025 paper notes that older systems trade speed against clear reasoning. Supervised detectors are quick but mute; generative models explain but lag.

The framework first turns frames into structured tuples of people, objects, interactions, and places. That compact form keeps the meaning that plain compression loses. A deduplication step then drops repeated events so the system keeps up in real time. Last, a language model tuned with chain-of-thought reasoning writes threat reports over the event stream. On two standard crime-video benchmarks, the system beat prior methods on accuracy, speed, and explanation quality. The authors aim it at live monitoring centers.
arxiv-2509-18771:
Language models grow by scaling size, data, and compute, but human text is running out and gains are shrinking. Xingkun Yin, Kaibin Huang, Dong In Kim, and Hongyang Du propose experience scaling in this 2025 paper. Their framework lets a deployed model keep evolving through its own interactions. Experience is captured, distilled, and shared among model copies.

Raw interactions are compressed into compact, reusable knowledge. Stored content is refined over time to stay relevant and efficient. Tests in simulated settings covered new but related tasks, repeated queries, and over-full knowledge stores. Across all three, experience scaling raised accuracy and held performance over time. Gains carried to novel situations the model had not met. The authors offer post-deployment learning as a path past the limits of static training data. It reframes deployment as a stage of learning, not its end.
arxiv-2509-18871:
Federated learning trains models on scattered data by sharing gradients, not the data itself. Tamer Ahmed Eltaras and four co-authors show those gradients can still betray the data in this 2025 paper. Gradient inversion attacks rebuild training samples from shared updates. Older analytical attacks worked mainly on simple layers and single examples.

The team extends their prior work with three new algorithms. One rebuilds samples from convolutional layer gradients, even with non-invertible activation functions. A second scales the trick to high-dimensional inputs. A third rebuilds whole mini-batches, not just one example at a time. Their key shift is to lean on gradient constraints rather than weight constraints. In some layers, under five percent of the previously assumed constraints sufficed. The results warn that gradient sharing needs stronger guards than many deployments assume.
arxiv-2509-19271:
Abdou Karim Kandji and four co-authors build a speech dataset for Wolof, a language spoken by more than ten million people in West Africa but rarely read or written. In Senegal, about ninety percent of people speak Wolof while literacy stays low, so voice services matter more than text. Their dataset, WolBanking77, targets banking intents: what a customer wants when speaking to a bank system. It holds about 9,800 written sentences and over four hours of spoken ones.

The team benchmarks text and speech models on the data, reporting intent scores and word error rates for the speech side. Early results are promising across the baselines tried. The paper also examines the dataset's contents in depth, comparing model families. Code and data are public, giving low-resource speech research a rare, realistic testbed in a domain people actually use.
arxiv-2509-19471:
Time series with many measured streams, such as sensors across a plant, strain the transformer models used to read them. Hunjae Lee and Corey Clark note that mixing all streams at once can add noise and blur the signal. Their method, DELTAformer, limits that mixing on purpose. A small set of stand-in tokens carries news between streams, while each stream keeps its own time pattern in full.

The tight gate forces the model to pass only the stream news that matters. Cost grows in a straight line as streams are added, not in a steep curve. Across test sets, the method beat standard transformers and set new best scores. It also kept its focus on the streams that carried real signal. The design shows that less mixing can mean both faster and better results.
arxiv-2509-19771:
Agents that learn from logged behavior can stray toward actions the log barely supports, and value estimates then go wrong. Hyunwoo Kim and Hyo Kyung Lee borrow an idea from physics: static friction. The logged actions form a smooth surface; moves along it are safe, while moves off it carry the main extrapolation error. That split yields a stability rule much like a friction threshold.

Their algorithm, Frictional Q-Learning, learns the safe directions with a contrastive autoencoder. Steps toward unsupported actions are damped before they corrupt values. Wide experiments test the method against rival offline learners. Offline learning matters where live trial and error is costly, from robots to medicine. A friction mindset offers a fresh handle on an old failure mode.
arxiv-2509-20171:
Patricia Schontag and four co-authors wrote this 2025 arXiv paper on underwater imaging. Testing camera systems underwater is hard to control or repeat. Water bends color, scatters light, and blurs contrast in ways that change with place, depth, and season. Most vision tests use one water type, so their results may not transfer.

The authors present Optical Ocean Recipes, a way to mix realistic test water in the lab. Calibrated color and scattering additives recreate chosen ocean conditions on demand. That control allows exact ground-truth data for tasks like image restoration and segmentation. It also supports visual navigation tests and water property estimation. They release a demonstration dataset and show the system at work on two vision tasks.
arxiv-2509-20371:
Light bouncing between two media follows rules that echo quantum mechanics, and Sayanho Biswas and Kolahal Bhattacharya work out that echo exactly in a 2025 arXiv paper. Their model treats a light ray like a wave function meeting a potential barrier. Remarkably, it reproduces Fresnel's classic reflection formula for one polarization. The authors apply the model to total internal reflection.

They establish a one-to-one match between quantum transmission through a barrier and frustrated total internal reflection at all incidence angles. Evanescent waves, which fade rapidly past the interface, fit the same picture. The model also yields the Goos-Hanchen shift, the small sideways displacement of a reflected beam. The treatment extends what standard optics texts present on these topics. It offers teachers and theorists a cleaner route to several classic results.
arxiv-2509-20571:
Stylizing a three-dimensional model for printing can quietly weaken it. Faraz Faruqi and nine co-authors guard against that failure with MechStyle, presented in a 2025 conference paper. Generative tools reshape geometry to match a text prompt, heedless of stress. MechStyle feeds mechanical simulation back into the stylization loop. Finite element analysis flags regions where stress is rising.

Feedback then restrains edits in those loaded regions while letting safer areas follow the style freely. The authors compared three control strategies for applying that feedback. They also compared three schedules for when to run the simulation, measuring time efficiency. A user interface lets creators produce models that are both stylized and structurally viable. Five example applications demonstrate the workflow, from decorative objects to functional parts.
arxiv-2509-20871:
Answering questions about an image often needs outside knowledge, and image captions are a noisy bridge to that knowledge. Yan Zhang and six co-authors present SCRA-VQA in a 2025 paper accepted at the DASFAA 2025 conference. The method improves knowledge-based visual question answering.

A vision-language model first turns the image into a caption. SCRA-VQA then summarizes the caption and reranks its parts, keeping what the question actually needs. It also generates contextual examples to guide the language model's reasoning. This cleaning step counters the excess noise that raw captions carry. The authors report stronger answers from the augmented language model. The approach shows how careful text preparation can beat simply feeding a model more text.
arxiv-2509-21071:
Four-dimensional flow MRI shows blood moving through the heart and vessels over time, but its images are coarse and noisy. Aurelien de Turenne, Remi Cart-Lamy, and Denis Kouame sharpen those images in a 2025 medical imaging paper. Their method solves an inverse problem explicitly, in the complex domain.

Clinical scanners provide magnitude and phase images, from which the authors rebuild synthetic complex-valued signals. Resolution loss is then modeled honestly, as a truncation of high-frequency components in k-space. Inverting that model recovers high-resolution velocity fields while denoising. Acquisition time limits keep raw 4D flow MRI blurry, so post-processing carries real clinical weight. Better flow images could sharpen diagnosis of complex hemodynamic conditions without longer scans.
arxiv-2509-21271:
Superchips fuse a graphics chip and a central chip in one package, changing how training should offload work. It comes from Xinyu Lian and 3 co-authors. A Superchip packs a graphics chip and a central chip in one package. That tight link offers high power and fast transfer. Offloading moves some training data to the central chip to save graphics memory. Past offload rules assumed loosely linked chips.

The authors present SuperOffload, a system built for Superchips. It uses the graphics chip, the central chip, and their fast link more fully. Methods include adaptive weight offloading, bucket repartitioning, and casting tuned for the chip. It also uses speculative execution, running steps ahead to hide delays. The work is the first study of offload training on this hardware type.
arxiv-2509-21771:
Alwyn Jose Raja, Rajesh Narayanan, and R. Ganesh write down ground-state wavefunctions for a chain of quantum magnets in this 2025 paper. The chain follows the one-dimensional Kitaev model, a standard test bed for entangled magnetism. Most known states for such models are written with helper particles called partons. States written directly in the spin basis are rare, and this paper supplies them.

The authors build their states from bonds between spins, classed as singlet-like or triplet-like. They check the states with a step-by-step method that starts from a lopsided limit, and the key features survive every step. For half-integer spins, many ground states appear together, under a rule that the triplet count stays even. For integer spins, one ground state remains, made only of triplets. Computer checks against exact results agree well.
arxiv-2509-21971:
Predicting whether a drug will bind to its target protein is a basic step in computer-aided drug discovery. Feng Jiang and six co-authors present GRAM-DTI in this 2025 paper. Earlier deep learning methods mostly read two inputs: a text form of the molecule and the protein sequence. That leaves out rich extra information available for both molecules and proteins.

GRAM-DTI pre-trains on four kinds of input at once, aligning them in a shared representation. Its contrastive method works with volumes rather than pairs, catching alignment across all inputs together. An adaptive dropout scheme turns each input stream up or down based on how informative it is during training. Where lab measurements of binding strength exist, they serve as weak guidance to ground the representations. On four public data sets, the framework beat the best existing baselines throughout.
arxiv-2509-22471:
Robbie Cruickshank and 5 co-authors built a flexible light lattice to make and study matter-wave solitons. A soliton is a wave packet that holds its shape as it moves. Their lattice works like an accordion: its spacing can be tuned over a wide range, as can its depth. The team details how they calibrate the lattice as the spacing changes.

They also prepare exact atom counts site by site using microwave pulses. Fast jumps in atom interaction strength and trap shape then create bright solitons in the lattice. By tuning jump length and final interaction strength, they found settings that keep solitons most stable. The setup suits controlled studies of nonlinear wave dynamics.
arxiv-2509-22771:
Pouya Asadi and 4 co-authors weigh what a future muon collider could add to the hunt for lepton flavor violation. Such violations, where one lepton type turns into another, would signal physics beyond the standard model. Low-energy precision searches are set to improve sharply and might see the first evidence. The team translates those searches into a set of effective operators. They then project the collider's reach on the same operators, with backgrounds and a parameterized detector model.

For most operators, the collider could confirm a low-energy signal. For some flavor pairings, it reaches scales far beyond low-energy probes. It also improves sensitivity to flavor-violating Higgs decays by about an order of magnitude over the high-luminosity LHC.
arxiv-2509-22871:
Rosa M. Mérida and 14 co-authors trace the star formation main sequence down to dwarf galaxies across most of cosmic time. The main sequence links a galaxy's star formation rate to its stellar mass and frames how galaxies grow. The team combined wide pre-JWST surveys for heavy galaxies with deep JWST and SHARDS data for light ones. The sample stays highly complete in both mass and star formation down to low masses, even at early epochs.

The overall sequence slope barely evolves up to redshift five. At low masses the slope steepens, though the strength of that bend depends on how measurement uncertainties are treated. A transition mass near ten billion suns holds across epochs. Scatter stays at canonical levels, even for dwarfs.
arxiv-2509-23071:
Training retrieval agents lacks the step-by-step traces that good supervision needs. Muzhi Li and 11 co-authors synthesize such traces from evidence, working backward. Their paradigm, EviPath, starts from question-answer pairs with supporting evidence. Stage one plans subtasks by abductive reasoning, in dependency order. Stage two answers sub-questions with the evidence as a stand-in environment.

Stage three turns full traces into dialogue form for fine-tuning. An eight-billion-parameter model trained on this corpus beat strong baselines. Exact match on open-domain questions rose by about fifteen points. The corpus gives agents grounded, executable practice paths.
arxiv-2509-23471:
Swapping in a better embedding model can force a costly rebuild of a whole vector database. Harshil Vejendla, the sole author, offers Drift-Adapter as a cheaper bridge. It is a small learned layer that maps new search queries into the old model's space. The old index then keeps serving, and the full rebuild can wait.

Three forms of the layer are tested: a rotation fit, a low-rank affine map, and a small residual network. Trained on a small paired sample, they kept almost all of the recall of a full rebuild on text and image tests with a million items. Query delay stayed tiny, and recompute costs fell by more than a hundredfold.
arxiv-2509-23571:
Defenders who hunt cyber threats by hand face more attacks than they can chase. Yuqiao Meng and 6 co-authors built CyberTeam, a benchmark that guides language models through blue team threat hunting in a standard way. Real hunts chain tasks from attribution to response, each with its own needs. CyberTeam maps those dependencies, then gives each task tailored operation modules, turning the hunt into ordered reasoning steps.

The benchmark holds thirty tasks and nine modules. Leading models and security agents were tested against open-ended reasoning styles. The guided design improved results, while free-form reasoning showed clear limits on real hunting work.
arxiv-2509-23971:
Traffic diffusion models draw lifelike streets where cars crash through each other and spawn inside buildings. Kargi Chauhan and Leilani H. Gilpin measured that failure on a leading simulator: half of its trajectories broke basic physical laws. Their fix, Validity-First Spatial Intelligence, treats validity as a requirement, not a hope. Energy-based guidance during sampling enforces collision avoidance and kinematic limits, with no retraining of the model.

Across two hundred urban scenarios from the Waymo Open Motion data, collision rates fell by two thirds. Overall validity climbed from about half to nearly ninety-five percent. Realism scores improved at the same time, which the authors highlight.
arxiv-2510-00071:
Dongqi Zheng wrote this 2025 paper on making large reasoning models cheaper to run. Such models often think far longer than a problem needs, wasting time, tokens, and energy. Zheng proposes Adaptive Reasoning Suppression, a method that watches a model's growing certainty as it works. When the model looks sure enough, the method trims the extra reasoning steps. The method needs no new training of the model itself.

Zheng tested the method on math reasoning tasks across several model designs. It cut token use by up to about half in the best cases. It also cut delay and energy use by large shares, while accuracy held steady or improved. Fixed cut-off rules did worse, because the method adjusts to each model's own path. The work matters for anyone paying to run reasoning models at scale.
arxiv-2510-00171:
Sreetama Das, Gian Luca Giorgi, and Roberta Zambrini published this 2025 paper on quantum reservoir computing. A reservoir computer lets a fixed, untrained system process signals over time, and only the readout is trained. Their system pairs one qubit with one bosonic mode, following the classic Jaynes-Cummings model of light and matter. They also test its dispersive limit, where the pair interacts more gently.

Both reservoirs were benchmarked on memory tasks that mix straight recall with nonlinear mixing. Unusually, the systems remembered nonlinear patterns better than simple linear ones. On the Mackey-Glass series, a standard chaotic forecasting test, they predicted comparably to known methods. Watching higher-order signals from the boson and slicing time into channels both boosted performance. The authors present the pair as a small, tunable building block for quantum machine learning hardware.
arxiv-2510-00271:
Nicole Crumpler and three colleagues published this 2025 astronomy paper hunting ultra-light dark matter through dead stars. If dark matter particles are extremely light, they form waves with a long coherence length. Such a field could swell or shrink white dwarfs in a spatially correlated pattern. The team asked whether catalog data could reveal that telltale correlation scale.

They first simulated the hunt, including dust, binaries, envelope differences, and noisy measurements. Only radius shifts near ten percent would stand out above that realistic noise, they found. Applying their routine to a Sloan survey catalog of more than ten thousand white dwarfs did show a correlation. Its scale sat near three hundred parsecs, with a striking average significance. Careful checks, though, traced the signal to biases in cool, nearby white dwarf measurements. The authors report a null result and a method ready for better data.
arxiv-2510-00471:
Yankai Jiang and three colleagues published this 2025 paper on the water footprint of supercomputing, an overlooked cost of big computation. High-performance systems drink water twice: directly for cooling and indirectly through power generation. Carbon emissions get the headlines, while water use stays largely unmeasured. Their framework, ThirstyFLOPS, quantifies both operational and embodied water for such systems.

The analysis folds in regional metrics for water use, power use, and the water intensity of local energy. Four famous machines serve as case studies: Marconi, Fugaku, Polaris, and Frontier. The authors compare water and carbon footprints side by side, exposing trade-offs between them. Regional water scarcity changes which machine looks greenest, they show. Nuclear-powered computing gets a careful hearing, with advantages and warnings both noted. The tool aims to ground future water-aware planning for computing infrastructure.
arxiv-2510-00671:
Nguyen and four co-authors introduce MILCO in this 2025 arXiv paper on multilingual information retrieval. Learned sparse retrieval represents queries and documents as weighted word lists, which is fast and transparent, but it has mostly worked in English alone. MILCO maps text from many languages into one shared English lexical space through a multilingual connector. A two-stage training recipe aligns those sparse representations first, then applies contrastive training to sharpen retrieval quality.

Rare names and entities can vanish when projected into English, so a LexEcho head adds a source-language view through a special echo token.
