The method is asynchronous, so an image can be read out at any moment. Reconstructions are noisier than neural results, yet clear enough for tasks like spotting fiducial markers.
arxiv-2510-20271:
Udit Saxena presents fast, differentiable tools for computing Euler Characteristic Curves, a topological summary of the global shape in imaging data. Topological features are useful in deep learning only if they can be computed quickly and differentiated through during training. His optimized graphics processor kernels report speedups ranging from sixteenfold to about two thousandfold over earlier graphics implementations on synthetic grids.

The kernels are tuned for Ampere hardware with coalesced memory access and hierarchical shared-memory accumulation. A PyTorch layer built on them learns thresholds in one direction through a smooth relaxation, enabling end-to-end training. Saxena also discusses downstream uses highlighted by earlier work and outlines batching and multi-processor extensions to broaden adoption of the method.
arxiv-2510-20671:
Subham Kumar, Lekhansh Shukla, Animesh Mukherjee, Koustav Rudra, and Prakrithi Shivaprakash address a hard clinic choice, deciding the right level of care for people seeking help with addiction. Beds and staff for live in care are scarce, so a wrong call wastes resources or leaves a patient with too little support.

Their system, GRACE, frames the choice as a graph learning task and builds a fair training graph to fight the severe imbalance in past records. Rare care levels are swamped by common ones. On real world data, scores for the rare class rise by wide margins over rival methods. Tuning the input features together with the graph model adds a further clear boost in accuracy.
arxiv-2510-20771:
Huijie Zhang and six co-authors dissect MeanFlow, a fast generative modeling method that learns average flow paths so images can be made in few steps. The method trains well in practice, yet the reasons for its success and its slow convergence in places were not well understood.

Gradient study shows its training goal splits into two parts, path matching and path consistency, that pull against each other and slow learning. The team defines a wider family of goals that unites MeanFlow with two rival methods, then trains with a schedule that eases from one part to the full goal. On a standard image task the new method beats MeanFlow at every scale, setting fresh best scores with plain transformer backbones.
arxiv-2510-20871:
Marta Gentiloni Silveri and two co-authors give the first quantitative exponential convergence guarantees for iterative Markovian fitting, a method for the Schrödinger bridge problem in transport and generative modeling. Earlier work proved only that the method settles in the limit, with no rate for finite runs.

Under mild structural demands on the reference measure and the target margins, with a strong enough starting fit, the team shows the error shrinks by a fixed factor at each round. That yields a clear time estimate for reaching a chosen accuracy, rather than a promise with no clock. Practical bridge matching methods inherit firmer ground, since their idealized core now has a proven speed.
arxiv-2510-21771:
Dharunish Yugeswardeenoo presents a low-cost robotic arm for everyday care tasks. Demand for assistive care is growing far beyond the supply of human caregivers. The arm is built from six servo motors, two cameras, and 3D-printed grippers. It learns by watching demonstration videos. No task-specific programming or manual labeling is needed.

Training data came from teleoperation with a leader arm. It covered feeding, cleaning spills, and fetching medicine across fifty thousand video frames. A new model design called PACT was paired with a smoothing method. In ten hours of real-world testing, it reached over ninety percent task accuracy. That beat comparison systems by a wide margin. Smaller models also stayed accurate under the same design.
arxiv-2510-21871:
Alphonse P. Magnus develops the mathematics of difference equations on special point grids, the discrete cousins of differential equations used when a problem lives on steps rather than a smooth line. The central question is which grids let a divided difference operator, a ratio of value change to step change, behave in a controlled algebraic way.

Magnus shows that when the starting function is a rational function of a given degree, the operator's output doubles that degree exactly on the right grids. In the most general case those grids come from an elliptic function sampled at evenly spaced arguments. Special and limiting cases are worked through, first and second order operators and equations are built up to the simplest elliptic hypergeometric level, and solutions show orthogonality properties.
arxiv-2510-22071:
Antonio Olivas-Martinez, Fei Gao, and Holly Janes work on trial designs that compare a new treatment against a proven one rather than against a placebo. Such non-inferiority trials are the right tool when effective options exist but a newcomer might be cheaper, safer, or easier to deliver, yet they carry a built-in weakness. With no placebo arm, the proven treatment's effect must be borrowed from history.

The classic rule demands the new option preserve a set share of that borrowed effect. When the standard treatment is very strong, a useful newcomer can fail the rule unfairly. Newer criteria instead ask whether the new option is effective enough against a hypothetical placebo. The authors propose a general framework that folds the existing analytic methods into one design and evaluation scheme.
arxiv-2510-22171:
Erum Mushtaq and five co-authors build a better gauge of model doubt. When a vision-language model is unsure, the gauge should say so. Systems that abstain on shaky answers generate less unsafe content. The usual gauges mash token probabilities together. They miss how tokens depend on each other. They also inherit biases from language habits.

Their method, HARMONY, reads hidden activations and outputs together. Surface probabilities are not trusted alone. Signals inside the network do carry news about image-text agreement. But the authors show that processing matters. How those signals are handled changes the quality of the estimate a great deal. The co-authors are Zalan Fabian, Yavuz Faruk Bakman, Anil Ramakrishna, Mahdi Soltanolkotabi, and Salman Avestimehr. The goal is selective prediction that catches bad answers before they ship.
arxiv-2510-22271:
Shanfeng Xiao, Huaxiong Huang, Robert Eisenberg, Zilong Song, and Shixin Xu model how the optic nerve washes itself. The brain's glymphatic system clears metabolic waste with flowing fluid. The optic nerve, a tract of central nervous tissue, must do the same to stay healthy and keep its ionic balance, yet the plumbing there is only partly understood.

Their multidomain electro-osmotic model couples water movement, driven by pressure and osmosis, with electro-diffusive ion traffic across four compartments. Axons, glial cells, the extracellular space, and the sleeves around blood vessels. Fluid enters along arteries, crosses glia and tissue. Leaves along veins, with exchanges through the water channel AQP4 and through gaps in glial endfeet giving two coupled transport modes, one for rest and one for activity. Parameter sweeps show what happens when the AQP4 route weakens.
arxiv-2510-22371:
Revanth Rameshkumar and four co-authors test whether large reasoning models, trained to argue step by step and check their own work, truly reason in general. High scores on graph and reasoning benchmarks had fed bold claims about such models. The team argues that those tests top out at modest difficulty, so they built a harder, scalable test set.

Their Deep Reasoning Dataset can produce endless examples at rising difficulty for graph connection and proof planning tasks. Model scores fell sharply once difficulty grew enough, showing weak generalisation. Most real world cases sit in the range models handle, but long hard tails remain.
arxiv-2510-22471:
Nivasini Ananthakrishnan and two co-authors study how a leader can do well in repeated dealings with an agent that learns from experience. Computing the best global strategy against such a learner can take a huge number of rounds, so exact planning is out of reach. The team shifts the goal to local equilibria, where no small change of plan helps the leader.

Within a smoothed analysis setting, they give an approximation scheme that runs in time polynomial in the agent action count. One cost grows fast as the allowed error shrinks, and they prove that cost cannot be avoided. The trade off makes local planning practical.
arxiv-2510-23171:
Zakaria Boutakka, Nouhaila Innan, Muhammed Shafique, Mohamed Bennai, and Z Sakhi benchmark setups for the variational quantum eigensolver on the silicon atom. VQE is a hybrid quantum-classical method for ground-state energies, and silicon is a heavy enough atom to be a hard test. Performance depends heavily on ansatz, starting point, and optimizer choices.

The team tries several ansatz families, including UCCSD and particle-conserving forms, paired with gradient and other optimizers. Their comparison shows which configurations estimate silicon energy best. Such benchmarks guide chemists who must pick practical VQE settings for near-term quantum hardware.
arxiv-2510-23471:
Shayan Kiyani, Hamed Hassani, George Pappas, and Aaron Roth study robust decision making when forecasts are only partially calibrated. Calibration is a foundation of trustworthy machine learning because, distribution-free and utility-free, the best policy is the one that trusts the predictions. But that promise holds only for fully calibrated forecasts, which are tractable to guarantee only in low dimensions.

For higher-dimensional problems, partial calibration is what practice can offer. The authors ask which decision rules stay robust under that weaker promise. Their results help policymakers act on modern forecasts without pretending those forecasts are perfectly calibrated.
arxiv-2510-23571:
Yash Jangir and nine co-authors built RobotArena Infinity, a framework for grading robot control policies without endless real-world trials. Testing robots in the physical world is slow, costly, hard to repeat, and risky at scale. Judging success is also tricky, since it often rests on subtle human views of how well a motion was carried out.

The framework turns video demonstrations from popular robot datasets into matching simulated scenes, using vision-language models, 2D-to-3D generation, and differentiable rendering. Inside these digital twins, policies are scored by automated model-guided ratings plus lightweight preference votes from crowdworkers. The team also perturbs scenes — changing textures, moving objects — to stress-test how well policies generalize. The result is a benchmark that keeps evolving while staying repeatable, aimed at real-world-trained manipulation policies.
arxiv-2510-23671:
Marmik Chaudhari and two co-authors ask how Mixture of Experts models organize knowledge inside, and whether the usual story from dense networks still applies. In dense models, superposition — storing more features than there are dimensions — is driven by how sparse and how important features are, with sharp phase changes. Mixture of Experts models, which route each input to a few specialist subnetworks, might work differently.

The authors find that neither feature sparsity nor importance triggers phase changes here. What matters instead is network sparsity, the share of experts active at once: sparser models show more monosemanticity, meaning single experts carry cleaner, single-meaning features. They propose defining expert specialization by that clean feature representation rather than by load balancing. With the right starting setup, experts settle around coherent feature combinations on their own, hinting that readable models need not cost performance.
arxiv-2510-23971:
Zhuo-Hua Chen and three co-authors predict a nonlinear layer Hall effect in layered antiferromagnetic insulators that respect combined parity and time-reversal symmetry. A linear version of the effect, driven by hidden Berry curvature, was recently seen in thin films of MnBi2Te4. It showed that the layer index itself can generate Hall transport, a fresh handle on fully compensated topological antiferromagnets.

The predicted nonlinear effect behaves oppositely in telling ways: its Hall conductivity is even in the antiferromagnetic order and odd in a vertical electric field. Two hidden geometric sources feed it, the Berry curvature dipole and the quantum metric dipole. Their currents obey different symmetries and flow in different directions, so an experiment can separate them. That separation is the point: the nonlinear signal offers a clean probe of the hidden Berry curvature dipole, a piece of quantum geometry that has been hard to isolate.
arxiv-2510-24171:
Abhiram Kaushik and two co-authors compute a missing piece of diffractive deep inelastic scattering, a process where a high energy probe strikes a proton and leaves it largely intact. They work in the dipole picture and calculate the contribution where a quark, antiquark, and gluon all take part, using exact kinematics.

The result is a finite part of the next order correction to the diffractive cross section. Earlier work had included this piece only in limiting cases for a soft gluon. Numeric checks show those limits do not approximate the full result well. The team also finds a soft quark contribution that matters just as much at high energy scales.
arxiv-2510-24271:
Krapivsky and Luck, two authors, study a playful problem in number theory. They look at endless products built from special whole numbers. Gauss numbers mix whole numbers with the square root of minus one. Eisenstein numbers use a cube root of unity in the same spirit. The pair ask what such products give once a smoothing rule tames them.

Their method follows Euler, who treated wild products with bold formal steps. Recent work by Muñoz García and Pérez-Marco gave one such product a clean value. That work found the product of all plain primes in this smoothed sense. Krapivsky and Luck push the same idea to the two richer number systems. They give explicit formulas for integers and for primes in each system. The result shows how far Euler style formal math can reach.
arxiv-2510-24471:
Yujie Zhu and seven co-authors propose a faster method for removing reverberation from single channel speech frame by frame online. Reverberation smears speech in rooms, harming communication and interaction systems. Forward convolutive prediction uses a neural network to predict the direct signal, then estimates a linear filter to suppress the remaining echo, but that filter is often excessively long and costly.

Their method decomposes the long filter as a Kronecker product of two much shorter filters. This cuts computation while keeping the dereverberation quality of the original approach. The result suits real time voice communication, where each frame must be cleaned with little delay.
arxiv-2510-24771:
Syon Bhattacharjee, Deepika Behmani, and Sudeep Bhattacharjee study how cold plasma in air changes plain water, and how that water then feeds young plants. The jet makes harsh oxygen and nitrogen forms at near room heat. When it hits water, the water gains a chem charge that shifts with dose time and amount.

They used a helium and air mix jet and checked the water for acid level, flow of charge, and dissolved solids. Light reads showed the mix made a more live discharge than pure helium, with more nitrate in the water. One dose and size pair worked best in their tests. They then gauged growth of chrysanthemum shoots in the charged water.
arxiv-2510-24971:
Kammoun leads a team with fifty one co-authors who give the first high grade X ray view of the galaxy NGC 7213, from the XRISM scope. Its Resolve tool can split iron lines that past scopes blurred as one. Fresh reads from two more X ray scopes and a ground scope back the main read.

The iron line splits in two: a thin core from a far dust zone, and a wider, slanted part from the disk close in. That wide part mirrors a twin peaked light line seen in plain light. Hot iron lines sit in the gap zone between disk and the broad line cloud. The whole set maps a stack of zones by range.
arxiv-2510-25071:
Ravi Kiran and A Taraphder map how waves of shake run through a flat grid of squares and eight side shapes. Such grids can host chiral shake waves, where the shake turns as it goes, when key mirror rules break. Their model is a spring and mass take, with pulls to near and more far points.

Mass gaps and spring pulls set where band gaps in the shake tones open and close. Speed of the waves shifts a lot with the way one looks, a slant born of the grid shape. Flat bands pile up in the state counts, and long pulls add more slant to sound spread. The map can guide new sound parts.
arxiv-2510-25571:
Phuc Tran and Nisheeth K Vishnoi bound perturbations for low-rank inverses. Their 2025 paper studies matrix inverse approximations under noise. Low-rank pseudoinverses approximate inverses in scalable computing. Machine learning and tuning use them widely. Real-world matrices are often observed with noise. Sampling, sketching, and quantization all present noise. Spectral-norm robustness remains poorly understood in literature.

They study spectral-norm error for symmetric matrices systematically. A noisy reading adds an error matrix to original. Best rank-p inverse approximations are compared against noisy versions. Mild noise assumptions support their theoretical study. Sharp non-asymptotic perturbation bounds are derived. Error scales with eigengap and spectral decay, they reveal. Noise matching with low-curvature directions also matters. Contour integral techniques are applied novelly here. Bounds improve over classic full-inverse adaptations largely. Empirical tests track true perturbation error closely. Classic values greatly overpredict error in tests.
arxiv-2510-25671:
Hongjin Du led four co-authors on hybrid power control. Rahul Rane, Weijie Xia, and Pedro P Vergara helped. Aleksandra Lekic closes the five-author team. Their 2025 paper controls hybrid AC-MTDC power systems. Renewable integration, especially offshore wind, presents uncertainty. Forecast errors and power fluctuations challenge stability.

Their approach integrates forecasts with optimal power flow. Random Forest models generate wind speed forecasts. A time-coupled optimal flow determines converter setpoints. Setpoints anticipate wind fluctuations before they occur. Real-time adjustment follows actual operating settings then. An changing droop scheme considers two deviations jointly. DC voltage and AC frequency deviations both matter. Hardware-in-the-loop runs validate the approach effectiveness. Stable, robust operation held under high renewable penetration. Hybrid systems mix alternating and direct current grids. Multi-terminal direct current adds control hardness there.
arxiv-2510-25871:
PA Crowther and JM Bestenlehner describe a new pipeline for measuring large samples of hot, massive OB stars in a uniform way. OB stars are the hottest and heaviest normal stars, and their spectra reveal temperature, gravity, and wind traits. Their tool fits each spectrum against a large grid of FASTWIND models, which simulate stellar air in detail, and it includes model errors in the fit.

Crowther and Bestenlehner test the pipeline on three large telescope surveys of stars in the Magellanic Clouds, the two small neighbor galaxies of the Milky Way. Results agree well with earlier careful work. Strong nebular glow, unseen companions, and disc emission still need human checks, and the tool now feeds a major survey pipeline.
arxiv-2510-26171:
Hasnain Iqbal, Zerina Begum, and Kazi Sakib cut wasted reruns in hunting order dependent flaky tests. A flaky test passes or fails unpredictably on the same code, and an order dependent test changes outcome based on which tests run before it. Such tests can fail a continuous integration pipeline without signaling a real fault. Finding them usually requires many reruns of unrelated tests.

Iqbal and the team prioritize likely order dependent tests by analyzing shared static fields in test classes, state that tests can silently share. On twenty seven project modules, their method placed all order dependent tests first in twenty three cases. Test executions fell by about sixty six percent on average, and unnecessary reruns fell by about seventy two percent.
arxiv-2510-26371:
Anton Chernev, Corina Cîrstea, Helle Hvid Hansen, and Clemens Kupke work in the theory of automata, the simple machines that read structures step by step. An unambiguous automaton allows at most one winning run for each structure, a trait that helps when checking reactive systems. Older work built such automata for thin trees, which are trees with few branches at each level.

Chernev and his three co-authors extend that building method from trees to thin coalgebras, a wider class of structures used across computer science theory. Their route passes through coherent algebras, a tool first made for studying such structures. Along the way they give a neat test: the languages these automata accept are exactly those that finite coherent algebras can pick out. That ties two views of the same thing together.
arxiv-2510-26771:
Marco Federici, with four co-authors, helps quantised AI models keep their accuracy at very low precision. Quantization stores a model's numbers in fewer bits to cut latency, power, and memory, but accuracy drops sharply when activations go below eight bits. Their method, STaMP, applies linear transformations along the sequence dimension of the data, where language and images have strong local correlation.

Federici and the team also keep a small number of tokens in each activation at higher precision, a mixed precision step. Together, the moves hold accuracy at lower average bit widths. Tests on recent vision and language architectures showed clear gains. The method complements established weight and activation quantization, including recent feature transformations.
arxiv-2510-27071:
Dengming Xu and Mengmeng Li construct constant dimension codes, a class of error-control codes used in random network coding. In these codes every codeword is a subspace of fixed dimension, and good constructions are prized because they raise how much data a network can carry reliably. The multilevel construction is among the most effective routes to such codes.

The authors first pick a skeleton code from binary vectors tied to one-factorization of complete graphs, meaning a splitting of all pairings into perfect rounds. They then build the full codes with quasi-pending blocks and compute dimensions using known optimal Ferrers diagram rank-metric codes. As a payoff, they improve known lower bounds for a key code size across several lengths. The gains give network coding designers stronger options.
arxiv-2510-27371:
Sagar Dutta, Banani Basu, and Fazal Ahmed Talukdar classify leg activities from radio waves creeping around the thigh. Creeping waves travel along the body surface, and their transmission between two flexible on-body antennas changes with leg motion. Six leg-based activities each produce unique time-varying signatures in that channel, offering a wearable-free sensing route.

The team applies discrete wavelet transforms for feature extraction, then compares classifiers including support vector machines, decision trees, naive Bayes, and nearest neighbors, plus time-warping and deep convolutional alternatives. Support vector machines with wavelet features outperform the others in each comparison. Safety simulations of specific absorption rate with the antenna directly on the thigh stay within the United States federal threshold, supporting practical activity monitoring use.
arxiv-2510-27571:
Zhuoning Guo and five co-authors argue in 2025 that video search tests are too narrow to build broad skill. Search models learn from small sets tied to one task, so they fail on new kinds of clips. The team built a joint plan that links a new test suite, new training data, and a new model.

Their test suite spans sixteen data sets to expose gaps by task and field. A build flow then made more than one and a half million matched pairs for training. A staged plan, called a Modality Pyramid, trains the model on linked kinds of data. The model leads on zero-shot tests, and partly matched clips prove to be a key, missed case.
arxiv-2511-00071:
Ertugrul Mutlu returns to wavelet-based parity finding as a testing of representation, not as a useful method, since parity is plainly read from the least significant bit. Integers up to ten thousand are encoded as fixed-width thirty-two-bit binary signals, split with a three-level Daubechies wavelet transform, summed up by coefficient sizes, and grouped per subband without watching.

The study asks how a standard signal process preserves, boosts, or hides symbolic information hidden in a numeric representation, and how that extends. Machine learning readers get a guided probe of representation dependence. Parity's known answer makes it a clean instrument for gauging what a process does to information.
arxiv-2511-00171:
Rahul Ghosh, Baishali Chaudhury, and Hari Prasanna Das propose CompAgent, an agentic framework for checking whether images and media obey complex, evolving policy rules in media, entertainment, and advertising. Task-specific models need costly labeled data and generalize poorly, while general multimodal models have broad knowledge but miss fine visual details and structured rule application on their own.

An agent structure combines those strengths, decomposing compliance checks into steps that use tools and detailed inspection. Computer vision readers get the first agentic approach to this problem, as framed by the authors. Automated compliance could scale content review where rules change faster than datasets can be rebuilt.
arxiv-2511-00371:
Erfan Al-Hossami and Razvan Bunescu formalize a teaching method called Socratic debugging, where an instructor guides a student to find a bug alone instead of handing over the fix. Most beginner bugs grow from misconceptions, false beliefs about how a concept works. A guided reasoning path can lead the student to a program behavior that clashes with the false belief, and the clash prompts a lasting belief update.

The authors define the task of generating such reasoning trajectories and build a dataset of debugging problems annotated with them, some written by hand and some by language models. They then test model-based generators for both the trajectories and the Socratic dialogues built on them. A large judge-based evaluation found most generated trajectories correct and nearly all dialogue turns valid.
arxiv-2511-00471:
Jian Zhang, Chenglin Wang, and Shihui Zhu resolve two conjectures about solitons of the cubic-quintic nonlinear Schrödinger equation in three dimensions. The conjectures, posed by Killip, Oh, Pocovnicu, and Visan, concern how soliton properties vary monotonically: one with frequency, the other with mass. Settling them required fresh control over the variational structure behind these self-trapped waves.

Both conjectures are now completely resolved, and uniqueness of the energy minimizer is proved along the way. With those pieces in place, the authors establish sharp stability for the solitons, the strongest form of the stability statement. They also give the first classification of normalized solutions for the equation. The work closes a coordinated set of questions about how these waves behave and persist.
arxiv-2511-01071:
Fengxing Zhu studies sequence reconstruction over a deletion channel, a communication setting where symbols can vanish from a transmitted binary codeword. The record notes the main mistake in an earlier version has been corrected. The receiver sees several distinct outputs, each missing up to a fixed number of symbols, and wants to narrow the original message down to a short list of candidates.

Zhu determines the minimum number of channel outputs needed to guarantee such a list reconstruction. The key step is computing the largest possible intersection of several deletion balls, the sets of outputs that different candidate codewords could produce after deletions. Knowing that intersection size exactly pins down when the received outputs can still be consistent with too many candidates.
arxiv-2511-01371:
Sagar Dutta, Banani Basu, and Fazal Ahmed Talukdar detect faults in induction motors without touching the machine. Induction motors are the workhorses of industry, and catching their faults early matters. Their sensor is a wide angle antenna, whose reflection and transmission coefficients change with the motor's condition.

Spectrograms of those two signals carry distinct signatures for varied fault conditions. A deep neural network learns the patterns and the boundaries between classes. Using the reflection coefficient alone gave about ninety three percent correct calls, the transmission coefficient alone did better, and both combined reached perfect accuracy in their tests. The paper also checks how the antenna's working frequency, its spot, and the signal length affect the score.
arxiv-2511-01471:
Mikhail Belov and five colleagues argue that the flow of executed trades, rather than price itself, is the basic engine behind market movement. They define execution flow as the rate at which traded volume accumulates over time, and they present experiments on real market data meant to show it driving the dynamics.

To compute the flow they build a numerical framework based on the Radon-Nikodym derivative. The method automatically picks out thresholds that could serve as trading triggers, and it extracts a characteristic time scale from an eigenvalue problem. A second framework, built on the Christoffel function spectrum, is offered as an alternative to principal component analysis that survives a wider class of transformations of the input data.
arxiv-2511-01971:
William Pannell, William Ronayne, and Andreas Stergiou examine a structural question about the renormalisation group, the machinery that describes how a quantum field theory changes with energy scale. In favourable cases the flow is gradient-like, following the slope of a single function. The authors check this property to four-loop order in theories mixing scalar and fermion fields, in four dimensions and just below.

A modified beta function, the beta shift, turns out to be central, and they derive the conditions it must meet for gradient flow. Over a thousand such conditions emerge, all scheme-independent and satisfied whenever the needed results exist. They also show that, as the number of fields grows, conformal theories with a nonzero beta shift dominate the landscape.
arxiv-2511-02271:
Yucheng Song, Yifan Ge, Junhao Li, Zhining Liao, and Zhifang Liao proposed a framework for automatically writing radiology reports from medical images, but the authors withdrew the submission from arXiv. In their withdrawal notice they stated that problems with the training epochs and training strategy had caused numerical errors in the results comparison table. They had decided to withdraw the preprint because of those errors. Its reported performance figures should therefore not be relied on.

As submitted, the work had described a system called HTSC-CIF that split report generation into three levels: aligning medical entities with image locations, tightening text-image alignment through masked modelling. It also applied a causal intervention to remove spurious correlations between image and text. The authors presented experiments claiming it beat current methods, claims that the withdrawal leaves unestablished.
arxiv-2511-02371:
Rohan Wandre, Yash Gajewar, Namrata Patel, and Vivek Dhalkari design a retrieval system for AI agents that learn continuously from streams of text, images, video, and audio. Retrieval-augmented generation grounds a language model's answers in stored evidence. A lifelong stream creates two headaches: keeping the index fresh without costly rebuilding, and keeping the distinct modalities semantically aligned as embeddings drift apart.

Their architecture, LUMA-RAG, tiers its memory, spilling embeddings from a fast index into a compressed tier under strict memory budgets. A streaming alignment bridge keeps audio and image representations consistent through incremental updates, and a telemetry layer bounds alignment drift and quantisation error to give explicit safety guarantees on the top-ranked results. Experiments showed strong text-to-image retrieval, gentle degradation when memory was compressed, and provably stable audio-to-image rankings.
arxiv-2511-02571:
Tetiana Manzhos, Tetiana Ianevych, and Olga Melnyk work out what a popular ranking metric should score when a ranking is pure chance. Recommender and search systems are graded by mean average precision at a cutoff, which rewards relevant items placed near the top of a list. To judge whether a real system beats luck, evaluators need the chance baseline and, just as much, the size of the random wobble around it.

The authors derive formulas for both the expectation and the variance of average precision at a cutoff under random rankings. Two evaluation settings are covered, the offline model and the online model. The expectation fixes the level a random ranker achieves on average, and the variance quantifies how far a single lucky or unlucky run can stray, which makes observed scores meaningfully interpretable.
arxiv-2511-02971:
Yige Li, Maria de los Angeles Resa, and Jose Zubizarreta estimate the effect of treatments that change over time, like a therapy adjusted month by month. Standard weighting methods wobble badly when some patients rarely get the treatment they in fact received. Their 2025 paper builds on a framework by Imai and Ratkovic and changes what gets balanced.

Instead of balancing raw patient traits, their estimator balances only the part of each trait that is new at each time point, the part not predicted by the patient's history. They prove the estimator stays consistent and well-behaved even where classic weighting fails. In simulations it matched the efficiency of model-based methods while shrugging off model errors better. A study of private versus public schooling in Chile showed stable, readable results.
arxiv-2511-03271:
Yize Liu, Yunyun Hou, and Aina Sui recast multi-turn attacks on chat models as a search for the best route through a map. Safety testers use long chats to coax models into banned replies, but many test methods wander and waste effort. The team models each talk turn as a step on a weighted graph whose weights shift over time.

On that base they build ABC, a search method modeled on how bee colonies forage together. Scout, worker, and follower roles share leads and chase the most promising paths. The authors report that the colony search finds strong attack paths with less overhead than prior ways. The point is defensive: cheaper, sharper red teaming can expose weak spots before real users suffer from them.
arxiv-2511-03471:
Ming Gu and colleagues frame AAA, a human-plus-model system for auditing web accessibility at scale. Most sites still fail accessibility rules, partly because careful audits demand heavy human effort. A standard step-by-step audit method exists but lacks practical support for large sites.

Two pieces carry the load: a graph-based sampler that picks pages covering a site fairly, using visual, text, and link cues, and a multimodal copilot that assists auditors across tasks. The copilot flags likely barriers and drafts findings for human review. The authors aim to keep expert judgment in charge while letting models do the sweeping. Wider audits could push more of the web toward equal use.
arxiv-2511-03671:
Bennett Lamb and Brandon B Le map the split fates of two coupled model neurons that each behave calmly alone. The Chialvo model captures a neuron's spiking and recovery in a few equations, and the pair here link with an uneven electrical coupling. Two kinds of long-run behavior coexist, one chaotic and one orderly.

The chaotic fate claims most starting states, while the orderly basin stretches to infinity through chance synchronization of the pair. Their shared border is fractal, so near it the tiniest change in starting state flips the ending. Such extreme sensitivity could matter for real neural circuits, where noise near a fractal border would make outcomes effectively unguessable.
arxiv-2511-03771:
Alif Elham Khan presents a self-supervised learning method for medical images whose labels form a tree, running from organ down to tissue and subtype. Standard training ignores that hierarchy. Khan makes the label tree a direct training signal and also a target for judging how faithful the learned features remain.

Two added objectives do the work. One weights contrastive pairs by shared ancestors, and the other uses a margin to separate groups at different levels. Tests on several benchmarks, including breast histopathology, show better features than strong baselines and closer respect for the taxonomy. The approach works with flat or curved embeddings and needs no change to the model design.
arxiv-2511-03871:
Mark S Bartlett is the lead author among twelve authors extending the Joint Probability Method to compound flooding in low-gradient coastal watersheds. Flood depth there comes from storm surge, rainfall, and river flow interacting, and older methods described drivers or single events rather than the long-term frequency of depths themselves.

Their extension couples storm characteristics with probabilistic rainfall realisations and random antecedent conditions, then pushes those processes through a flood response model. The output is a full distribution of compound flood depths. That statistical basis supports mapping transition zones, attributing depth shares to different causes, and choosing design events on firmer ground for flood planning.
arxiv-2511-03971:
Victor Mattos, Joao Henrique Schmidt, Amit Bhaya, Alan Oliveira de Sa, Daniel Sadoc Menasche, and Gaurav Srivastava model covert man-in-the-middle attacks on water treatment plants. Digital intrusion there can threaten health, safety, and the environment. Their systematic approach uses system identification to design an attacker's covert controller.

A second-order linear model with time delay stands in for plant dynamics, and stealthy attacks are simulated against a process-aware anomaly detector. System noise and errors in the attacker's own plant model change how stealthy an attack can stay. Those sensitivities, the authors argue, show why industrial control defences need stronger detection built for quiet, model-aware intruders.
arxiv-2511-04271:
Sergio Bengoechea, Paul Over, and Thomas Rung present a complete quantum time-marching algorithm for multi-part linear transport problems with arbitrary boundaries. It is the first such application reported. Adapting the linear combination of unitaries method block-encodes diffusive dynamics, while edge conditions shape whether the scheme stays practical on fault-tolerant hardware.

Images enforce general edges at a cost of one extra qubit per spatial dimension. Neumann conditions can instead be encoded directly by splitting the discrete marching operator. Success chances stay optimal and time stays linear, the authors argue. State-vector runs of the heat equation with Neumann, Dirichlet, and mixed edges demonstrate the method.
arxiv-2511-04371:
G M Delgado and J E G Silva study an electron confined to a twisted cylindrical surface, a model for nanotubes, heterostructures, and curved quantum devices. Strain from twisting changes the surface metric, and da Costa's formalism turns that geometry into a quantum potential inside the Schroedinger equation even without external forces.

Bound states and energy levels are computed in linear and nonlinear torsion regimes. Both twists imprint a geometric phase on the wave function while leaving the da Costa potential unchanged, so the bound spectrum stays twist-independent, a surprising split. Two scattering setups, a twisted section inside an infinite cylinder and a finite twisted cylinder, show how transmission responds to geometry and strain.
arxiv-2511-04571:
Leonid Positselski, writing alone, studies pseudo-dualizing complexes for torsion modules in an MGM duality setting. This work returns to two earlier papers and a section of a third. A commutative ring carries a weakly proregular, finite ideal at the center.

Three classes of torsion and contramodule classes are compared against a chosen dualizing complex. Maximal, abstract, and minimal versions each get their triangulated equivalences. A special case covers semiderived categories for adically coherent rings with a ring map between them. Such dualities organize how local cohomology and completion interact across modern algebra.
arxiv-2511-04671:
Maximus A. Pace leads eight authors with X-Diffusion, training robot policies from human videos. Human demonstrations are plentiful, but human and robot bodies differ sharply. Many human actions cannot be copied directly by a robot arm.

Still, the videos carry rich cues about objects and task intent. The key move treats human actions as noisy versions of robot actions. Ambient Diffusion then uses low-quality data only at high-noise steps of training. That way, intent transfers while unworkable human motions fade out. The method aims at robot skills learned from coarse guidance alone.
arxiv-2511-05071:
Tommaso Proietti and a co-author revisit how climate normals and anomalies should be estimated. A normal is the baseline level and seasonal pattern of a measure like rain or heat, and an anomaly is the gap from that normal.

Such gaps drive study and forecasts of the El Niño and Southern Oscillation pattern. The standard normal is a plain 30-year mean, but that rule is now in doubt as climate shifts over time. The authors weigh methods that can track a moving baseline, so anomalies reflect real change rather than an old fixed frame.
arxiv-2511-05171:
Davide Marincione and co-authors show that merging two models can fix a flaw in a bioacoustic base model. NatureLM reads animal sounds well after fine-tuning, but that tune-up hurt its skill at following mixed prompts.

For one case, it named a species well by common name or by Latin name, yet failed when both were asked at once. A simple blend of NatureLM with its base language model brought back prompt skill while it kept sound skill. The fix is cheap, and it warns that fine-tuning can quietly trade away broad use.
arxiv-2511-05271:
Jack Hong and co-authors introduce DeepEyesV2, a multimodal model built to act, not just to see and describe. An agentic model should call tools like code runs and web search, and fold their results into its reasoning.

The team found that direct reinforcement learning alone did not yield firm tool use. So they built a two-stage run: a cold start that sets tool habits, then reinforcement to sharpen them. They cover data building, training, and tests. The lesson is that tool skill must be seeded before it can be tuned.
arxiv-2511-05371:
M. de Berg and co-authors build star-based separators for intersection graphs of colored pseudo-segments, shapes formed where curves cross. Separators split a graph into balanced parts by removing a small set, a trick that speeds many algorithms.

Planar graphs have classic separators, but disk-like intersection graphs do not. Past work gave clique-based separators for disk graphs, later widened to other disk-like shapes. The authors add a star form for this colored pseudo-segment case. Such splits can bring fast, divide-and-conquer methods to graphs that come from geometry in the flat plane.
arxiv-2511-05471:
Antônio Catão and co-authors present TUPANN, a satellite-only neural model for very short-term rain forecasts, built for places with no dense radar net. Radar-based nowcasts are sharp, but the places most hit by climate extremes often lack radar cover.

TUPANN splits the task into physical parts. A variational encoder reads motion and intensity fields from recent images, under flow guidance. A transformer block then evolves the hidden state by lead time. A physics-based shift step builds the future image. The design aims to transfer across regions with no radar at all.
arxiv-2511-05571:
Xiaofei Wang, Stephen Price, and Chao Li present C3-Diff, a method to sharpen spatial transcriptomics maps. These maps show where genes are active inside tissue, but current platforms give blurry, low-resolution readings. Sharper maps would help reveal how tissue works at a fine scale.

C3-Diff uses microscope images of the same tissue as a guide. It first refines contrastive learning so features shared across image and gene data, and features unique to each, are both kept. It then adds noise-based augmentation and a training trick that fills in missing data. On four public data sets, the method beat rival approaches by a clear margin.
arxiv-2511-05771:
Seyed Alireza Javid and Nuria González-Prelcic improve how wireless systems estimate their radio channels when few pilot signals are available. Accurate channel knowledge drives both communication and sensing in next-generation networks. Classic methods degrade in complex settings with sparse pilots, while pure learning methods need huge data sets and explain little.

Their physics-informed neural network starts from a model-based estimate, then refines it with a deep network that also reads maps of signal strength in the environment. Cross-attention fuses the two inputs. On ray-traced urban data the method cut estimation error by a clear margin over leading rivals. Gains were strongest when pilots were scarcest, and the method held up across frequencies with little retuning.
arxiv-2511-06171:
Xi Chen and five co-authors prove a hardness result for testing halfspaces, a basic class of yes-no rules also called linear threshold functions. The setting is property testing with relative error, where distance is measured against the number of inputs a function accepts. That model suits sparse functions, which accept only few inputs.

Halfspaces can be tested with a constant number of queries in the standard model, independent of input size. Under relative error, the authors show any testing method needs on the order of log n oracle calls. Halfspaces become the first well-studied class where relative-error testing is provably harder than standard testing.
arxiv-2511-06571:
Haiyan Zhao and colleagues ask how much of a text survives inside a single internal vector of a language model. Models turn writing into hidden numerical patterns, but what those patterns retain is murky. Rep2Text tries to rebuild the original words from just one hidden representation taken from the model.

For short texts near sixteen words, the method recovered about half the original words while keeping the overall meaning. Longer texts resist exact recovery, though their main ideas still come through. The findings open a window on what models store internally and flag a privacy concern: shared hidden representations may leak parts of the input text.
arxiv-2511-07071:
Marcel Müller's dissertation applies multi-agent reinforcement learning to a warehouse problem: autonomous mobile robots that block each other and deadlock. Fleets of such robots make intralogistics flexible, but deadlocks degrade throughput and reliability, and most planners ignore deadlock handling during planning, falling back on rigid rules that cannot adapt. The dissertation develops a step-by-step approach for integrating learning-based control into logistics planning and operations.

Reference models formulate pathfinding problems that explicitly allow deadlocks, enabling side-by-side comparison of plans in grid-based simulations. Learning methods based on PPO and IMPALA, above all with centralized training and decentralized execution, outperformed rule-based methods in complex, congested settings. In simpler layouts with ample space, rule-based methods stayed competitive thanks to lower computational demands, so the dissertation stresses tailoring the approach to context.
arxiv-2511-07171:
Sébastien Thuau, Siba Haidar, and Rachid Chelouah compare plans for detecting violence in surveillance video without centralizing the footage. Federated learning trains models across sites while data stays local, protecting privacy, but fine-tuning huge vision-language models that way costs serious energy. The study tests three methods under realistic non-identical data splits on the RWF-2000 and RLVS data sets. They are zero-shot vision-language models, LoRA fine-tuning of a seven-billion-parameter video model, and a personalized 3D convolutional network.

All three exceeded ninety percent accuracy on binary violence detection. The smaller CNN calibrated best and used roughly half the energy of federated LoRA tuning, while the vision-language models offered richer contextual reasoning. Semantic category grouping lifted their multiclass accuracy sharply on UCF-Crime. The authors recommend hybrid deployments that default to efficient CNNs.
arxiv-2511-07471:
Ratun Rahman, Sina Shaham, and Dinh Nguyen combine quantum computing with federated learning to spot anomalies. Anomaly detection matters in surveillance, medicine, and industry, yet labeled examples are scarce and data cannot always be pooled. Quantum federated learning spreads training across many quantum clients instead.

Real clients differ in hardware, circuit design, noise, and how they encode data. One shared model can fit such varied clients poorly. The authors move toward personalized models tuned per client. Their discussion weighs privacy gains against uneven quantum behavior. The work maps a path for private anomaly detection on near-term quantum networks.
arxiv-2511-07671:
Yasir Zubayr Barlas, Sabina Sloman, and Samuel Kaski design experiments that stay trustworthy when the model is wrong. Bayesian optimal design picks experiments by expected information gain, but a wrong model corrupts both inference and those gain estimates. Real science rarely guarantees a correct model.

Generalised Bayesian inference swaps the likelihood for a loss function, gaining robustness. Building optimal design on that foundation yields experiments chosen for reliable learning even under mismatch. The framework keeps the tidy bookkeeping of Bayesian design while dropping its most fragile assumption. Fields from psychology to engineering could plan studies that degrade gracefully instead of misleading confidently.
arxiv-2511-07771:
Yanxian Tao, Lingyun Wan, and Xiongzhi Zeng predict molecular wavefunctions with a hybrid quantum-classical learner. Molecular dynamics needs fresh electronic states at every atomic arrangement, and solving them self-consistently each time is the bottleneck, especially for large or strongly correlated systems.

Quantum-centric machine learning couples quantum circuits with a Transformer. Early training on diverse molecules teaches broad patterns, then the combined model predicts wavefunctions and observables directly. Skipping repeated self-consistent solves could stretch simulations to bigger systems and longer times. The approach also gives quantum hardware a concrete chemistry workload where learned classical structure does much of the heavy lifting.
arxiv-2511-08071:
Ying Wang and colleagues introduce Radar-APLANC, an unsupervised method for sensing heartbeats with radar and no contact. Frequency modulated radar can pick up tiny chest movements, but noise degrades older signal processing methods. Learning based methods resist noise better, yet they usually need costly labeled recordings for training.

The framework builds positive samples from the heartbeat range and negative samples from noise ranges in the radar matrix. A noise contrastive triplet loss trains on pseudo labels from a traditional method, so no true physiological labels are needed. Adaptive label selection cleans those pseudo labels, and results rival supervised methods on two data sets.
arxiv-2511-08171:
Bangti Jin, Fengru Wang, and Jun Zou develop a stable iterative direct sampling method for elliptic inverse problems with partial Cauchy data. Problems in impedance tomography, optical tomography, and cardiac electrophysiology all ask where hidden inhomogeneities sit inside a body. Missing boundary information and measure noise make that reconstruction delicate, and unstable methods blur or misplace the targets.

Three pieces work jointly: a data completion scheme rebuilds missing boundary values, a regularized Dirichlet to Neumann map sharpens probing functions, and a stabilization correction guards the numerics. The method carries a provable stability guarantee, adapts to varied measure layouts, and improves resolution in the three test applications.
arxiv-2511-08571:
Mainak Singha, Jose Aguilera-Toste, and Vinayak Lahiri test whether two simple signals, trend and momentum, can earn steady profits in gold futures. Their backtest runs from 2015 to 2025 with a rolling design: ten years of training, then six months of trading, repeated across nearly twenty-eight hundred trading days.

Positions are sized with a fractional Kelly rule adjusted for market impact, with volatility targets and ATR-based exits, and costs are charged throughout. Out of sample, the authors report a Sharpe ratio near two point nine and a maximum drawdown of about half a percent. Returns show almost no link to spot gold moves, which they read as benchmark-neutral performance. Statistical checks, including bootstrap intervals and SPA tests, support the result under cost and delay stress.
arxiv-2511-08671:
Si-Rui Ge and four co-authors use the James Webb Space Telescope to check whether dust is hiding the true power sources inside distant galaxies. Optical emission lines usually classify what ionizes a galaxy's gas, but heavy dust can block the optical view and fool the classification.

Near-infrared line ratios, which suffer less from dust, are applied to spectra of fifty-five galaxies seen as they were within the universe's first ten billion years. About ninety percent agree with the optical verdict. Three galaxies that look star-forming in optical light read as active galactic nuclei in the infrared, which the authors interpret as buried black hole activity. Three others flip the other way, explained by hidden star formation or unusual nitrogen enrichment.
arxiv-2511-09071:
Mou Cai, Josef Dick, and Takashi Goda approximate complicated functions from scattered evaluations using lattices with many shifts. Their setting is a weighted Korobov space, a family of periodic functions whose smoothness is tuned by weights. The workhorse is the rank-1 lattice rule, a structured grid beloved in quasi-Monte Carlo integration.

Estimating Fourier coefficients from one lattice invites aliasing errors, where different frequencies masquerade as each other. Running many shifted copies of the same lattice and recovering each coefficient by least squares cancels the confusion. The cost grows like the squared logarithm of the lattice size per dimension. The authors prove the method achieves the optimal worst-case convergence rate for uniform approximation, and with random shifts the optimal rate for squared-error approximation as well. Numerical experiments mirror the theory.
arxiv-2511-09571:
Margaret R. Martin and Soha Hassoun ask large language models to simulate how molecules break apart in a mass spectrometer. Metabolomics stalls because most measured spectra never get annotated, and fragmentation patterns are the key to naming unknown compounds. Their framework, GIF, guides pretrained models through the simulation with structured prompting instead of ad hoc questions.

Tagging, structured inputs and outputs, system prompts, and iterative refinement steer the model's reasoning. On a question-answering dataset derived from MassSpecGym, GPT-4o and its mini version scored best. They reproduced true spectra more faithfully than newer and domain-specialized models. GIF also outperformed several deep learning baselines. The authors highlight human-in-the-loop, explainable workflows as a further benefit.
arxiv-2511-09771:
Yu Deng, Teng Cao, Hikaru Shindo, Quentin Delfosse, Jiahong Xue, and Kristian Kersting present STORM. The system estimates and tracks an object's six-dimensional pose from a single reference image. Robots need this skill, but many pipelines demand a ready-made 3D model or a hand-drawn mask in the first frame, and they fail quietly under occlusion or fast motion.

STORM fuses reference and live images through a hierarchical attention design that can also use language-based cues to tell similar instances apart. A trained verifier scores tracking quality continuously, spots drift, and triggers automatic re-initialization when tracking breaks. On the LM-O and YCB-Video benchmarks it beat strong baselines at annotation-free tracking and recovered reliably from heavy occlusion and rapid viewpoint changes.
arxiv-2511-09871:
Hyung-Jun Moon and Sung-Bae Cho design a continual learning system that stores no old examples yet keeps what earlier tasks taught. Older methods isolated each task, forcing networks to relearn similar features or push them too far apart. Their design uses two differentiable memories: one for features shared across tasks, and one that combines shared features into traits unique to each sample.

A memory adjustment module prunes key slots and expands capacity only slightly for each new task. Orthogonal regularization keeps preserved and newly learned components geometrically separate, limiting interference and forgetting. Against fourteen leading methods on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny-ImageNet, the system finished ahead, and its learned features came closest to an upper-bound reference.
arxiv-2511-09971:
Peter Røysland Aarnes and Vinay Setty probe whether language models can judge the truth of claims involving numbers. Models do well on knowledge-heavy fact checking, yet numerical reasoning is a known weak spot. The authors evaluate leading systems on veracity prediction for numerical claims paired with evidence, applying controlled perturbations, including probes that flip labels, to see how fragile the judgments are.

Even top proprietary systems lost accuracy heavily under some perturbations, with drops reaching about sixty-two percent, and no model stayed robust everywhere. Longer context generally hurt accuracy, although enriching that context with perturbed demonstrations helped most models recover substantially. The findings frame numerical fact checking as an open robustness problem for current models.
arxiv-2511-10271:
Xin Sun, Daniel Ståhl, Kristian Sandahl, and Christoph Kessler examine the quality of code that large language models generate, beyond whether it merely works. Guided by the ISO quality model, they combine a review of 109 papers, two industry workshops, and an empirical study in which three models patched real software issues. The empirical focus fell on security, maintainability, and performance efficiency, the attributes both sources flagged as critical.

Research attention concentrates on those same attributes while neglecting others, they find, whereas practitioners prize maintainability and readability and fear faster technical debt. Prompt-based attempts to optimize quality traits proved unstable in practice. The authors call the mismatch between academic focus, industry priorities, and model behavior a case for built-in quality assurance.
arxiv-2511-10571:
Reginald Zhiyan Chen, Heng-Sheng Chang, and Prashant G. Mehta introduce Belief Net, a framework for learning hidden Markov models by turning the forward filter into a structured neural network. Hidden Markov models are fundamental for sequential data, but the classic Baum-Welch algorithm is slow and gets stuck in local optima, while spectral methods can output invalid probabilities.

In Belief Net, the learnable weights are exactly the logarithms of the model's initial distribution, transition matrix, and emission matrix, so the network stays fully interpretable. Training runs end to end with gradient descent on next-observation prediction. On synthetic data, the method converges faster than Baum-Welch and recovers parameters in settings where spectral methods fail, and the authors also compare it with transformer models on real language data.
arxiv-2511-10971:
Anzhe Cheng, Shukai Duan, and their colleagues present ERMoE, a sparse model design that sends each input to only a few expert parts. In older designs the router that picks experts can clash with how each expert works inside, which wastes experts and slows training. Extra balancing losses help, but they can blur what each expert is good at.

ERMoE rebuilds each expert in a learned set of axes and scores matches by how well the input lines up with those axes. Routing then follows content, stays steadier, and needs no balancing loss. Tests on image sorting and image-text search gave top scores with more even expert loads.
arxiv-2511-11071:
Ziyi Li, Qingyu Mao, and their colleagues present Online-RepNeRV, a method that stores video as the weights of a small neural network. Such neural video storage can shrink files and speed delivery, but richer network designs often cost more to run and fit poorly into other tools. Model size also caps how much detail the stored video can hold.

Their design trains with many parallel paths to boost capacity, then merges those paths into a single path once training ends. Extra cost therefore stays in the encoding stage, while playback stays fast. Broad tests show the approach lifts quality without the usual overhead, which makes neural video storage more practical.
arxiv-2511-11471:
Samuel Tomlinson and Demetrios Papageorgiou model steady laminar boundary layers, the thin sheets of slowed fluid that hug a surface, over small-scale textured surfaces. The texture is far thinner than the boundary layer, yet it changes the flow through an effective slip length at the wall. Matched asymptotic expansions split the flow into outer, boundary-layer, and inner regions to make the problem tractable.

The inner solution's far field yields a slip condition for the boundary layer, with a closed solution for small slip and a numerical scheme for any slip. Applied to superhydrophobic surfaces and riblets, the frame shows how slip alters velocity, wall shear, and layer thickness, plus the stability of the flow.
arxiv-2511-11571:
Guangxuan Xiao, Junxian Guo, Kasra Mazaheri, and Song Han study Mixture of Block Attention. This design lets language models read long texts at low cost. The model attends to just a few blocks of stored keys and values. The idea is promising. But why it works, and how to run it fast, were both unclear.

A statistical model shows the key skill is the router's. The router must tell useful blocks from useless ones. A signal-to-noise ratio ties that skill to design choices. Guided by the analysis, the team improves the method. They also supply a fast GPU version. Long-context models stand to gain speed with no loss in quality.
arxiv-2511-12071:
Rosario Napoli and four co-authors ask whether graph embeddings miss hidden knowledge in sparse data. Embeddings turn a knowledge graph into vectors for tasks such as classifying nodes or predicting links. Because they come only from stated links and features, key implied facts can be left out.

Their pipeline adds a knowledge completion step before embeddings are made. It infers hidden links for transitive relations, using decay-based rules that reshape the graph itself. Tests with GraphSAGE and Node2Vec, in a case study on COVID-19 spread, show the embedding space changes a great deal. Completion, they conclude, is a core step, not a minor extra.
arxiv-2511-12271:
Zhiyu An and Wan Du tackle moral decision making by language model agents, which increasingly shape human choices. Past work mostly judged such decisions rather than steering them. The hard case is new scenarios unlike training data, where an agent must still apply a moral framework in a consistent way.

The team builds Moral-Reason-QA, a dataset of high-ambiguity moral cases with reasoning traces written for utilitarian, deontological and virtue ethics frameworks. Their learning method rewards both the final decision and the framework-specific reasoning behind it. Tests on unseen scenarios show clear gains in alignment scores for at least the utilitarian and deontological frameworks.
arxiv-2511-12371:
Yiqing Shen and three co-authors define a harder version of text-to-video search, where the query does not name what to find directly. Standard retrieval works when the wanted content is described in plain terms, but implicit queries need reasoning to decide which videos fit. The system must also point to the objects that satisfy the query.

Their approach first turns each video into a digital twin, a structured scene description built by specialist vision models. A query is split into parts and matched against those descriptions to find candidates. A large language model then reasons over the twins for the final ranking, avoiding the loss that comes from compressing long video into visual tokens.
arxiv-2511-12471:
Youming Chen and Zhaoqiang Liu present Diff-OneBit, a diffusion-model method for recovering a signal from measurements kept at just one bit each. One-bit quantization is cheap for hardware and storage, and appears in compressed sensing and logistic models. Recovery is hard because the link between signal and bits can be non-smooth or have no explicit form.

The authors replace that link with a smooth surrogate likelihood, so gradient steps become possible. The surrogate sits in a plug-and-play loop where any pretrained diffusion model acts as a denoiser, keeping data fit and prior separate. Tests on three large image datasets report high-fidelity reconstructions that beat the best prior methods.
arxiv-2511-12571:
Bikramarka S Choudhury, Md Khalid Hossain and Farook Rahaman construct a new class of traversable wormholes. Their shape comes from the geometry of a catenoid. A catenoid is the minimal surface formed by a soap film between two rings. Their spacetime keeps exact spherical symmetry. Starting from the metric, they derive its curvature properties step by step.

From the curvature they compute the Einstein and stress-energy tensors, finding the wormhole is held up by an anisotropic fluid. Checking the energy conditions shows exotic matter is required, as in most traversable designs, and sets the limits on physical viability. Further analysis covers whether the wormhole can be crossed, how it would bend light, and its stability, and shows the structure has bounded spatial extent.
arxiv-2511-12671:
Tushar Anand, Advik Sinha, and Abhijit Das present DensePercept-NCSSD, a vision model that estimates optical flow and depth-like disparity maps in real time. Optical flow tracks how pixels move between frames, and disparity infers depth from paired images; both are basic tools for robots and vehicles that must sense a three-dimensional world. Their model fuses the two input images inside a non-causal state space block, a Mamba-style design adapted for dense image tasks.

The authors report that the model lowers inference time while keeping accuracy high and graphics memory use low. Tests and validation in a real-life scenario back the claim that one model can serve both flow and disparity work. For builders of real-time perception systems, the appeal is a single fast model that does not need heavy hardware to keep up with a moving scene.
arxiv-2511-12771:
Anna Wienhard surveys a new notion of positivity in real semisimple Lie groups, written for the proceedings of a major mathematics congress. Positivity generalizes two older ideas at once: total positivity in split real Lie groups, and positive semigroups in Hermitian Lie groups of tube type. The article explains how positivity connects to higher Teichmüller spaces, then describes the theory and its open questions.

The second half takes a non-commutative turn. For Hermitian Lie groups of tube type, positivity suggests viewing their geometry through non-commutative algebra, and Wienhard explains how that perspective is built. It leads to applications such as non-commutative versions of Markov numbers, a classical topic in number theory. As a survey, the piece maps a young field for other mathematicians: definitions, links, results, and the problems its founder considers most promising.
arxiv-2511-13071:
Michal Levin and Itzik Klein calibrate cheap accelerometers without leveling them. Low-cost motion sensors in phones, robots, and navigation gear suffer bias errors, and standard calibration needs the sensor held level or rotated through known orientations, which is slow in the field. Their learning-based method estimates the bias while the device sits still, with no knowledge of its orientation and no rotation steps at all. A neural network learns the correction directly from stationary data.

Validation used a dataset of over thirteen hours recorded from six accelerometers. The method's errors came out more than half lower than traditional techniques, consistently across the devices. The authors present it as a fast, practical, scalable fix for rapid field deployment. Better bias estimates mean more reliable position and motion sensing from inexpensive hardware, which matters for the many scientific and industrial settings that cannot afford precision instruments or careful bench calibration.
arxiv-2511-13171:
Niccolò Paglierani and four co-authors turn a drone into a passive listener that locates phones on a 5G network. Their UAV does not serve the network or relay traffic; it simply flies, synchronizes to standard uplink sounding reference signals. It identifies and localizes multiple user devices from those transmissions alone. Narrowband signals of one point four megahertz keep device power and complexity low while allowing many devices to share resources.

The onboard chain achieves reliable synchronization and multi-device identification even when devices share the same resources, and positions are estimated from measurements gathered along the flight path. Simulations and a full-scale field campaign gave localization errors under eight meters in urban settings and under three meters in rural ones.
arxiv-2511-13771:
Shaowei Guan and 4 co-authors present ExplainableGuard, a defense for language models that explains each protective action it takes. Adversarial text attacks nudge model output in harmful directions, and most defenses silently rewrite or block input, leaving users unsure what happened. Their guard uses the chain-of-thought skill of a reasoning model as the defense engine itself.

Tailored prompts steer the model through character, word, structural, and semantic checks, then produce a cleaned output with a readable justification. Early tests on standard language benchmarks showed promising protection. Human raters judged the explanations clearer and more actionable than stripped-down variants, and gave the system a strong deployability-trust rating for real use.
arxiv-2511-14171:
Denis Bodrov and 29 co-authors present a track finder for the Belle II particle physics experiment that hunts kinks. A kink appears when a charged particle decays or scatters inside the detector, suddenly changing direction, and the standard tracking algorithm mostly misses these broken paths. The Kink Finder was built specifically for that signature.

Benchmark studies show reconstruction efficiency near forty percent, against about eleven percent for the standard algorithm. The new finder also sharpens the measured parameters of the secondary track, cuts down cloned duplicate tracks, and reduces misidentification between kaons and pions. Better kink recovery opens physics channels that depend on in-flight decays.
arxiv-2511-14271:
Weimin Bai, Yubo Li, Weijian Luo, and four co-authors let a vision-language model judge 3D generations while they are being made. Text-to-3D systems still miss fine prompt details and botch spatial relations, assembling parts in impossible ways. Their framework, VLM3D, repurposes the big model as a differentiable critic of both meaning and geometry.

The critic signal comes from the model's yes-or-no log-odds, scored along semantic and spatial axes. Plugged into optimization-based pipelines as a reward, it beat existing methods on standard benchmarks. Used as test-time guidance for feed-forward generators, it steered sampling to correct severe spatial errors, showing one signal can serve both paradigms.
arxiv-2511-14471:
Hanyu Cheng, Liangqi Cheng, and Xiwen Bai model fleet choices for tramp shipping under new carbon rules. Tramp ships take cargo where demand appears, so firms face shifting fuel prices, freight rates, and demand. A new international carbon intensity rule adds a further limit on deployment. The authors build a two stage stochastic model for long term planning.

The model jointly sets routes, cargo loads, and ship speed under uncertainty. A fast heuristic finds solutions close to optimal for real use. Their analysis finds a paradox where the current rule can raise total emissions and cut profit. Planning for uncertainty also closes much of the gap to perfect foresight.
arxiv-2511-14571:
Partha Kumar Paul, Sujit Kumar Sahoo, and Narendra Sahu study singlet-doublet Majorana dark matter and the role of conversion driven processes. The model mixes a singlet fermion with a doublet, set by a mass splitting and a mixing angle. Earlier work assumed Dirac dark matter and found a limited allowed range. The nature of dark matter is still unknown.

Assuming Majorana dark matter widens the space that matches the observed relic density. Direct detection limits can also be satisfied over that larger range. Masses up to much higher values become viable. The authors map the new ranges in detail. Their results guide future searches for this dark matter candidate.
arxiv-2511-14671:
Kristi Topollai and four co-authors present a search augmented approach to streamline industrial contract management. Reviewing clauses that set rights and duties is slow, and proposed revisions can be problematic. Labeled data are scarce and legacy contracts are largely unstructured. Their modular system joins several language model steps into one pipeline.

Lab made data creation and semantic clause search feed an acceptability classifier. Reward based alignment then helps flag bad revisions and draft better alternatives. Built with an industry partner, the system tops eighty percent accuracy on both flagging and improving revisions. Performance holds under real low resource conditions. The work offers a practical path to faster, safer contract review.
arxiv-2511-14871:
Saeed Shaebani studies a relaxed kind of graph coloring in which the color classes need not follow the usual rules. In a fair and tolerant coloring, each vertex must see the same share of neighbors in its own color and in every other color. The largest number of colors for which this is possible is called the FAT chromatic number.

Shaebani takes up a question left open by the researchers who introduced the idea, who asked whether a bound links this number to the degrees of the vertices. The paper gives conditions under which such colorings exist and studies how the number behaves. It adds a new tool for splitting networks into balanced groups.
arxiv-2511-15071:
Ashwin Karthikeyan, Hengyu Liu, and two co-authors present the first practical zero-knowledge proofs for statements in the complexity class PSPACE. A zero-knowledge proof convinces a checker that a claim is true while revealing nothing else. Efficient versions existed only for the smaller class NP, even though theory allows them for all of PSPACE, which covers far harder claims.

The team makes the leap by proving quantified Boolean formula evaluations, the canonical PSPACE-complete task, inside zero knowledge. They encode resolution-style proofs of those evaluations so that checking becomes cheap arithmetic. On a standard benchmark, most evaluations and winning strategies are verified within a hundred seconds, which brings a long-theoretical tool into practical reach.
arxiv-2511-15371:
Eddie Conti, Álvaro Parafita, and Axel Brando rank the features a model relies on by comparing the counterfactual worlds where it says yes and no. Feature importance scores explain single predictions, but the field lacks ground truth to grade the graders. Their method, CID, generates sets of positive and negative counterfactual examples around a case, changed just enough to flip the model's verdict.

Density models fitted to those two counterfactual clouds are then compared feature by feature with a dissimilarity measure built to satisfy strict metric properties. Features whose counterfactual clouds differ most are the ones the decision truly turns on. Benchmarks against established local explainers test whether the principled construction also wins in practice.
arxiv-2511-15671:
Mihir Rao frames scientific discovery as a thermodynamic process, where an agent spends physical work to gain information about its surroundings under a fixed work budget. Automation of science raises a practical question: how much can be learned per unit of work spent? Rao builds on established results about the thermodynamics of computing, which link information handling to energy costs.

He derives bounds, for a finite budget, on information gain across rounds of sequential Bayesian learning, where beliefs update step by step as data arrive. A metric for information-work efficiency is proposed. He also compares learning in one undivided system with federated learning split across parts, under matched budgets, offering guidance for scientific automation efforts.
arxiv-2511-15771:
Yue Li, Qing Xu, and nine co-authors adapt a powerful general image segmentation model for ultrasound scans. Segmentation outlines structures in an image, and the Segment Anything Model 2 does this well on natural photos but poorly on ultrasound, whose grainy physics differ sharply. Adapting it must stay light on parameters and must run in clinics with limited computing power.

Their UniUltra system adds a context-edge adapter that sharpens fine detail across ultrasound types while tuning only a small fraction of parameters. A distillation step then transfers knowledge into a tiny encoder, cutting the final model size by over ninety percent against the original. Extensive experiments show it beats leading methods and generalizes well across modalities.
arxiv-2511-15871:
Özgür Ökcü derives the Friedmann equations, the core laws of cosmic expansion, from a changed law of energy sharing at the horizon. The work merges horizon thermodynamics with a generalized uncertainty principle. That principle sets a smallest length that can be measured, and alters how energy is shared among degrees of freedom. Verlinde entropic gravity, where gravity emerges from entropy, supplies the frame.

The new laws give a highest energy density at the start of the universe and a highest expansion rate. Both point to a start with no singularity. A curvature check backs that up. A negative value of the new parameter fits the early acceleration best. The setup also offers a route to the cosmic excess of matter over antimatter.
arxiv-2511-15971:
