Donny Dwiputra, Mir Faizal, Francesco Marino, and Freddy P. Zen study how work is distributed when a gapless quantum system is suddenly or slowly changed by a quench. Work statistics describe the spread of energy costs over many repetitions, summarized by cumulants, which capture mean, width, and shape. For systems with no energy gap, the authors ask whether that spread follows universal scaling laws.

Cumulants scale as separate power laws in fast and slow quench regimes, echoing the Kibble-Zurek mechanism for defect formation in phase transitions. A spin chain tuned to its critical state, described as a Tomonaga-Luttinger liquid, confirms the analytic scaling against exact numerics. Finite systems show oscillations that fade in the large-system limit, aiding quantum computing thermodynamics.
arxiv-2511-16371:
V. Blavatska, Ja. Ilnytskyi, and E. Lähderanta model adsorption on branched polymer structures with star and comb topologies for wastewater cleaning. Waste capture by flocculation and heavy metal capture by chelation both act like adsorption onto polymers at large scales. Branched adsorbents beat linear ones in lab tests, so shape stats of branched forms matter. Lattice polymer models capture those stats with ease.

Star polymers have a point like core, while comb polymers have a 1D rigid core. Branch number and length are varied across both families. Adsorbing speed follows from how conformations expose binding capacity. Comparing the two simplest branched architectures isolates topology effects. Results guide design of polymer adsorbents where architecture, not just chemistry, controls cleaning results.
arxiv-2511-16471:
Clemens Pollak, Kersten Diers, Santiago Estrada, David Kügler, and Martin Reuter present FastSurfer-CC, an automated pipeline for measuring the corpus callosum, the brain's largest bridge between hemispheres, from MRI scans. The structure is a key marker in aging and disease research, yet few public tools analyze it in full.

The pipeline finds the mid-sagittal slice, segments the corpus callosum and fornix, locates the anterior and posterior commissures to standardize head position. It produces thickness profiles, subdivisions, and eight shape metrics. It beat existing tools on each task. Applied to Huntington's disease, it revealed clear differences between patients and healthy controls that the current best tool missed, showing the value of a thorough automated measurement.
arxiv-2511-16571:
Md. Tawfique Ihsan and four co-authors attack severe class imbalance in tabular data, where the rare class is often the one that matters. They generate extra minority examples with latent-space diffusion driven by gradient-boosted trees. Standard generative oversamplers wrestle with tabular data's mixed types, training instability, and privacy risks.

Their family of methods runs conditional flow matching in a compact latent space, with trees as the vector-field learner, then decodes back to the original features. Three variants use principal component, learned, and attention-based embeddings. Across eleven datasets from health care, finance, and manufacturing, the attention variant achieved the best average minority recall with competitive precision and privacy scores. The simpler variants generated data much faster at similar quality.
arxiv-2511-16771:
Le-Chris Wang and six co-authors reanalyze the JWST transmission spectrum of WASP-96 b, a hot Saturn, and overturn an early claim about its skies. The first analysis saw a steep blue slope hinting at high-altitude haze; the new work finds no such slope and instead a clear atmosphere above a low gray cloud deck.

Combining the JWST data with VLT, Hubble, and Spitzer spectra gives coverage from the near ultraviolet to five microns. Abundances for water, potassium, and sodium are constrained, and the carbon-to-oxygen ratio and metallicity sit tentatively below the star's values. Interior models then imply a massive core of roughly forty Earth masses, suggesting the planet formed beyond the water ice line, migrated inward, and gathered its atmosphere inside the carbon soot line. A broadened sodium feature hints the two limbs of the planet differ.
arxiv-2511-16871:
Marshall Rosenhoover and Huaming Zhang introduce Graph Linear Transformations, a way for graph neural networks to gather information from distant nodes in one step instead of stacking message-passing layers. Standard networks only mix direct neighbors per layer, so reaching far across the graph means going deep, with the usual training headaches.

The transformation is a single linear operator derived from the graph, computed by interpreting the graph as a walk-summable Gaussian graphical model and running Gaussian belief propagation. Each node then aggregates direct and indirect neighbors without enumerating multi-hop paths. Different precision matrix constructions give interpretable propagation biases, from selective edge-level mixing to uniform smoothing. On homophilic and heterophilic benchmarks the approach matched or beat local message-passing networks and dynamic neighborhood aggregation models.
arxiv-2511-17071:
Jan-Ole Koslik and five co-authors improve a tool ecologists use to read animal movement data: the hidden Markov model. These models sort a time series into hidden behavioral states, but the analyst must guess a probability curve for each state, and a wrong guess distorts the results. Flexible spline methods avoid the guess yet can produce wiggly, two-peaked curves that make little biological sense.

The team's method forces each estimated curve to have a single peak, by constraining the spline pieces that build it. Simulations and a case study of narwhal dive records show steadier estimates and better performance than the unconstrained approach. The result is a middle path for telemetry studies: nearly as flexible as the free-form method, but with results researchers can interpret with confidence.
arxiv-2511-17271:
Sebastian Böhm and three co-authors cut the cost of performance testing for configurable software. Systems with many options need testing across configurations, but remeasuring everything after each change is expensive, while sampling configurations can miss regressions that hit only a few of them. Their tool, ConfFLARE, takes a different route: it estimates whether a change can affect performance by tracing data flow into performance-relevant code, and identifies which features participate in those interactions.

Profiling then focuses on the configurations those features touch. On synthetic and real-world systems, ConfFLARE caught performance regressions in almost every case, found the relevant features nearly always, and cut the configurations to test by roughly three quarters or more. The savings amount to hours of testing time per change, without giving up completeness where it matters.
arxiv-2511-17571:
Yves Matanga, Yanxia Sun, and Zenghui Wang improve a family of optimization algorithms that hunt many peaks at once. Multi-swarm particle methods split a population into niche swarms, each exploiting a promising region, and clustering-based versions are among the most effective. Their weakness is resolution: distance-based clusters usually probe only one peak each, so nearby peaks get lost. The authors add two enhancements to fix that.

First, a preliminary local search scouts the initial particles so every region is checked before collaboration begins. Second, a new clustering step analyzes concavity to detect several sub-niches hiding inside a single cluster. The resulting algorithm, tested on the standard CEC2013 niching benchmark suite against three rival methods from the same family, found a better share of the peaks on almost every test function. The work matters wherever many good solutions are wanted, not just one.
arxiv-2511-18071:
Rasmus Sorensen, Margherita Guido, Allan Peter Engsig-Karup, and Daniel Kressner speed up simulations of nonlinear water waves. Each time step requires solving a large Poisson problem to keep the flow volume preserving. Iterative solvers dominate the cost, and a better starting guess can cut their work substantially.

They extend a subspace acceleration method to use the complete history of past solutions, weighted so recent ones count more, removing repeated sketching steps. Inside a high order finite difference solver, the method sharply reduces iteration counts on two wave benchmarks, including flow over a submerged bar, without losing accuracy. The technique works with other discretizations too.
arxiv-2511-18971:
Tommaso Ruggeri, Ferdinand Thein, and Qinghua Xiao prove existence and uniqueness for self similar, radially symmetric flows of a relativistic gas. The gas laws come from relativistic kinetic theory, in the Synge energy form for single atom gases and its extension to two atom gases. The flows include the spherical piston problem, a classic test where a piston drives a shock.

Their solutions hold for all values of the relativistic parameter, from the classical limit to the ultra relativistic regime. Key traits of the Synge energy are shown along the way: a strict bend sign in its pressure response and a monotone link between wave speed and the parameter. Classical self similar theory thus gains a full relativistic form.
arxiv-2511-19371:
Bibhuti Kumar Jha, Lisa A Upton, Greg Kopp, and Odele Coddington reconstruct the Sun's surface magnetism across more than two centuries. Direct magnetic maps cover only recent decades, yet long records are needed to study solar cycles, predict future activity, and rebuild how the Sun's brightness has varied. Their approach generates synthetic active regions, the magnetic patches tied to sunspots, for solar cycles one through twenty-four, spanning 1755 to 2020, driven solely by the historical sunspot number record.

Those synthetic regions feed a flux transport model that simulates new regions emerging and then being carried across the surface by solar flows, producing full-Sun magnetic maps. Earlier reconstructions are extended and unified by the catalogue. The result gives solar physicists a consistent magnetic history where before there were mostly spots and gaps.
arxiv-2511-19571:
Jerrold Franklin challenges a textbook claim about point charges: that an electron carries infinite electromagnetic self-energy. Many standard texts present that result, the author notes, while admitting they do not really understand it. Franklin argues the conclusion is wrong.

The paper contends that electrons must instead be point particles with no electromagnetic self-energy at all. The argument is offered as a correction to how classical electromagnetism treats the energy a charge's own field would assign to it. Readers get a short, pointed dispute with a long-standing piece of textbook doctrine, defended from the author's reading of the theory.
arxiv-2511-19671:
Rishab Sharma, Iman Saberi, Elham Alipour, Jie JW Wu, and Fatemeh Fard present FISCAL, a framework for teaching small models to check financial claims. Financial uses of language models demand factual reliability and efficiency, yet current systems invent details and lean on huge models. FISCAL generates synthetic claim and document pairs tailored to finance, and that generated data set trains a lightweight verifier specialised in numerical financial claims. The kind where a wrong figure is the whole error.

The small verifier beats its own baseline, outperforms GPT-3. 5 Turbo and open models of similar size, and approaches the accuracy of systems twenty times larger. On two external financial fact-checking data sets it rivals flagship commercial models while beating others. The lesson is that domain-shaped synthetic data can substitute for raw scale in verification work.
arxiv-2511-20071:
Canevari, Cherednichenko, and Zarnescu chase a ghost term that appears when equations meet tiny holes. Their 2025 paper studies Laplace's equation in periodically perforated domains. The material is pierced by small holes. Robin conditions, a mix of value and flux rules, govern each hole's edge. The Robin coefficient scales inversely with total hole surface.

In one critical scaling regime, something extra survives homogenization. The smoothed limit equation gains a zero-order term. That term depends nonlinearly on the Robin coefficient. It is built from a Steklov-type spectral problem. There the eigenvalue appears in both equation and boundary rules. As the Robin parameter shrinks to zero, the term vanishes. As it grows without bound, a classical term returns. That limit matches the capacitary strange term of Dirichlet problems. Cioranescu and Murat coined strange term for such effects. The paper traces exactly where this one comes from.
arxiv-2511-20271:
Devyver, Dupaigne, and Thizy sharpen a Sobolev inequality on a weighted hyperbolic space. Their 2025 paper extends Caffarelli-Kohn-Nirenberg theory to curved settings. Sobolev inequalities bound function size by gradient energy. Sharp constants mark the best possible bounds. On hyperbolic space the classical version gains a correction term.

Conformal invariance links Euclidean and hyperbolic forms. For plain Sobolev, sharpness holds in dimension four and up. Dimension three breaks sharpness in the classical story. The weighted CKN setting has an effective dimension instead. Call that effective dimension n in their notation. Improvement becomes possible when n lies between three and four. Below and above that window the picture changes. Extremal bubble functions drive the subtlety here. Aubin-Talenti bubbles are not compactly supported on the ball. Spectral bottoms of the Laplacian enter the constants. Weighted inequalities inherit the same dimensional drama. Analysis on curved spaces gains a precise boundary case.
arxiv-2511-20371:
Mukherjee, Sen, and Gangopadhyay ask what fast motion does to quantum coherence. Two particles share an entangled state here. A moving observer sees that state transformed.

Generalized Gaussian wave packets model the two particles. Two scenarios structure the whole analysis. One particle is boosted while its partner rests. Then both particles ride different boosted frames. Two coherence measures quantify what remains. The l1-norm and Frobenius-norm measures agree qualitatively. Coherence decays as packets grow wider. Larger boost speeds erode it further as well. Boosting both particles degrades coherence the most. Mass, width, and entanglement angle all enter the formulas. Results hold across the generalized packet family. Relativistic motion acts as a coherence tax. Space-based quantum links must budget for it. The framework extends their earlier single-particle study.
arxiv-2511-20571:
Im, An, Kim, Lim, and Jeong watch water droplets freeze through X-ray eyes. Their 2025 paper studies sessile droplets, drops sitting on a cold surface. A freezing drop grows a sharp point at its top. Water expands as it turns to ice, forcing that tip. The tip angle was thought to be universal across conditions.

In situ X-ray imaging shows the angle shifts with surface temperature. Trapped bubbles during freezing cause the drift from the classic value. Three-dimensional tomography measured the ice-water density ratio directly. Bubbles lower the effective ratio below the pure value. Feeding that ratio into the theory reconciles the angles. A bubble-free drop frozen in vacuum showed the classic angle again. The team also measured three-phase boundary angles during freezing. Those readings validate the geometric theory of tip formation. High-resolution X-ray imaging proves a sharp tool for ice research.
arxiv-2511-20671:
Zhaoxin Chang and colleagues present in 2025 WiRainbow, a Wi-Fi sensing system that tells which direction a target lies in while using only one antenna. Wi-Fi sensing reads distortions in radio signals to detect presence or movement without any worn device. Finding direction normally takes an array of antennas, which costs more. WiRainbow instead uses a frequency-scanning antenna, which naturally sends different subcarriers, the slices of a Wi-Fi channel, toward different angles.

The team's coupled-resonator antenna widens the view sharply, reaching a 60-degree field of view in the 5 GHz band. Earlier scanning antennas managed only about 22 degrees there. A processing step based on sensing signal-to-noise ratio, how clearly the target stands out from background echoes, then pins down direction even in rooms full of reflections. Prototype tests and real-world case studies showed accurate, robust direction estimates.
arxiv-2511-20771:
Sebastian Bruchhold and Mathias Weller speed up in 2025 a hard question in evolutionary biology: does a phylogenetic network contain a given tree? Networks generalise trees by allowing reticulations, the merges caused by hybridisation and horizontal gene transfer. Tree Containment is NP-hard, and its firm yes-or-no answers break on poorly supported branches, producing false negatives.

The soft version, introduced by Bentert, Malík, and Weller in 2018, tolerates uncertainty by letting high-degree vertices resolve into binary trees. Bruchhold and Weller's algorithm exploits scanwidth, a measure of how tree-like a network's extension is, introduced by Berry, Scornavacca, and Weller in 2020. Real networks tend to have low scanwidth. Their running time is exponential only in the tree's out-degree times a scanwidth-based parameter, and merely polynomial in the input size otherwise, improving on treewidth-based approaches whose exponent grows quadratically. The work comes from Bruchhold's master's thesis.
arxiv-2511-20971:
Marwa Ennaceur settles in 2025 when numerical approximations preserve two delicate spectral invariants of an operator: ascent and descent, the steps at which kernel and range chains stabilise. A transport example shows the danger. The continuous operator has ascent 1, but a central-difference grid gives ascent infinity at every mesh size, while its eigenvalues misleadingly cluster near zero. An upwind scheme keeps ascent 1 and behaves.

Ennaceur proves stability holds exactly when a computable test value, the discrete reduced minimum modulus, stays positive as the mesh refines. The condition is both necessary and sufficient under strong resolvent convergence, the right notion for non-selfadjoint, singular problems. B-Fredholm theory extends the result to powers of the operator, and a Volterra-type example shows the closed-range hypothesis cannot be dropped. Stabilised schemes such as SUPG keep the test value positive even in convection-dominated regimes, which the theory now explains.
arxiv-2511-21171:
Number theorists Lennart Gehrmann, Xavier Guitart, and Marc Masdeu present a 2025 study of Bianchi rigid meromorphic cocycles. These are special objects from p-adic analysis, where numbers are measured by divisibility by a prime. Darmon, Gehrmann, and Lipnowski introduced the cocycles as a wider analogue of classical special values. Such values often encode deep arithmetic facts about number fields, the systems built by adding roots of equations.

Gehrmann and his coauthors build the tools needed to actually compute these cocycles at a class of points called big ATR points. Their calculations give the first numerical check of a standing conjecture. The values are algebraic, meaning each one solves a polynomial equation with whole-number coefficients. The values also behave much like values of Borcherds products on Hilbert modular surfaces at big CM points, a parallel the authors flag for further study.
arxiv-2511-21271:
Xinyan Xie and seven coauthors redesign indoor lighting so the same lamps sense people, carry data, and stay comfortable to sit under, in 2025. Visible light communication uses LED light to transmit information, a candidate technology for sixth-generation networks. Prior work chased data rates and sensing accuracy while burning power and ignoring visual comfort, so the team made energy saving a primary goal of their integrated framework.

Xie and her coauthors split the receiving plane into an activity area and a calmer surround, then locate the user with non-line-of-sight sensing, which reads reflected light. The user's position flips the system's goal: inside the activity area it minimizes transmit power while guaranteeing communication and lighting quality, and outside it evens out signal strength. Simulations delivered about 54 percent energy savings over a non-adaptive system and roughly 58 percent better signal uniformity, with localization accurate to about 7 centimeters.
arxiv-2511-21571:
Freddie Illingworth, Arjun Ranganathan, and Ella Williams settle two questions about ordered graphs in a 2025 combinatorics paper whose title promises all and nothing. In an ordered graph, vertices come in a fixed sequence. The relative Turán density of a pattern is the largest fraction of edges one can always keep while deleting its occurrences. The ordered theory, begun recently, proved subtler than the classical one.

The 'all' result is a single family of host graphs that is simultaneously optimal for every ordered pattern, a universal worst case. The 'nothing' result characterizes exactly which patterns have zero relative density: precisely those containing no monotone path of length two, the simplest increasing two-step walk. Their example family makes the contrast vivid: relative densities shrink to zero while ordinary Turán densities climb toward one. Order can make a pattern trivially avoidable and nearly unavoidable at once.
arxiv-2511-21671:
Nicholas Davidson, Jonathan Kujawa, and Robert Muth build diagrammatic categories that encode superalgebra representation theory, in 2025. Webs draw algebraic structures as string diagrams, turning products into pictures. Working over a characteristic-zero domain, the authors define an affine web supercategory attached to any locally unital Frobenius superalgebra. It extends their earlier finite web category.

The new category wears three faces: an affinization of the finite webs, a thickened version of the degenerate affine wreath product algebras, and a Frobenius deformation of earlier affine webs. The team constructs an asymptotically faithful family of functors from it into endofunctors of modules over general linear Lie superalgebras, for every rank. Those functors yield a basis of morphism spaces made of decorated double coset diagrams, the diagrammatic analogue of a basis theorem. A cyclotomic quotient, cut down by a chosen datum, gets matching basis results.
arxiv-2511-21971:
Jaffarove and colleagues use Parker Solar Probe data to ask where the solar wind's quiet stretches originate. In March 2025 the probe skimmed about 9.8 solar radii from the Sun and caught a fast wind stream almost pristine, before expansion and collisions with other streams could stir it. Some intervals in the stream show unusually low magnetic variability, marked by small changes in the radial field. The team traced those intervals back to their source regions on the Sun's surface.

Using magnetic connectivity models, they estimated each parcel's solar footpoint and its source variability. About half of the low-variability periods were associated with low source variability. Quiet periods sitting between switchback patches, dramatic folds in the magnetic field, likewise showed statistically less source variability than the patches themselves. The pattern points to a solar origin for the calm stretches.
arxiv-2511-22171:
Li, Zhang, Quan, and colleagues generate CAD models the way language models write text. Boundary representation is the faces-edges-vertices format CAD depends on. It mixes continuous geometry with discrete topology in structures that change size from part to part, which pushed earlier generators into pipelines with errors. Their BrepGPT tokenizes everything through a Voronoi Half-Patch representation, which assigns each face region to its nearest boundary half-edge. The representation unifies geometry and topology into units a transformer can predict one token at a time.

Dual vector-quantized autoencoders compress vertex topology and half-patches into token sequences. A decoder-only transformer learns to generate them autoregressively. BrepGPT reports state-of-the-art unconditional B-rep generation, and the model handles conditional generation from category labels, point clouds, text, and images. It also handles autocompletion and interpolation between parts, suggesting autoregressive modeling suits CAD geometry better than expected.
arxiv-2511-22271:
Claudet, in his doctoral thesis, settles when exactly two quantum graph states hold the same entanglement. Graph states, workhorses of measurement-based quantum computing, are entangled states pictured by graphs, and two have the same entanglement when local operations convert one to the other. Restricting to local Clifford operations gives LC-equivalence, fully captured by a graph move called local complementation; but counterexamples killed the conjecture that the broader LU-equivalence, allowing all local unitaries, coincides with it.

The thesis introduces generalized, r-local complementation and proves it captures LU-equivalence exactly. The moves form an infinite strict hierarchy of equivalences between LC and LU, and the characterization yields a quasi-polynomial algorithm deciding LU-equivalence of two graph states. It also proves LU and LC coincide up to 19 qubits, up from 8, and studies universal graph states.
arxiv-2511-22371:
Khaitovich and Özgün build a logic of intention, formal rules for what an agent can be said to intend. Intentions obey simple principles like consistency, but must not be closed under logical consequence: you can intend a tooth filling while knowing it will hurt, without intending the pain. The authors argue a good logic must also avoid closure under equivalence, the weaker rule treating two statements with the same truth conditions as interchangeable.

Their system makes intention depend on the decision problem the agent faces, borrowing from inquisitive semantics, which tracks the questions at issue, and topic-sensitive accounts of mental states. They show the closest existing frameworks prove too much by validating some cases of closure under equivalence. The team gives a sound and strongly complete axiom set for the logic, meaning the rules prove exactly what the semantics makes true.
arxiv-2511-22471:
Huang and colleagues ask whether a big vision model can spot AI-generated images from unseen generators. Existing detectors tend to memorise the fingerprints of specific synthesis models and fail badly on new ones. Testing the frozen DINOv3 foundation model with no fine-tuning at all, the team finds it already works surprisingly well as a cross-generator detector, and analyses why across frequency, spatial, and token views.

The evidence points to global, low-frequency structure as the transferable cue: real and synthetic images differ in broad layout statistics, while the high-frequency details detectors usually chase are generator-specific. Building on this, their FGTS strategy ranks tokens by authenticity information and keeps only a small subset, followed by a lightweight linear probe. The resulting detector improved accuracy across all datasets without training the underlying model, and a frozen CLIP backbone alone reached 55.9 percent accuracy on unseen commercial generators.
arxiv-2511-22671:
Mondal and Sadhukhan listen for echoes from a wormhole. The geometry, built by Maldacena, Milekhin, and Popov, joins two near-extremal black hole mouths to a long throat, held open by fermions' quantum negative energy. They derive the effective potential for scalar waves and find, in the stretched tortoise coordinate, two sharp, widely separated barriers, a resonant cavity from the mouths' near-horizon geometry.

Simulating a scalar wave packet inside the throat, they find the late-time signal carries a distinct train of echoes, the packet bouncing between barriers and leaking out in pulses. The echoes depend strongly on angular momentum: higher modes face taller, more reflective barriers, so trapping is more efficient and echoes are stronger and narrower. The monopole mode, lacking a centrifugal barrier, produces essentially no echoes. Linking echo strength to angular momentum gives the wormhole a testable signature for gravitational wave observations.
arxiv-2512-00071:
Prime numbers follow patterns that are simple to state and hard to prove. Yung-Hua Chen studies correlations between primes separated by a fixed shift, in a 2025 study. The sequence involved has no multiplicative structure and no Euler product, which blocks many standard analytic tools.

Chen builds a framework based on Mellin-Laplace kernels to expose structural obstructions in these correlations. Work at this level is theoretical, aimed at showing what cannot happen as much as what can. It contributes to analytic number theory, where prime pair patterns remain among the deepest open questions. Such results clarify where analytic methods reach their natural edge and map terrain for later work.
arxiv-2512-00371:
In open-source games, players submit computer programs instead of choosing actions directly. Swadesh Sistla and Max Kleiman-Weiner evaluate large language models in that setting in 2025. Submitted programs are interpretable, transparent to other agents, and formally verifiable.

Programs also enable program equilibria, outcomes that exploit the transparency of code and are unreachable in ordinary game settings. Testing models as program-writers probes both their coding skill and their strategic reasoning. The setting offers a clean laboratory for studying how AI agents compete and cooperate when everyone can read everyone else's strategy. Open-source games are a public arena, so model strategies can be inspected by anyone. That openness is the feature the whole setting is built to exploit.
arxiv-2512-00471:
Quantum chaos is often measured by correlators that deliberately scramble the order of operations in time. Andrew Hunt studies out-of-time-order correlation functions in single-body systems in 2025. These correlators quantify how fast quantum information spreads and becomes inaccessible.

Maldacena and co-authors conjectured a universal, temperature-dependent bound on that scrambling rate. Single-body systems are the simplest arena in which to test such claims, free of many-body complications. Hunt's analysis helps clarify whether the bound reflects deep principles or artifacts of the complicated systems where it was first proposed. Single-body systems strip quantum chaos down to its simplest possible stage. If the bound fails there, its claimed universality needs rethinking.
arxiv-2512-00671:
Four physicists, J Altmann, L Bernardinis, P Skands, and V Zaccolo, tackle a puzzle from the Large Hadron Collider in 2025. When protons collide, the share of strange hadrons grows as more charged particles are made. A hadron is a particle built from quarks, and strange ones carry a strange quark.

The widely used Pythia event generator, with its default Monash tune, predicts no such growth. The authors test a possible fix called string closepacking. In that picture, overlapping strings from the collision form a background field, mostly along the beam line. Checking this idea may help event models match what detectors see.
arxiv-2512-00871:
Na Wang and five coauthors search for rhythmic flickers in blazars in a 2025 astronomy paper. Blazars are galaxies whose jets point almost straight at Earth, making them look bright and variable. A quasi-periodic oscillation is a rough rhythm in that flickering, which hints at regular motion near the galaxy's black hole.

Using data from the Zwicky Transient Facility, the team picked ten blazars as their sample. Four of them showed possible signs of such rhythmic modulation. The authors name each candidate and treat the signals as indications, not proof. Firmer rhythms, if confirmed, could clock the inner workings of blazar jets.
arxiv-2512-00971:
Yunfeng Lin and six coauthors present H-Zero in a 2025 robotics paper on humanoid walking. Humanoid robots need controllers that keep them stable and efficient as they move. Most existing controllers are built for one robot design, so each new body demands fresh tuning of rewards, physical parameters, and training settings.

H-Zero pretrains locomotion across humanoid bodies, learning shared walking skills that are not tied to one design. The authors show that this cross-humanoid pretraining enables few-shot transfer to new embodiments. A robot maker could adapt the controller to a fresh design with little extra training, speeding up development across product lines.
arxiv-2512-01271:
Pratik Chattopadhyay works on rules for very soft light in an expanding universe. In quantum theory, soft photons are light parts with very low energy. Known rules link them to how charged parts scatter. Past work dealt with heavy charged parts in de Sitter space, a model of fast growth.

The light-mass case was left unclear in that past work. Taking the mass to zero gave a muddy result. Chattopadhyay works out the fix for that case step by step. Clear rules for soft light help check that quantum sums in curved space stay sound.
arxiv-2512-01471:
Luis Reis, Mario Baldiotti, and Orfeu Bertolami study gas falling onto coupled black holes. Some black holes may gain mass from the cosmos itself as space expands. Dark fluids drive that expansion. The team asks how such a fluid falls onto those holes.

They focus on a fluid called generalized Chaplygin gas. To keep the fluid's global traits, they use the McVittie metric. That metric blends a black hole with an expanding cosmos. The study shows how inflow shifts with coupling. Results feed the debate on whether black holes can grow with the universe.
arxiv-2512-01671:
Aurelien Drezet and Bernard Nabet link Maxwell theory to the de Broglie-Bohm view in a tiny cavity. In an optical microcavity, a photon acts like a massive particle. Its energy law comes from Maxwell's equations. The Bohm view tracks a probability fluid for that particle.

The pair show the two conservation laws match in form. That formal match ties wave energy flow to Bohm trajectories. Such links help interpret quantum optics tests. They also clarify what Bohm paths mean for light in confined spaces. Two-dimensional cavities keep the match exact, giving a clean case where looser analogies in higher dimensions can be judged against truth.
arxiv-2512-01771:
Ahsan Raza Siyal and co-authors register medical images with learnable edge kernels. Registration aligns images from distinct scans, times, or subjects. Diagnosis and treatment plans rest on that alignment. Classic methods strain with contrast gaps, warps, and modality traits.

Their method learns edge kernels that guide the match. Edges stay more stable across modalities than raw brightness. The approach covers both rigid and non-rigid alignment. Steadier alignment helps doctors compare scans over a treatment course without hand fixes at each visit. Edge kernels are learned per task, so the same frame adapts to brain, lung, or joint scans without hand-set filter banks.
arxiv-2512-01871:
Stein spaces are a central setting in complex geometry, and mathematicians have long wanted an equally clean version in non-archimedean geometry, where distance works differently. Tom Biesbrouck's 2025 paper builds that version algebraically, starting from a new class of Banach algebras he calls Liu algebras.

He defines non-archimedean Stein algebras as inverse limits of these locally affinoid algebras, then shows the spaces match the algebras in a complete, functorial way through their Berkovich spectra. In doing so, the paper settles a conjecture posed by Michael Temkin. The result gives non-archimedean geometers a firm dictionary between spaces and their algebras.
arxiv-2512-02171:
The brightest objects in the universe, quasars, X-ray binaries, and gamma-ray bursts, pour out energy drawn from gravity or spin. Elisabete Dal Pino's 2025 paper reviews how such high-energy sources work when the central object has no event horizon, the point of no return that defines a black hole.

Converting gravitational or rotational energy into radiation, jets, and relativistic outflows is the engine in all these sources. If the central body is a horizonless compact object rather than a black hole, the extraction mechanisms and their signatures change. Understanding those differences gives observers a way to test what really sits at the heart of these cosmic powerhouses.
arxiv-2512-02371:
Tensor accelerators, the specialized circuits behind modern AI chips, are powerful but notoriously hard to program beyond matrix multiplication. Yihong Zhang and three co-authors present in 2025 a user-schedulable language that lets developers direct these accelerators at a wider range of workloads themselves.

Today most programmers must use vendor kernel libraries, which confine tensor hardware to traditional machine learning and scientific computing shapes. A schedulable language hands scheduling decisions to the user instead of the library. Opening tensor accelerators to general computation could reclaim a large and growing share of the world's computing capacity for new tasks.
arxiv-2512-02571:
Kobe Grobben, Phablo F. S. Moura, and Hande Yaman study approximation schemes for hard covering and packing problems. Such mixed integer programs include multidimensional knapsack, facility location, and supplier selection. Exact solutions grow too slow on large inputs, so near optimal answers with guarantees are prized.

The authors first study the vertices of the linked polytope, the shape that encodes the problem. They then split problems into knapsack cover cases with one continuous variable per dimension. Structure aware splitting is a classic route to schemes that run in reasonable time while staying provably close to optimal. The split turns one hard nut into many small ones, each of which a fast code can crack with care.
arxiv-2512-02971:
A. D. Lindsay, S. Rhebergen, and B. S. Southworth speed up fluid flow simulation at high Reynolds number. Their solver uses a hybridizable discontinuous Galerkin method on the linearized Navier-Stokes equations. Fast, turbulent like flows make such systems hard to solve iteratively without a good preconditioner.

Their preconditioner rests on an augmented Lagrangian form of the full discretization. Unlike standard grad div augmentation, theirs builds on divergence conformity. Better solvers shorten design cycles for aircraft, ships, and turbines, where high Reynolds flow decides performance and fuel use. Fast solves mean more shapes can be tried per day. More shapes tried is how a wing or a hull gets good in the end, not by one big guess.
arxiv-2512-03071:
Mixed data, with both numbers and labels, are hard to group. Loup-Noé Levy, Guillaume Guerard, Sonia Djebali, and Soufian Ben Amor offer a new tool in this 2025 work. Their method, called PretopoMD, rests on pretopology, a flexible way to define closeness.

The tool builds groups in layers without first shrinking the data down. It uses plain logic rules that users can set to fit their own needs. Users can also tune settings to shape the groups they get. Such control helps when data sets differ a lot from one field to the next. For data teams, the appeal lies in rules they can adjust without rebuilding the whole method from scratch each time.
arxiv-2512-03271:
Muslims pray toward the Kaaba in Mecca, a direction called the Qibla. Duaa Abdullah reviews ways to find that direction in this 2025 work. Muslim scholars and astronomers have worked on the problem for centuries with great care.

Old methods use tools like the astrolabe and compass. Newer methods use spherical trigonometry to compute the Qibla angle from any place on Earth. Abdullah compares astronomical and geometrical approaches. The study joins history of science with a live religious need for accurate prayer direction. Trigonometric methods give a precise azimuth for any site, once its coordinates are known.
arxiv-2512-03371:
Partial processes need a math frame that respects their limits. Marcello Lanfranchi and Jean-Simon Pacaud Lemay set out such a frame in this 2025 work. Older frames for partial work exist, but the authors seek new ones that fit more cases.

They present three new frames: local, partial, and inclusion types. In the local type, objects are resources that can be reached in part, and maps are processes that link them. Such frames help model work that may fail or lack full data. They may serve the study of code, data banks, and systems where some inputs are missing by design.
arxiv-2512-03671:
Beatrice Savoldi and a large Italian team survey how a nation's adults actually use generative AI, and who gets left behind. Nearly two thousand Italian-speaking adults answered their 2025 questionnaire on adoption, skills, and habits. Chatbots are remaking daily information work, but access alone may not equalize gains.

Adoption lagged among older, less-educated respondents and those less at ease with technology, with forty percent naming competence as a barrier. Among users, prior AI training best predicted purposeful uses like creating, learning, and building skills. Casual uses, including companionship and lookups, ignored training levels. Gender split both uptake and frequency, a divide running through every result.
arxiv-2512-03771:
A harmless-looking word can smuggle a banned meaning into a language model, if earlier examples quietly teach the substitution. Itay Yona and colleagues name that trick Doublespeak in a 2025 preprint on language model security. Across several in-context examples, a harmful keyword is swapped for a benign one, and the swap is placed before a harmful request.

Inside the model, the benign token's representation drifts toward the harmful word's meaning, layer by layer. Early layers keep the innocent reading, while later layers settle on the disallowed one, so a prompt about the harmless word is treated as a banned instruction. The attack needs no optimisation, transfers across model families, and succeeded often on both open and closed systems. The authors argue that safety training must therefore work at the level of internal representations, not only surface wording.
arxiv-2512-03971:
Imagine learning a hidden decision tree by asking it questions, one answer at a time, with a guarantee the questions are nearly optimal. Zunchen Huang and Chenglu Jin pursue that goal in a 2025 preprint on logic in computer science. Instead of entropy heuristics, they encode every candidate tree of bounded depth into SAT formulas.

Each possible question's value is estimated by counting, approximately, how many candidate trees it would rule out. An approximate model counter measures the shrinking hypothesis space after every answer, so the learner strengthens its formula step by step. If counting stalls, an equivalence check tests whether surviving trees compute the same function. In experiments, the method converged to the correct tree after a handful of queries. The rigorous foundation suits formal analysis and verification settings.
arxiv-2512-04271:
Susan Jane Colley, Gary Kennedy, and Corey Shanbrom continue a two-part study of Goursat distributions, a topic in pure math tied to how certain systems of directions spread across a surface. Their first paper covered what they call structural invariants, traits that mirror those of curves drawn on surfaces. This second paper, posted on arXiv in 2025, turns to a second family of traits.

The new traits come from the small growth sequence of a distribution, a record of how fast its directions fill space step by step. The authors show how these growth traits line up with the structural ones from the first paper. The work runs through a tall stack of spaces over a surface, nicknamed the monster tower. It also ties the results to the study of sharp points and folds in curves on surfaces.
arxiv-2512-04471:
Daniel Borin, Danilo Rando, Edson Leonel, and Diego Oliveira study how a spinning, kicked system settles as it nears a tipping point. The system is a relativistic rotator with friction, kicked at steady beats. As a control knob nears its threshold, each beat can double the pattern period. Their 2025 arXiv paper pairs hand-derived formulas with large computer simulations to track the slowdown.

Near the threshold, the motion follows a simple normal form. Distance from the settled path shrinks as a power law over beats. From that law the team derives a set of critical exponents. Below the threshold, settling is exponential, with a time scale that blows up in a fixed way. Simulation numbers match the formulas closely. The match places this rotator in the same broad family as simple one-dimensional maps, a unity that helps physicists predict behavior across systems.
arxiv-2512-04771:
Roberto Garrone argues that two very different lenses, used together, give a fuller portrait of agent-based models. Such models simulate crowds of simple agents to study markets, crowds, and ecosystems. One lens, the epsilon-machine of computational mechanics, captures a time series' predictive structure: how much of the past a system truly uses to make its future. His 2025 arXiv paper adds a second lens from generative AI.

Diffusion models read the other axis: the shape of whole outcome distributions at a moment in time. They learn the surface on which population-level results live and can synthesize fresh, plausible outcomes. Garrone shows formally that the two tools act on distinct domains, processes versus distributions. Joined, they give a two-axis chart of a model's behavior, temporal order against distributional shape. Modelers gain a sharper way to compare simulations and spot what each one is really doing.
arxiv-2512-04971:
Caroline Violot, Vera Sosnovik, and Mathias Humbert study how French politics played out on YouTube during the snap elections of 2024. After the far-right National Rally won the European vote, President Emmanuel Macron dissolved parliament and called legislative elections two weeks later, and much of the whirlwind campaign unfolded online. The team tracked news outlets, politicians, and the commenters who gathered under their videos.

Their dataset covers dozens of channels and millions of comments across the campaign. Far-right and left-wing channels posted the most and drew far more views, likes, and comments than centrist ones, and their commenters formed tighter clusters. A small share of commenters ranged across the political spectrum and posted far more than loyal in-group users. News channels mostly hosted guests who matched their own leanings, and a politician's appearance pulled more of a channel's viewers into political commenting.
arxiv-2512-05071:
David Wang, Wilson Chen, Tianju Wang, and Jiale Zhang survey the technologies that let surfaces sense touch and gesture. What began with infrared light frames grew through infrared vision methods. Those methods trap light inside a pane, or scatter it across its back. The line ends in the capacitive sensing that now dominates phones and tablets. The survey follows that arc and turns to the newer contenders reshaping the field.

Vision-based and acoustic sensing get close treatment, along with approaches still in development such as millimetre-wave radar and vibration sensing. Each technique is weighed on how it works, how sharply it resolves contact, how well it scales to big surfaces, and where it is used. The authors also discuss blending several methods into one surface. They close with the obstacles — accuracy, power draw, and privacy — and with how new sensing methods could make interactive surfaces common and smart.
arxiv-2512-05271:
Rafael Frongillo, Mary Monroe, Eric Neyman, and Bo Waggoner study how to combine expert forecasts so the combination is provably hard to beat. The sobering background result is impossibility: merging experts' stated probabilities alone can do no better, in the worst case, than picking an expert at random. The authors change the game by letting the aggregator ask the experts structured follow-up questions, and they design the questioning so honesty is each expert's best strategy.

Within a model of independent but overlapping expert signals, optimal aggregation becomes achievable in the worst case, with questioning costs bounded by the number of agents. Accuracy improves in a clean tradeoff with the number of questions, and the error vanishes once queries engage enough agents and reasoning depth. Modest, well-chosen questions, they argue, dramatically strengthen what a crowd can know.
arxiv-2512-05371:
Changwen Xing and eleven co-authors present ChipMind, a framework that helps language models reason over circuit design specifications far longer than any context window. Chip designs are documented in vast, intricate specifications, and automating chip development with language models founders on that length: relevant facts sit many hops apart. ChipMind first converts a specification into a domain knowledge graph, built by a construction method aware of circuit semantics.

Reasoning then runs over the graph. An information-theoretic retrieval step dynamically traces logical dependencies through the graph, while intent-aware filtering prunes irrelevant material, balancing completeness against precision. On an industrial-scale benchmark of specification questions, ChipMind beats leading baselines by about a third on average, with much larger gains on the hardest questions. The authors frame the work as a bridge between academic language-model research and the practical realities of industrial hardware design.
arxiv-2512-05671:
Zhitao He, Haolin Yang, Zeyu Qin, and Yi R Fung tackle a gap in AI tutoring: teaching a whole group at once. Models do well one on one, but a ward round tutor guides many trainees at once. Their 2025 paper builds a system for clinical teaching in the Socratic style, where the tutor leads by questions.

First comes ClinEdu, a multi-agent simulator that mimics group dynamics among students. From it the team built ClinTeach, a large set of Socratic teaching dialogues. On top sits ClinTutor-R1, a vision and language agent with an explicit inner thinking step. It tracks each student's beliefs and the group's shared ground at the same time. Tests ranged from static benchmarks to live sessions in the simulator, expert review, and a study with two hundred users. The tutor beat its base models by more than a fifth and matched strong commercial models.
arxiv-2512-05771:
Hanjin Jo leads a ten author team modeling why high power thin-disk lasers lose output even when their beam stays clean. In these lasers, a pump beam bounces many times through a thin crystal disk. Pumping warps the disk slightly, and that warp shapes the cavity light. Their 2025 model starts from measured maps of the disk's optical path differences.

The simulation couples a multi-pass absorption model for the pumped crystal with propagation of the cavity field. Run on an ytterbium based disk laser, it reproduced the leftover pump share and predicted output power, beam size, and beam quality to within a few percent. Breaking the warp into Zernike shapes showed simple defocus alone would allow full power, while higher order warps steal light from the main mode. That modal loss is the real ceiling on power scaling. Builders must fight the disk's fine deformation, not just its focus.
arxiv-2512-05971:
Mohammadhossein Ghahramani, Yan Qiao, NaiQi Wu, and Mengchu Zhou bring gene inspired thinking to the factory floor. A gentelligent system is factory equipment whose components carry inherent information, like genes. The prize is reliable fault detection. Their framework chooses which sensor features to watch while also tuning how well faults get classified, treating the two goals as one problem rather than two.

The optimizer is a dominance based evolutionary algorithm that returns Pareto optimal trade-offs in a single run: no single best answer, but a frontier of options balancing feature count against detection quality. Two real world datasets from different industries validate the approach, and it generalizes across both. The goals genuinely conflict: cheaper monitoring pulls against better detection. Engineers get the whole frontier, not one compromise.
arxiv-2512-06071:
Francisco Mercado and nine co-authors stage a three way contest between galaxy simulations and the sky, over a simple question: when do small satellite galaxies stop forming stars? The fraction of satellites that go quenched is a sharp test of galaxy physics. Three simulation suites are aligned with survey observations under uniform selections.

On mass, everyone agrees: lower mass satellites quench more. Radial trends are messier. Observations show quenching easing gently with distance from the host; TNG50 matches best, FIREbox stays consistent, while FIRE-2 suppresses quenching at small distances, traced to unusual paired analog systems. Mass quenching looks settled; the spatial pattern still discriminates.
arxiv-2512-06271:
Bethan James and the CLASSY team compare the metal content of gas in nearby star forming galaxies, in two states at once. These galaxies stand in for far away ones from the young universe, which are too faint to probe in such detail. Gas that is calm and neutral can be read from the light it blocks, while hot charged gas glows and can be read from the light it gives off.

For a set of about thirty galaxies, the team weighed nitrogen, oxygen, sulfur, and iron in both states. Oxygen and sulfur, made by short lived giant stars, were mixed well between the two. Iron lagged in the charged gas, perhaps held in dust. Nitrogen stood out: the charged gas held far more, and the gap grew with galaxy size and outflow speed. The pattern points to fast enriching of new gas by young stars.
arxiv-2512-06371:
Viktor Lavrukhin works in topology, the study of shapes up to smooth bending, on a refinement of a classic way to tell shapes apart. Closed shapes can be compared through numbers built from their Stiefel Whitney classes, and two shapes count as alike in the cobordism sense when they jointly bound a higher shape. Lavrukhin starts from any relation among those numbers for shapes of a given size. From it he builds a new invariant for shapes one size down. Those shapes carry extra structure and bound nothing.

In a special case his invariant turns out to be a known one, the Kervaire semi characteristic. He also builds a new cobordism group that extends the classic unoriented one, and proves his invariant fully decides the classes in it. He further shows both the invariant and the class behave in a quadratic way in a known technical sense.
arxiv-2512-06571:
Zifan Xu, Peter Stone, and their co authors teach a humanoid robot to kick a soccer ball well despite noisy senses. A kicking robot must swing its leg fast, balance on one foot, and cope with shaky sensing and bumps from opponents. Their system learns by reinforcement, through a teacher student setup. A teacher policy trains on perfect information. Then a student learns to copy it using only the noisy signals a real robot gets.

Training runs in four stages, from chasing the ball over distance to placing kicks by direction, then distilling the teacher into the student, then refining the student under noise. Tailored rewards, realistic noise models, and a constrained online learning step close the gap between simulation and the real machine. In simulation and on a physical robot, the kicker scored reliably across varied ball and goal positions.
arxiv-2512-06971:
Ben Jacobsen and Kassem Fawaz study prediction with expert advice under a strict privacy rule. In the classic problem, a forecaster blends the guesses of several experts and learns over time which to trust. Local differential privacy adds a twist: each data point must be scrambled on its owner's side, so nothing raw ever leaves. The authors first show a classical algorithm already respects that rule, then build two that do better.

One, RW-AdaBatch, exploits the fact that privacy noise makes the forecaster switch experts rarely, and turns that slowness into stronger privacy on easy data at almost no cost in accuracy. The other, RW-Meta, privately chooses among experts that are themselves full learning algorithms, something earlier work had not handled. On hospital data from the COVID-19 pandemic, the meta method beat both the classical baseline and a leading central-privacy algorithm by a wide margin.
arxiv-2512-07271: Alex Bergman revisits the Beurling-Malliavin theorem, a classic of harmonic analysis that limits how short an interval a band-limited signal can be forced to vanish on. Bergman shows that the multiplier side of the theory also works for radial functions of many variables, and the route is a lifting trick of unexpected directness. His simpler argument replaces a harder one due to Vasilyev. It also settles a question Vasilyev had raised about the Cartwright form of the theorem.
arxiv-2512-07471:
N. Saidi, A. Abbad, W. Benstaali, and K. Bahnes wrote this 2025 materials science paper. It studies a family of full Heusler alloys built from cobalt, lead, and one further metal. That metal is technetium, titanium, zirconium, or hafnium, giving four related compounds.

All calculations run inside density functional theory, the standard tool for electronic structure. Two approximations handle the exchange and correlation energy, one tuned for better band gaps. The team computes structure, electronic behavior, magnetism, elasticity, and heat-driven electricity. All four alloys act as half-metallic ferromagnets in the results. That means one spin channel conducts while the other stays blocked. The alloys also prove mechanically stable, with a ductile character. Their thermoelectric signs are positive, and their efficiency figures are high. Such traits suit spintronic devices, which use electron spin for logic. The authors also point to embedded systems in cars as a use.
arxiv-2512-07571:
Nicolas Calbucura, Jose Guillen, and Valentin Barriere wrote this 2025 paper on giving language models ears. Text-only models miss what a speaker's voice reveals in tone and delivery. The authors add speech to a pretrained model for classification tasks, cheaply.

The obstacle is bulk: audio turns into far more tokens than text. A speech tokenizer built for recognition produces long streams from a huge vocabulary. Feeding all of that into a language model is costly and clumsy. Their trick is a lasso-based selection over a bag-of-words picture of both inputs. Only the audio tokens that matter for the task survive the cut. A self-supervised step then adapts the model to those few tokens. Fine-tuning on the real task follows at the end. The method shines on spotting argumentative fallacies, where audio was thought harmful. It also helps on emotion tasks from a widely used dataset.
arxiv-2512-07671:
Hao Zou wrote this 2025 mathematical physics paper on mirror symmetry for supermanifolds. Gauged linear sigma models are field theories whose phases describe different geometries. Their A-twisted versions can have complex Kähler supermanifolds as geometric phases.

Zou revisits those models with fresh questions about their other phases. For abelian models with no superpotential, he describes the non-geometric point explicitly. That Landau-Ginzburg point gets an orbifold description in his hands. He also gives a systematic rule for the tricky R-charge assignments there. The paper then turns to topological super Landau-Ginzburg models. It derives their chiral ring relations and genus-by-genus correlation functions. Those formulas become tools for testing a mirror proposal. The proposal follows the Hori-Vafa pattern known from ordinary manifolds.   The paper supplies concrete formulas.
arxiv-2512-07871:
Andrew Kiruluta wrote this 2025 report on a new kind of reasoning machine. Quantum Circuit Reasoning Models aim to do logic with quantum-style machinery. They extend tunable quantum circuits beyond their usual homes in energy problems and sorting tasks.

The core claim is a natural match between quantum moves and reasoning moves. Superposition maps to branching among rival guesses. Entanglement spreads constraints from claim to claim. Interference checks that claims agree, and a final readout settles the choice. On that basis he builds a tunable circuit design. Logical rules become unitary gates acting on claim qubits. Training runs by plain gradient descent over the circuit's settings. Runs on ordinary hardware show how the pieces would work today. A Quantum Reasoning Layer packages the idea as a hybrid building block. Such layers could slot into larger modular reasoning systems. Science, medicine, and chemistry are named as target fields.
arxiv-2512-07971:
Km Nitu Rai, Neelam Panwar, Jeewan C Pandey, and three co-authors wrote this 2025 astronomy paper. Most stars are not alone, yet telescopes see close pairs as single points. Air turbulence and the diffraction limit blur their true separations away.

Speckle interferometry is a cheap trick for beating that blur from the ground. Fast snapshots freeze the turbulence into speckles that encode fine detail. The team applies the method at India's Devasthal Optical Telescope. Its mirror ranks in the medium, four-metre class of instruments. Binary systems are resolved, with separations and position angles measured directly. Faint companions defeat the conventional analysis in some systems. For those, Bayesian inference models the speckle patterns instead. Orbital parameters then come out with high precision from the fit. The work establishes a working recipe for the telescope as an interferometer. Indian astronomy gains a proven path into high-resolution stellar studies.
arxiv-2512-08071:
Pingchuan Ma, Chengshuai Zhao, Bohan Jiang, and colleagues, computer scientists, posted a methods paper on arXiv in December 2025. Their system, called CAMO, classifies social media posts during crises, sorting text and images into useful disaster information. The hard part is generalizing to new kinds of disasters the model has never seen, where performance usually falls apart.

CAMO is guided by causality. An adversarial objective pushes the model to separate true causal features from spurious ones that only fit past disasters. A unified representation also aligns text and image features in one shared space, so single modality generalization methods can extend to both. Experiments across datasets show the approach performs best on unseen disaster scenarios. For emergency teams, a classifier that holds up on a novel crisis could sharpen situational awareness when it matters most.
arxiv-2512-08171:
Zhi Hao Cui, Hao Wu, and Wei Xu, probabilists, posted a research paper on arXiv in December 2025 about the excursions of reflected Levy processes. A Levy process is a random motion with jumps, and reflection at its past low point cuts its path into repeated excursions. The authors study the rare excursions that last long or climb very high.

For an oscillating process drawn to a stable law, long lived excursions need not be tall ones. Scaled properly, they behave like stable excursions with lifetime or height above one, extending work by Doney and Rivero. The negative drift case behaves very differently. There, under a heavy tail condition, long life and large height become the same event in the limit. Conditioned on either, excursions settle into a single jump process whose jump size follows a Pareto law. The contrast sharpens the picture of how rare paths form.
arxiv-2512-08571:
Gourab Panigrahi and Phani Motamarri present methods to speed up large quantum chemistry calculations that use finite elements in space. Their work targets density functional theory, a widely used way to find the ground state of atoms and materials. The main cost comes from applying a large sparse operator again and again inside a solver.

The authors build matrix free methods that compute those steps on the fly instead of storing huge matrices. They use structured tensor work, careful data layouts, and mixed precision to reuse cache well on three major supercomputers. Tests show clear speed gains over the standard cell matrix approach, with larger gains for all electron cases. When paired with a filtered solver, the methods also cut total time to solution.
arxiv-2512-08771:
Patricia Goncalves, Martin Hairer, and Maria Chiara Ricciuti study scaling limits of a random interface model with a weak global perturbation. The model starts from classic corner flip dynamics on a discrete torus. A small asymmetry in the growth direction is added, and its sign switches based on the total area under the interface.

The slopes of the model can be seen as an exclusion process at half filling with rates that depend globally on the system. For a key parameter value, the authors show the large scale density follows a joined evolution: part viscous Burgers dynamics and part heat dynamics, in time sequence. For a stronger range and prime system size, equilibrium fluctuations converge to an infinite dimensional Ornstein Uhlenbeck process. The results show how a tiny global feedback can reshape both the average behavior and the random fluctuations of a growing interface.
arxiv-2512-08871:
Joseph Dill and coauthors report low resistance electrical contacts to a wide bandgap nitride semiconductor with very high aluminum content. Such contacts are vital for electronic and photonic devices, but they are usually made by a lift off process with high temperature alloying. That heat can deform structures and imposes a harsh thermal budget on the whole device.

The team instead forms non alloyed contacts that work as deposited, with no high temperature step. Resistivity and contact resistivity are among the lowest reported for this composition, with clean linear current voltage behavior. Two fabrication routes achieve the same quality, one based on metal first patterning and one on lift off with an oxygen cleaning step before metal deposition. Growth on a high quality single crystal substrate and a smooth surface help isolate the junction physics. A standard emission model fits the results and yields a clear barrier height.
arxiv-2512-08971: A large group of Bulgarian physicists presents the national input of the Bulgarian particle physics group to the European Strategy for Particle Physics. The text sums up the group view and vision for how the field should develop, seen from a Bulgarian viewpoint. It outlines current activities in particle physics in the country. It also rates the strengths and weak spots of the research field as it stands. Finally, it sets out the group interests for the future growth of the science and tech landscape in the field.
arxiv-2512-09371:
Yukun Luo and colleagues improve the boundary physics of Babcock-Leighton dynamo models, the leading framework for explaining the Sun's eleven-year magnetic cycle. Surface flux transport models describe the Sun's visible magnetic field very well. The authors argue those models should therefore constrain what a dynamo model is allowed to do at its outer boundary.

They propose a new boundary condition with zero radial diffusion, derived directly from the magnetohydrodynamic induction equation. They test it against two alternatives, a purely radial boundary and the same boundary combined with strong near-surface pumping. For a single bipolar magnetic region, the new condition keeps the dynamo's surface evolution consistent with flux transport simulations, suppressing leakage across the surface. Inside a full dynamo model, it reproduces the basic properties of the solar cycle and yields a surface field that is not purely radial, matching observations more closely.
arxiv-2512-09671:
Hikmatullo Ismatov gives a deliberately friendly exposition of a proof that a simple stationary mean field game has one solution. Mean field games model many interacting agents, each optimizing against the average behavior of the crowd. They are described by a coupled pair of equations: a Hamilton-Jacobi equation for each player's value, and a transport equation for the density of players.

Working on a torus, Ismatov uses the monotone operator method. He first builds a general Hilbert space framework, adding a coercive regularization and applying Minty's method to obtain a solution. Then he specializes to an explicit Hamiltonian, a quadratic term minus the density, and checks every assumption so the abstract theorem delivers existence and uniqueness for the game. The exposition is slow and elementary, aimed so that a motivated undergraduate can follow each step, making the paper as much a teaching text as a research contribution.
arxiv-2512-09871:
Yimin Zhu and Lincoln Linlin Xu propose DPS4Un, a method for unmixing hyperspectral images. Each pixel in such an image mixes light from several materials. Unmixing means naming the pure materials, called endmembers, and estimating each one's share in every pixel. Two difficulties dominate: knowing expected spectra beforehand, and handling spectral variation across a scene. The authors work in a Bayesian frame, where the answer is a posterior distribution combining the observed data with prior knowledge.

Their sampler uses a pretrained diffusion model of spectra as the prior engine. They build endmember bundles from the image itself, within small uniform regions called superpixels, rather than borrowing a library that could bias results. Starting from noise, the method updates material shares and endmembers in turns, which captures spectral variability. On three real world benchmark datasets, DPS4Un beat the leading unmixing methods.
arxiv-2512-09971:
Robert Ehrlich reviews a bold claim about the famous supernova SN 1987A: that its neutrino data reveal the actual masses of the three neutrinos. Ordinarily, cosmology and laboratory experiments give only upper limits on those masses. In 1988, Ramanath Cowsik argued the supernova burst could do better, yielding values rather than bounds. His result needs the neutrinos to have been emitted nearly all at once, within less than a second. That clashes with standard emission models, which include a cooling phase lasting more than ten seconds.

Ehrlich explains why those standard models might be mistaken. If the models are wrong about the burst's duration, Cowsik's masses could still be right. That would be surprising, because the suggested masses exceed the upper limits implied by cosmology and direct experiments. The review lays out the tension honestly, as an open challenge to the standard picture.
arxiv-2512-10071:
Junjie Bai leads a large team in the 2025 BEHAVIOR Challenge, a robotics contest on long household tasks. The BEHAVIOR-1K suite covers everyday chores people most want robots to help with, in simulated homes. These tasks demand mobile manipulation over long horizons, far beyond pick and place demos. The team's system, Openpi Comet, finished a close second and clearly outperformed the remaining submissions. It builds on a recent vision language action foundation model, and the report focuses on careful study rather than a single trick.

Through careful ablation studies, the team measured how training techniques and data choices affect performance. They found scaling benefits in both pretraining and post training phases. Their validation score far surpassed previous state of the art on the benchmark. The report distills practical lessons and design advice for adapting powerful foundation models to complex embodied settings.
arxiv-2512-10171:
Gustavo O. Carvalho, Fábio P. Machado, and J. Hermenegildo R. González study the frog model, a toy system of hopping particles that wake each other up. Frogs sit at integer sites; when visited by an active frog, sleeping frogs activate and hop randomly, but each frog lives only a random lifetime. The twist here is that each particle draws its own survival parameter, with a distribution whose shape near perfect survival is governed by an exponent and a slowly varying factor. The question is the classic one for such systems: does activity spread forever or die out?

A universal threshold in the exponent decides the outcome. At the boundary, sharp criteria involving the slowly varying factor decide the outcome. The proof combines a percolation comparison with sharp displacement estimates.
arxiv-2512-10471:
L Celestine and co-authors examine two lead-free halide perovskites, materials chased for clean energy devices because they convert light and pressure into electricity without toxic lead. Their study compares cesium germanium chloride and rubidium tin bromide, both alone and joined at a germanium-tin finished interface, using density functional theory.

The team analysed the bulk crystals, their main surface, and the joined interface under two levels of theory. The uneven atomic arrangements at surfaces and interfaces turned out to give notably strong optoelectronic and piezoelectric behaviour. They checked the piezoelectric promise directly with electromechanical coupling calculations for each surface cut. The findings point to these lead-free pairings as plausible material for harvesting renewable energy, with the interface itself doing much of the useful work.
arxiv-2512-10571:
Haojie Zheng and co-authors build AVI-Edit, a tool for editing single objects inside a video while keeping the sound in step. Recent video generators show that believable content needs audio and picture to move together. Yet most editing methods ignore sound and give users only coarse control over where and when an edit lands.

The framework sharpens a rough user-drawn mask into a precise outline of the chosen instance, refining it step by step with awareness of the detail level needed. A self-feedback audio agent curates clean audio guidance, giving fine control over timing as well. The team also built a large dataset with instance-level links between video and sound and detailed annotations. In their tests, AVI-Edit beat leading methods on visual quality, following instructions, and audio-visual synchronisation.
arxiv-2512-10771:
Tomofumi Shimoda, Wataru Kokuyama, and Hideaki Nozato build a test rig that can shake a vibration sensor in three directions at once, slowly and over long strokes, while baking or freezing it. Triaxial sensors, including cheap MEMS accelerometers, are everywhere, but their accuracy drifts with temperature. And certifying one for earthquake work demands reference measurements under realistic conditions.

Their system integrates a triaxial exciter with an environmental chamber spanning deep cold to hot conditions, reproducing the long, low-frequency sway of a huge earthquake. Reference readings come from a laser interferometer and reference accelerometers calibrated inside the system itself, so its readings are good to better than a quarter of a percent. As a demonstration, the team measured how a MEMS accelerometer performs on earthquake signals across the temperature range. And the paper lays out the rig's layout and testing steps in full.
arxiv-2512-10871:
Benjamin Anker and Dripto Debroy make quantum error correction robust to broken hardware. Fabrication defects knock out qubits and couplers, and recent work showed the surface code can cope by leaning on the state partway through an error-correction cycle. This paper improves that prescription in two directions, both about choosing what to measure and in what order.

First, they quantify what a richer set of gauge operators, proposed earlier for the hexagonal surface code, buys on the standard square grid. And add a method for cutting away qubits that are effectively unused. Second, they use the LUCI framework as an intermediate language and let integer linear programming search its large space of valid circuits for high performers. On a distance-eleven surface code with realistic dropout and noise, the optimisations improved performance by a clear double-digit margin over four rounds of syndrome extraction.
arxiv-2512-10971:
Tianyu Fan and co-authors introduce AI-Trader, a live test bed for language model agents that trade in real financial markets. Agents must react in real time, gather fresh information, and adapt as prices move. The benchmark covers United States stocks, Chinese A-shares, and cryptocurrencies at several trading speeds.

Agents receive only basic starting context and must search for, check, and combine live market information on their own, with no human help. Six major language models were tested across the markets. Most earned poor returns and managed risk badly, even when they reasoned well in other settings. The authors find that risk control, more than general intelligence, decides whether a strategy holds up across markets.
arxiv-2512-11071:
Maida Wang and Panyun Jiang address a growing abuse in online media, where bad actors re edit a creator's content so it looks the same but means something different. Detecting such semantic changes requires a model of each creator's personal style. Individual bloggers, though, usually have very few example samples to train on, so classical detectors overfit or fail.

Their system, Q-BAR, pairs classical processing with a small variational quantum circuit to spot anomalies in that low data setting. Features from several media types are mapped into a quantum space where the creator's normal pattern forms a compact region. Tested on a curated set of one hundred creators, the quantum enhanced approach detected anomalies robustly while using only hundreds of trainable parameters. The authors present it as a path toward personalised media forensics.
arxiv-2512-11171:
Mostafa Atallah and colleagues compare strategies for avoiding barren plateaus, the flat training landscapes that stall a leading quantum algorithm. The variational quantum eigensolver estimates molecular energies by tuning a quantum circuit, but its gradients can vanish as systems grow. Many fixes exist, yet how they trade off against computing budget was unclear.

The team benchmarked four mitigation approaches against the standard algorithm on molecules ranging from small to a fourteen qubit case, tracking gradient strength over deep circuits and accuracy over many iterations. Which method won depended on both system size and iteration budget. One approach led early on larger systems, while another overtook it given more iterations and reached near exact energies on small molecules. The lesson is to match the strategy to the budget rather than judging by gradient size alone.
arxiv-2512-11571:
Andreu Matoses Gimenez and co-authors work on how robots plan both what to do and how to move. Older planners often simplify the physics, so plans can fail when a robot must push, slide, or lean on objects. Plans that ignore the real motor controllers can also miss the best motion.

The team runs many plan trials at once in a fast physics simulator on a graphics chip. A sampling method called cross-entropy then tunes the controller settings toward low cost plans. Because the same controllers drive the real robot, it can carry out the plan at once. Tests show the robot using walls and edges to move objects.
arxiv-2512-11671:
Miriam Resch and co-authors present a smarter way to clean noise from quantum sensors. Quantum sensors can beat classic ones in precision and detail, but the same traits make them fragile to noise from their surroundings. Standard fixes use facts about the noise to undo its harm.

Their method first profiles the device, then adapts to how complex the noise growth is. It also flags the best sensing times for the cleanest reads.
