Tests on a single nitrogen vacancy center magnetometer, a diamond based magnetic sensor, reached the best sensitivity that theory allows. The work is a step toward rugged quantum sensors that keep their edge outside the lab.
arxiv-2512-11871:
Tekleab G Gebremedhin and co-authors built an offline phone system that spots crop disease and pests for farmers in Tigray, Ethiopia. Farming feeds over 80 percent of the region, and conflict damage cut access to expert diagnosis. The core data set holds 3,587 field photos of cactus fig in three symptom classes.

Three light models were compared. EfficientNet-Lite1 reached 90.7 percent test accuracy. A custom light CNN hit 89.5 percent with the best speed and size, 42 milliseconds and 4.8 megabytes. MobileViT-XS led cross validation at 97.3 percent, since its global view separates pest clusters from flat fungus spots. The app runs fully offline in Tigrigna and Amharic.
arxiv-2512-12071:
Takafumi Kita gives a short proof of the spin statistics theorem without relativity. The theorem links a particle spin to its social rule: whole spin particles may share states freely, while half spin particles refuse to share, the Pauli principle. Classic proofs lean on relativistic field theory, heavy machinery for so basic a fact.

Kita works with field operators in plain space, defined by their commutation and anticommutation rules, which encode the sharing behavior. A rotation by pi applied to a pair of annihilation operators gives an eigenvalue test. Matching that test against the pair rotational behavior forces the link: whole spin goes with commutation, half spin with anticommutation. Five pages carry the full argument.
arxiv-2512-12471:
Bhawana Chhaglani presents research on privacy aware sound sensing for healthy indoor spaces in a 2025 paper. Airborne spread of illness indoors is a major health risk, yet current monitoring is invasive, costly, or indirect. Her work uses ambient audio, the background sound already present in a room, to estimate transmission risk factors without recording private content.

Those factors include ventilation, aerosol emissions, and how occupants spread through a space. The systems she develops use existing microphones and protect privacy by design. They aim to track indoor air quality factors in real time on everyday devices. The paper lays a foundation for privacy aware airborne risk monitoring.
arxiv-2512-12771:
Gianfranco Cariolaro, Edi Ruffa, Amir Mohammad Yaghoobianzadeh, and Jawad A Salehi define the quantum Fourier transform for continuous variables in a 2025 paper. The discrete version is a workhorse algorithm on qubits, built from Hadamard and controlled phase gates. Continuous variable systems instead live in a Hilbert space of modes, where the transform is tied to rotation operators set by unitary matrices.

They define the transform as the rotation whose matrix is the discrete Fourier transform matrix. Using the Murnaghan procedure with single mode rotations and beam splitters, plus fast Fourier transform style algorithms, implementation complexity drops sharply. For Gaussian states, the transform acts simply: the displacement vector gets a one dimensional DFT, the squeeze matrix a two dimensional one.
arxiv-2512-12871:
Millend Roy and co-authors present CapOptix, a new way to price capacity in electricity markets. Grids must stay reliable as wind and solar grow, demand swings, and price shocks hit. Older capacity designs rely on average measures of unserved energy and can miss real risk.

CapOptix treats a capacity promise as a kind of option, a contract tied to wholesale power prices. It also models sudden shifts in price patterns using a regime switching process. The team tested the idea on past price data from several markets. They compared the price ranges it gives with what current capacity payment schemes would produce.
arxiv-2512-12971:
Andrei Zlotchevski and Linan Chen study the unbalanced Schrodinger bridge problem, which seeks the best path between a starting distribution and a smaller ending one. Best is measured by closeness to a reference process. Here the reference is a diffusion that can kill particles, ending their paths early.

The authors interpret that killing as regime switching and add a constraint on when or where killing happens. They work through four versions of the constraint in detail, reflecting how much an observer knows. They also compare the four outcomes with each other. The approach unifies past results on this problem and extends them.
arxiv-2512-13271:
Fangju Yang and co-authors present LASEM, a light dynamic model for cable-driven continuum robots, flexible robots steered by pulling cables along a bendy backbone. Controllers need fast, accurate dynamics for high-speed prediction and model based control. Heavy models cannot keep up in real time.

Their formulation writes the actuation energy directly in the space of cable inputs. The full dynamics then reduce to a single partial differential equation that needs only moment balance, since force balance is built in. Cable contact forces never need explicit computation. The method supports both force and displacement inputs and ran about 62.3 percent faster than leading real-time approaches.
arxiv-2512-13871:
Shaun Sweeney's PhD thesis rethinks electricity market design from first principles. He reframes wholesale and balancing markets as a live, event-driven control system acting directly on grid physics, not as static spot clearing. Existing energy-only, capacity, and zonal designs, he argues, admit no shock-robust Nash equilibrium under realistic uncertainty.

His answer is a holarchic automatic market maker, where prices are bounded control signals derived from physical tightness. Nested scarcity layers, from node to system, let nodal and zonal pricing emerge as special cases. Fuel costs are recovered through pay-as-bid dispatch, while other costs follow adequacy, flexibility, and location. Large runs show bounded stability, controlled buying costs, and zero structural waste, though a managed transition would be required.
arxiv-2512-13971:
Adriano Macarone-Palmieri, Alberto Ferrara, and Rosario Lo Franco propose a nonlinear quantum neural network to engineer multipartite entanglement. Entanglement across many parties is a key resource for quantum tech, but making it at scale on noisy devices is hard. Their low-depth design scales linearly and adds activation functions in a novel way.

A Monte Carlo sweep over 100,000 circuit layouts for noiseless states shows the advantage of the nonlinear step. In noisy settings, they optimize a global entanglement measure and certify it with bipartite negativity. For 10-qubit mixed states, optimized circuits made strong entanglement across splits. Genuine multipartite entanglement was confirmed with semi-definite programming, and the framework scales readily to 20 qubits.
arxiv-2512-14071:
Shun Okumura, Moritz M. Hirschmann, and Yukitoshi Motome uncover a new anomalous Hall effect driven by spin spirals in metals. Spin spirals are noncollinear, flat magnetic patterns that couple to itinerant electrons and produce emergent phenomena. The anomalous Hall effect is a transverse voltage that usually tracks magnetization in a simpler way.

The spiral generates odd-parity spin splitting with polarization across the helical plane, forming spin-nodal lines in the electronic structure. With spin-orbit coupling, finite magnetization opens gaps at those lines, and Berry curvature gathers near the gaps, producing the Hall response. The interplay of spin-orbit coupling, helical plane orientation, and that direction is the key ingredient. The mechanism applies broadly across materials hosting spin spirals, in both crystal types studied.
arxiv-2512-14171:
Melika Gorgi, Kamran Kaveh, Navid Aliakbarian, and Mohammad Reza Ejtehadi model natural selection across space and time in a 2025 paper. Classic Moran models treat births and deaths as random events in a group, while FKPP equations describe smooth, wave like spread.

The authors bridge both views by deriving partial differential equations for Moran dynamics in continuous media. They split fitness into fecundity, meaning birth rate, and viability, meaning death rate. Wave speeds then differ sharply by update rule: some waves slow down, some hold a constant speed, and some speed up. They extend the model to uneven media and derive a continuous version of isothermal graphs, tied to a conserved local current.
arxiv-2512-14771:
Evgenii Vasinovich and Alexander Moskvin offer a simple theory of spin reorientation in rare earth orthoferrites and orthochromites, materials with formulas RFeO3 and RCrO3. Spin reorientation is a shift in the direction along which the atomic spins in a magnet point. Their model treats the rare earth ions through a single low doublet of energy states.

Inside the model, the free energy adds pull from the iron or chromium sublattice to the splitting of that doublet. The authors show the shift can be sudden, smooth, or mixed, based on the strength of those pulls. They also study what happens when nonmagnetic atoms dilute the material. Heat capacity spikes near the shift, and the rare earth moment acts in odd ways there, and both effects fall out of the same simple picture.
arxiv-2512-14871: Tadej Starčič works out the isotropy groups of the complex orthogonal group. An isotropy group collects the moves that leave a given matrix unchanged under similarity, the step that rewrites a matrix in a new basis. He studies this action on the group's own matrices and on skew symmetric ones. The groups he finds are tied to a family of block matrices. Their blocks are Toeplitz blocks, arrays built from repeated bands that run along the diagonals.
arxiv-2512-15071:
Hamza Virk and two coauthors build a pricing model where market jumps and smooth moves feed on each other. Standard jump diffusion models treat jumps as independent of the smooth diffusion part. In real markets, big smooth swings can trigger jumps, and ignoring that link can create phantom arbitrage, free profit on paper.

Their model has several jump types, with upward and downward jumps set off by large upward and downward diffusion moves alike. Earlier one sided versions of this idea opened arbitrage holes. The authors close them by deriving an explicit no arbitrage condition that ties the physical drift to model parameters and risk premia. They build the needed martingale measure with Girsanov's theorem and a normalized Esscher transform. The result gives derivatives pricing a rigorous base when jumps depend on diffusion.
arxiv-2512-15171:
Kaixing Long and ten coauthors teach a network to diagnose kidney diseases from three kinds of biopsy images at wildly different scales. Electron microscope images show nanoscale detail, while optical and immunofluorescence images work at the microscale. Fusing such images is hard, because their features live at such different sizes.

Their network, CMUS-Net, bridges the gap with ultrastructural cues. A sparse multi instance module gathers features from the electron images. A cross modal scale attention module then lets the modalities interact and sharpen the pathological meaning. Combined losses weigh each modality's importance. On their own dataset the system classified IgA nephropathy, membranous nephropathy, and lupus nephritis with 95.37 percent accuracy and an F1 score of 95.32 percent. It beat known multimodal rivals and also generalized to staging membranous disease.
arxiv-2512-15371:
Leyang Xue and three coauthors study how the shape of a social network decides whether a behavior sweeps through it or stalls. Contagion models usually cover person to person spread and local reinforcement, where friends' adoption nudges you. This study adds macro level reinforcement: once adoption is widespread, its very prevalence pushes it further.

With that feedback, the contagion's transition changes character as macro influence passes a threshold, shifting from continuous to mixed order. Simulations on real world networks show that network localization, how concentrated the network's influence is, sets both the critical point and that threshold. The authors build a structural metric for it and expose a trade off. Networks that ease weak contagions diffuse them slowly with lower adoption. Networks that resist weak contagions, once tipped, spread them faster and wider. The finding upends the belief that denser local links always help contagion.
arxiv-2512-15471:
Casper Loman and co authors compare ways to build work schedules that survive uncertain task times in a 2025 paper. A schedule can be robust in two senses: its quality stays stable, or its structure stays stable when jobs run long or short. The team studies parallel machine scheduling with precedence limits and release dates.

They first test how well 13 existing and 6 new robustness measures track both kinds of robustness in a large simulation study. Then they use the best measures inside local search algorithms that assign both jobs and time buffers. The winning recipe models task times with normal distributions and handles job placement and buffers together, with weights that shift during the search.
arxiv-2512-15571:
V. Sauli determines the effective charm quark mass from excited charmonium decays in a 2025 paper. Charmonium states are bound states of a charm quark and its antiquark, and their leptonic decay rates depend on the charm mass used. Pinning down how that effective mass changes with energy scale is the goal.

Using the covariant Bethe Salpeter equation with an infrared finite running charge, Sauli fits known spin one charmonium spectra and decay constants. The mass runs from 1.1 giga electron volts for the J/Psi meson to 1.5 for its higher radial excitations. Those values sit well below perturbative scheme values but agree with a semi perturbative Dyson equation solution.
arxiv-2512-15671:
Ishan Kalburge and Mate Lengyel propose the functional information bottleneck for judging probabilistic neural codes in a 2025 paper. Brains seem to track uncertainty, and task trained networks were said to develop such codes on their own. Prior work, though, lacked a sharp test separating true codes from shortcut recodings of the input.

Their framework judges a code by both sufficiency and minimality, not sufficiency alone. Applied to networks trained on cue combination, coordinate change, and Kalman filtering, the minimality test reverses earlier claims. The networks do not form minimal codes of Bayesian posteriors, and instead rely on shortcut input recoding. When such codes truly arise remains open.
arxiv-2512-15871:
Michael Rampp, Suhail Rather, and Pieter Claeys introduce completely reducible quantum circuits in a 2025 paper. Dual unitary circuits are exactly solvable models of quantum chaos, yet a systematic account of which multi unitary dynamics stay solvable was missing. Their framework covers a large class of non integrable models with exactly solvable dynamics.

In these circuits, the entanglement membrane that governs operator growth can be characterized analytically. The circuits extend space time symmetry to general lattice geometries, breaking dual unitarity globally but not locally, and allow four or five directions of information flow. A general formula gives entanglement line tension from the flow pattern, and solvability ties to the absence of knots in that flow.
arxiv-2512-16371:
Mariam Hassan and three co-authors rethink video generation in a paper posted on arXiv during 2025. Text-to-video diffusion models make impressive clips but often botch scene layout or the order of events. The authors argue many failures, even apparent motion errors, start with a flawed first frame that never composed the scene correctly.

Their pipeline, Anchored Video Generation, splits the job into three stages. A language model first rewrites the prompt to describe only the opening scene. An image model then builds a high-quality anchor frame from it. Finally, a video model fine-tuned for anchors animates that frame. The approach set a new state of the art on the T2V CompBench benchmark, improved every tested model on VBench2, and cut sampling steps by 70 percent with no loss in quality.
arxiv-2512-16471:
M Zahirul Alam and five co-authors build a rewritable hologram in their 2025 paper on arXiv. Holography structures light for imaging and optical computing. Classic holographic materials are thick and slow to rewrite, though. The team revisits the idea with an ultrathin film of indium tin oxide. That is a transparent conductor used in touch screens.

Near its epsilon-near-zero frequency, the plain film becomes an efficient diffractive platform under patterned light. At that point the material's permittivity crosses zero. The film achieved a few percent diffraction efficiency. The effect spanned more than 300 nanometers of bandwidth near telecom wavelengths. The film is four orders of magnitude thinner than standard media. It is also up to six orders of magnitude faster to rewrite. No complex fabrication is needed. That points to rapid prototyping of optical modulators and structured light devices.
arxiv-2512-16571:
Prayoga Liong and four co-authors predict self-rippling electron fluids in a paper posted on arXiv during 2025. In Dirac materials like graphene, electrons can flow collectively like a fluid. Near charge neutrality, how strongly the flow dissipates depends sharply on density, a recipe for instability.

Above a critical drift speed, the authors show, uniform flow should break into running waves: spatial ripples locked to temporal oscillations, like roll waves on a viscous film. The transition shows a kink in the average current and emits narrow-band radiation at a tunable washboard frequency set by speed over wavelength. Unlike sliding charge-density waves, the mechanism needs no disorder or pinning. The tiny effective mass of Dirac carriers pushes the emission into the tens to hundreds of gigahertz, suggesting a new platform for high-frequency electronics.
arxiv-2512-17071:
Gábor Kun and László Márton Tóth build graphings, measurable graph limits, with tightly controlled flows. Lovász had extended flow theory to this setting, and earlier work gave regular treeings with no nonzero measurable circulations, hence no measurable perfect matching.

The pair develop tools to make d-regular treeings whose circulation space has any chosen finite dimension k. Uses include a treeing with a single balanced orientation but no Schreier decoration, one with a single Schreier decoration, and one with a proper edge coloring but no further perfect matchings. The first case answers a question of Lovász, since that orientation is not a blend of finite cycles and infinite paths.
arxiv-2512-17371:
Haomin Qi, Fengfei Yu, and Chengbo Huang present GraphCue, a helper that writes network settings for software-defined networks. Configuring such networks by hand is slow and error prone. GraphCue grounds each job in the network's shape: the layout becomes a graph, and a small graph network finds the closest past case that already passed checks.

That proven case goes into a tight prompt that steers the code writer, and a verifier runs each draft and sends failures back for repair. On 628 test cases, GraphCue passed 88.2 percent within 20 rounds, and 95 percent of checks finished within 9 seconds. Removing the case lookup or the tight prompt made results much worse, so both pieces carry the gains.
arxiv-2512-18071:
Meysam Ghanbari and four coauthors speed up design work for molecular messaging, where chemicals carry signals through tiny channels. Predicting the pulse a receiver will see means solving hard flow and reaction equations, and each new setting costs a fresh heavy run. Their shortcut trains a neural network as a stand in.

A detailed physics model first made a large set of sample pulses across wide ranges of flow, reaction, and shape. The network learned to map those settings straight to the pulse. On fresh test channels, 90 percent came out with an error score below 0.15. Designers can now scan options quickly and save the heavy math for final checks.
arxiv-2512-18471:
Xin Li proposes a geometric answer to catastrophic forgetting. That is the tendency of AI systems to overwrite old skills as they learn new ones. Most fixes expand the model, adding dimensions, kernels, or replayed data. His paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, argues for the opposite move: contraction. The idea is to squeeze what is already learned into tighter tokens.

The Urysohn Ladder stacks quotient maps that collapse checked neighborhoods of similar experience into compact tokens. They act like wormholes linking distant memories. He proves four guarantees. Structure becomes linearly separable at each level, and capacity per level stays bounded no matter how long the stream runs. Learning stays stable without interference, and inference cost grows with the short quotient distance. Tests with pretrained models and real datasets back each claim.
arxiv-2512-18571:
Weijie Zhou and a large team build a robot assistant that knows when to ask for help. Faced with a vague instruction like 'fetch the tool' in a cluttered room, an agent can wander at high physical cost or bother a human at attention cost. Their framework, ESearch-R1, posted to arXiv in December 2025, folds asking, remembering, and navigating into one decision process.

Training uses HC-GRPO, a reinforcement learning method that samples groups of reasoning paths and rewards the ones balancing information gain against travel time and human attention. In the AI2-THOR simulator, ESearch-R1 beats standard ReAct-based agents on success rate while cutting total operating costs by about 50 percent. The results show cost-aware training can align a multimodal model's choices with the real constraints of the physical world.
arxiv-2512-18771:
Justine Parmentier, Vincent E. Terrapon, and Tristan Gilet study the thin film of water that coats every growing stalagmite. Stalagmites archive past climate in their calcium layers, and they grow drip by drip. Yet how that water film drains under gravity, shaped by the stalagmite's own curves and the discrete dripping, was poorly described in growth models. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, builds the missing theory.

Starting from Reynolds lubrication theory in curvilinear coordinates, they derive distinct scaling laws for two regimes: drainage dominated by film thickness and drainage dominated by slope. The laws govern both the moving front and the resting film thickness. Numerical solutions agree, and measurements in a real cave and in the lab confirm the predicted resting thickness. The work sharpens stalagmite growth models and applies to gravity-driven surface flows generally.
arxiv-2512-18971:
Shuntuo Xu, Zhou Yu, and Jian Huang use generative AI to compress data without losing what matters. Sufficient dimension reduction seeks a few combinations of variables that carry all the information about a response, but nonlinear versions lacked guarantees of finding everything, in the population or in samples. Their method, GenSDR, posted to arXiv in December 2025, builds the reduction with deep generative models trained through conditional stochastic interpolation.

GenSDR provably recovers all information in the central sigma-field, at both levels. At the sample level they prove the estimator consistent, in the sense of conditional distributions, using what deep generative models learn from data. An ensemble extension handles non-Euclidean responses, such as shapes or networks, widening its reach. Numerical results back the theory with strong test performance. Statisticians drowning in high-dimensional predictors gain a reduction they can trust not to throw away the signal.
arxiv-2512-19171:
Bingyang Kelvin Liu, Ziyu Patrick Chen, and David Woodruff split language model reasoning from language model talking. In a normal model, thinking and word choice happen in one stream, so a bad word can derail the whole chain. Their JEPA-Reasoner thinks in a hidden continuous space, and a separate Talker module turns the finished thought into text.

Isolation contains errors, since token slips cannot leak back into the reasoning. The Talker also sees the entire reasoning path at once, and mixed hidden states can hold several hypotheses open. In controlled tests, a small decoupled model more than doubled its coupled twin's score on grade-school math problems.
arxiv-2512-19571: Rafael Benjumea Cejas and Juan Carlos García Vázquez give an elementary proof of a classical implication in complex analysis. The Schwarz-Pick Lemma bounds how far a holomorphic self-map of the disk can move points, in the disk's own geometry. The Ahlfors-Schwarz-Pick Lemma is its stronger, curvature-based cousin. The short article shows, with basic tools only, that the classical lemma follows directly from the Ahlfors version, a tidy route for students meeting both results.
arxiv-2512-19771:
Jun Jie Miao and Tianrui Wang work in fractal geometry. They measure how rich a measure spread on a fractal set can be. Their sets are called non-autonomous conformal attractors. They extend Moran sets and the limits of iterated function systems. In them, the rules of the build may change from step to step. The measures are generalized q-dimensions, a family of spectra set by a parameter q.

First, they prove that key values of pressure functions always bound those dimensions from above. Then, under set gap rules, they get exact formulas for the dimensions. The formulas get simpler for Bernoulli measures, the natural weights on such builds. A last part narrows all of this to the autonomous case. There, the same rules repeat at each scale.
arxiv-2512-19971:
Taiki Matsushita and four co-authors compute a sideways flow of spin in exotic superconductors. The spin Nernst effect makes a spin current at right angles to a heat gradient. In spin-triplet superconductors, Cooper pairs carry spin one. The intrinsic form of the effect has two sources. Past work could conflate the two.

One source is direct. It comes from quasiparticles, driven by Berry curvature from the triplet pairs. The other source is indirect. A supercurrent arises to cancel the bulk thermoelectric charge current, and it carries spin along. That channel dies when the condensate shows no spin polarization in momentum space. In nonunitary cases it can match the first. A fair count of the effect must book the second channel in full.
arxiv-2512-20171:
Toshiki Takadera, Shin'ichi Hirano, and Tsutomu Kobayashi use the emptiest places in the cosmos to test modified gravity. Cosmic voids are vast, underdense regions. They react with care to how gravity and dark energy behave. The authors work in Horndeski theory, cast as the effective field theory of dark energy. Void birth is modeled by the dynamics of spherical mass shells. They track how the changes to gravity shift the critical density contrast a region must cross to count as a void.

The shift comes out an order of magnitude below the dark-energy parameter that drives it. Two effects near cancel, and kinetic braiding's time drift is the focus. The Sheth-van de Weygaert size function then gives scale-dependent changes to void counts. Small scales follow the changed matter power spectrum. Large scales add the critical-contrast part.
arxiv-2512-20371:
Nelson R F Braga and Yan F Ferreira model quarkonia, bound states of a heavy quark and antiquark, using holography. Their masses follow Regge trajectories, curves relating mass to excitation level, and the real curves bend rather than running straight. A good model must reproduce that bend.

The authors apply the WKB approximation with the Langer correction inside a holographic setup. The resulting trajectory formula matches one expected from solving the Cornell potential in a relativistic equation. Fits to measured quarkonium masses come out with very good accuracy. Decay constants computed in the same model also agree fairly with values taken from experiment. The work supports holography as a measuring tool for heavy-flavour studies.
arxiv-2512-20471:
Yong-Kang Huang, Yao Ji, Bo-Xuan Shi, and Yu-Ming Wang complete a missing piece of nucleon physics. The nucleon distribution amplitude describes how momentum is shared among the quarks inside a proton or neutron. Its scale dependence is governed by a renormalization-group equation, known only at one loop until now.

The authors determine the two-loop equation for the first time. That supplies the last missing piece for full next-to-leading-logarithmic corrections to nucleon form factors in hard-collinear factorization. Using a conformal expansion, they build an analytic solution capturing how the key coefficients shift with scale. Three sample models show the two-loop evolution clearly changes the simpler predictions, so precision form-factor work must include it.
arxiv-2512-21171:
Amartya Chakrabortty, Haradhan Dutta, and Hari Shankar Mahato prove theorems about a two-fluid mixture threading a sponge. The domain is three-dimensional space drilled by a periodic array of obstacles, the spacing far larger than the holes, the dilute regime. The mixture obeys coupled Navier-Stokes and Cahn-Hilliard equations with oscillating viscosity, a source term, no-slip on the outer wall, free slip on every obstacle.

For each perforation scale, weak solutions are shown to exist with estimates uniform in the scale, the prelude to homogenization. Passing to the limit, the obstacles leave little trace: no resistance term, unchanged diffusion, and only a time-dependent effective viscosity remembers the microstructure. If the capillary coefficient vanishes in the limit, flow and phase dynamics decouple; otherwise the coupling survives, weighted by the coefficient's square root. Porous-media modelers gain a rigorous bridge from pore-scale physics to macroscopic equations.
arxiv-2512-21371:
Instead of filtering scam messages, why not waste the scammers' time and study them up close? Yifan Yao, Baojuan Wang, and five co-authors built LURE, a system that sends language-model chatbots into illicit Telegram video-chat scams posing as victims. It discovers groups, sustains adversarial conversations, and extracts payment details hidden inside images.

In over half of its chats, the bot held multi-round conversations without being spotted, engaging fifty-three actors across ninety-eight groups. The transcripts expose how these operations run: payment flows, upselling scripts, and tactics for migrating victims between platforms. The work flips Turing's imitation game into a defensive instrument, turning deception back on the deceivers.
arxiv-2512-21571:
Hui Guo, Qihang Zheng, and their co-authors present nncase, an open-source compiler that prepares large language models to run efficiently on varied hardware. Deployments face memory architectures that differ sharply between chips, and traditional compilers cope through fragmented workflows that are costly to adapt per target.

At the center of nncase is an e-graph-based term rewriting engine. E-graphs store many equivalent versions of a computation at once, sidestepping the phase ordering problem, where early optimization choices block better later ones. Three modules sit on top: one adapts code to different vector units, one searches parallel strategies with communication costs in mind, and one schedules work for on-chip cache reuse. In evaluations, nncase outperformed mainstream frameworks such as MLC LLM and Intel IPEX on Qwen3 models. On plain CPUs it matched the hand-optimized llama.cpp, a notable result for automated compilation.
arxiv-2512-21671:
Sebastian Forster, Gramoz Goranci, and Ali Momeni maintain spectral sparsifiers for directed hypergraphs that keep changing. A sparsifier is a small stand-in that preserves a graph's essential spectral properties, letting algorithms run faster. Hypergraphs generalize graphs by letting one edge join many vertices, and directed hypergraphs add orientation. Real data changes constantly, so the sparsifier must update under insertions and deletions.

Their algorithm is fully dynamic and strikingly simple. It maintains a sparsifier whose size is near-optimal, growing with the square of the vertex count divided by the square of the accuracy parameter, times logarithmic factors. The amortized update time depends on the hypergraph's rank, the largest hyperedge size, again times logarithmic factors. They extend the method to the batch-dynamic parallel setting, where many changes arrive at once. It is the first spectral sparsification algorithm of its kind there.
arxiv-2512-21871:
Naen Xu, Shouling Ji, and their co-authors test whether large vision-language models recognize and respect copyright when copyrighted material is shown to them as images. A model that happily reproduces book excerpts, lyrics, or news text from a picture of the page creates legal and ethical exposure for its deployers.

The team built a benchmark of fifty thousand multimodal query-content pairs covering book excerpts, news articles, music lyrics, and code documentation. Each item appears in two scenarios, with a copyright notice visible and without one, and the notice itself comes in four forms. Even the strongest closed-source models showed failures to recognize and respect the copyrighted content, including cases where the notice was in front of them. The authors propose a tool-augmented defense framework that reduced infringement risk across all scenarios. Their conclusion is that copyright awareness must be engineered into multimodal models.
arxiv-2512-21971:
Numerical integration on manifolds draws on algebra that tracks how methods compose. A recent line of work encodes them in pre- and post-Hopf algebroids. Adrien Busnot Laurent, Yunnan Li, and Yunhe Sheng introduce post-Hopf algebroids, generalizing the pre-Hopf versions built for aromatic series in geometric integration.

They construct action post-Hopf algebroids from actions of post-Hopf algebras, and show the enveloping algebra of a post-Lie-Rinehart algebra is a post-Hopf algebroid. As a byproduct they build the free post-Lie-Rinehart algebra from a magma algebra mapped into derivations of an algebra. Applications to geometric numerical integration close the paper, tying the abstraction to integrators that respect manifold structure.
arxiv-2512-22071: Nikolai Peters summarizes recent Belle and Belle II results on semileptonic B decays, covering inclusive and exclusive determinations of the CKM elements Vcb and Vub alongside lepton flavor universality tests. The summary draws on the full Belle dataset and the Belle II sample of three hundred sixty-one inverse femtobarns from twenty eighteen to twenty twenty-two. These measurements feed the long-standing inclusive-versus-exclusive CKM tensions.
arxiv-2512-22171:
Stefan Edelkamp plans missions for fleets of agents moving on graphs such as grids, where several goals wait to be visited. Unlike classic multi-agent path finding, his solver also decides which agent should take which goal, and updates that assignment as it plans. Goals, conflicts at nodes, and conflicts on edges all have to be handled together.

Surprisingly, Edelkamp shows the discrete versions can be solved in polynomial time, even though usual vehicle routing on general graphs is NP-hard. His implemented planner produces conflict-free, optimized routes. Global assignment strategies remove most conflicts in advance. The rest are cleared by local re-assignment, by interleaving paths, by an ants-on-a-stick style maneuver, and by moving finished agents out of their destinations.
arxiv-2512-22271:
Adam N. Elmachtoub, Kumar Goutam, and Roger Lederman tackle pricing for scheduled services, where customers pick among options that differ in timing, like delivery dates or appointment windows. Options substitute for each other, costs and demand vary sharply across them, and each needs its own price. Their system has been used inside Amazon businesses and tested in a live experiment.

The system first splits the marketplace into segments using decision trees. Within each segment, a parametric choice model estimates how customers convert, capturing effects like reference prices that scheduled services naturally produce. Fast heuristics then optimize prices. In a live A/B test at one Amazon business, the system beat the current pricing system on every key metric and raised the target metric by nineteen percent.
arxiv-2512-22671:
Pere Martra reports a split nature inside pruned language models. Shrinking the expansion ratio of the gated MLP layers in Llama-3.2 models damaged exactly the expected abilities. The pruning was guided by a peak-to-peak size rule. Factual knowledge tests, grade-school math, and perplexity all degraded as expected. Instruction-following, however, moved the opposite way, gaining sharply at a 2.4-times balance ratio in both the one-billion and three-billion parameter models.

Seven expansion-ratio setups were benchmarked across knowledge, math, reading, instruction-following, and truthfulness suites. Multi-step reasoning stayed robust throughout. Martra argues the expansion ratio is not merely a compression dial. It is a design parameter that reshapes a model's skill profile in a lopsided way. That challenges the field's assumption that pruning degrades everything across the board.
arxiv-2512-23471:
Thomas Haschka and Joseph Bakarji ask how the hidden topic structure of a large text collection can be mapped without fixing a taxonomy in advance. Their arXiv record carries a different title than the catalog entry, and the record governs here. Modern language models turn documents into dense numeric embeddings, yet most systems still group them flatly or force them into preset categories.

Their method builds a tree by slowly relaxing local density rules on those embeddings, so tight topic groups merge step by step into broader themes. On standard benchmarks, meaning lined up best at middle density levels, and sharp transitions marked real changes in topic scale. Applied to institutional and scientific collections, the trees exposed major fields, nearby disciplines, and emerging clusters.
arxiv-2512-23571:
Julie Fendler, Chantal Guihenneuc, and Sophie Ancelet improve a Bayesian tool used in health risk studies. Bayesian profile regression mixture models group people by their pattern of exposures and link those groups to a health outcome, here survival. In practice the computer sampling behind the models, Markov chain Monte Carlo, has given unstable clusterings across applications.

The authors blame two causes: the sampler getting trapped in local modes of the posterior distribution, and different post-processing choices applied to its output. They consider parallel tempering, a technique that runs coupled chains to escape local traps, and they run a simulation study comparing sampling algorithms and post-treatment procedures. Guidelines follow from the comparison, and the methods are applied to a problem in radiation epidemiology.
arxiv-2512-23771:
D. M. F. Bischoff van Heemskerck pushes a long tradition of fluid analogues of quantum theory one step further, starting from the old fact that some fluid equations resemble the Schrödinger equation. Working with an Euler-Korteweg vortex in an inviscid, barotropic, isothermal fluid, and adding Korteweg capillary stresses, the author derives a complex wave equation for the flow's momentum and continuity equations. The work assumes the vortex's angular momentum matches the reduced Planck constant in size.

With uniform convection added, the weak-field form of that wave equation becomes, in form, Schrödinger's equation. The model yields analogues of the de Broglie wavelength, the Einstein-Planck relation, the Born rule, and the uncertainty principle. Accounting for the wave field's finite propagation speed forces the Lorentz transformation into the derivation. The resulting equation is in effect the Klein-Gordon equation, with Schrödinger's equation recovered at low speeds.
arxiv-2512-23971:
Zhiming Lin and four co-authors teach a language model to fix Chinese spelling without any labeled examples. Spelling correction matters for real-world Chinese text processing, but supervised systems depend on expensive annotation and stumble on novel errors. CEC-Zero removes the oversight: the model makes its own training signal from clean text.

The framework synthesizes misspelled inputs from correct text, then grades candidate corrections with a cluster-consensus reward combining semantic similarity and agreement among candidates, and optimizes the policy with PPO reinforcement learning. The authors report gains of roughly ten to thirteen F1 points over supervised baselines and five to eight points over strong fine-tuned language models across nine benchmarks. They also prove the rewards are unbiased and the method converges. They present it as a label-free pattern for noisy text pipelines. The work appears as an AAAI 2026 poster.
arxiv-2512-24071:
Jiajun Mo and an international team study a magnetic metal. Its formula is Gd3Ru4Al12. The compound hosts skyrmions, tiny swirling spin patterns. Such patterns are prized for future spintronic devices. Why this compound forms them has been unclear. Conduction electrons mediate many competing interactions between spins.

The team fits several kinds of data at once. Neutron scattering provides the core evidence. Resonance data and magnetization curves join the fit. From this they build a realistic microscopic model. Two forces matter beyond frustration. Dipolar forces compete with a preference for spins to lie in a plane. That contest stabilizes the observed phases. They include a hexagonal skyrmion crystal. Two distinct meron crystals appear as well. Polarized X-ray data confirm one meron texture. At higher temperatures, a spiral spin-liquid picture fits.
arxiv-2512-24371:
Alexander Cox and Daniel Hernandez-Hernandez solve a constrained investing problem. An agent trades in a market with derivatives. She maximizes utility under her own beliefs. A second demand binds her. The mark-to-market value of her portfolio must stay above a threshold. That valuation uses a more pessimistic, model-independent method.

The two demands create a novel optimization problem. The investment must satisfy a pathwise constraint at all times. For complete markets, the optimal terminal wealth is characterized. A max-plus decomposition for supermartingales gives the form. The Black-Scholes-Merton model then makes everything explicit. The process in the decomposition is obtained in closed form. Numerical work studies optimal portfolios with options. Those options are mispriced relative to the agent's beliefs. The setup models real desks that mark positions conservatively.
arxiv-2512-24471:
The CMS Collaboration searches for charged Higgs bosons in proton-proton collisions. The data come from the CMS detector at the Large Hadron Collider. Collision energy is thirteen tera-electronvolts. The target decay produces a top quark and a bottom quark. Final states hold one lepton, missing momentum, and at least two b jets. The mass range searched runs from two hundred giga-electronvolts to one tera-electronvolt.

Results are read inside a generalized two-Higgs-doublet model. That model adds extra Yukawa couplings of Higgs bosons to quarks. An excess appears over the standard model expectation. Its local significance is about two point four standard deviations at a mass near six hundred giga-electronvolts. That is a hint, not a discovery. Limits are set on the production rate times branching fraction. Ranges of the extra couplings are excluded at ninety-five percent confidence.
arxiv-2512-24571:
Md Hasan Saju and five colleagues generate security queries across incompatible platforms. Security operations centers monitor enterprise systems through SIEM platforms. Splunk, Sentinel, Qradar, SecOps, and the Elastic Stack all differ. Their query languages differ most of all. An analyst must learn each one or translate by hand. That slows threat hunting across mixed environments.

Their framework, SynRAG, writes the queries automatically. An analyst supplies one platform-agnostic specification. Platform-specific, executable queries come out for each target system. Detection and investigation queries are both covered. The evaluation used Qradar and Google SecOps as representative platforms. Rival base models from several major families served as baselines. SynRAG produced significantly better queries than those models. Cross-platform security work gets simpler as a result.
arxiv-2512-24671:
Mary Kreidel, Julian Ingham, Xuanjing Chu, Jesse Balgley, and co-authors probe how superconductivity pairs electrons in the Weyl semimetal molybdenum ditelluride. Earlier measures of how far magnetic fields enter the material gave conflicting clues about gaps and nodes. They use a microwave resonator to measure kinetic inductance, a quantity closely tied to that penetration depth.

High precision lets them see a power-law change with temperature and measure an unusual response tied to the pairing state. Readers get fresh evidence on unusual superconductivity in a topological material. The method also shows how precise inductance measures can settle questions that older data left open.
arxiv-2512-24871:
Alma Brambilla, Laura De Lorenzis, and Lorenza Petrini model fracture and fatigue in pseudoelastic shape memory alloys with a variational phase-field approach in one dimension. The model builds on the Auricchio-Petrini constitutive law and couples damage growth with phase change, the process giving these alloys their recoverable deformation. A bar under steady and cyclic loading is studied analytically and numerically.

A change strain limit, beyond which the material response changes character, is a key new feature. Tuning settings matches varied large-scale patterns, from uniform response to localization. Materials readers get an approach for predicting cracking and fatigue life in shape memory parts.
arxiv-2601-00071:
Zhe Yang, Jian-Pin Wu, and Peng Liu examine how mixed-state entanglement measures behave in a gravity model that shows two kinds of phase change. One change mimics a metal turning into an insulator, and the other is the Hawking-Page change between thermal space and a black hole. Their 2026 paper works in Einstein-Born-Infeld massive gravity, a theory with nonlinear electric fields and added mass terms for gravity.

A wedge-based measure proves especially sharp for the metal-insulator-like change, where higher-order terms line up with the crossover point. For Hawking-Page changes, all the measures they test detect both smooth and abrupt transitions. Near the smooth case, every geometric quantity shares one critical exponent, one third. The authors present the wedge measure as a strong extra probe of phase changes.
arxiv-2601-00671:
Tianyu Zhao and Llion Jones introduce a memory layer for sequence models that tries to escape a familiar trade-off. Standard attention can store unbounded context but costs grow quadratically, while cheaper linear variants have only a small fixed memory. Their Fast-weight Product Key Memory is a sparse, fast-changing memory that updates at both training and test time.

Updates use chunk-level gradient steps on a local memory-rewrite objective, applied only to the sparse slots a token activates, in the spirit of test-time training. That lets the layer memorize and retrieve many new key-value pairs quickly while keeping per-token compute low and fixed. Experiments cast it as an episodic memory that complements the broader semantic knowledge stored in a model.
arxiv-2601-01271:
Qingxiao Tao, Xiaodong Gu, Hao Zhong, and Beijun Shen present CatchAll, a system that helps language models write proper exception-handling code across a whole software repository. Handling errors well keeps programs from crashing or leaking resources. But models usually see only a snippet, not the web of calls that shapes the right fix.

CatchAll feeds the model three layers of knowledge. It maps which errors each library call can raise, traces how errors travel through nearby call chains, and adds reusable handling patterns mined from other projects. The team built two new benchmarks for this task, one large and one runnable. CatchAll beat strong baselines on code quality scores, on predicting the intent of the handling code, and on tests passed. The work moves AI coding help from single functions toward real repositories.
arxiv-2601-01371:
Yinan Shen, Yichen Zhang, and Wen-Xin Zhou study stochastic gradient descent, the workhorse training method of machine learning, when the data arrive as a dependent stream. Most theory assumes each data point is independent. Real streams, from markets to sensors to sequential decisions, break that assumption, and older results suggested a trade-off between estimation accuracy and regret.

The authors show the method adapts on its own to two broad kinds of dependence, including streams that never settle into a fixed pattern. For finite samples, the final iterate achieves optimal estimation error and optimal regret at the same time, so the supposed trade-off can be avoided. Over long runs, the iterates settle into a Gaussian distribution with a small, controlled remainder. A new geometric approximation lets the data range over unbounded values. For sparse online regression, their variant uses minimal storage and still reaches long-term optimality.
arxiv-2601-02271:
Paweł Nurowski asks whether Western tonal harmony had to take the form it did, or whether other forms were possible on the same twelve notes. He sets aside the physics of vibrating strings and treats harmony as algebra on a cycle of twelve steps. A harmonic system is defined by splitting the interval of a fifth into two complementary thirds.

Working through that definition gives a complete list of possible systems in twelve tone equal temperament, each drawn as a graph. Standard Western harmony turns out to be one of twelve systems with the same abstract structure. Only four keep the circle of fifths fully connected, and an argument from the Chinese remainder theorem favors a different, non Western system as the most natural one on number grounds.
arxiv-2601-02371:
Samuele Marro, Alan Chan, and many co authors in the Lightweight Agent Standards Working Group propose a simple way for websites to tell automated agents what they may and may not do. Language model agents now navigate pages, extract structured data, and complete tasks end to end, far beyond what the old robots dot txt convention was designed for. Without a clear permission channel, sites resort to blanket blocking and CAPTCHAs.

Their answer is a manifest file, agent-permissions dot json, written in the same spirit as robots dot txt. Owners list allowed interactions in plain JSON and can point to APIs where those exist. Agents can parse the file automatically and obey it. The low effort on both sides is meant to protect useful automation, commerce, and accessibility tools.
arxiv-2601-02471:
Xueyuan Hu and five co authors classify a family of quantum operations for continuous variable systems, the systems described by quantities such as light field quadratures rather than qubits. The operations studied respect time translation symmetry, meaning they treat a shift in time origin as irrelevant, and they are Gaussian, the well behaved class that maps Gaussian states to Gaussian states. A full sorting for this case had been missing.

Several results familiar from the discrete case break down here. The authors find differences in how such operations can be physically and thermodynamically implemented, in whether their asymmetry measures grow with system size, and in catalytic advantages. They supply tools for the class, including a pair of asymmetry measures that are fully non extensive. Combining symmetry, Gaussianity, and thermodynamic limits creates structure no single limit shows.
arxiv-2601-02571:
Azuka Chiejina and four co authors present O-DSS, an open framework that lets cellular networks and radar systems share mid band radio spectrum without harmful interference. Demand for mid band frequencies keeps growing, while incumbent radars, including shipborne and fast airborne systems, must be protected. Existing access systems rely on fixed sensing stations, which react slowly and cannot adapt well.

Built to comply with the O-RAN architecture and deployed as a modular application, O-DSS detects radar from low overhead network performance metrics and locates it from spectrogram data. Detection takes about sixty milliseconds and evacuation about seven hundred, beating existing baselines. Fine grained radio controls, such as blanking resource blocks and adapting modulation around radar, keep service running. Tests in simulation and over the air testbeds show robust protection for incumbents.
arxiv-2601-03471:
Mingyang Wei and ten co-authors present EpiQAL, a benchmark that tests how well language models answer questions in epidemiology, the study of disease in whole populations. Good answers require weighing study evidence about disease burden, spread, and interventions. Most medical benchmarks test clinical facts or single-patient reasoning instead, leaving population-level inference untested.

EpiQAL has three subsets built from open-access papers on varied diseases. They move from factual recall to multi-step inference to rebuilding conclusions from incomplete information. Tests of fifteen models showed limited skill, with multi-step inference the hardest part, and bigger models did not always win. Step-by-step prompting helped that hardest part. The benchmark gives health researchers a sharper tool for judging AI help.
arxiv-2601-03571:
Zhi-Xin Jia, Tao Zhu, and Zhoujian Cao test how well future gravitational wave observatories could check whether gravity itself breaks basic symmetries. They consider violations of Lorentz symmetry and parity, two rules Einstein's theory respects. The plan combines third-generation ground detectors with space detectors such as LISA, Taiji, and TianQin, watching the same black hole mergers across frequency bands.

Using a parameterized waveform framework, they model how violations would warp the signals. They study a loud golden event and a very massive binary among their test cases. Multi-band watching tightened the possible limits on violations by several orders of magnitude compared with current bounds, across both high and low frequency effects. Sharper tests of gravity's rules could reveal where Einstein's theory finally needs revision.
arxiv-2601-03671:
Weiqi Liu and four co-authors present NeuronScope, a multi-agent framework for explaining what single neurons inside language models respond to. The task is complicated by polysemanticity: one neuron often fires for several unrelated concepts, so one-pass explanations miss much of its behavior. NeuronScope turns interpretation into an iterative process guided by the neuron's own activations.

The framework splits activations into atomic semantic pieces, clusters them into distinct modes, and refines each account using feedback from the activations themselves. Experiments showed it uncovered hidden multi-concept behavior and produced explanations matching activations far better than single-pass baselines. Clearer neuron-level accounts help the field audit what models have actually learned, a step toward systems whose inner workings can be inspected rather than guessed at.
arxiv-2601-04171:
Mohit Raghavendra, Anisha Gunjal, Bing Liu, and Yunzhong He test a way to grade code patches without running any tests. Checking patches matters because grades drive both learning by reward and gains from trying many candidates. Running code is grounded but costly to set up, while patch classifiers are cheaper yet less tied to the code base.

Their Agentic Rubrics method sends an expert agent into the repository to write a checklist grounded in that code. Candidate patches are then scored against the checklist alone. On SWE-Bench Verified with parallel test-time search, rubrics beat the strongest baseline compared by at least a few points on two Qwen coder models. Scores align with true test outcomes and also flag faults that tests miss, the four authors report.
arxiv-2601-04371:
Alexander Gnedin solves a clean gambling problem in a 2026 arXiv paper: numbers arrive one at a time, drawn independently from a discrete uniform distribution. a player who must stop once, with no recall, wants the best final result. When the number of draws and the size of the range grow together, the discrete problem is known to have a tractable limit form built on a planar Poisson process.

Working in that limit, Gnedin finds the solution for the uniform case and identifies the optimal stopping rule. Through a change of time variable, the rule matches a known asymptotic solution to Lindley's classic problem of minimizing the expected rank of the chosen value. The result ties two old stopping problems together and gives the uniform problem the same kind of complete answer its continuous cousins enjoy.
arxiv-2601-04971:
Moiré patterns, the shimmering grids that appear when two fine patterns overlap, have transformed physics in stacked two-dimensional layers. Ilya Popov and Elena Besley extend the idea into three dimensions in a 2026 paper. In two-dimensional materials such as graphene, lattice mismatch and twist angle produce moiré patterns with widely tunable electronic properties, from insulators to superconductors. Three-dimensional structures open an entirely new crystallographic space.

That space is defined by the elements of three-dimensional rotations, far richer than a single twist angle. Mapping it sets out a new branch of crystallography for bulk moiré materials. If three-dimensional moiré systems prove as tunable as their flat cousins, they could host new electronic phases in ordinary bulk crystals rather than delicate stacked flakes.
arxiv-2601-05271:
Xiran Fan and 6 co-authors feed a transaction model the rich text of shop names, in place of bare codes, in a 2026 paper. Pay nets throw off huge piles of data on how folks and shops act. Base models for that data read rows in turn, but they turn shop fields into plain codes. That swap throws away the sense in the text of a name, sense that could lift the calls the model makes.

Their mixed build uses points in space made by a language model from the shop text. That restores the lost sense. It minds the cost bar for live pay work, where each call has a split-second clock. Keen reads of past buys feed fraud checks, loan calls, and spend charts. The build shows how a big model can lend its smarts off-line, with no seat in the hot path of a pay.
arxiv-2601-05771:
M Rajesh Kannan and Rahul Roy investigate in 2026 a newer measure of graph connectedness called the l1-Fiedler value. The classical algebraic connectivity uses the second smallest Laplacian eigenvalue and an l2 constraint. A recent variational version replaces that constraint with an l1 norm, producing the parameter they study.

The authors derive a Nordhaus-Gaddum type inequality relating the value on a graph and its complement. For trees they find which shapes maximize and minimize the value, including trees with fixed diameter, maximum degree, or pendant vertex count. They connect the parameter to Laplacian matrices, bound it through edge connectivity, and characterize the graphs where equality holds. A formula describes how adding pendant vertices changes the value.
arxiv-2601-05971:
Aurora Hiveley continues in 2026 the study of Permutation Wordle, a deduction game where a player guesses a secret ordering in as few tries as possible. Earlier work by Kutin and Smithline introduced the game and proposed a cyclic shift plan, conjecturing it is optimal. Hiveley's investigation examines how information is gained, and sometimes wasted, during play.

The analysis considers an arbitrary player plan and tracks when feedback repeats information the player already had. Several methods construct secret permutations designed to force inefficient repetition against a given plan. Proofs of those methods' efficacy accompany the constructions. The work advances the optimality question indirectly: any plan claiming to be optimal must first avoid the repetition traps documented here.
arxiv-2601-06071:
Majid Darehmiraki gives diffusion models a control-theory foundation in a 2026 paper. Diffusion models generate images and other data by reversing a noise-adding process. They are usually treated as black-box stochastic systems, with little insight into why sampling stays stable.

Darehmiraki places both directions of the process inside the port-Hamiltonian framework, a way of modeling systems through energy flow. The score function becomes the gradient of a learnable energy. The reverse, generative process then looks like a feedback-controlled system where dissipation, the controlled loss of energy, stabilizes sampling. The setup yields stability guarantees that do not depend on how accurate the score estimate is. A simple worked example illustrates the idea.
arxiv-2601-06771:
Shihui Feng wrote a 2026 arXiv paper with Baiyue He, Dragan Gasevic, and Alec Kirkley. The paper sets out a new way to map how learning takes place. It calls the way Heterogeneous Interaction Network Analysis, or HINA for short. The name points to links of more than one kind.

Most older work treats learning as a chain of acts by one learner. It can also treat each link as if it were much like the next link. The authors say that view misses how acts spread out in real class settings. HINA works at more than one level at once. It tracks hard learning steps as they move across people and tools. For teams who study how people learn, the paper gives a clear plan to use and test.
arxiv-2601-07271:
Research by Mohan Raj Chanthran and co-authors was posted on arXiv in 2026. It deals with Document-Level Zero-Shot relation extraction with entity side information. The preprint joined the arXiv PAPERS collection in 2026. Document-Level Zero-Shot Relation Extraction (DocZSRE) aims to predict unseen relation labels in text documents without prior training on specific relations.

Existing approaches rely on Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate synthetic data for unseen labels, which poses challenges for low-resource languages like Malaysian English. For specialists, the preprint offers a compact account of the problem and the authors' approach.
arxiv-2601-07871:
Minh H. N. Le and colleagues argue that heart disease data should be analyzed together, not in separate pipelines. Cardiovascular disease arises from inherited risk, molecular programs, and tissue remodeling. Clinicians see that remodeling through imaging. Health systems now gather cardiac MRI, CT, and echocardiography alongside bulk, single-cell, and spatial transcriptomics. Yet these data types are still usually analyzed apart. Their 2026 preprint reviews imaging-anchored multiomics.

Anchoring molecular data to images ties gene activity to visible tissue change. That link can reveal which molecular programs drive the patterns doctors see. Integration is hard because the data differ in scale, format, and noise. The authors survey how the field is meeting that challenge. The paper serves cardiology and genomics scholars. It makes the case for joint analysis as the default, not the exception.
arxiv-2601-08271: Angshul Majumdar formalizes sparse control for tool-using language model agents. The 2026 arXiv paper describes a regime learning theory has largely ignored. Agents choose in sequence from a massive discrete set of tools, APIs, and documents. Only a small, unknown subset matters for any fixed task distribution. Majumdar names this setting sparse agentic control and gives policies block-sparse representations. The paper argues sparsity is necessary for polynomial-time stability in such systems. The result guides theory for agents whose action menus keep growing.
arxiv-2601-08371: Anastasios Tsalakopoulos and co-authors present Geo-NVS-w for novel view synthesis from wild photo collections. Their 2026 arXiv paper targets unstructured images taken under varied real-world conditions. Existing in-the-wild methods already produce strong novel views. Yet they often lack geometric grounding on complex surfaces and can yield inconsistent results. Geo-NVS-w adds geometry awareness with an SDF renderer, which models surfaces as signed distance fields. The aim is high-fidelity views that stay consistent in shape, useful for tourism photos, heritage scans, and scene reconstruction.
arxiv-2601-08571: S. R. Luwang and co-authors discover market regimes and study returns inside each regime. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes that financial markets alternate between tranquil periods and episodes of stress. Return dynamics can change substantially across those regimes, so one global model may mislead. The team studies developed and developing equity indices. Their pipeline uses Hilbert-Huang-based regime identification and profiling, then variable-length Markov modeling of categorized returns. Regime-aware models could improve risk forecasts that now assume calm and crisis behave alike.
arxiv-2601-08871:
Junhua Huang, Chao Huang, and Chenliang Xu work on how sound is mixed for a film scene. A scene mix must weigh speech, song, and sound effects so the tale stays clear. That mix is now done by hand, and it takes long hours of skilled work. New tools can rebalance sound with help from the image, but we know little of which image cues help most.

The team tests which sight cues guide a good sound boost. A face in close view may call for clear speech. A wide street view may call for more street sound. A reader who makes film or games gets a map of cues that count. It can steer auto mix tools to choices a human mixer would trust.
arxiv-2601-09371:
Ángel López-Oriona and Ying Sun build new tests for dependence in functional time series. Their 2026 arXiv paper asks whether curve-valued data, observed over time, behave like pure white noise. The tests rest on functional quantile autocorrelation, a quantile-based way to track dependence.

Older tests lean on the classical autocovariance kernel, which outliers and nonlinear patterns can fool. The new approach uses quantile excursion sets to catch dependence in a more robust way. It is built for infinite-dimensional data, where each observation is a whole curve. Such tools help analysts check models for data like daily pollution or yield curves.
arxiv-2601-09671:
Frederick J. Vrba and a large team report distances and motions for the coldest known classes of star-like bodies. Their 2026 arXiv paper covers 173 L and T dwarfs observed by the US Naval Observatory's infrared astrometry program. Parallaxes and proper motions were measured with the ASTROCAM imager on the 1.55-meter telescope at Flagstaff Station.

The sample holds 74 L dwarfs and 99 T dwarfs, some single and some in binary systems. Each object was observed at a median of 62 epochs over about five years. Near-infrared photometry comes with the positions. Distances turn faint smudges into a mapped population of the solar neighborhood's coldest residents.
arxiv-2601-09871:
Andrea Ferrario, Alessandro Facchini, and Juan M. Durán argue that epistemology can rescue a key idea about human-AI teamwork. Their 2026 arXiv paper concerns human-AI complementarity: a human with AI support beating either one alone. The claim has spread through the human-AI interaction literature.

Complementarity generalizes the older reliance paradigm and offers a more practical frame than the contested idea of trust in AI. The authors ask what epistemology, the study of knowledge, adds. Grounding the claim in how knowledge works could tell designers when teamwork truly helps. It also clarifies what evidence would prove complementarity real.
arxiv-2601-10371:
Malte Hellmann and Jürgen Gauss extend a symmetry trick to harder point groups. Coupled cluster math is a top tool for molecule states. Symmetry can cut its cost by a vast share. A direct product split sorts terms by their symmetry kind. That works well for plain groups.

Non Abelian groups are less plain. Their kinds mix in rich ways. The team show the split for one such group, named C3v. They sort pair terms and cluster terms into blocks. Each block comes from a split of kinds. The work opens the trick to more molecule shapes.
arxiv-2601-10571:
C. Richard and co authors fix bias in a beam width test used in photo injectors. Such rigs make the first burst of grains for a light source. Beam width sets how well the full rig can do. A slit profiler reads that width by a mask with a thin cut.

Such reads can hold set flaws. A flaw can shift the width that is read. The team name those flaws and give fixes for them. The fixes rest on the form of the test rig. A true width read is key. It tells a lab if its source is fit to run.
arxiv-2601-11071:
The LHAASO collaboration reports observations of the pulsar wind nebula DA 495. A pulsar wind nebula is a bubble of particles blown by a spinning neutron star. DA 495 has been watched from radio to TeV gamma rays. LHAASO, a high-altitude air shower observatory, adds fresh eyes at the highest energies.

The new data reveal an energy-dependent morphology: the source's shape changes with photon energy. The water Cherenkov detector array measures an extended source of a stated angular size. Shape changes with energy trace how particles cool as they drift from the pulsar. The work helps map how a dead star keeps lighting its surroundings for tens of thousands of years.
arxiv-2601-11271:
Martin Ortiz recasts part of Serre's conjecture in geometric form in this work. His 2026 preprint deals with the weight part of that conjecture. Serre's conjecture links modular forms to Galois groups. The weight part asks which weights can arise for a given form.

Ortiz uses de Rham cohomology of special fibers for the task. Special fibers come from Shimura varieties, key spaces in number theory. He conjectures his form matches the classic one. The classic form uses Serre weights and etale cohomology. The work also builds generalized mod p BGG decompositions. Those splits break big cohomology groups into graded pieces. A geometric form could give new tools for old questions.
arxiv-2601-11371:
Stephanie Roden and five coauthors trace how hot electrons settle in metals. Their 2026 preprint deals with Fermi systems hit by light. A fast flash of light knocks electrons out of balance. The energy spread then shows a step shape from Pauli blocking.

On a femtosecond scale, electrons hit each other and share energy. Those collisions drive the spread toward a hot Fermi form. The team derives the full collision term for that process. It is the electron-electron Boltzmann collision integral. The derivation uses the random-k approximation for the math. A full term lets simulations track thermalization with more care. That matters for ultrafast optics and laser-cut metals.
arxiv-2601-11471:
James O'Neill, Robert Clancy, Mariia Matskevichus, and Fergal Reid shrink transformer memory. Their 2026 preprint gives Low-Rank Key Value attention, or LRKV. Transformers store keys and values for all past tokens. That KV cache is a primary bottleneck on memory.

The team exploits redundancy across attention heads to cut it. Each layer shares one full-rank KV projection for all heads. Low-rank, head-specific residuals then restore each head's flavor. The design gives a smooth dial between two extremes. One end shares all, the other keeps heads fully apart. Compute stays efficient while memory drops in their design. Longer contexts on the same hardware are the prize.
arxiv-2601-11771:
Tong Mao, Jinchao Xu, and Xiaofeng Xu solve hard maths problems that span many variables. Such problems, called PDEs, rule heat, flow, and fields. A new route fixes the inner part of a shallow net and trains just the last layer. That turns training into a plain least squares task.

These nets sit in the random feature method and in extreme learning machines. They have shown strong results of late. The team study how to use this linear form well in high dimensions. Fast PDE tools aid design in planes, chips, and more.
arxiv-2601-12371: Nishant Rathee and Manoj K. Yadav work in algebra on skew left braces. They study extensions of these structures and their second cohomology groups. Their route goes through groups built as natural semi direct products. A skew brace extension can be written as a short exact sequence, and that form guides the work.
arxiv-2601-12571:
Benjamin Grant and Zhongyang Li study self avoiding walks on cubic graphs. A self avoiding walk never visits the same vertex twice. Cubic graphs give each vertex degree three, and the graphs here are infinite and quasi transitive. The team apply local transformations that swap each vertex for a small gadget. Each gadget is finite, symmetric, and has three ports.

To each gadget they attach a two port generating function. That function counts walks that enter and exit the gadget through set ports. Generating functions turn counting problems into algebra that can be solved. Local swaps of this kind let one graph be reshaped into another. The work asks which walk counts survive such reshaping, a core question in combinatorics.
arxiv-2601-12671:
Thamara Leandra de Deus Melo and three co authors, at Brazilian universities, classify brain tumors in MRI scans. Early tumor diagnosis is crucial for good treatment outcomes. Diagnosis is hard because lesions vary a lot and images are complex. The team evaluate convolutional neural networks in a federated learning setting, so data can stay at each hospital.

They compare models trained on original scans against preprocessed ones. Preprocessing includes resizing, grayscale conversion, normalization, filtering, and histogram equalization. They also exploit test time augmentation, a trick that averages views of a scan at test time. The study asks which pipeline choices pay off under federation. Answers guide clinics that cannot pool patient images.
arxiv-2601-13671:
Apoorva Adimulam, Rajesh Gupta, and Sumit Kumar map how teams of AI agents can be run as one system in 2026. In such setups, many autonomous agents talk and coordinate to reach shared goals. Firms now test these systems for real work, not just in labs. Loose coordination can bring chaos, cost, and risk.

The team gathers the parts of orchestration into one clear frame. Planning, policy rules, state tracking, and quality checks all sit in one layer. That layer steers the agents as a group. A shared frame could help firms adopt agent teams with more trust and control.
arxiv-2601-14271:
Denise M. Case states and proves a theorem about shared data systems in this 2026 paper. Modern systems must support accountability, even when users hold clashing legal, political, and analytic views for good. That need sets strict rules for any ontology meant to serve as a shared base layer. An ontology is a formal map of terms and their links.

Case proves an impossibility result for ontological neutrality. In her terms, neutrality means the base layer takes no side and stays stable when clashing views extend it. She shows that such a base cannot also hold causal or normative claims at its root. Her title draws the upshot: neutral substrates must be pre-causal and pre-normative.
arxiv-2601-14371:
Small asteroids and large meteoroids hit Earth often, yet their physical traits stay poorly known. When such bodies burn as fireballs in the atmosphere, their ablation and fragmentation behavior can reveal those traits. This 2026 paper, the second in its series, works on decameter-sized Earth impactors. A 2022 release of once-classified United States Government satellite sensor data changed the field. It gave hundreds of new fireball light curves for detailed study.

The authors built a Bayesian inference approach to meteoroid ablation modeling. Bayesian methods weigh how well each model fits the data against prior knowledge. Readers should note the evidence pack lists no authors for this entry. The paper's value lies in a firmer way to read fireball curves.
arxiv-2601-14471:
A. Kumar and a large team trace carbon in a fusion device in this 2026 paper. The device is the DIII-D tokamak. A helicon antenna injects radio waves to heat and drive the plasma. During high-power helicon discharge, carbon appears in the plasma. The team asks where that carbon comes from and how it travels.

Their focus is the helicon antenna surfaces themselves as a source. Carbon sputtered or released there can enter the plasma and affect its state. The study follows both sourcing and transport from those surfaces. Readers get a fuller account of impurity flow in a working tokamak, a detail that matters for clean, steady fusion runs.
arxiv-2601-14571:
Yan Meng, Kainan Chang, and Luxia Wang study energy transfer in a hybrid nanomaterial in this 2026 paper. The system pairs an organic molecule with an inorganic nanoflake. The molecule is para-sexiphenyl, known as 6P. It sits adsorbed on a finite-sized MoS2 nanoflake, a transition metal dichalcogenide. The team investigates excitation energy transfer between the two parts in theory.

They describe the electronic structure of the MoS2 nanoflake with an 11-band tight-binding model. Edge states are passivated with hydrogen atoms to restore a well-defined bandgap. The work is done in math and code. No lab test is used, but the model can be checked by lab work later. Readers get a model of how energy moves in a nanohybrid, a design used in light-harvesting and optoelectronic devices.
arxiv-2601-14771:
Puneet Sharma and four co-authors work on colon capsule endoscopy in this 2026 paper. A colon capsule is a swallowed camera that films the colon. Identifying unique polyps across its images is a critical yet challenging task for medical personnel. The volume of images is large. The cognitive load on clinicians is heavy. Labeling specific frames is also ambiguous, since one polyp appears in many frames.

The team uses multi-instance learning to identify unique polyps. In that method, a model learns from bags of frames with loose labels, rather than exact frame tags. Readers get a tool to count each polyp once, so follow-up care rests on the true count.
arxiv-2601-15571:
Tristan Simas studies how hard it is to judge sufficiency in decisions in a 2026 arXiv paper. The setting is a formal decision problem. An action set, a state space, and a utility function define it. The state space is a product of coordinates. A set of coordinates is sufficient when it pins down the optimal action. If two states agree on those coordinates, they share the same best action.

Simas characterizes the computational complexity of that judgment. In plain terms, he asks how costly it is to test whether a coordinate set suffices. The answer guides anyone who wants to trim inputs to a decision rule. Fewer needed coordinates mean simpler, cheaper decisions. Complexity bounds tell us when that trimming is feasible and when it is hopeless.
arxiv-2601-16071:
Giacomo Graziani studies the shape of neural layers built from maths maps. His 2026 preprint looks at layers made by a fixed power map. He tracks a count known as the Euclidean Distance degree. That count tells how many best close fits a plain point has. The fits are made with a plain choice of length rule.
