Graziani asks when that count stays firm as terms shift. Firm counts help teams know what a layer can and can not do. The study uses the shape maths of these layer sets. It links deep learning form to pure maths of curves and sets. The result gives a firm base for later work on layer shape.
arxiv-2601-16371:
Jiwon Jang and coauthors test a trade scope set for sky views. Their 2026 preprint sets out the PIXIS 1300BX cam and its mate scope parts. Trade sets must be checked as a whole ere use in night work. The team runs the set through lab and sky tests. Tests span sharp grade, noise and true light counts.

A full trait map tells users what the set can and can not do. It also gives a base line for later wear checks. Trade sets at low cost serve schools and small teams well. Firm trait maps help those teams plan night work. The work is a tool note for sky users.
arxiv-2601-16771:
Jiahao Li, Yunpeng Bai, Yongkang Dai, Hao Guo, Hongping Gan, and Yilei Shi build a new way to make 3D parts by machine. Parts in design files are stored as B-reps. A B-rep lists the faces, edges, and links of a solid. Past AI tools split shape and links into two tracks. That split blocked the use of text-style AI models.

Their 2026 preprint packs the whole B-rep in one token chain. Text-style models can then learn and make parts in one flow. The chain keeps both shape and links in full. This could let firms draft parts from prompts. It could also speed search in vast part stores.
arxiv-2601-17071:
Jisui Huang, Andreas Alpers, Ke Chen, and Na Lei split shots in the face of harsh light gaps. Some shots mix bright and dim zones in stark ways. Plain splits fail where light shifts that hard. Their 2026 preprint takes a two-step path. First, pixels group in small tiles called superpixels. A lean least-squares step does that group work fast.

Next, tiles merge in whole zones by a spread gauge. That gauge is the squared 2-Wasserstein gap. It weighs tile trait spreads, not just means. Clean splits feed car, scan, and scope tools. The path runs fast for big shot sets.
arxiv-2601-17171:
Yehya Cheryala, Mokhtar Z. Alaya, and Salim Bouzebda work on a hard math problem in optimal transport. The field asks how to compare and align several chance distributions at once. It is used in machine learning and statistics, where such joint matching comes up often.

The authors present one full Kantorovich duality theory for this multi-way case. The theory holds on general Polish product spaces. It needs only a bounded, continuous cost function. A clear duality result helps users check solutions and build methods on firm ground. Readers in math and data work gain a single frame where older split results now fit together.
arxiv-2601-17371:
Shuning Zhang and seven co-authors present Collab, a web plugin to help users flag deepfake videos. Deepfakes shift in space and time in subtle ways. One viewer can miss signs that a group would catch. Platforms also lack tools that scale human review. Collab lets users mark and share notes on videos as a team.

Joint annotation pools many eyes on one clip. Notes build a record that moderators can use. The tool aims at social media, where fakes spread fast. It treats viewers as partners, not just targets. That shift could raise the quality of public checks. It also gives platforms richer proof than a lone flag.
arxiv-2601-17871:
Huy Trinh, Sebastian Ratto, Elliot Creager, and George Shaker build a bridge between radar simulation and the real world. Their 2026 preprint is about FMCW radar, a type that sweeps its tone to sense range. Training radar models on real data is costly. It needs controlled tests, repeated setup, and long hours of labeling. Many teams cannot pay that price.

The team uses a digital twin shaped by physics to stand in for real rooms. Their light frame trains models in the twin for tasks like spotting people in a room and counting them. The goal is that the models still work when moved to real radar. Less time in the lab means faster progress for sensing tools.
arxiv-2601-17971:
Junior Cedric Tonga, Chen Cecilia Liu, Iryna Gurevych, and Fajri Koto turn language models into sources of cultural knowledge. Their 2026 preprint starts from a simple fact. Models soak up cultural know-how from vast and varied web text. That know-how is rich, but it sits inside the model in a loose, hidden form. Hidden knowledge is hard to check, share, or build on.

The team draws the knowledge out into a graph of cultural commonsense. Nodes and links state what people in a culture take for granted. An iterative process pulls the facts out step by step. A structured graph can serve search, teaching, and cross-cultural tools. It also lets scholars inspect what the model has absorbed.
arxiv-2601-18571:
Maël Dumas and Aliaume Lopez study when a set of graphs can be sorted by a kind of well rule. A well rule here means no chain of graphs in the set drops for ever, and no set of graphs in it all fail to hold each other. The graphs in view have a cap on how wide their tree-like form can be. Their points can bear tags.

The pair show that one can tell, from a finite plan of the set, if the set is well ruled in this sense. That is a strong claim: a finite check can settle a trait of a set with no end. Such checks sit at the base of proofs that some searches must end. They also serve the maths of graphs with caps, a field that feeds code checks and chip design.
arxiv-2601-18671:
N. Balabanova, H. Duong, and C. Hilbe study a game of give and take in which the two sides move in turns, not at once. The base game is a famed one: each side can help or cheat, and joint help pays best for both in the long run. In the turn form, one side gives first and the next side then picks its move with that gift in view. That break of step fits real trades, such as gift chains.

Each side can hold a long mind of past moves. The team ask which ways of play grow strong as groups of such players change over time. Long minds let a side tell a slip from a cheat. That skill can keep joint help alive when a same-time game would kill it. The work adds to the maths of how trust grows.
arxiv-2601-18771:
Yanming Liu and nine colleagues build Dep-Search, a way for language models to reason through hard asks with the help of search. Such models can call on out-side facts as they work, step by step. The field has grown past plain fetch-and-read plans, in which facts are pulled once and the reply is wrote at once. New plans search in rounds, with each round set by what the last round found.

Those rounds lean on each other: a late search rests on the facts and picks of the rounds ahead of it. If those links are lost, the chain can drift or loop. Dep-Search learns traces that keep the links in view as it goes. It also keeps a store that lasts across rounds, so past finds stay in hand. A chain that minds its own links should reach sounder ends.
arxiv-2601-18871:
Zoe Le Conte and nine colleagues find a small disc of stars at the heart of a far galaxy, from a time when space was young. Such discs are built by bars: long lines of stars that sweep gas to the core. The gas then forms new stars in a tight ring or disc. To find a disc of that kind at such a young age is to find that bars did their work far back in time.

Past work had shown bars in place a few years of space time past the start. This disc shows the next step: a bar that has had time to build a core disc. That means bars can shape a galaxy from its youth, not just in its old age. The find rests on sharp shots of a galaxy at what the field calls cosmic noon.
arxiv-2601-19171:
Seokhyeon Park and six co-authors study the gaps between what users want and what AI interface builders give. Generative tools can now draw polished interfaces from text prompts. Yet users often cannot state their design intent in words, and they struggle to judge or refine what comes back.

The team names these the gulfs of execution and evaluation, and offers semantic guidance to bridge them. Guidance in terms of meaning, not pixels, helps users steer by intent. The work speaks to a broad design problem: tools that generate well still fail if people cannot direct them.
arxiv-2601-19571:
Antonio Lei and Katharina Müller bring a deep number theory method to the study of graphs. Iwasawa theory tracks how algebraic objects grow across towers of number fields. Here the tower is made of directed graphs, stacked in layers with a regular symmetry. Two groups are watched as the tower climbs: the Picard group and the Bowen-Franks group of each graph.

The authors formulate and prove main conjectures for these groups in this graph setting. A main conjecture links an analytic object to an algebraic one, and proving it is a strong check on the theory. Their towers are indexed by prime powers in several directions at once. The work shows that ideas born in number theory can govern combinatorics too.
arxiv-2601-19771:
Deeksha Arun, Kevin W. Bowyer, and Patrick Flynn work on identifying people by their ears. Ear shape is stable and distinctive, making it a useful biometric. Vision transformers are strong recognisers, but they cut images into rectangular tokens. For an ear, those rectangles pull in background and hair, which pollutes the signal.

Their method, PaW-ViT, warps the ear image before recognition. The warping is rooted in anatomical knowledge of how ears are shaped. Normalising the image this way makes the transformer's job cleaner. The team tests the approach on ear verification, deciding whether two images show the same ear. Preprocessing guided by anatomy could lift other biometric systems too.
arxiv-2601-20171:
Kazuma Yamasaki and five colleagues ask who writes project documentation now that AI agents contribute code. As software work moves toward what they call SE 3.0, agents carry out more tasks and open pull requests of their own. The authors compare documentation pull requests written by agents with those written by humans.

Their study looks at how much agents contribute and how human reviewers step in. That pattern shows where trust in agent work is high and where people still check closely. The results matter for teams setting rules on agent use, since docs shape how well a project can be maintained.
arxiv-2601-20371:
Kenta Fujisawa and seven colleagues monitor a methanol maser in the star-forming region G33.641-0.228. Masers are bright, narrow radio signals from gas clouds. This one, at a frequency used to trace young massive stars, shows burst-like flashes for unknown reasons. The team watches its flux and circular polarization at high cadence.

They observe with left and right circular polarizations at the same time. The polarization pattern can reveal magnetic fields and the geometry of the bursting gas. Pinning down why these masers flare would sharpen a tool astronomers use to study how massive stars are born.
arxiv-2601-20571:
Anna van Elst, Igor Colin, and Stephan Clémençon study robust distributed learning on resource-constrained edge devices. Algorithms there must be communication-efficient, robust to corrupted data, and light in memory. Gossip-based methods meet the first need, but robustness is harder to achieve.

The authors turn to asynchronous decentralized ADMM methods for estimating quantiles, starting from the median, which resists corruption better than the mean. Edge networks, from sensors to phones, must learn without a central server and despite bad actors. Robust quantile estimation gives such networks a trustworthy summary of their data.
arxiv-2601-20871:
Rylan Malarchick measures how much trust survives each step of quantum circuit optimization. The 2026 paper spans the full compilation stack. It runs from high-level gate optimization down to pulse-level control. A modular framework links a C++ circuit optimizer with pulse simulation. The pulse model uses Lindblad dynamics, which account for noise and decay. Hardware parameters come from the IQM Garnet quantum processor.

Four optimization passes come under the lens. They are gate cancellation, commutation, rotation merging, and identity elimination. Each pass simplifies a circuit, but each can also cost fidelity. The study evaluates that cost in a systematic way. End-to-end numbers show where simplification helps and where it hurts. The work guides compiler writers who must trade neat circuits against true accuracy.
arxiv-2601-20971:
The Spherical-Rindler Framework is built in this 2026 paper as a new view of flat spacetime. It starts with Rindler-type pictures of Minkowski space. The standard hyperbolic map is shown to be one of an infinite family. Each member is a new coordinate map of the same flat space. The authors add cyclic coordinates to this family. Unlike the usual Rindler wedge, these mark out a compact region.

From that start, the frame reaches toward curved settings. Its subtitle promises a path to black hole and cosmology solutions. Compact regions of flat space give a controlled test bed. Lessons learned there can guide work on horizons and expanding worlds. The paper is a theory build, dense with geometry. It serves relativists who craft new coordinate tools.
arxiv-2601-21171:
Kamal Berahmand and four co-authors hunt abnormal nodes in networks with very few labels. Their 2026 paper presents AC2L-GAD, a method for graph anomaly detection. The task is to spot abnormal patterns in networks. Label scarcity and extreme class imbalance make it hard. Anomalies are rare almost by definition. Graph contrastive learning offers a strong unsupervised route. Old versions of it suffer two key flaws.

Random changes can break meaning in positive pairs. Naive negative sampling yields trivial, useless contrasts. The method's name answers both: active counterfactual contrastive learning. Counterfactual cases are crafted to inform, not to randomize. Active selection spends effort where the model is unsure. The work targets fraud, intrusion, and fault detection in network data.
arxiv-2601-21271:
Tram Thi Minh Tran and eight co-authors ask what augmented reality built on sound, not sight, could do in daily life. Smart glasses with speakers are already on the market. Hearing is a main way people sense context, sense change coming, and move through social space.

Yet sound-based augmentation is still little studied next to visual overlays. The authors map out uses, needs, and open design questions for everyday settings. Sound can guide without blocking the view or drawing stares. The work lays ground for tools that help people notice and navigate the world through their ears.
arxiv-2601-21371:
Sifat Chowdhury, Yihsu Chen, and Yu Zhang plan power grid upgrades that hold up against more than one hazard. Extreme weather is growing more common and knocks out power for long stretches. Some defenses help against one threat but hurt under another, such as floods versus high winds.

The authors build a two-stage plan that adapts as conditions unfold. Early choices set up the grid, and later choices respond to the hazard that arrives. Weighing clashing threats together avoids defenses that backfire. The approach gives utilities a way to spend hardening money where it protects against the widest range of storms.
arxiv-2601-21471:
Ruicheng Ao, Hongyu Chen, Siyang Gao, Hanwei Li, and David Simchi-Levi study how to find the best option when judges are cheap but biased. A language model can grade many samples at low cost. True labels from human audits are accurate but expensive, so they can only be bought for a few samples.

Unlike classic setups, the cheap judge is biased in ways that depend on the option and the context. Ground truth also arrives only where the team chooses to look. The authors design a method with firm guarantees for this setting. It fits modern evaluation, where AI judges do the bulk grading.
arxiv-2601-21571:
Neil Rathi and Alec Radford shape what a language model can do by filtering its training data before training starts. Most attempts to remove unwanted skills happen after training and can be bypassed. Filtering the data itself attacks the skill at its root.

On a test task of removing medical skills, simple filtering proved highly effective. It also held up against attempts to undo it and cost little at large scale. The result suggests data curation is a strong safety lever. Builders could decide early which skills a model should never gain, rather than patching them out later.
arxiv-2601-21671:
Divya D. Joshi, Trupti R. Sharma, and Prashant M. Gade study pattern formation in a two-dimensional grid of excitable neuron-like units. Each unit follows the Chialvo map, a simple model of a neuron that can fire. Neighbors are linked by nearest-neighbor coupling, in two different styles.

One coupling style grows ring-like patterns, and the rings widen as coupling strengthens. The other style grows spirals, which break into turbulence and fade at strong coupling. The contrast shows how the wiring rule alone can flip a system's whole behavior. Such maps help explain waves seen in brain tissue, heart muscle, and other excitable media.
arxiv-2601-21771:
Hadi Banaee and Stephanie Lowry model abstract concepts as regions in a geometric space, using chess strategy as the test case. Concepts like attack or sacrifice unfold over time and resist crisp definitions. In their framework, each concept is a region across interpretable quality dimensions.

A game becomes a trajectory moving through that space. When the path heads toward a region, the intended strategy can be recognized. The chess study is a proof of concept for the wider idea. If it generalizes, the same geometry could track strategy in teaching, sport, or negotiation, where plans are real but hard to name.
arxiv-2601-21971:
Lorenzo Mazza and co-authors teach robots to imitate surgeons. Imitation learning works well for ordinary robotic manipulation, but surgery is harder. Data are scarce, workspaces are tight, and the needed safety and predictability are exceptional. A small error at an operating table is not like a dropped cup.

The team presents a supervised mixture-of-experts architecture built for surgical tasks that unfold in phases. Specialized expert networks handle different phases of a procedure, under supervision that keeps behavior structured. Their 2026 preprint aims at policies that are both capable and predictable. Surgical robots that learn from expert surgeons could extend specialist skill to hospitals that have none on staff.
arxiv-2601-22071:
Pranav Nagarajan and co-authors debunk a sensational claim about the star BE Lyncis. BE Lyn is a well-studied pulsating star of the delta Scuti type, with large brightness swings. A recent analysis of decades of its peak-light timings claimed it is an extremely eccentric binary hosting the nearest known black hole.

The team's 2026 preprint uses astrometry from Gaia and Hipparcos, precise measurements of the star's position and motion, to test that claim. Their conclusion stands in the title: BE Lyn is not a black hole binary. The paper is also a lesson in method, showing how a timing pattern alone can mislead. And how independent data can settle an extraordinary claim before it hardens into fact.
arxiv-2601-22171:
Jort de Groot extends a framework from quantum geometry to a new setting. Spectral triples are the core objects of noncommutative geometry. Each triple has three parts. They are an algebra, a Hilbert space, and a Dirac operator. Together they encode a space and its geometry. De Groot works with the group SU(1,1), a non-compact group central to relativity and representation theory.

Using harmonic analysis on that group, he shows that a triple built from Kostant's cubic Dirac operator forms a pseudo-Riemannian spectral triple. His 2026 preprint adapts the machinery, which was designed for Riemannian cases, to the indefinite metric of pseudo-Riemannian geometry. That widens noncommutative geometry toward the spacetime-like settings where it may eventually meet physics.
arxiv-2601-22571:
Zhipeng Chen and a large team built PerfGuard, an agent that watches the true limits of its tools. Their 2026 preprint notes that most agent frames assume each tool call works, and judge tools by text blurbs alone. Real tools for visual content have sharp performance edges that blurbs hide.

PerfGuard tracks what each tool can really do, and plans with those bounds in view. That should cut failed runs and poor picks in image and video tasks. The work is a dose of realism for agent design. It treats tool skill as data, not faith.
arxiv-2601-22871:
Alexander Loth, Martin Kappes, and Marc-Oliver Pahl study how easily people fall for false content made by AI. As large models write with near-human fluency, telling real from synthetic text gets harder. Their work uses two tools, JudgeGPT and RogueGPT, to probe that weakness.

The framework splits two questions: does a text feel authentic, and who or what made it? Keeping those apart shows where human judgment fails first. The findings matter for news, schools, and platforms fighting large-scale deception. Separating authenticity from attribution also helps platforms decide whether to label, limit, or remove suspect content at scale.
arxiv-2601-23071:
Massimo Bocus and Louis Vanduyfhuys present ThermoLIB, a Python library for free energy surfaces. Such surfaces summarize how likely each state of a molecule is, and what barriers separate them. The library builds these surfaces from of molecules model run output.

It can also convert surfaces between different collective variables and pull out thermodynamic and kinetic properties. The package is free on GitHub, with docs and many guides. A shared, tested tool saves labs from rewriting the same analysis code for every project. Tutorials and extended docs ship with the library, lowering the barrier for groups new to free energy methods.
arxiv-2601-23171:
Anthony Almudevar revisits the lost submarine problem as a test case for statistical inference. The example, highlighted by Morey and co-authors in 2016, targets blind faith in confidence intervals. It asks where a lost submarine likely lies, given limited sonar-style information.

A decision-theoretic treatment weighs actions by their costs and risks, not by interval habits alone. The case shows how a tidy interval can mislead when the real question is what to do. It remains a sharp teaching example for applied statisticians. The submarine story's role is diagnostic: it exposes where confidence interval practice breaks as a formal inference statement.
arxiv-2602-02471:
Edwin Kys and 1 co-author add a detection head to stop medical image models from hallucinating anatomy, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Deep learning auto-segmentation outlines organs for radiotherapy planning. Standard models sometimes paint target structures onto slices where none exist, producing false positives that anatomy rules out.

Their gated multi-head transformer builds on a Swin U-Net design and uses context from nearby slices. A parallel detection head judges, slice by slice, whether the structure is present, and its output gates the segmentation stream. Training uses a slice-wise Tversky loss to handle lopsided class counts. On a prostate data set full of hard edge cases, the gated model's error collapsed compared with a segmentation-only rival. Detection scores tracked real presence closely, nearly wiping out spurious outlines. Valid slices kept their segmentation quality, a key need for use in clinics.
arxiv-2602-02671:
Francesco Leonardi and 2 co-authors add continuous spherical attention to machine-learned interatomic force fields, in a 2026 paper. Such force fields now power accurate atomistic runs, but most rely on fixed angular expansions that limit how freely local shapes can be weighted. Attention, if made rotation-aware, could weight each neighbor's share on the fly.

Their module extends spherical attention from tasks about rotation alone to the full molecular symmetry group, using neighbors' angular and radial coordinates. It handles equivariant interactions at low cost, meaning predictions rotate as they should with the molecule. The module plugs into current models such as MACE with no structural changes. Across benchmarks it sharpened energy and force predictions, cut high-error events, and raised robustness. The authors argue the method is a general operator for atomistic models, not a one-model trick.
arxiv-2602-02771:
J. Brandon Carter and 1 co-author review Markov random fields for categorical spatial data, with a shared tool of their own, in a 2026 paper. These models capture spatial dependence on discrete domains and are workhorses for binary observations or latent binary variables. Their behavior, however, depends heavily on formulation choices.

Core structural properties come first: clique factorization, conditional independence, and the role of neighborhood structure. Phase transition, where tiny setting changes flip the field's global character, gets careful treatment for what it does to model specification and inference. The central addition is response functions, a prior-analysis tool showing how different formulations shape implied marginal and joint distributions. A case study of direct-data models with covariates shows how formulations encode dependence in different ways. Though focused on binary fields, the principles extend to richer categorical models, and the review supplies practical guidance for reading and extending them.
arxiv-2602-02971:
A droplet coated with surfactant in an electric field is modeled by Michael A. McDougall and 2 co-authors in a 2026 paper. The drop is a leaky dielectric, meaning it conducts electricity weakly. A uniform direct-current field can deform it, and past a threshold it can start rotating steadily, an instability called Quincke rotation.

Their three-dimensional theory keeps surface charge convection, often dropped in simpler models. Coupled equations track the drop's shape, dipole moment, and surfactant distribution. In the weak-field regime the drop stays a spheroid. In the rotation regime, weakly diffusing surfactant lowers the threshold field. Surfactant elasticity can raise or lower that threshold depending on diffusion. Observed hysteresis in rotation speed can also vanish.
arxiv-2602-03071:
Finding the right moment in a video without training is the aim of Sunoh Kim and 2 co-authors in a 2026 paper. Weakly supervised grounding locates a queried segment using only video-sentence pairs, without exact boundary labels. Recent methods represent candidate segments with Gaussian proposals, bell-shaped ranges over time, but convert them to boundaries with heuristic rules that localize poorly in practice.

Their framework, Gaussian Boundary Optimization, instead solves a principled optimization problem. It balances covering the proposal against keeping the segment compact. A closed-form solution is derived, with optimality analyzed under different penalty regimes. The method is training-free and fits single or mixture proposal systems. Experiments across standard benchmarks reached state-of-the-art localization, with efficiency and generalizability shown.
arxiv-2602-03171:
Zhe Xu's solo proposal speeds up reinforcement learning by scoring every step instead of waiting for the end. Sparse, delayed rewards slow convergence in complex environments. Xu's Psychological Regret Model turns that sparse signal dense. After each decision, it computes regret as the gap between the expected value of the best action and the value of the action actually taken in that state.

That step-wise score gives immediate feedback throughout an episode. In benchmark tests including Lunar Lander, the method reached stable performance substantially faster than a standard proximal policy optimization baseline. Benefits were strongest in continuous control tasks and settings with delayed feedback. Xu frames the signal as formalized counterfactual thinking, bridging behavioral economics and reinforcement learning for uses like robotics and adaptive education.
arxiv-2602-03371:
Empty voxels waste computation in scene completion, and Zhiwen Yang, working with 1 co-author, offers multi-detail matching as auxiliary supervision. Camera-based three-part meaning scene completion assigns occupancy and meaning labels to every voxel around a vehicle from images alone, supporting autonomous driving perception. Most voxels in driving scenes are empty, though, so supervision from voxel labels alone limits tuning speed and model results in sparse three-part grids.

Their method projects image traits into multi-detail three-part traits and aligns them at scene level by fusing discriminative seed traits. A cubic meaning anisotropy module scores each voxel's meaning significance against its neighbors. Critical voxels then anchor a spread matching loss across resolutions. Code is publicly available. The authors frame matching as extra supervision that sparsity otherwise denies the model.
arxiv-2602-03671:
Checking whether a phone app actually obeys privacy law is harder than reading its privacy policy. Cornell Ziepel and 3 co-authors propose mopri in a 2026 paper, a framework for unveiling privacy violations in mobile apps. Regulations like the GDPR grant users informational self-determination, but enforcement needs evidence about what apps really do.

Mopri organizes existing analysis tools into one modular pipeline mixing static and dynamic methods. A prototype extracts app permissions and tracking libraries, records network traffic, and decrypts it where possible. Enrichment and reporting features present the findings clearly for users and enforcement bodies. The authors stress that the framework must keep adapting as the app ecosystem evolves.
arxiv-2602-03871:
When a high-resolution NMR spectrum reads the same forwards and backwards, algebra is usually the reason. Dmitry A. Cheshkov and 1 co-author examine that mirror symmetry in a 2026 theory paper. Their subject is the spin Hamiltonian, the matrix that encodes how nuclear spins interact.

Two routes to the symmetry emerge from the analysis. One is plain geometry: the Hamiltonian matrix is itself mirror-symmetric in a suitable basis, as in balanced spin systems. The other is deeper, resting on two spin systems sharing the same spectrum when parameters are exchanged. Readers gain clear conditions for when a palindromic spectrum must appear.
arxiv-2602-04371:
Some Feynman integrals live on curves far richer than circles, and Claude Duhr and 5 co-authors show how to compute them anyway. Their 2026 proceedings paper treats integrals tied to elliptic curves or Calabi-Yau varieties, arising in collider physics and gravity-wave work.

Equations in canonical form simplify such integrals and expose their analytic structure. The authors present a step-by-step construction of canonical equations even when answers exceed polylogarithms. The two-loop sunrise case carries the show, with details deferred to the original papers. Frontier work, from particle colliders to binary black hole waveforms, depends on exactly this machinery.
arxiv-2602-04971:
Sensors must report over wireless links so a distant controller can track a system, but fading channels and limited power force hard choices about which sensor transmits when. The work is by Minjie Tang and 2 co-authors. The authors study scheduling for many sensors sharing a multiple-antenna channel.

They propose sending sensor readings combined over the air, weighted by meaning rather than treated as raw numbers. Framing scheduling as a finite-horizon planning problem, they show the best policy adapts on the fly to the current estimation error and channel quality. A mathematical bound then yields a practical, low-complexity scheduler and estimator. In simulations, the scheme beat existing methods on both accuracy and power use, which matters for battery-powered sensor networks.
arxiv-2602-05071:
Harvesting a fish stock spread across a stream web raises a planning question: where should effort go? Tung D Nguyen and 5 co-authors model that question in this 2026 applied mathematics paper. Two aims compete, keeping the most total biomass in the water and taking the most total yield out, under a fixed overall harvesting effort.

For a two-patch web the authors fully pin down the best plan for each aim. Above a key growth rate, one plan wins on both aims at once. For larger webs where all patches share the same growth rate, they focus on the high-growth case and show the best plan picks patches by their competition rates. A net flow score set by the web's links guides the rest of the choice. The scheme runs to 27 pages and blends population dynamics with optimization.
arxiv-2602-05571:
Graph neural networks learn from node features and links, but a graph built in one domain may have a different structure in another, which breaks transfer. Rishabh Bhattacharya and Naresh Manwani argue that domain-invariant structure is not locked to one topology; it shows up as consensus across several graphs built from links and feature similarity. Their first method, EdgeMask-DG, trains an edge masker to find the worst-case soft masks under a sparsity limit.

A task network must then perform well under those adversarial masks, which forces it to rely on robust edges. The extended method, EdgeMask-DG*, applies the same trick to an enriched graph that adds feature-derived edges. That lets the model find stable structure even when the given topology is noisy. The authors back the approach with robust optimization arguments and report new state-of-the-art results on varied benchmarks, including citation networks.
arxiv-2602-05771:
How fast electrons settle after a laser pulse, in samples whose electrons break spin symmetry, is hard to read without heavy fitting. Alexander Bartenev and 8 co-authors present a nematic response model that pulls out the electronic cool-down time, with no fitting. The method joins spin-filtered pump probe tests of the nematic response with a two heat model of particle settling.

The response is built as a gap between scaled shine signals. Its sharp sub picosecond peak yields the typical cool-down time. Tests on two iron based superconductor films gave time constants in a narrow flash range, matching standard two heat fits of the same data. The authors note the approach applies to any sample with electronic nematic order. It offers a map of settling times for nematic samples, dodging hard fitting steps. The work should catch flash-fast light labs that study linked superconductors.
arxiv-2602-05871:
Short video generators stumble on long clips, because small errors pile up frame after frame until the scene drifts. Xunzhi Xiang and 9 co-authors introduce Test Time Correction, a training free method for distilled autoregressive diffusion models, the fast models used for real time synthesis. Existing test time optimization works on images or short clips but fails on extended sequences, thanks to unstable reward landscapes and touchy distilled parameters.

The correction uses the initial frame as a stable reference anchor. Intermediate stochastic states along the sampling path are calibrated against that anchor as generation proceeds. Experiments show the method plugs into various distilled models with negligible overhead. Generation lengths grow while quality matches resource intensive training based methods on thirty second benchmarks. The authors frame anchoring, not optimizing, as the right test time move for long video. The work targets video generation researchers who need longer coherent output without retraining.
arxiv-2602-05971:
When people name things they know, they move through meaning in steps, one idea leading to the next. Felipe Toro-Hernández and two co-authors turn that movement into paths through embedding space, built from transformer text models. Each path is built from cumulative embeddings, and the team tracks its shape and motion: distance to the next point, distance to the centre, entropy, speed, and change in speed.

They test the frame on four task sets in several languages, covering neurodegenerative cases, swear-word fluency, Italian property listings, and German tasks. The paths tell clinical groups apart and sort concepts, with cumulative paths best on longer runs. The same pattern shows up across embedding models, which points to a shared shape in learned meaning. The frame offers a low-effort way to study thought in motion, for clinics and cross-language work.
arxiv-2602-06071:
Shrinking huge data sets into small sketches is a core trick in randomized linear algebra. Rajat Vadiraj Dwaraknath and 2 co-authors noticed that the random sparsity which makes sketches cheap also fights against graphics processors. Irregular memory access wastes the speed these chips offer.

Their answer pairs a new sketch family, BlockPerm-SJLT, with a custom graphics chip kernel called FlashSketch. The sketch layout is shaped so the hardware can move data in neat blocks. One tuning knob trades raw speed against sketch quality. Tests on standard benchmarks and on a data attribution pipeline showed speed gains over the best prior chip sketches, with quality intact.
arxiv-2602-06271:
Misophonia is a condition where ordinary sounds like chewing or tapping trigger intense anger or panic. Kurumi Sashida and Gouhei Tanaka work toward assistive tools that can spot those trigger sounds in everyday audio. Their task is sound event detection: marking when each trigger sound starts and stops in a continuous recording.

Real recordings of this kind are scarce, so the pair synthesized soundscapes tailored to the task. Their detection model pairs a frozen, pretrained sound network with a trainable time-sequence module, testing several recurrent designs. Two-directional sequence models consistently did best, with the bidirectional gated recurrent unit on top. The study is a first step toward technology that could soften daily distress.
arxiv-2602-06371:
Ask a language model about Taiwan's sovereignty in Chinese and in English, and the answer may change with the language. Ju-Chun Ko benchmarks that bilingual bias across many models, using questions about the Republic of China (Taiwan) posed in both languages. Consistency on politically sensitive topics, he notes, is understudied.

Most of the tested models showed measurable differences between their Chinese and English stances. Models of Chinese origin showed the severest issues, including flat refusals and answers echoing one party's official narratives. Only one small model earned a perfect consistency score in both languages. Ko proposes two new scoring metrics for language bias and consistency, and releases the benchmark openly for others to extend.
arxiv-2602-06471:
The shape of a transformer has barely changed in years: feed-forward blocks swell wide, then narrow again. Feng-Ting Liao and 4 co-authors question that convention. Theory and tests suggest hourglass blocks, wide then narrow then wide, stay expressive despite their bottleneck, so the team built Hourglass Transformers around them.

Hourglass attention also separates the residual stream's width from attention width. Squeezing the feed-forward middle allows wider streams and fewer layers at the same parameter count. Across scales up to billions of parameters, the hourglass models matched conventional ones on language and downstream tasks, with better training efficiency at matched accuracy. After long-context extension, the largest model beat its baseline across context lengths, with cheaper attention at the longest settings.
arxiv-2602-06571:
The Cahn-Hilliard equation models how mixtures separate into phases, and P O Mchedlov-Petrosyan and 2 co-authors study a sixth-order variant of it. The standard equation is fourth order; here the thermodynamic potential is modified so the square gradient coefficient depends on the order parameter, and a squared Laplacian term appears. Those changes raise the order and add nonlinear terms.

The authors find several exact solutions, both static patterns and traveling waves, and study how those solutions change with the system's parameters. Exact solutions matter because they give clean test cases for numerical methods and reveal the solution landscape of a complicated equation. The convective-viscous form of the equation targets systems where flow and dissipation shape phase separation.
arxiv-2602-06771:
Fengpeng Li, Kemou Li, Qizhou Wang, Bo Han, and Jiantao Zhou tackle a tension in making image generators safe. Concept erasure retrains a diffusion model so it can no longer produce a harmful concept. Methods tend to improve either robustness, resisting attacks that reactivate the concept, or retention, keeping unrelated abilities intact, at the other's expense. Their framework, AEGIS, aims at both at once without needing extra retention data.

The approach is adversarial: it guides the erasure with gradient information so that the model resists semantically related prompts that try to revive the erased concept, while leaving other concepts alone. Because it needs no retention dataset, it sidesteps the cost of assembling one. The authors present it as a practical step toward erasure that survives real prompt attacks without visibly degrading the model.
arxiv-2602-06971:
Anastasios Manganaris and three co-authors survey how formal methods can make learned robot policies safer and more trustworthy. As robots take up deep learning, their policies grow highly capable yet rigid, fragile, and hard to read, resisting old-style formal analysis. Researchers have answered with new formal and semi-formal tools for setting goals, guiding learning, and checking learned policies.

The survey sorts the field into two pillars: policy learning and policy checking. For each it highlights typical techniques, compares how they scale and how much they can express, and sums up how they improve realistic robot safety and correct behavior. It ends with the obstacles that remain and hopeful paths forward, aiming to bridge strict specification with data-driven control.
arxiv-2602-07271:
Wave equations with degenerate coefficients break the standard tools for edge control, because the usual Dirichlet-to-Neumann machinery does not apply. Donghui Yang and one co-author develop a solution theory for second-order degenerate hyperbolic equations with non-homogeneous edge inputs.

They prove weak answers exist and are regular in weighted Sobolev spaces, and they build a Dirichlet map for that case. They also derive energy bounds and show the problem is well posed even for rough edge inputs. As a use case, they prove a near-control test that extends the Hilbert Uniqueness Method. Applied math experts get a method that carries classic wave control into such settings.
arxiv-2602-07471:
Electronic structure codes need checking, and the GW approximation for quasiparticle energies has only lately gained a thorough benchmark in the GW100 data set. M. Bonacci and six co-authors assess Yambo's GW code against that reference.

They compare the Godby-Needs plasmon-pole model with the newer multipole model on how right they are, how fast they settle, and how stable they stay. Materials experts get a careful answer to which approximation to trust in Yambo, and where each one wobbles, backing repeatable many-body work. Reliable GW numbers matter because those energies feed forecasts of band gaps and photoemission spectra.
arxiv-2602-07771:
Monte Carlo simulations of nuclear reactors demand enormous memory to track particles at high fidelity. Ethan Lame and three co-authors test compressed sensing, a technique that rebuilds signals from far fewer samples than traditional sampling requires, by collecting tallies in overlapping cells.

More samples improve reconstruction, though gains taper off, and the sparsity setting in the reconstruction algorithm strongly affects quality. Across three test cases, memory falls by up to 81 percent for two-dimensional and 96 percent for three-dimensional reconstructions, with some errors within one standard deviation of high-fidelity references. Reactor modelers gain a path to detailed simulations on far more modest hardware.
arxiv-2602-07871:
Reproducing a software failure starts with setting up its environment, a fiddly job of dependencies, build systems, and missing documentation. Xiang Li and four co-authors argue that success should be judged by executable evidence, not by whether packages merely installed. They propose a three-level Environment Maturity Hierarchy culminating in running the project's main entry point.

Their HerAgent system builds environments incrementally, validating and repairing through execution at each step. Tested on four public benchmarks, it outperforms prior approaches. Builders and teams who waste hours on setup will appreciate both the stricter yardstick and a tool that treats a runnable program, not an installed package list, as the goal.
arxiv-2602-07971:
Quantum computers need gates, and high-dimensional gates can outperform qubit gates for some tasks. Huan-Chao Gao and two co-authors describe entanglement-based optical controlled-SWAP gates acting on a qubit plus two qudits, encoding control in photon polarization and targets in spatial modes.

Their circuit uses only 2 plus 3d linear optical elements, beating an earlier count of 14 for the two-dimensional case, with circuit depth 5 instead of 11 and fidelity reaching 99.4 percent. The construction is deterministic, needs no borrowed ancillary photons or measurement-induced nonlinearities, and works for dimensions above 2. Optical quantum computing researchers gain a leaner, higher-fidelity building block.
arxiv-2602-08471:
Generating random directed acyclic graphs uniformly is a basic task for testing algorithms, yet efficient exact-size samplers are scarce. Wojciech Gabryelski and two co-authors propose two algorithms for the job, including an asymptotically optimal sampler. Their arXiv paper builds on a statistical sampling model for graph counting functions and exploits decompositions of directed acyclic graphs.

The optimal sampler uses about half the square of the node count in operations and random draws, plus lower-order terms. The new methods improve on prior art in theory and run markedly faster in practice. Readers get a clean, fast way to draw uniform random DAGs at exact sizes for experiments and benchmarks.
arxiv-2602-08671:
Dual-path models dominate source separation, but their cost grows with frequency bins, forcing a band-split shortcut that is rigid and parameter-heavy. Kohei Saijo and Yoshiaki Bando propose Spectral Feature Compression, which compresses frequency features with a single sequence-modeling module. Their arXiv paper targets music and cinematic separation at high sampling rates.

Unlike band-split encoders with a dedicated module per subband, the new module adapts to each input and shares parameters, with variants based on cross-attention and on Mamba. Biases inspired by band-split design keep the compression suited to frequency data. Tests show consistent wins over band-split across separator sizes and compression ratios. Readers get a leaner, adaptive front end for separation models.
arxiv-2602-08971:
World models let robots imagine what happens next, but tests of them usually grade video beauty, not usefulness. Yu Shang and twenty co-authors introduce WorldArena, a unified benchmark that scores both sides. It grades perception quality across sixteen metrics in six areas, and functional value as data engines, policy judges, and action planners, with human judgment included.

A single holistic index, EWMScore, rolls the dimensions together. Across fourteen representative models, a clear perception-functionality gap emerges: pretty video does not guarantee capable embodied decisions. The benchmark and public leaderboard aim to steer the field toward world models that truly work, not just look good.
arxiv-2602-09171:
Radio-quiet narrow-line Seyfert 1 galaxies are usually thought to shine mainly by heat from their accretion disks. Vineet Ojha and six co-authors test that picture against recurring 37-gigahertz radio flares seen in seven such galaxies by the Metsähovi observatory, flares that hint at non-thermal, jet-like processes. They combine high-cadence optical light curves from ZTF with long-term mid-infrared curves from WISE, plus broadband spectral modeling.

Every galaxy shows significant long-term optical variability, growing stronger toward bluer wavelengths. Three show bluer-when-brighter trends and rising variability across optical bands, signs of a non-thermal contribution. Intrinsic mid-infrared variability appears in three of four sources tested, with significant lags between bands. The evidence suggests jets contribute more to these supposedly quiet galaxies than assumed.
arxiv-2602-09271:
The CMS Collaboration maps the Lund jet plane of high-energy jets in lead-lead crashes and sets it beside proton-proton crashes. Jets are narrow sprays from high-energy quarks and gluons, and the Lund plane logs each puff's sideways push and angle as the jet is step-by-step unpicked. The study looks at angle spreads in two sideways-push slices for jets of radius 0.4 and push 200 to 1000 giga-electronvolts.

Lead-lead data from 2018 and proton-proton data from 2017, both at 5.02 tera-electronvolts per nucleon pair, test whether the earliest puffs come before quark-gluon plasma birth. Within error bars, no big gap shows in high-push puffs between the two crash setups, matching those puffs occurring early, before much plasma contact.
arxiv-2602-09771:
Battery matter speed-up platforms need joining paired ways and linking mixed lab sets. A 2026 paper led by François Cadiou tackles this in a large multi-mode program with fifteen labs across Europe. Joint tests run on top graphite and lithium nickel oxide full cells. They ask two questions. Does liquid mix impact pole traits, and how does pole matter evolve as cells cycle to end-of-life?

A workflow runs from sample making to sending through labels, making seventy-five joined sets shared by partners. Joint work shows findings depend deeply on the signal chosen for pole traits and the test way used. Two-dim signal-way patterns serve as multi-trait views. Each pixel holds yes, no, or unsure answers to a science question. They sort matter ways and way fit by set user demand, showing links between test choices, taken knobs and science reading.
arxiv-2602-10071:
Power price forecasting guides grid operation and market choices, and deep learning has diversified its models rapidly. A 2026 review led by Runyao Yu, with ten co-authors, surveys deep learning for day-ahead, intraday, and balancing markets. It introduces a unified map splitting models into backbone, head, and loss parts for fair comparison.

Using that lens, the review traces trends toward chance-based, microstructure-centered, and market-aware designs. It also names gaps, including thin coverage of intraday and balancing markets and a need for strategies tuned to each market. The result pulls together a fast-moving literature and points later work at its open questions.
arxiv-2602-10171:
Coding benchmarks usually grade static results and assume fixed power during runs, missing how agents improve as they iterate. A 2026 paper led by Wentao Zhang, with five co-authors, presents EvoCodeBench, a benchmark for self-changing language-model coding systems across coding languages, matched against human coders. It tracks scores beside speed gauges such as solving time, memory use, and better algorithmic design over repeat attempts.

Results show self-changing systems gaining clearly in speed over time, and human-matched plus multi-language looks reveal insights scores alone hide. Cross-language toughness and long-tail language strength, often thin, are covered under one set of rules. The benchmark sets a base for judging coding intelligence as it changes during runs.
arxiv-2602-10771:
Krishna Kanth Nakka and Vedasri Nakka test whether driving vision-language models understand cycling in a 2026 paper. Cyclists face safety-key urban situations, yet model tests stay vehicle-centric, never probing perception and thinking from a cyclist's viewpoint. That blind spot matters for assistive systems meant to support riders.

Their benchmark, CyclingVQA, probes perception, spatio-time grasp, and traffic-rule-to-lane thinking from the cyclist's perspective. Evaluating more than thirty-one recent models spanning general-purpose, spatially aided, and driving-specialized systems, the authors find encouraging capabilities alongside clear gaps. The benchmark gives teams a cyclist-centered yardstick for models that will share roads with vulnerable users.
arxiv-2602-10971:
Bandit problems get harder when noise levels shift and rivals tamper with feedback. Sanghwa Kim and two co-authors propose HCW-GLB-OMD, a method for generalized straight bandits under uneven noise and hostile corruption. It pairs an online mirror descent estimator with weights built from curvature data.

The authors prove a corruption-proof confidence sequence and a new possible lemma for the mix of corruption and adaptive weights. For self-concordant models, they give a high-chance regret bound and matching lower bounds for its main terms. The method needs one update per round and modest storage. It matters because it keeps strong guarantees while staying cheap to run in messy, shifting settings.
arxiv-2602-11171:
LoRA tuning is cheap, but its settings are fussy and costly to search. Baek Seong-Eun and three co-authors propose a Bayesian tuning frame that uses a pretrained language model as a mapping from settings to a continuous space. Language prompts inject domain lore about LoRA settings and their roles.

A learnable token captures residue that prompts cannot easily state, and proxy training on a data subset speeds the search further. With only about thirty iterations, the found settings beat standard settings by more than a fifth, against a search space of tens of thousands of combos. The paper shows that language-aware tuning can tame a hyperparameter hunt that brute force cannot afford.
arxiv-2602-11271:
Four planets around one red dwarf straddle the radius valley. Thomas G. Wilson and a large team profile the LHS 1903 system with transit photometry and radial velocity data. Orbital periods span days to about a month, and the planets cross the gap between super-Earths and sub-Neptunes.

Densities show the innermost planet is rocky, while the next two carry extended atmospheres. The outermost planet, though farthest from its star, holds no gaseous envelope at all. That pattern points to formation from gas-depleted material, rather than later atmospheric stripping alone. One system thus tests two competing stories for the radius valley at once.
arxiv-2602-11471:
Radar around corners relies on weak multipath bounces off walls. Kainat Yasmeen and two co-authors apply a reconfigurable intelligent surface to steer incident beams into non-line-of-sight regions, strengthening around-the-corner sensing for security, surveillance, and automotive look-ahead warnings.

Tests at five point five gigahertz show micro-Doppler signatures of walking humans can now be captured without direct line of sight, through strategic surface deployment. The work turns a marginal multipath trick into a practical sensing channel, showing that engineered surfaces can redirect radar energy where direct paths cannot reach. The demonstration uses walking humans, a realistic and demanding test case.
arxiv-2602-11571:
Dark matter may talk to ordinary matter through a new force tied to baryon number, carried by a charged scalar particle. Taramati and four co-authors build such a model, in which a fermionic dark matter candidate interacts with quarks through that scalar mediator. The leftover abundance of dark matter then depends not only on ordinary annihilation but also on coannihilation. How strong that second process is hinges on the mass gap between the dark particle and the mediator.

Scanning the model against cosmology, direct and indirect searches, and collider data, the authors find workable regions beyond the simplest versions of the idea. Many of those regions should come within reach of upcoming XENONnT and Cherenkov Telescope Array searches. The same model also predicts linked signals in rare flavor-changing decays, giving a second, independent way to test it.
arxiv-2602-11671:
Code models shine on standalone snippets but fade when a task spans a whole repository. There, cross-file dependencies and structure matter more than surface similarity. Minh Le-Anh and six co-authors trace part of the failure to retrieval methods borrowed from natural language processing. Chunking breaks coherence between code units. Similarity search misses true dependencies like helper functions and global variables.

Their framework, Hydra, treats code as structured code instead. Hydra indexes repositories as hierarchical trees of functions, classes, and variables. A lightweight retriever finds true dependencies explicitly. A hybrid design blends that retrieval with similarity search for usage examples. On two demanding benchmarks built from real repositories, Hydra sets a new state of the art. It beats the strongest baseline by over 5 percent across open and closed models, and lets smaller models match or pass much larger ones using older retrievers.
arxiv-2602-11771:
Species distribution models output odds, but ecology and conservation need binary presence-absence maps. Converting odds to yes-or-no maps is usually heuristic, and it can badly distort prevalence and community composition figures. Sébastien Gigot-Léandri and six co-authors propose MaxExp, a decision-driven framework that picks the most probable species set by directly maximizing a chosen score, with no tuning data needed.

A second method, Set Size Expectation, offers a fast alternative that predicts sets from expected species richness. Across three case studies spanning diverse taxa, species counts, and metrics, MaxExp matches or beats widely used thresholding and tuning methods, especially under strong class imbalance and high rarity. Set Size Expectation stays competitive while staying simpler, giving practitioners robust, reproducible tools for mapping many species at once.
arxiv-2602-11971:
Cheyne Glass and one co-author give a short proof that two ways of building homotopy theory agree on key geometric sites. The local projective model structure and the Cech projective model structure turn out to be the same. Their result covers smooth manifolds with open covers, and also cartesian spaces with good open covers.

Take a presheaf of sets over one of these sites, and the gain is plain. Applying the plus construction just once is enough to sheafify it. No repeat pass is needed, so a step that might have taken rounds of work now ends in one move. That single-step result makes a basic tool of sheaf theory easier to use.
arxiv-2602-12271:
Real-time video generation with diffusion transformers chokes on the quadratic cost of three-dimensional self-attention, especially in few-step, autoregressive modes where errors build up. Krish Agarwal led this work with seven co-authors, finding that video attention is not reliably sparse. It mixes strong periodic structure from position with sparse semantic links and dense mixing, beyond even oracle top-k capacity.

Their answer, MonarchRT, factorises attention with Monarch matrices in aligned blocks, extended with a tiled form, keeping expressiveness while cutting cost. Fine-tuning and custom Triton kernels remove the overhead. On Self-Forcing, it reaches 95 percent attention sparsity with no quality loss, beating FlashAttention kernels by 1.4 to 11.8 times and reaching true real-time video at 16 frames per second on one RTX 5090.
arxiv-2602-12671:
Hom-tridendriform and Hom-post-Lie structures extend old algebra by twisting ops with a homomorphism, and their dual coalgebra versions are less built out. Damien Houndedji led this work with one co-author, Ibrahima Bakayoko, giving Hom-tridendriform coalgebras and Hom-post-Lie coalgebras as dual notions of the matching algebras.

Traits tied to them are given, then ties between them and their link with post-Hom-Poisson coalgebras are studied. Next, using Yau twisting in the modules case, builds of comodules over post-Hom-Lie coalgebras are given by twisting either the comodule structures or the post-Hom-Lie coalgebra structures. Readers get a systematic dual frame for Hom-type structures, linking tridendriform, post-Lie, and Poisson coalgebras.
arxiv-2602-12771:
People live in three-dimensional space but meet on flat screens, and that mismatch may quietly shape online talk. Yihuan Chen and four co-authors compare two video layouts on the Ohyay platform: a standard gallery grid and a room layout where participants sit in a circle on screen. In a social support task, room users focused more on the group overall and showed stronger self-awareness.

In a debate task with teams facing off, room users used spatial cues to signal allegiance, engaging more with distant participants and empathising more with near ones. Spatial effects also showed up in hiding from the spotlight, taking others' perspectives, and using gestures. The authors argue that screen layout deserves design attention, since where people sit online changes how they relate.
arxiv-2602-12871:
Language models are more and more put forward as aids for mind-health testing, but most mind-health benchmarks use social media posts or caring chats, not formal diagnosis. Hoyun Song and nine co-authors present MentalBench, a benchmark that tests whether models can use DSM-5 rules and tell-apart diagnosis rules under varying doubt. Its spine is MentalKG, a knowledge graph built and checked by mind-health doctors spanning 23 illnesses.

From that spine the team made 24,750 mock cases that vary in fullness and hardness. Tests show leading models do well on clean knowledge questions but struggle to tune trust when illnesses share signs. That gap raises doubts about how much to trust them in real diagnosis help and argues for testing that mirrors the messy doubt doctors face in real life.
arxiv-2602-12971:
Finding objects in 3D scenes from queries that mix hierarchy, attributes, negation, and chained spatial relations is hard for existing maps and memories. YukTungSamuel Fang and seven co-authors propose INHerit-SG, a layered semantic scene graph that grows over time, with retrieval to match. Geometric and semantic processing run asynchronously, and event-driven maintenance organises observations into a hierarchy expressed in plain text. That same memory supports direct reading by strong hosted models or parsed structured retrieval for smaller local models.

Direct reading wins with powerful models, while structured retrieval helps smaller models and cuts per-query API cost for hosted ones. Tests on 6,084 queries across 36 scenes plus three real environments show INHerit-SG beating the strongest baselines, with an overall success lead of 9.8 points on real robots and the largest gains on attribute and compositional queries.
arxiv-2602-13071:
Mobility data power smart-city planning, but many cities cannot share real trajectories, leaving generation methods stranded. Shuai Liu and four co-authors pose a new setting: trajectory generation conditioned on bus data, with zero target-city trajectories available. Generation uses only source-city mobility data plus public bus timetables from both cities.

Their method, MobTA, brings task arithmetic into trajectory generation for the first time. It models the parameter shift from timetable-based to mobility-based generation in the source city, then applies that shift to the target city through arithmetic on task vectors. Experiments show MobTA beating existing methods and approaching models fine-tuned on target-city data. Stability is also analysed theoretically across base and instruction-tuned language models.
arxiv-2602-13171:
Fast matrix multiplication schemes often use complex coefficients, which cost extra arithmetic and limit practical speed. Yoav Moran, Oded Schwartz, and Shuncheng Yuan ask when a complex-coefficient scheme can be converted into an equivalent real- or rational-coefficient one. They give a systematic method that, for any complex scheme, either builds equivalent rational algorithms as a family or proves that no such scheme exists. It uses only basic linear algebra of similarity transformations.

The method recovers earlier ad-hoc results from Dumas, Pernet, and Sedoglavic, extending them to rational coefficients and square roots, with the imaginary unit as a special case. As applications, they prove no rational scheme matches Smirnov's 4,4,9,104 algorithm over Q[sqrt(161)], and no real scheme matches Kaporin's 4,4,4,48 complex algorithm. The framework can also rule out integer-coefficient schemes.
arxiv-2602-13271:
Intrusion detection must catch attacks, but security teams also need to see why a system raised an alarm. This framework pairs deep learning with explainable AI for that dual goal, testing on the NSL-KDD benchmark. It combines convolutional and long short-term memory networks to read traffic sequences over time, and both models reached 0.99 accuracy, with the memory network ahead on macro-averaged precision, recall, and F-1 score.

To open the black box, the authors add SHAP explanations, which flagged error-rate features as most influential for both models. A trust survey with experts, run through an interactive interface, probed whether analysts would rely on the system in practice. Md Muntasir Jahid Ayan leads the work with eight co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13471:
With the fourth LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA observing run ending without a new confirmed neutron star merger, kilonova samples will stay scarce. That scarcity will persist even as gravitational-wave watching continues. This paper explores a complementary route. Bright short gamma-ray burst afterglows can flag kilonovae for the Rubin Observatory's Legacy Survey of Space and Time, whose depth makes such detections feasible without a gravitational-wave trigger.

Nearly on-axis afterglows, viewed within 30 degrees, could lift kilonova detection rates in the LSST g-band from about 29 per year to about 91 per year. Event colors can further separate merger counterparts with and without kilonova emission, and detectable events should appear near peak for rapid follow-up. Haille M. L. Perkins leads the work with four co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13871:
Sai Ravela and six co-authors set out a 2026 arXiv paper on a unified view of ensemble inference. At its center sits the conditional Gaussian law, the full posterior for a Gaussian prior with linear observations. Kalman filtering, they stress, is just one way to compute that law under dynamics, not the law itself.

Their synthesis, called Ens-CGP, builds the prior from ensemble moments, which may be low-rank, and then conditions exactly. By splitting representation from computation, the framework links Kalman filters, ensemble variants, and iterative schemes to one object. It also ties the same law to MAP estimation, kernel-style regression, and classic regularization, clarifying how probabilistic and variational views fit together.
arxiv-2602-14171: Yuriy A. Drozd, writing alone, links two representation worlds: algebras whose radical squares to zero, and species. The stable category of the algebra sits inside the representation category of its species, and the Auslander-Reiten quiver of the algebra can be rebuilt from that of the species. The short paper offers a clean link for this class of algebras.
arxiv-2602-14271:
A. G. Acar leads a large CLAS12 team reporting a 2026 arXiv first measure of beam spin tilts for pion pairs. The measure covers pi-plus pi-zero and pi-minus pi-zero pairs in semi-inclusive deep inelastic scattering. A 10.6 GeV long-spinning electron beam struck a proton target at Jefferson Lab.

A photon sorter based on gradient boosted trees, trained on runs, cut false combo pi-zero background and raised stats up to fivefold over prior CLAS12 pi-zero studies. A non-zero sin phi tilt was seen. The result probes the little-studied twist-3 PDF e(x), coding quark-gluon links, and gives first proof for isospin ties in the helicity-tied dihadron split function.
arxiv-2602-14371:
Mahesh Godavarti, writing alone, reframes a 2026 arXiv pair of channel concepts: diversity and degrees of freedom in Gaussian fading channels. Classic definitions divide capacity growth and error-rate decay by log signal-to-noise ratio, hiding a two-step process. First, one must find the gauge on which capacity or reliability truly grows; second, one normalizes by the right atom.

For coherent MIMO channels, both gauges happen to be log SNR with unit atoms, masking the distinction. Outside that calibration case, the paper makes the process explicit via a Bhattacharyya-frontier construction. A capacity-packing sandwich theorem recovers the capacity gauge, while a binary-endpoint theorem identifies the zero-rate diversity gauge. Endpoint degrees of freedom and diversity then follow by dividing raw coefficients by atom coefficients.
arxiv-2602-14971:
Banks argues that gravitational scattering in high dimensions strains the usual picture of a unitary S-matrix. For finite energy windows, he says, final states appear as normalizable coherent states in Fock space. As the window center moves to infinity, black hole physics predicts those states turn orthogonal to every finite-particle state. Since energy spectral measures follow from Poincare invariance, the S-matrix cannot be unitary in Fock space, despite finite matrix elements and perturbative unitarity at every order.

Banks finds the same conclusion in regimes of the BFSS matrix model and in CFT-correlator definitions of the S-matrix. He reviews a scattering theory built from a finite set of fermionic oscillators, whose algebra tends toward the Awada-Gibbons-Shaw algebra. A class of limiting states there meets the demands of physical unitarity, he argues, leaving only a proof of Poincare invariance for the amplitudes still missing.
arxiv-2602-15171:
Villarroel and colleagues answer a critique by the Watters team of statistical analyses in two 2025 papers on claimed technosignatures in POSS1-E photographic plates. They argue it mixes up object-level validation with ensemble-level statistical inference. It also leans on a reduced, oddly trimmed subset built for a different scientific purpose.

They further question whether the heavily filtered subset truly raises sample purity, given a twenty-fold cut in sample size. Their simple visual check suggests it does not. The subset also lacks full temporal information and is too weak for testing the claimed Earth-shadow deficit. The horizontal gap metric for plate assignment and timing, they note, needs the cosine-of-declination factor for geometric sense; omitting it would shift assignments and inferred times. With no error bars or error tracking in that response, they conclude the main 2025 findings stand intact.
arxiv-2602-15471:
López-Soriano and colleagues tackle the puzzle of setting the Gauss bend on the disc and the edge bend on its rim via an angle-true shift of the ruler. In this work the case of minus Gauss bend is covered, a zone for which the foaming acts of near answers is not so well grasped. This is due to the likely rise of blow-up answers with runaway span and size.

They give a proof under guesses on the bends which are fairly plain, in view of some blocks built-in to the puzzle. Their plan is energy-based and leans on the study of set groups of near cases. By doing a fine blow-up study for answers with capped Morse index, they prove tightness.
arxiv-2602-15571:
Casnici and colleagues speed up predictive coding, a brain-inspired training rule that updates each layer locally and so allows parallel learning. In practice, error signals still crawl from output to early layers through many inference steps, and feedback fades exponentially along the way, leaving early layers with vanishing updates. The team answers with direct Kolen-Pollack predictive coding, or DKP-PC, which tackles delay and decay together while keeping updates local.

Learnable feedback links run straight from the output layer to every hidden layer, giving errors a direct path. That change cuts error propagation time from order depth to order one, removing depth-driven delay. Tests show performance at least matching standard predictive coding, often better, with lower latency and compute cost, a profile that suits custom hardware built for efficient learning.
arxiv-2602-15771:
Székelyhidi works alone on neck pinch singularities in two-dimensional Lagrangian mean curvature flow of surfaces in a Calabi-Yau surface. He introduces a notion of nondegenerate neck pinch singularity. He shows that such singularities can occur. He shows they stay stable under small perturbations. He shows any neck pinch singularity can be perturbed into a nondegenerate one near the singular time. That machinery answers questions raised by Neves and Joyce.

He also introduces nondegenerate teardrop singularities. He shows that these cannot occur for embedded flows. The paper thus draws a sharp line. Neck pinches are generic and robust in this setting. Teardrops are ruled out for embedded flows. Geometers gain a precise account of which singularities can appear and which cannot along Lagrangian mean curvature flow.
arxiv-2602-15871:
Abbonato built CheckIfExist, an open web tool that checks whether a cited work truly exists. Fake cites are a growing risk as language models spread through academic work. Such fakes have turned up even in papers taken by top machine learning venues such as NeurIPS and ICLR.

Old reference tools file cites but do not check them live. Paid fake-cite detectors often cap free use or charge high fees. CheckIfExist fills the gap by checking each cite in turn against CrossRef, Semantic Scholar, and OpenAlex. It scores each match for closeness and handles one cite or a batch of BibTeX records. It returns checked APA cites and BibTeX records that can be saved, all within seconds.
arxiv-2602-16071:
Joseph Root and Evan Sadler lay axiomatic foundations for the utility functions used in network games, where each player interacts with many others through a network. A common feature of such games is bilateral strategic interaction, and the authors show it matches exactly the case where player utilities split additively across opponents. Utilities built from a linear aggregate of opponent actions turn out to be strategically equivalent to such separable utilities.

With real-valued actions, a constant rate of substitution between opponents forces a utility that is linear in opponent actions. The authors then pin down the classic linear-quadratic utility with precise conditions: linear best replies plus midpoint indifference. Together these results give theorists interpretable building blocks and principled generalizations, clarifying which assumptions drive the familiar forms used across network game models.
arxiv-2602-16171:
Ryosuke Nishide and Kunihiko Kaneko propose a minimal model for how bioelectricity might self-organize in early cells. Directional ion transport across membranes keeps living systems out of balance. It underlies chemiosmotic energy change. Yet the physical origin of collectively organized ion transport in early cell systems remains unclear. In their model, ion pumps align as a group through feedback between ion transport and electrostatic interactions.

That transport generates a membrane voltage. The resulting electrochemical voltage biases pump orientation, closing a feedback loop that yields self-organized lining up. Simulations and mean-field analysis reveal a shift from a disordered state with no net transport to an aligned state with sustained membrane voltages. Critical traits match the mean-field Ising universality class, though the effective field arises on its own from nonequilibrium transport. Protocell asymmetry can bias voltage polarity, offering a generic physical route toward chemiosmotic coupling in protocells.
arxiv-2602-16471:
A. N. Ignatenko, S. V. Streltsov, and V. Yu. Irkhin present an extensive Monte Carlo study of the classical Heisenberg model on a simple cubic lattice with antiferromagnetic exchange between first, second, and third neighbors. The study covers a broad region of exchange ratios and heat. The character of the phase transitions is analyzed with the Binder cumulant method.

The Néel temperature and the frustration ratio, the ratio of the Curie-Weiss magnitude to the Néel temperature, are found. A comparison with the Tyablikov approximation is carried out, and the strength of frustration effects is explored. Possible applications to antiferromagnetic perovskites such as calcium manganese oxide and mercury manganese oxide are discussed, grounding the abstract model in candidate real materials.
arxiv-2602-16571:
Zhuqian Zhou and co-authors tackle a snag in sharing math tutoring transcripts. Numbers that are part of teaching often look like dates or ID numbers. Generic privacy tools then over-redact the lesson itself. The team builds MathEd-PII, the first benchmark for privacy detection in math tutoring dialogue. It was annotated with human-in-the-loop language model help. False redactions cluster in math-dense passages, confirming numeric ambiguity as a key failure mode.

Four detection strategies are compared. Domain-aware prompting wins clearly. Math-aware and segment-aware prompts score far above a Presidio baseline. They also cut numeric false positives. Education researchers get a benchmark and a practical lesson. De-identification of tutoring data must understand the subject matter to preserve its value.
arxiv-2602-16671:
Jaid Monwar Chowdhury, Chi-An Fu, and Reyhaneh Jabbarvand present SPARC, a neuro-symbolic frame for automated C unit test generation. Direct intent-to-code synthesis often fails by leaping to code with no grounding in program structure, yielding tests that do not compile, invented signatures, low branch coverage, and weak assertions. SPARC bridges that gap in four stages.

The stages are control flow graph study, an operation map grounding model reasoning in checked helpers, path-targeted test synthesis, and an iterative self-correction loop using compiler and runtime feedback. On fifty-nine real-world and algorithmic subjects, SPARC beats vanilla prompt generation by large margins in line coverage, branch coverage, and mutation score, matching or beating the symbolic tool KLEE on hard subjects.
arxiv-2602-16871:
S. Deng and co-authors report a full study of BaFe2Se3, a chain-like superconductor with no inversion symmetry. Spin-ladder compounds in this family can be seen as dimensional cuts of two-dimensional iron-based pnictide planes. Despite their slim form, they keep unusual ground states. One is superconduction under pressure beyond ten gigapascals, following a structural shift at four gigapascals.

The team joins sharp single-crystal X-ray diffraction, infrared spectra work, and first-principles sums. Together they resolve the true nature of the pressure-induced superconducting phase. Diffraction alone shows a symmetry drop from one crystal form to another, but cannot pin the precise space group. Spectra work plus density functional theory give clear proof for a polar space group with no inversion center. That revises the structural assignment and establishes a key ingredient for unconventional superconduction.
arxiv-2602-17071:
Rong Fu led a five-author team hardening graph neural networks against messy, unfriendly graph structure.
