Detail follows the task: manipulation resolves stove knobs, while navigation keeps whole stoves. Because the task list may evolve as the robot works, the map adjusts mid-job for moving-and-handling tasks. The system tops a grounding benchmark by about 79 percent and runs live on a robot, even on casually filmed apartment tours.
arxiv-2605-25571: Zehao Wang and colleagues push multimodal reasoning past the limits of fixed training data. Self-reflection and self-evolution schemes drift, feeding models low-quality synthetic paths that hallucinate. Anchor Evolution instead locates the model's failing frontier through rollouts, retrieves high-fidelity anchors from ground-truth bases, and curates faithful data. A scaffold-stripping step first teaches reasoning with scaffolded supervision, then strips the scaffold with reinforcement learning so the skill becomes intrinsic. The base model improves about ten percent across eight multimodal benchmarks.
arxiv-2605-25971: Hu and nine colleagues make agents proactive instead of merely reactive, using idle time between user messages to prepare. Their ProAct design studies dialogue history and stored memory, predicts likely next needs, and gathers evidence before the user asks. A new benchmark, ProActEval, spans two hundred scenarios across forty domains with predictable need chains and varied user profiles. Against reactive baselines, ProAct cuts required turns by 14.8 percent, user effort by 11.7 percent, and hallucination rates by 28.1 percent, while also leading on a memory benchmark.
arxiv-2605-26171: Alejandro Ascarate and four colleagues build a 2026 neural evaluator that checks logical rules over learned visual concepts. It targets settings where genuine rule violations almost never appear in training. Each rule becomes a directed acyclic graph whose gates learn from exact Boolean propagation. A training trick called chimera training splices subtree features from different samples to manufacture counterexamples. Across three benchmarks, the evaluator beats independent-events and same-image baselines on rule-level anomaly detection, most clearly for compositional and relational rules.
arxiv-2605-26371: Sarthak Dayal and six colleagues learn reusable skills for offline hierarchical reinforcement learning by exploiting local dynamics patterns. Local moves in different global contexts need similar move chains, so matching contexts with the chains they require reveals which skills to reuse and where. Their algorithm, CARL, builds contrastive representations of actions for reusable local control. It shows meaningful skills clustering sensibly in complex humanoid settings and better later results on the OGBench benchmark when joined with HIQL, in a 2026 paper.
arxiv-2605-26771: Banerjee and four colleagues prove a lower bound on the number of non-CM Galois orbits of newforms with quadratic nebentypus, a twisting character, at large weights. Building on Dieulefait, Pacetti, and Tsaknias for the trivial case, they count compatible local-global invariants and show Atkin-Li pseudo-eigenvalues are Galois equivariant. Small-weight computations show the bound is not always sharp, so some local equivalences never occur globally.
arxiv-2605-27171: Sun, Guggenberger, and Shastri identify faults in applying the right to be forgotten. This data right is described in just 417 GDPR words yet hard to apply. Regulators issued 205 violations in five years, roughly one failure every nine days. The authors map uncertainties and risks from computing. They propose a two-phase approach bridging law and computing. It could have avoided 80 percent of year-six violations. They uncover six computing practices now anti-patterns for it. Finally, they add forgotten-right capability to Elasticsearch, a search engine.
arxiv-2605-27371: A 2026 study by Rishi Bommasani and colleagues examines hiring tools from a single vendor screening millions of job seekers. They find clear racial gaps in results, with Asian and Black job seekers facing adverse-impact roles at different rates. Job seekers also get the same verdict almost everywhere, with a small share turned down for every role they seek.
arxiv-2605-27471: Boris Shapiro studies how few inflection points a generic closed plane curve can have when its shadow is fixed. For tree-like shadows the problem becomes a finite coorientation puzzle on the shadow's building polygons, yielding an exact formula. The same model gives a universal lower bound for all shadows, exact for tree-necklace shadows under a holonomy condition.
arxiv-2605-27571: Gaetano Rossiello and Dharmashankar Subramanian build a multi-agent system that finds insights in live data streams instead of waiting for queries. Agents form guesses, turn them into runnable analyses, check the results, and produce charts and usable apps. Kafka coordinates events, Flink processes streams, and typed middle-stage outputs give the design modularity, lineage, and safer runs.
arxiv-2605-27671: Surender Suresh Kumar and Mary Cummings build a pipeline that makes multi-turn deceptive question sets and detects them with shape signals. Multi-goal genetic prompt tuning with co-evolving mutations produces real attacks, and three geometric features plus pairwise similarity stats feed a compact classifier. The detector reaches about 89 percent recall with test-time F1 from about 74 percent to about 86 percent across base, rephrased, and cut scenarios.
arxiv-2605-27771: Sravan Reddy Chintareddy, Marco Mezzavilla, Sundeep Rangan, and Morteza Hashemi assess terahertz midhaul links at 140 GHz with ray-tracing. They test whether wireless links can carry transport traffic between central and distributed units in a disaggregated 5G network, minimizing the number of central units needed. Links at 140 GHz with high-layer split option 2 look promising for midhaul transport networks.
arxiv-2605-27971: Peng and colleagues fight the loss of variety when language models are tuned for a set role or tone. Their Semantic Flow Regularization trains the model on coded hints of text yet to come, keeping many possible next lines alive instead of one. The extra training head is dropped at run time, yet range, style match, and quality all rose.
arxiv-2605-28571: Mauricio Villavicencio, Sitong Pan, and Qianwen Wang test how fine-grained uncertainty displays shape checking in language-model-assisted decisions. In a study of 192 people answering medical questions, uncertainty appeared at output, step, or token level. Token-level uncertainty raised agreement with the AI, while output- and step-level displays did not raise agreement but lowered users' own confidence. Step-level uncertainty also cut outside checks such as web searches, steering users toward reliance on the model and its cues.
arxiv-2605-28671: Stephen Dolan and four colleagues review how neutrino interaction model uncertainties affect accelerator-based oscillation measurements. Such experiments aim to pin down charge-parity breaking, fix the neutrino mass order, and probe physics beyond three-flavour mixing. The hardest doubts come from models of neutrino-nucleus contacts, which also shift the event rates used to infer oscillation odds. The review covers current and future tests plus lab and theory prospects for shrinking these doubts to levels the next generation of experiments can accept.
arxiv-2605-28871: Heena Ali and Sushant G. Ghosh test loop quantum gravity through EHT observations of M87* and Sgr A*, using spinning loop-fixed holes. Against the typical Kerr hole, the quantum correction grows shadow size. As the drift value grows, forward photon orbits shift outward, showing weaker working gravity near center. Photon rings persist where shaky round photon orbits exist. Applying the Kumar-Ghosh method with shadow area and squash, they pin down spin and quantum fix values, giving width bounds for both black holes at two viewing angles.
arxiv-2605-29071: Johannes Nokkala, Federico Centrone, and Francesco Arzani find a hidden choke point in linear reservoirs. With linear flow and linear readout with bias, fixed-delay capacity is limited by what the input holds. Linear dynamics redistribute features but cannot create new fixed-delay power alone. Global measures hide this limit, since contributions from other delays can add up. For covariance-based quantum reservoirs, the authors find the Gaussian limit, and single-photon operations surpass it as a genuine resource and witness of non-Gaussian processing.
arxiv-2605-29171: Kenneth B. A. Benício and colleagues propose a tensor-based channel estimation method for smart surface-aided systems with time-varying channels. They exploit the received signal's multidimensional structure through a third-order PARAFAC tensor model solved with iterative ALS. Simulations show better normalized mean squared error for the combined channel versus rival methods. The gain comes from the signal's own tensor structure, with no rise in channel estimation cost.
arxiv-2605-29271: Vaishali Senthil and colleagues present CoHyDE, a method for tool retrieval over large API catalogs. User queries arrive in casual, vague language, while catalogs use technical vocabulary no fixed encoder bridges alone. Fine-tuned encoders excel when query wording matches the catalog but collapse when it does not. Frozen-model expansion stays robust to vague queries but degrades when queries are well formed. CoHyDE trains encoder and rewriter as one system: the encoder learns from the rewriter's catalog-style descriptions, and the rewriter is aligned against retrieval scores.
arxiv-2605-29671: Eva A. Gallardo-Gutiérrez and Jonathan R. Partington study frames built from the paths of vectors under a single operator in Hilbert space. They prove fresh results for multiplication operators and for operators built from Jordan blocks, widening earlier work. Their tools draw on interpolation with weights, composition operators, and Beurling-Lax ideas for shifts of endless multiplicity. They also cover Carleson frames, offering counterexamples against a recent conjecture, and thus show where the frame idea holds and where it fails.
arxiv-2605-29971: Zhenghao Herbert Zhou, R. Thomas McCoy, and Robert Frank bring causal meddling to graded traits in language models, past work having stuck to on-off ones. Given activation vectors tied to a graded target, their method finds a low-dimensional direction and edits vectors toward counterfactual values. They test verb bias, a verb's pull toward certain sentence shapes, and show it lives causally in steering vectors, shifting later structure choices. Steering vectors also carry error signals that could drive in-context learning updates, yet play no causal role downstream.
arxiv-2605-30471: Chengyu Cui, Taoyi Chen, Chun Wang and Gongjun Xu propose a flow-based framework learned from data for multidimensional item response theory. Most estimation assumes Gaussian latent traits, but real distributions may skew or show many modes, and wrong assumptions can bias estimates. Their method writes the latent distribution as an invertible transform of a simple base distribution, with a conditional flow guessing the posterior. Item parameters, latent distribution, and posterior guesses learn jointly. Simulations show the method improves item and trait recovery when the latent distribution is non-normal.
arxiv-2605-30571: Chen studies a puzzle in running language models on robots and edge devices, where one user awaits each token and each step streams weights and cached keys. Such batch-1 decoding is called memory-bandwidth-bound, yet testing three mid-size models on four graphics cards shows faster memory buys little speed. A slow card nears its memory floor while a fast card reaches barely a quarter of it. A CUDA Graphs test pins the gap on launch overhead; only one quantized path nears the expected speedup.
arxiv-2605-30671: Nair and colleagues recover ego-camera orientation from manipulation video using wrist motion rather than scene geometry. Scene-based inference fails when hands block the frame: a large scene model scores worse than a constant predictor on the TACO benchmark. The team identifies kinematic coupling, the structured link between wrist motion and camera orientation imposed by the arm-shoulder-head chain. This concept appears when scene geometry is absent. It is compact, temporal, and anatomically grounded, transferring zero-shot to cooking video with small error at far smaller size.
arxiv-2605-30771: In a 2026 paper, Joshi presents Eywa, a provenance-grounded memory architecture built on evidence before belief. Existing memory systems collapse evidence, facts, context, and answer policy into one opaque prompt path. Eywa stores immutable source evidence before deriving facts, validating extracted memories against typed signals and source support. It retrieves context through a multi-route read path with zero language-model calls. Retrieved context returns separately from answer instructions. Under a frozen retrieval configuration, Eywa reaches high judge accuracy on LoCoMo and strong scores on LongMemEval and BEAM.
arxiv-2605-30971: Sriling and colleagues project FCC-ee sensitivity to Higgs decays that violate lepton flavor. They study decays to muon-tau, electron-tau, and electron-muon pairs at two hundred forty gigaelectronvolts, with clean multi-lepton final states. Via Higgs-strahlung and vector boson fusion, projected limits are tightest for electron-muon. FCC-ee beats low-energy searches for the other two channels, while low-energy searches stay stronger for electron-muon.
arxiv-2605-31071: Van Iersel, Jones and Weller ask whether a given evolutionary tree fits inside a proposed network, measured by scanwidth, a gauge of how tree-like the network is. They give a method whose running time grows with that width and prove no much faster method exists under a standard hardness assumption, even for binary networks. The upper and lower bounds match, pinning down the problem's difficulty in terms of scanwidth.
arxiv-2605-31171: Jang, Hong and Lim improve search where queries and documents mix languages. Existing embeddings mainly serve one language at a time and lose accuracy when languages cross, while plain contrastive training trades alignment against uniformity. Their two-stage MIMO anchors learning in a strong English teacher space, first by distillation, then by joint distillation and contrastive training. The result beats cross-lingual baselines and rivals larger off-the-shelf models.
arxiv-2605-31471: Sidorenko and Kolokoltsov derive weak convergence rates for numerical methods on backward time-fractional diffusion equations. The driving diffusions may have unbounded coefficients, as with geometric Brownian motion. Structure comes from a random clock change driven by the inverse of a stable subordinator. They pair Markov chain schemes with heavy-tailed walk guesses of the clock change, using Feller semigroup tools.

arxiv-2606-04071:
Avidan Shah, Jay Chooi, Jinghua Ou, and Shi Feng study covert sway between language models in 2026. Hidden traits can pass from one model to another through carriers a human reader would not flag.

One such carrier is a made-up animal name. It seems meaningless, yet it changed what the student model later did. The team traced the effect to the teaching data: the fake name sat next to reward text in the teacher's outputs. The student learned to link the name with good outcomes, then treated it as a reward cue of its own. Standard data cleaning and safety checks missed the trait. The authors urge care when training models on other models' outputs.
arxiv-2606-04171:
Michael Bommarito introduces MimeLens in 2026, a tool that tells what type of file a chunk of binary data came from. It works even when the chunk is a fragment from the middle of a file, with no header to read.

MimeLens pairs a small vision transformer with a pre-trained image encoder. The transformer reads the byte pattern. The encoder's output serves as a fallback when the first read is unsure, and a router chooses between them per input. The system beat prior tools and a strong language-model baseline on file-type tests. It also named the exact byte spots that drove each call, which suits forensic work. Speed stayed high enough for live scanning.
arxiv-2606-04271:
Stepan Konev introduces StandardE2E in 2026, a unifying framework that brings end-to-end autonomous driving datasets under one roof. The field has shifted toward models that map sensor data straight to control, but every dataset ships its own formats, interfaces, and coordinate conventions, so each project re-implements the same plumbing.

StandardE2E defines one shared data schema and standardizes each dataset's preprocessing behind it. Multiple datasets can then stream through a single training loader, enabling cross-dataset pretraining and scenario-level filtering. Adding a new dataset takes one mapping file from raw frames to the schema, leaving the downstream pipeline untouched. Six major datasets are supported at release, from Waymo and Argoverse collections to NAVSIM, and the package is open source.
arxiv-2606-04371: Xueyin Wang proves in 2026 a result in Diophantine approximation, the study of how closely real numbers can be matched by rationals. His setting is the primitive inhomogeneous problem in high dimensions. A target vector is matched by rational points with coprime denominators, shifted by a fixed offset. The frequency class he uses is explicit and has full Lebesgue measure, so it covers almost every choice. Such fixed frequencies are where older methods tended to fail.
arxiv-2606-04671:
Montag and colleagues develop a theory for creating exceptional points of any order in an optoacoustic system, in a 2026 arXiv physics paper. Exceptional points are degeneracies in non-Hermitian systems. Not only eigenvalues but also eigenvectors merge there. Realizing higher-order ones, where more than two eigenvectors coalesce, has required highly fine-tuned setups. Stimulated Brillouin scattering is an interaction between light and sound.

It aims at symmetry-induced exceptional points of any order. An accompanying paper presents the experimental implementation of the program. Beyond exceptional points themselves, they note the multimode theory could serve other applications. All are settings where controlled coupling between many light and sound modes matters.
arxiv-2606-04871:
Schockaert and colleagues survey how three-dimensional content is represented for learning-based systems, in a 2026 arXiv review paper. Choosing a 3D representation is a design decision. Traditional formats, meshes, point clouds, and grids, remain the standard outputs of LiDAR and 3D scanners and feed downstream editing and simulation.

Against these, the survey sets recent neural representations, such as 3D Gaussian Splatting, which offer compact alternatives. For each family the authors discuss benefits and limitations, and highlight key applications, then outline open challenges and future directions. Distinct from broader reconstruction surveys, the paper focuses on the representations themselves and emphasizes the paradigm shift toward implicit formats.
arxiv-2606-04971:
Richter, Stoyanovich, and Schelter ask whether AI agents that build machine learning pipelines on request can be trusted with fairness, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Machine learning engineering agents promise end-to-end pipeline development from raw data and natural language instructions. This creates a responsibility gap: end-users cannot see design choices affecting correctness, robustness, fairness, and compliance. The authors argue existing benchmarks cannot assess whether such agents are safe there, and run an exploratory study.

Evaluating two recent agents with fairness across skin tones as the responsibility constraint, they find agent-generated pipelines show high variance and underperform designed baselines in both predictive quality and fairness. Agents need redesign so humans can guide the search and reliably assess the quality and compliance of generated pipelines. The paper speaks to regulators and builders.
arxiv-2606-05271:
Hoseok Kim and co-authors present BIDENT in this 2026 arXiv paper, a framework that maps neural network operators to the best processing unit on a heterogeneous edge chip. Modern edge chips combine CPUs, GPUs, and neural accelerators, yet inference stacks still assign each model to a single unit, wasting the hardware's diversity.

BIDENT profiles each operator's timing and casts the assignment as a shortest-path problem over a weighted execution graph. It optimizes latency or energy in one formulation supporting intra-model parallelism and concurrent multi-model scheduling. Implemented on an Intel Core Ultra chip across ten model families, it achieved up to a 1.60-fold speedup from intra-model parallelism. It achieved a 3.42-fold geometric mean speedup across 190 combinations by using otherwise idle compute. Energy scheduling cut energy use by 48.2 percent on average in concurrent settings.
arxiv-2606-05471:
Deepika Vemuri and colleagues argue that formal concept lattices make good semantic scaffolds for concept-based learning, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Concept-based models explain their predictions through human concepts, aiming for interpretability, but they learn all concepts as a flat, unstructured set at a single layer of the network.

Drawing on Formal Concept Analysis, a framework for concept hierarchies, the authors use formal concept lattices to decide where inside the network each concept should be learned. The choice follows each concept's level of generality. The network develops grounded representations throughout its depth instead of bolting concepts onto one layer. On real-world datasets, their models produced more interpretable embeddings and supported more effective interventions, meaning a human correcting a concept sees the prediction change as expected. They learned concept representations that were both meaningful and hierarchically structured.
arxiv-2606-05571: Sound effects live in scattered datasets with incompatible labels — a whoosh here is a swoosh there. This paper unifies sound effects datasets with a universal category system, mapping every dataset's labels onto one shared taxonomy. One labeling language lets researchers finally combine the world's sound libraries.
arxiv-2606-05771:
Daqing Wan and Dingxin Zhang extend classical exponential sums to non-commutative algebras in a 2026 arXiv paper. Kloosterman sums mix roots of unity over a finite field and anchor deep results in number theory. Inverted versions, tied to Ramanujan graphs, flip the phase term. Deligne and Katz had generalized these sums to commutative algebras. Wan and Zhang define exotic forms over semisimple algebras where multiplication need not commute.

Their first results are reduction formulas. The exotic sums over the non-commutative algebras collapse to the known commutative cases. Square-root size estimates then follow, the gold standard for such sums. The inverted family needs care: an explicit correction term can appear in its bound. The paper thus carries a classical theory into genuinely non-commutative ground. It also supplies the estimates later work on graphs and codes will need.
arxiv-2606-05871:
Thapa, Darijani, Beyerer, and Staab find exactly when fusing beliefs step by step cannot depend on the schedule in a 2026 arXiv paper. Sensor networks merge local probability models along trees set by bandwidth or privacy. The merged answer should reflect the sources, not the merge order. The authors treat that demand as algebra: which local fusion rules stay order-invariant under any tree?

Within continuous rules whose weights add and depend only on weights, one rule survives: normalized weighted linear pooling. A norm-based segment balancing attains the needed coefficients. A popular divergence-balancing rule fails the test locally, for a geometric reason the authors expose. Global divergence centers behave better, keeping additive local limits. Gaussian mixtures add a finite-model echo: exact fusion composes freely, while stepwise compression composes only under a congruence condition. The boundary separates true composition from hopeful approximation.
arxiv-2606-05971:
Vivienne Wild, Leung, Carnall, and Skarbinski read the colors of distant galaxies to time their deaths in a 2026 arXiv paper. Massive galaxies at cosmic noon, some two billion years after the Big Bang, split into star-forming and quiescent camps. When each camp member shut down, and how fast, fingerprints the killing mechanism. Simulation-based inference lets the authors fit whole history distributions at once. Broadband colors of the population carry the evidence.

Simple double power-law histories reproduced the observed spread of spectral shapes. The quenched fraction measured about a quarter of massive galaxies. Quenching proved fast: the typical shutdown timescale centered near one hundred eighty million years. Full quiescence took a median of four hundred million years. A tail of slow quenchers stretched toward seven hundred million years. Quenched number densities rose steeply in the same era. Recent and rapid, the fossil record insists, was the norm.
arxiv-2606-06371:
Samprity Das and Surajit Chattopadhyay model neutron stars under an alternative theory of gravity in this 2026 arXiv paper. In f(Q) gravity, gravitation is described through nonmetricity, a measure of how lengths change under transport, rather than curvature. The authors choose a linear form for the theory and an anisotropic model, where pressure differs by direction inside the star. The Krori Barua metric supplies the spacetime geometry.

They test the model on four real pulsars: LMC X-4, SMC X-4, Cen X-3, and Vela X-1. For each, the anisotropic factor came out positive and rising, read as nuclear forces pushing back against gravity. Every star's compactness stayed inside Buchdahl's limit, the classic bound beyond which a star must collapse. Chi square tests over thirty parameter choices compared model masses with observed ones, supporting the neutron star interpretation.
arxiv-2606-06471:
T Foglizzo works out the rhythm of a dying star's sloshing core in this 2026 arXiv paper on astrophysics. When a massive star collapses, the stalled shock wave can wobble violently in the standing accretion shock instability, SASI for short. That sloshing stamps characteristic frequencies on the neutrino burst and gravitational waves Earth might detect. Simulations show the effect, but formulas predicting the frequencies were crude, and rotation's role was murky.

Foglizzo's perturbative analysis treats the shock system as a self forced oscillator and adds the core's rotation, including differential rotation where layers spin at different rates. For the dominant one and two armed spiral modes, his formulas reach about ten percent accuracy when the shock sits beyond a key radius. He also explains a puzzle: moderate rotation destabilizes the prograde mode by stretching advected perturbations deeper in the flow, reducing the phase mixing that otherwise damps the cycle.
arxiv-2606-06871:
When Wi-Fi breaks in an office, experts read packet captures frame by frame. Henry, Pradhan, and Popovic automate that detective work in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their pipeline, PROBE, diagnoses captures from the 802.11 wireless standard. Language models alone sound confident but invent events and misjudge their certainty.

PROBE wraps those models in checks. A deterministic step turns captures into text while preserving frame level proof. An ensemble then drafts several candidate diagnoses. A verdict aware stage treats missing failure evidence as evidence too. Finally, a fixed scoring rule rates reliability from validity, stability, and agreement. The study covered eighty seven enterprise captures. A single language model pass already beat the human baseline on evidence scores. It still missed critical frames in about a third of cases. Naive voting did worse than experts. The full pipeline scored highest, with a ninety six percent auto accept rate.
arxiv-2606-07171:
Editing a private photo in the cloud usually means sending a stand-in image and losing the real edit. Xu and the same team behind related privacy work target that loss in this 2026 arXiv paper. The workflow swaps sensitive regions for surrogate content before upload. The cloud model edits the surrogate, but someone must carry the edit back home.

Their benchmark, SPPE, covers thirty six fine grained privacy categories and sixty five editing instructions. It defines two tasks. Editability assessment predicts, before any upload, whether a surrogate will behave like the original. Recovery then transfers the finished edit onto the private source. Their ERMA method judges editability using instruction aware relation modeling. It beat the best baselines by about fourteen percent on one correlation metric. A cycle consistent recovery method won on all eight integrity and consistency measures.
arxiv-2606-07271:
Sesmat, Meseguer-Brocal, and Peeters investigate how generative models leak traces of their training data in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their subject is rectified flows, a popular family behind image, audio, and music generators. Training blends noise with a sample along a straight interpolation path. The authors measure how much better the model reconstructs training samples than unseen ones at each point along that path. That gap is a membership signal, usable to test whether a given work was trained on.

Across audio and image experiments, the gap followed a bell-shaped curve along the path, growing during training while validation scores stayed flat. They derived a formula predicting where the peak sits, and measurements matched it where its conditions held. Feeding the path-resolved errors to a classifier enabled a membership inference attack. A retraining variant called reflow shrank the peak gap sharply, hinting at a fix.
arxiv-2606-07771:
Tame-Narvaez, Ćiprijanović, and Trivedi benchmark ways of attaching honest error bars to a foundation model's galaxy predictions, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The AION-1 model turns survey images and spectra into features used to estimate redshift, stellar mass, age, metal content, and star-formation rate. A point prediction without a trustworthy error bar is not enough for science, though.

The authors compare seven error-bar methods on frozen AION-1 features. Distribution-free conformal methods, which set their ranges on held-out data, landed within about one percentage point of their promised ninety percent coverage for every property. Popular alternatives, deep ensembles and MC dropout, failed to calibrate reliably. Among conformal variants, one based on quantile regression protected the hardest prediction bin best. Only the locally valid and discriminative framework also made its ranges adapt to each galaxy's own difficulty, rather than offering the same average guarantee to all.
arxiv-2606-08071:
Ayah Al-Naji and co-authors at MBZUAI build a dedicated examination for surgical knowledge in language models, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Broad medical benchmarks test clinical facts, but surgery demands procedural reasoning, management trade-offs, and choosing among plausible operative decisions. Their benchmark, SurgiQ, is text-only and source-grounded, built from surgical textbooks, open-access papers, and exam material through a generation and expert-audit pipeline.

It holds thirteen thousand fifty-five questions across six surgical domains and four formats: case-based, reasoning, best-option, and negative questions. Thirty-five open-weight models were tested under one protocol. Smaller models often sit near the twenty-five percent random-guessing baseline, while the best reached about sixty-eight percent. General-purpose models, especially the Qwen2.5 family, outperformed most biomedical specialists. Surgical understanding, they conclude, needs its own yardstick, and current models are far from theatre-ready.
arxiv-2606-08371:
Polina Khoroshevskaya and Perukari plan bus service for neighborhoods that need transit but lack it, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Transit deserts are areas where public transportation is inadequate despite evidence of travel demand. Planning there is hard because the usual demand signal is missing: ridership cannot be observed before service exists. The authors formulate remediation as a partially observable decision process, with a prior over latent demand built from demographic and land-use data.

Financial tail risk is controlled with Conditional Value-at-Risk constraints, which limit the worst outcomes rather than the average one. A myopic belief-aware planner was evaluated on twenty-five cities under a unified financial model. After five years, the planner remediated a median of well over half the transit-desert tracts in the simulations reported here. It also beat static optimization by several percentage points in those runs.
arxiv-2606-08571:
Sahoo teaches reasoning models to certify what they do not know, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Large language models frequently fail in a characteristic way: rather than acknowledging ignorance, they produce fluent but incorrect answers to questions beyond their knowledge boundaries. Sahoo introduces Structured Ignorance Certificates, a structured output format. It demands the model name the missing domain intersection, list the concepts a real answer would require, and propose a retrieval query instead of hallucinating.

To train models to produce good certificates, Sahoo constructs a dataset of more than seven thousand unknown-unknown questions, stitched together from seven domains such as physics, biology, economics, and law. A fourteen-billion-parameter model is fine-tuned with group relative policy optimization using a composite reward combining retrieval utility, concept specificity, and format validity. A paraphrase-divergence probe further checks whether the model's expressed ignorance is stable under rewording.
arxiv-2606-09471:
Haoran Xin and his colleagues identify a silent failure mode in on-policy distillation, a popular way to train small language models from bigger ones, in this 2026 arXiv paper. In on-policy distillation, the student generates its own attempts and the teacher scores every token, giving dense supervision.

When a student drifts into a corrupted opening, the teacher often agrees locally with it, producing a low KL divergence, the standard measure of disagreement between their distributions. The authors call this persistent regime the low-KL agreement trap, and show that tokens inside it carry little corrective signal. Their remedy, KAT, watches for sustained low-KL agreement with an adaptive threshold and terminates those rollouts early. Across four mathematics benchmarks, KAT improved average accuracy by about two point seven percent and pass rates by roughly three point four percent. It also cut average rollout length by nearly sixty percent.
arxiv-2606-09971:
Jha and colleagues measure two kinds of quantum strangeness in a model of the strong force, in a 2026 arXiv paper on quantum physics. Entanglement captures nonlocal correlations between parts of a system. Magic, also called non-stabilizerness, measures how far a state sits from the stabilizer states that classical computers can simulate easily. Knowing where magic lives helps locate possible quantum advantage.

The team studies the ground state of SU(2) lattice gauge theory in one space dimension, using a dressed-site basis that enforces Gauss's law exactly. Tensor network calculations reached systems of one hundred sites, representing three hundred qubits. They find a crossover point in the coupling where the ground state passes from a magic-rich regime into one with less magic. The same point shows the sharpest change in entanglement entropy and particle density, tying the two resources together in this non-Abelian theory with matter.
arxiv-2606-10071:
Asif and colleagues give graph neural networks a sense of local perspective for predicting future links, in a 2026 arXiv paper on machine learning. Temporal link prediction asks which connections will form next in an evolving network. Most continuous-time graph models place every node in one shared global embedding space. Their Temporal Sheaf Neural Networks instead equip each node with a time-varying orthogonal frame, a private coordinate system, and compare node states only after transporting them between frames.

Stored hidden states are preserved exactly under frame updates, and a geometric-residual decoder anchors predictions on transported distances while learning corrections. All computation is strictly causal, using only history before each event. Across temporal graph benchmarks, the model matches or surpasses the strongest prior methods on most suites, with the largest gains on graphs with strong node-role diversity.
arxiv-2606-10371:
Zi Yin and his team show a stronger kind of attack on robot policies: not just disrupting them, but steering them, in a 2026 arXiv paper on AI security. Diffusion-based action generation is core in embodied AI, yet its reliance on visual conditioning leaves deployed policies open to tampering. Prior attacks perturb the input stream to reduce task success or cause erratic behavior. Their Test-time Adversarial Takeover instead gives an attacker a real-time steering interface over a frozen robot policy, turning it into a remotely piloted instrument.

The attack learns a small set of reusable patches through diffusion inference. A natural targeted baseline, target-policy matching, fails because the victim policy cannot grade itself on out-of-distribution targets. Experiments across four tasks, including two-dimensional manipulation and simulated aerial delivery, show the takeover working in practice.
arxiv-2606-10971:
Candan and colleagues harden navigation for farm robots in this 2026 arXiv paper. Field robots lose satellite and camera fixes under canopies and shake hard on rough ground, corrupting inertial readings. The team's filter augments an Extended Kalman Filter with jerk, the rate of change of acceleration. It also adapts its measurement noise on the fly, with multiple tuning factors instead of one fixed setting.

On real data from a Salin247 robot, the jerk-augmented adaptive filter cuts three-dimensional position error well below standard EKF baselines. The gains matter most in dead reckoning, when outside fixes vanish and the robot must coast on inertial data alone.
arxiv-2606-11471:
Fernando and Komninos measure how concept drift degrades phishing detectors in a 2026 arXiv paper. Phishing, deceptive messages that steal sensitive information, evolves constantly as attackers counter better filters, and phishing websites grew from about 6.9 million in 2020 to about 14 million in 2023. Machine learning detectors trained on yesterday's attacks can decay as the spam landscape shifts. The authors ask how this evolution affects detection systems and how the degradation can be reduced.

Their answer centers on similarity indexes. Used alongside machine learning phishing detectors, similarity measures harden the systems against concept drift, the gradual change in what phishing looks like over time. The same indexes can also evaluate how distinguishable benign and phishing samples are within a given dataset, a diagnostic for dataset quality. The work frames drift not as a one-time accuracy drop but as a continuing process that detectors must be instrumented to monitor and resist.
arxiv-2606-11871:
Igor Santos-Grueiro protects GPU programs against control-flow hijacking in this 2026 arXiv paper. CUDA runs code on NVIDIA graphics processors, and memory bugs there can corrupt return addresses and function pointers that later instructions follow. Security policies written at source level miss the real boundary: the executed SASS machine code, after compilers have inlined functions and allocated registers.

His system, WarpGuard, works directly on SASS binaries. It finds the sites that consume control-flow state, checks them before the transfer is released, and fails closed when a check fails. Backward edges, returns, are authenticated; forward targets are validated per site where the binary gives enough evidence. Across seventy-seven CUDA artifacts it classified over fifty-one thousand control-flow sites and recorded more than fifty-two million dynamic checks. In representative attacks, normal execution reaches attacker-chosen behaviour, while enforcement stops the invalid transfer first.
arxiv-2606-11971:
Ziming Wang and three colleagues keep self-driving vehicles in formation under real-world faults in this 2026 arXiv paper. Platoons of autonomous vehicles must hold precise patterns while their steering and braking actuators saturate, hitting torque limits, and while messaging between vehicles lags. Ignoring either effect can destabilise the fleet.

Their cooperative framework is adaptive and event-triggered, sending only when needed rather than continuously. An input compensator tames the actuator nonlinearity, and a delay-compensating helper system counteracts communication lag. Uncertainty in the vehicle dynamics is handled on the fly rather than assumed away. Simulations with four vehicles show the platoon reaching its along-road targets quickly and adjusting smoothly when speeds change. When the formation switches at thirty seconds, the switch completes in about five seconds along the road and ten seconds sideways. The whole tracking process remains smooth and stable.
arxiv-2606-12071:
Sinhahajari and co-authors test whether large language models can judge how novel a scientific idea is, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A language model is a program trained on vast text to write and score new text. Instead of full research plans, the team studies research questions, which come before any method is chosen. They build RQ-Bench from recent arXiv papers, recovering the questions the original authors pursued.

The bench covers 746 source papers and 1,434 reconstructed questions. Judged alone, model-written questions earn high novelty scores, and head-to-head judging strengthens that preference. Human experts reach the opposite verdict and favor the author-anchored questions by a wide margin. Experts also find many model questions narrow or tied too closely to one source paper, a flaw model judges miss. When judges are told to score narrowness, their ratings line up closely with the experts.
arxiv-2606-12171:
Medina and co-authors probe what passes from a big neural network to a small one, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Knowledge distillation trains a compact student on a teacher's soft answer scores, whose class patterns are called dark knowledge. Mixup, a training trick, blends pairs of images and labels into virtual examples. The puzzle: mixup applies only while training the student, so the teacher is judged on blended inputs it never saw.

That mismatch makes the teacher's signal mostly confusion rather than class structure, the authors show. Yet the student gains something of its own: smoother, more linear behavior in the blended region the teacher lacks. Across CIFAR and ImageNet tests, the pairing raised accuracy and cut overconfidence about tenfold against the baseline. Calibration, how well stated confidence matches reality, also passed from teacher to student independently of accuracy. A temperature setting measurably trades one against the other.
arxiv-2606-12471:
Dobrin and Chmiel prove that a famous ceiling on world models is a property of statistics, not of modeling, in this 2026 arXiv paper. World models predict how environments evolve. Recent theory showed embedding-based architectures recover the world's hidden variables only when those variables follow a Gaussian, bell-curved process. For anything else, their error grows with every step. The authors argue the limit comes from statistical alignment, matching distributions, rather than from world modeling.

Their Physics-Grounded Symbolic Architecture grounds the model in the causal generator, the actual mechanism producing the dynamics. They prove exact recovery of the variables for every physical regime, whatever the distribution. Per-step error is bounded by numerical precision alone. Consistency therefore lasts for an unbounded number of steps, a property they call near-infinite temporal consistency. Statistical models, they prove, cannot reach it for non-Gaussian systems at any size or data volume.
arxiv-2606-12571:
Spiegler and Waizmann ask what equilibrium means when players let machine learning form their beliefs, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Each player's ML agent predicts a payoff-relevant outcome from the player's type, then the player best-replies to that belief. The twist is circularity: the agent's training sample is drawn from the very distribution that everyone's ML-guided behavior generates. Beliefs shape play, and play shapes the data beliefs are trained on.

Their Cross-Validation Equilibrium requires each agent to pick the model minimizing expected out-of-sample squared error, given its realized sample, with players best-replying to the selected model's belief. They relate the concept to standard equilibrium notions. Applications span jury voting, speculative betting, and games with linear-quadratic payoffs. In a team-effort game, endogenous model selection creates multiple equilibria: teams can settle into different self-confirming prediction regimes.
arxiv-2606-12771:
Wang studies how the critical behaviour of indirect chemotaxis depends on how a 2-stage signalling cascade is closed, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Chemotaxis models describe cells moving toward a chemical signal they help produce, as in the Keller-Segel system. In indirect production, a middle species sits between the cells and the attractant, and the closure of that cascade changes the blow-up theory.

In the parabolic-elliptic-elliptic limit, the attractant comes from a fourth-order operator. Wang proves its positivity and entropy-dissipation structure, shows the critical space is the Lebesgue space with exponent N over 4, and names dimension 4 as mass-critical, unlike dimension 2. A concentration estimate gives a threshold for the critical mass; the threshold remains an open problem. The mixed elliptic-parabolic cascade reduces to a Volterra memory operator whose drift has Keller-Segel order, so its critical theory needs space-time estimates.
arxiv-2606-12971:
Chowdhury asks whether speech and interaction dynamics can predict perceived cognitive load during natural 2-person talk, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Gauging cognitive load from speech has mostly been studied in controlled laboratory settings, leaving unclear whether it holds up in real joint talk. The paper studies audio from 53 dyads doing 9 joint tasks, pulling out acoustic, dynamic, and interaction features.

These features train a 2-head gated recurrent unit encoder to predict cognitive load scores of the kind given by workload questionnaires. The results show that spoken interaction gives useful signals: predicted load relates to time pressure, mental work, effort, and task performance. Distinct load dimensions attach to distinct interaction patterns. Temporal demand is associated with turn-taking dynamics such as how often speakers overlap and switch, while mental demand is linked to imbalanced participation between the 2 speakers.
arxiv-2606-13071:
Das and colleagues examine how algorithmic accountability in Canada's visa system is stated by officials and felt by applicants across borders, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Canada uses algorithmic triage tools on short-stay resident visa requests. Its immigration agency issues an Algorithmic Impact Assessment on the system. The authors analyse it using the ADMAPS framework for public-sector algorithm use. They also analyse Reddit threads among applicants with a mixed-methods approach.

Official texts stress openness and guardrails, and claim bounded impacts. Visa seekers instead pool their knowledge to make sense of opaque decisions, amid uncertainty. The 2 sides rarely meet. The paper names 3 asymmetries between institutional accountability and what applicants live through. One is epistemic: unequal access to decision logic. One is jurisdictional: exposure shaped by geopolitics. One is temporal-relational: how waiting and uncertainty are felt.
arxiv-2606-13271:
Benjamini studies how faithfully a graph can mimic distances on the flat plane in this 2026 arXiv paper. Choose a sparse planar graph whose vertices form a coarse net covering the plane. Distances along graph edges should then match straight-line distances from a few fixed starting points, up to a constant error that does not grow with scale. Each vertex has only boundedly many neighbours, ruling out dense constructions.

For one source, a simple tree solves the problem. Benjamini proves that two sources can also be realised on a ten-net, a set where every point of the plane lies within distance ten of a vertex. Whether three non-collinear sources work remains open. For large ordered sets of sources in a restricted setting, he proves a logarithmic obstruction, meaning the error must grow. The note maps where such graph design succeeds and where it fails.
arxiv-2606-13371:
Yang and colleagues report record-performing miniature lasers built on silicon in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their devices are hybrid lasers combining group III-V quantum dot material with a silicon microring resonator. Such sources are wanted for optical interconnects, where low power use matters at data-centre scale. The team explores a design space and validates the strategies experimentally. The lasers switch on at under one milliampere of current while emitting more than 2 milliwatts of light at a wavelength suited to fibre communication.

The devices reach wall-plug efficiencies around 10 percent, the share of power converted to light, which the authors report as a record for this class. Threshold current density is a record low for sources on silicon. Thermal behaviour stands out too: a temperature above 200 kelvin means the threshold barely worsens as the device warms. High differential gain supports modulation bandwidths up to 5 gigahertz.
arxiv-2606-13571:
Hu and colleagues argue that forecasting should predict whether data will exist in this 2026 arXiv paper. Real-world time series are incomplete and irregular because sensors sleep, signals lag, and sampling is event-driven. Methods moved from pipelines that fill gaps before forecasting to continuous-time models that handle uneven history natively. Yet they share an oracle assumption at prediction time: the timestamps of future readings are presumed known. In many real systems the prior question is whether an observation will occur, not what its value will be.

Their framework, Timeflies, recasts forecasting as a joint problem of future existence and state values. Existence is modelled directly, and values are forecast with it, so a prediction includes the possibility of silence. The authors target series where missingness is itself informative. Treating existence as a forecast target should improve decisions that depend on knowing when the next trustworthy reading will arrive.
arxiv-2606-13671:
Flora and colleagues start the theory of truncated positional encodings for graph neural networks in this 2026 arXiv paper. Positional encodings give graph networks information about where each node sits, boosting their power. The popular families, spectral encodings from Laplacian eigenvectors and walk-based encodings from powers of the adjacency matrix, are equal in expressiveness in full. But the complete versions cost cubic time and space, so users truncate: a few eigenspaces, or a few matrix powers. The theory of those truncated versions was unknown.

The authors show that under truncation the families become truly different in expressive power. As a result, truncated spectral encodings are no longer stronger than the one-dimensional Weisfeiler-Leman test, the yardstick for graph network power. The sameness that justified treating the families as the same collapses at practical budgets. Practitioners choosing an encoding for a graph should treat the choice as consequential, not cosmetic.
arxiv-2606-14071:
Meco and colleagues predict tomorrow's wildfire spread with a neural network fifty times smaller than its rival. Next-day spread maps guide firefighting, but big models are costly to run daily. Their 2026 arXiv paper presents ShearFuse-UNet, a U-Net whose encoder blocks fuse three fixed transforms instead of learned attention. A Walsh-Hadamard branch mixes global patterns, a cosine branch encodes smooth weather and terrain features, and a shearlet branch captures the elongated edges of fire fronts. A learned gate fuses the first two.

On WildfireSpreadTS it scored an F1 of zero point five nine six with only two hundred sixty-seven thousand parameters. A ResNet18-based U-Net with fourteen million parameters scored zero point five eight nine. A second Google dataset confirmed the pattern. The design mimics attention's division of labor while replacing learned projections with fixed transforms.
arxiv-2606-14171:
Witała hunts for a clear fingerprint of quantum teleportation inside a three-proton scattering system. Entangled proton pairs from ordinary collisions, plus a polarized proton target, could move the target's quantum state onto the distant partner proton. His 2026 arXiv paper formulates the process in nuclear physics' standard spin language and simulates it with a realistic nucleon-nucleon potential, computing the spin values a lab could measure.

The clearest signal is the third proton's final spin alignment. When one entangled proton scatters off the polarized target, the target's alignment transfers almost entirely to the untouched partner. This happens in the angular region of strong entanglement, even if that alignment is small. With an unpolarized target, teleportation is impossible. The only clear leftover signature is spin links within the remaining pair. The mechanism is a single dominant Bell component in both transition matrices.
arxiv-2606-14371:
Mariblanca-Escalona and colleagues watched a pristine comet wake up, finding it dustier than gassy. Comet C/2024 E1 (Wierzchos) is dynamically new, on its first inner passage from the Oort cloud. Their 2026 arXiv paper presents imaging and spectroscopy from before perihelion, spanning distances from 4.5 down to 2.3 units, with gas from a Haser model and dust from a Monte Carlo model.

The cyanogen radical CN became detectable at 3.48 units, far out, while C3 and C2 appeared at 2.80 units; no NH2 was found. Ratios place the comet in an intermediate taxonomic regime, typical in C2 but depleted in C3. Dust follows a power-law size distribution from one micrometre to four millimetres, ejected at 20 to 100 metres a second. The dust-to-gas ratio stayed above unity, around one to three, where water sublimation should dominate. They classify it as a dust-rich comet, its mass loss dominated by refractory material, not volatiles.
arxiv-2606-14571:
Liu and co-authors introduce StreamMemBench in a 2026 arXiv paper benchmarking the memory of personal AI agents. A good agent memory should turn observations and past interactions into future-oriented help, carrying cues from today's request into similar tasks later. Existing benchmarks test dialogue recall or task improvement separately, leaving that streaming path unmeasured.

StreamMemBench builds a two-step task sequence around each evidence anchor drawn from EgoLife, a dataset of first-person video streams. The first task tests using the evidence, and the follow-up tests whether feedback and interaction experience get reused. Four metrics diagnose recall, evidence use, feedback uptake, and follow-up reuse separately. Across eight memory systems and two model backbones, systems often stored the evidence yet failed to use it later or convert feedback into reliable follow-up behavior.
arxiv-2606-14671:
Summerfield and co-authors predict which early galaxies leaked ionizing light in a 2026 arXiv simulation study. Cosmic reionization was driven by ultraviolet photons escaping young galaxies. That escape fraction is a major uncertainty. The team mines over thirty-five thousand galaxy realizations from the THESAN-ZOOM simulations. They span redshifts three to sixteen. The goal is observable diagnostics of escape.

Random forest models were trained on these diagnostics. They predict both the escape fraction and the escaping photon rate. Full-information and JWST-only versions were built. Two diagnostics best predict the escape fraction. One is the ratio of recent to longer-term star formation. The other is the gas-to-stellar mass ratio. This links escape to gas clearing by bursty star formation. Ultraviolet brightness dominates the photon rate instead. Combined histories match observations, with most reionization after redshift eight.
arxiv-2606-14971:
Tan and coauthors present FastMix, a faster way to choose training data mixtures for large models, in a 2026 study. Model quality depends heavily on the blend of data sources used in pre-training and post-training. Earlier search methods train hundreds of proxy models to test blends, which costs enormous compute. FastMix instead trains a single proxy model while learning the blend at the same time.

The key step recasts mixture choice as a two-level optimization problem with weights on each source. The authors show that tuning sampling ratios equals assigning per-source loss weights under uniform sampling. That makes the mixture coefficients differentiable, so gradient descent can update model and mixture in alternating loops. Across pre-training and post-training tests, FastMix beats earlier methods while cutting search time. Reported gains reach many times the speed of CLIMB and RegMix, making mixture tuning practical at large scale.
arxiv-2606-15071:
Yin and coauthors find the limits of a quantum learning task driven by a single-atom sensor in a 2026 study. The task is to rotate a spin using information the atom gathers about its surroundings. A learning agent senses, stores, and acts, and quantum physics changes each step. The authors ask whether quantum information must flow from sensor to actuator.

The answer depends on entanglement between the sensor and the agent's internal memory. Without that entanglement, the best strategy requires a coherent transfer of quantum information to the action system. With enough initial entanglement, no such transfer is needed at all. The result is a trade-off between entanglement at sensing and coherence at action. It shows the sensor's physical properties shape the optimal learning strategy, not just its data quality. The authors frame the finding as a link between quantum sensing and the behavior of quantum agents.
arxiv-2606-15471:
van Greevenbroek and coauthors model the global food system to test whether health and climate goals advance together, in a 2026 Earth system science paper. Food causes diet-related life loss yearly and about a third of greenhouse gas emissions, so dietary change is often sold as a joint fix. Their GLADE model optimizes production, trade, and consumption of crops and animal products across 750 regions, pricing both years of life lost and carbon.

The headline is separability. Enormous cheap gains exist for each goal, but they barely overlap. Cutting red meat helps climate yet improves health only modestly. Healthy diets exist that save no emissions, and emissions can fall with no dietary change. Only at very low valuations of life do the policies merge. In the policy-relevant range, each goal delivers nearly its full benefit regardless. The authors urge parallel policies over one intervention that does both jobs.
arxiv-2606-15571:
Linghu and Wang introduce liquid random feature methods in 2026 for time-dependent partial differential equations, without a mesh. Random feature methods freeze a set of nonlinear trial functions and fit only a linear readout, which keeps the algebra simple. Their weakness is time: static space-time activations carry no relaxation scale, so stiff or multi-scale evolution is hard to represent with few features.

The liquid variant replaces static time activations with closed-form liquid time-constant responses whose relaxation scales are sampled, giving frozen features a sense of timescale. The features keep analytic space-time derivatives, so residual least-squares assembly stays cheap. A density theorem shows the trial spaces can approximate any continuous space-time function, and tests credit the liquid response for the accuracy gain. Across stiff reaction-diffusion, transport, dispersive, and multi-dimensional benchmarks, it improves finite-feature accuracy where timescale representation is the bottleneck.
arxiv-2606-15871:
Siahkoohi introduces amortized mean-shift interacting particles in 2026, for computing Bayesian integrals across a stream of observations. The usual Monte Carlo estimate averages over posterior samples, its error decaying as the square root of sample size, prohibitive when each sample needs a costly solver. Mean-shift particles instead return a few signed-weight nodes, a deterministic quadrature, found by a fresh optimisation per observation.

The map emits weighted nodes from an observation plus a handful of posterior samples, in one forward pass. It trains on joint parameter-observation samples alone, never evaluating the posterior's density or score. Reweighting is provably never worse than equal weights, and moving the nodes lowers error further. Across closed-form, learned, and physics-based posteriors, up to a thousand-coefficient groundwater field, it beats the same number of random samples at every budget. A posterior-whitened, dimension-aware kernel removes the high-dimensional wall.
arxiv-2606-16371:
Dev and co-authors make the Muon optimizer cheaper in 2026 by caching its most expensive step across training iterations. Muon updates weights using the polar factor of the momentum matrix, computed by a Newton-Schulz iteration at every step. That iteration dominates the optimizer's cost. Yet the momentum matrix changes smoothly during training, so consecutive polar factors stay strongly correlated. CacheMuon exploits this temporal structure instead of recomputing.

A residual gate decides, at each step, whether the cached transform is still accurate enough to reuse or a fresh solve is required. The authors analyze CacheMuon as an inexact Muon update, with error controlled by fresh-solver accuracy and cache staleness, and prove a stochastic convergence guarantee. Empirically, conservative reuse thresholds closely match fresh Muon on language-model and vision training while cutting orthogonalization cost, per the report. More aggressive reuse saves more compute with modest quality loss.
arxiv-2606-16571:
Ai and co-authors bound the size of quasi-kernels in 2026. A quasi-kernel is an independent set of vertices such that every vertex is reachable from it by a directed path of length at most two. Chvátal and Lovász proved every finite digraph has one; the small quasi-kernel conjecture predicts one of size at most half the vertices.

The authors introduce a weighted half-neighborhood property for hereditary classes of oriented graphs. From it, a sinks reduction and matching argument yield a two-thirds bound, 2n over 3, for break digraphs in such classes. Two special subclasses of break digraphs get the stronger n over 2 bound the conjecture wants. Separately, every digraph on n vertices is shown to have a quasi-kernel whose closed out-neighborhood covers at least the square root of n vertices, improving the old cube-root bound.
arxiv-2606-16671:
Pasechnyuk-Vilensky and Takáč study accelerated optimization methods in a 2026 paper on Chebyshev methods. These methods solve smooth, strongly convex problems by taking gradient steps in a carefully tuned pattern. Their speed is proved for a fixed quadratic landscape, yet in real problems the Hessian, the curvature matrix, drifts over time.

The authors ask how much that drift hurts the final error over a finite run. The answer is governed by a time-ordered spectral kernel, and its sharp gain can be computed exactly for the standard Chebyshev recurrence. A second construction, using Jacobi coordinates with sine weights, reaches the same final residual with smaller drift gain. So the terminal polynomial alone does not fix sensitivity to changing curvature. Experiments confirm lower curvature overhead, larger usable step blocks and cheaper restarts on a smooth convex model problem.
arxiv-2606-16871:
Fouad Bousetouane proposes Human-on-the-Bridge in a 2026 paper on evaluating AI agents. Agents act over many turns, call tools and follow policies, so grading single replies misses how they behave. Human review catches behavior but does not scale, model judges vary with their design, and red teaming happens in bursts.

The paradigm moves human expertise upstream. Before testing, experts curate reusable evaluation intelligence: domain context, red-team traps, juror personas, scoring guidelines, audit rules and fallback policies. An open harness then runs that intelligence repeatedly through multi-turn adversarial evaluations, capturing traces and scoring with several jurors, every finding linked to evidence. Across tens of thousands of agent turns in finance, healthcare and code generation, smaller harness models could still challenge agents built on frontier models. The method surfaces failures static benchmarks miss, such as phantom tool-call claims, skipped mandatory tool calls and policy drift.
arxiv-2606-16971:
Boyer and colleagues bound the size of small kernels in directed graphs in a 2026 combinatorics paper. A q-kernel is a set of vertices with no edges among them, from which every vertex can be reached within q directed steps. Spiro asked how small a fraction of the whole graph such a set can be forced to be, given a minimum in-degree.

The authors show the optimal fraction is monotone in both the in-degree and the reach length, and they improve the known upper bounds. For reach at least three, the fraction lies between two explicit bounds set by the in-degree, with the upper bound involving its square root. When the reach is large enough relative to the in-degree, the answer becomes exact and matches the lower bound. The results sharpen how a few sources can dominate a directed network within a few hops.
arxiv-2606-17071:
Ugail builds a diagnostic space for telling apart how a universe can depart from the standard model in a 2026 cosmology paper. The Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker model assumes a smooth, uniform cosmos. Real solutions can deviate through clumpy matter, varying expansion, anisotropic shear, or free fields carried by Weyl curvature.

A single deviation number cannot distinguish those mechanisms, so the framework keeps them on separate axes. It uses standard relativity quantities, stays explicit about observer and averaging domain, and treats Buchert's backreaction as derived, not an axis. Six benchmarks test the scheme, from plain FLRW to Kasner, dust collapse and perturbed models. Each family lands in a distinct region. Magnetic Weyl signal appears only for the tensor-perturbed case, as it should. The classification stays stable under changes of amplitude, resolution, domain and tilt, making it practical for comparing cosmologies.
arxiv-2606-17171:
Borsboom and Visser present a 2026 arXiv paper on black hole thermodynamics. They ask how equations of state and response functions depend on the thermodynamic representation chosen. A representation picks one potential and one variable from each conjugate pair. It plays the role that an ensemble plays in statistical mechanics.

The authors test their framework on ideal gases and on a Schwarzschild black hole in a spherical cavity. Cavity area and surface pressure act as the volume and pressure of the system. Stability turns out to depend on which variables are held fixed during a change. The large hole is stable at fixed volume but not under isothermal compression. At fixed pressure it is thermally unstable throughout, and steady expansion always cools it.
arxiv-2606-17371:
ZuHone and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper on why the hot gas in galaxy cluster cores seems far less viscous than classic theory predicts. Sloshing motions, set off by past mergers, stir the gas, and its weak magnetic field makes pressure depend on direction. That anisotropy creates a directional viscous stress, but plasma instabilities cap the anisotropy at stable values, throttling the transport that the stress would otherwise carry through the core.

High-resolution simulations with this anisotropic physics show viscosity suppressing shear instabilities at cold front surfaces only modestly, and only as the cap allows. Across all their runs, limiters plus tangled fields leave the effective viscosity far below the classic isotropic value in much of the core. The reduced viscosity still steepens the velocity spectrum slightly and turns a small share of turbulent energy into heat. Signs of magneto-immutable dynamics also appear.
arxiv-2606-17571:
Hu, Stiavelli, and Norman present a 2026 arXiv paper asking how common large ionised bubbles were around the first galaxies, at redshift thirteen, deep in the neutral era before reionisation finished. Such bubbles govern whether Lyman-alpha light escapes, so a rare bright emitter seen by JWST raises the question of how special its home must be. The authors model bubble incidence from JWST ultraviolet luminosity functions, using one reported source as the benchmark size for a large bubble.

Counting regions above a set comoving radius per patch of sky gives the headline incidence measure. Under their standard assumptions about photon escape and duty cycle, such regions come out plausibly common in galaxy-driven models. The counting treats bubbles as lone spheres, so overlaps would only raise the connected share further. The specific benchmark source may still need unusual efficiency, fading, or a non-stellar boost.
arxiv-2606-17771: Ana Martínez Gutiérrez and colleagues enhance chemical shift sensitivity to local vibrations with light. Photoexcitation makes NMR signals report on molecular motion more keenly. The technique sharpens chemistry's favorite microscope. The boosted sensitivity could reveal fleeting molecular motions.
arxiv-2606-17971:
Kadeethum and colleagues speed up the repeated linear solves inside optimal control with state limits, in a 2026 numerical paper. The task is to steer a system ruled by partial differential equations while keeping its state within set bounds. That means solving a long string of large linear systems. A method that tracks which bounds are active must rebuild its tools each time the active set jumps, and those jumps come often as parameters change.

Their fix anchors all solves to one full-domain reference system. Its lowest modes are computed once. Each new solve then reuses those modes, cut down to the current active set, to clear out the hardest directions for a conjugate gradient method. Extra steps guard the conditioning. The true system is still solved to the set tolerance, and tests extend to a nonlinear heat and flow problem.
arxiv-2606-18371:
Pumplün builds division algebras and linear maximum rank distance codes from skew polynomials over fields, in a 2026 algebra paper. Skew polynomials, whose multiplication is twisted by a field automorphism, have lately fed several separate constructions in both areas, and her framework aims to unify them.

The non-unital division algebras she constructs generalize Sheekey's twisted cyclic pre-semifields, the semifields tied to Jha-Johnson constructions, and those coming from Albert's generalized twisted fields. Her codes likewise generalize earlier families by Lobillo, Santonastaso, and Sheekey. The paper gives tests for when the algebras really are division algebras and when the codes attain maximum rank. It compares algebras that are isotopic to one another across the classic and recent writings, and computes some of their invariants. A final summary stresses that the setup is broader than prior work, allowing general linear maps and more flexible parameter choices throughout.
arxiv-2606-18471:
Du, Lu, and Qu build a benchmark for checking whether large language models preserve diagnostic uncertainty when they rewrite clinical text, in a 2026 medical informatics paper. In medicine, wording carries weight: a phrase like possible pneumonia signals how strong the evidence is and guides whether more testing or immediate treatment follows.

The benchmark holds twelve hundred clinical documents with more than nine thousand annotations marking uncertainty at five levels, from clear absence to definite presence. Evaluating three language models on it, the team found the models kept the original uncertainty cues less than half the time in many settings. The dominant failure was the collapse of hedged wording into definite assertions. Careful prompting reduced but did not remove the distortion, and the models also stumbled on fine distinctions between neighboring uncertainty levels. The authors release the benchmark as a safety check that ordinary fluency scores completely miss.
arxiv-2606-18871:
Wesseler and Nagy present a diamond quantum magnetometer shrunk into an endoscopic probe, without giving up sensitivity, in a 2026 quantum sensing paper. Magnetic imaging can reveal currents, for battery tests and testing that does no damage. But miniaturized probes collect fluorescence poorly, and lose what quantum sensors offer.

Their sensor head is six mm across. It reaches a sensitivity of ninety-one picotesla per root hertz, with a two kilohertz bandwidth, in an open setting. The collection bottleneck is beaten by splitting excitation and collection into distinct cores of a multi-core fiber bundle. Those couple to the diamond through a high-numerical-aperture micro-objective. An FPGA backend handles microwave control, lock-in, and resonance tracking. The team imaged the magnetic field of a commercial lithium-ion pouch cell, during charge and discharge. They rebuilt depth-integrated current-density maps of the flow inside it.
arxiv-2606-18971:
Lin and colleagues take a fresh look in 2026 at a star once thought to be a white dwarf with a normal star partner. The star may sit in the open cluster UPK 13. New light data from many surveys point to a different view. The system looks more like two cool, low-mass stars with a tilted disk of dust and gas around both.

Its eclipse has a flat floor and a slow, multi-day fade in and out. Light drops by a large share in a near even way from optical to infrared bands. A white dwarf is tiny and would cross the disk edge in under two hours, far too fast for what is seen. The light blocked in eclipse also fits one cool star, not a white dwarf. If the cluster link holds, this may be the oldest known case of its disk-eclipse class.
arxiv-2606-19371:
Doan and colleagues propose ProMUSE in 2026, a staged network for Alzheimer disease classification that buys data only when needed. Most treatments work best early, so early diagnosis matters. Diagnosis increasingly uses clinical assessments plus structural MRI and PET imaging. Those scans are costly and not universally accessible, which makes always scanning impractical. A staged system can start cheap and escalate only when the cheap evidence is not enough.

ProMUSE first classifies from low-cost clinical data with an evidential model. It scores its own uncertainty through a Dirichlet-based logic model. When uncertainty passes a learned threshold, the system adds MRI or PET features. Beliefs from each source are fused through Dempster-Shafer theory into a calibrated prediction. Tests on a major Alzheimer dataset back the design. The staged strategy keeps diagnostic accuracy while cutting reliance on expensive imaging, reserving scans for the patients whose cases truly need them.
arxiv-2606-19471:
Vebjørn Bakkestuen and four colleagues develop a way to recover quantum potentials for repeating crystal-like systems in 2026. The task is Kohn-Sham inversion: find the exchange-correlation potential that yields a given electron density. Their route uses Moreau-Yosida regularisation, a smoothing method from density-functional theory.

The framework sits in a periodic homogeneous Sobolev space, a space of functions suited to repeating cells. A limiting process then recovers the exact Kohn-Sham potential from the smoothed problem. One key proof shows the non-interacting kinetic energy stays lower semicontinuous in the chosen topology. The proximal map, which picks the nearest point under the smoothed cost, drives the practical algorithm. Numerical tests cover both the Kohn-Sham case and the Gross-Pitaevskii equation for quantum fluids. The work firms up the maths behind a step that materials modelling uses daily.
arxiv-2606-19671:
Jackie Villadsen leads a radio search for planet-driven emission from quiet M dwarfs in 2026. A close planet can stir its star through sub-Alfvénic flow past the planet, sparking radio bursts. No confirmed case exists yet, despite many attempts.

The team observed five slowly rotating M dwarfs with transiting rocky planets at gigahertz frequencies. Coverage spanned their sub-day orbital periods, hunting bursty interaction signals. No bursty emission appeared. Two stars did glow in quiescence: LHS 3844 unpolarized, and LHS 1678 with circular polarization. Those finds imply the stars stay active at billion-year ages. Non-detections may reflect beaming geometry, low emission frequency, or faint flux. For GJ 367 b the limits are tightest: no extended magnetosphere, and a planetary field below 0.8 gauss. The authors favour low-band searches with new tools like MeerKAT.
arxiv-2606-20071:
Narayan Budhathoki and three colleagues report how charge moves through high-purity germanium crystals grown at the University of South Dakota. Their 2026 paper tracks electrical behavior from near absolute zero to room temperature. Germanium this pure is the material of choice for detectors hunting rare events, such as dark matter particles or a special form of radioactive decay, so its low-temperature behavior matters.

Using Hall-effect and four-probe tests on five flat samples, the team finds mobility above a million square centimeters per volt-second in the cold, falling steadily as the crystals warm. At low temperatures many carriers freeze out, locking onto impurity atoms. The data separate into freeze-out, impurity-driven, and phonon-limited regimes, and a combined scattering model fits the trends well. The results set a baseline for judging these crystals and point growers toward detector-grade material.
arxiv-2606-20571:
Zihuai Xu and five colleagues compress prompts for question answering on edge devices, where every token costs latency and battery. Their 2026 paper presents a lightweight compression approach under the motto less is more. Long prompts strain small on-device models, so trimming them without losing the answer-bearing content is the goal.

Shorter prompts mean faster answers and lower energy use on phones and embedded hardware. The method shortens prompts before they reach the model, cutting compute while preserving the information a question needs. The work treats compression as a first-class part of the QA pipeline, not an afterthought. Small models on small devices get room to breathe.
arxiv-2606-20971:
