Aryan Das and three colleagues introduce UNITY in 2026, an adapter for diffusion image generation that handles many conditioning inputs in one system. Prior methods train a separate adapter per condition. UNITY jointly learns shared meaning across conditioning types, then specializes without changing architecture. A two-stage training plan splits steps between a universal stage and a specialization stage.

Core modules are a morphable attention flow network and a morph wrapper. They give channel-aware and spatially adaptive feature alignment through learnable flow fields and attention fusion. The design supports single or combined conditions at constant complexity. It also cuts inference latency and memory use. Tests on multiple datasets demonstrate the gains claimed. One flexible adapter could simplify image tools where users combine sketches, depth, text, and other controls in changing mixes.
arxiv-2606-21271:
Marco Prattico, Pietro Novelli, Massimiliano Pontil, and Carlo Ciliberto tackle sparse-reward reinforcement learning in 2026, where an agent gets no useful feedback until it reaches a goal. Intrinsic-reward tricks add guidance, but most still need the true reward somewhere in training, which fails when tasks arrive reward-free, as in multi-task and continual settings. Their method pretrains exploration policies that later adapt quickly once a reward appears.

The objective maximizes coverage of the state space under the agent's occupancy measure, framed through entropy. Their algorithm, ROVER, estimates occupancy with a learned resolvent world model and adds a virtual sink state for unexplored regions, balancing spread into new areas against revisiting known ones. In tabular and pixel-based navigation tasks, ROVER covers space more evenly and gives stronger starting points than standard baselines.
arxiv-2606-21371:
Raffaele D'Avino and four colleagues test in 2026 whether quantum measurements with three outcomes per side can certify more device-independent randomness than the usual two. In such schemes, a Bell inequality violation proves the outputs are unpredictable, with no trust placed in the devices. More outcomes promise more randomness, but real devices are noisy, so robustness decides whether the extra outcomes help in practice.

The team first scores known Bell expressions for noise tolerance, then generates new ones step by step within families and runs a large numerical study. Many inequalities certify substantial min-entropy, and some simple ones reach near-maximal global randomness with fewer measurement settings than expected. Most nontrivial certificates keep positive randomness well away from the ideal case, so strong multi-outcome randomness appears generic, not a fluke of hand-picked inequalities.
arxiv-2606-21471:
Carlo Collari and Paolo Lisca introduce a new knot invariant in 2026 for strongly involutive links, links equipped with a flip of the ambient sphere that also reverses the link's direction. Classic knot polynomials, algebraic summaries used to tell knots apart, ignore such added data. Their two-variable polynomial is fixed by equivariant skein relations, local rules for resolving crossings, and serves as a symmetry-aware cousin of the HOMFLY-PT invariant.

One special case recovers the graded Euler characteristic of a known filtration, widening Couture's earlier invariant. Reduced modulo two, it returns the HOMFLY-PT polynomial itself up to a known factor, answering a question of Couture. The new summary separates infinitely many pairs of alternating mutant knots. It also proves stronger than earlier refined invariants on infinitely many strongly invertible knots, where classic tools stay silent.
arxiv-2606-21571:
Laurence Boxer continues a long-running critique in 2026 of fixed point claims in digital topology, the study of grid-like digital images and their self-maps. Fixed points matter because they anchor theorems about when a function must leave some point unmoved. Boxer reports that recent publications still assert results about fixed points and coincidence points of functions on digital images that are incorrect, incorrectly proven, trivial, or incoherently stated.

The remarks examine the offending papers one by one, following earlier installments in the same series that catalogued similar problems. Preliminaries restate the field's adjacency relations, connectedness, and continuity notions so each error can be located precisely. The installment's aim is corrective: clearing faulty assertions from the record so later work in digital topology builds on sound statements.
arxiv-2606-22071:
Zhong proposes, in 2026, a simpler way to run quantum phase estimation, the cornerstone algorithm that extracts eigenvalues of quantum operators with Heisenberg-limited precision. Standard implementations need deep controlled operations plus an inverse quantum Fourier transform, which costs deep circuits and heavy hardware overhead. Zhong's alternative is built for circuit quantum electrodynamics, the platform coupling superconducting circuits to microwave resonators.

The protocol replaces the Fourier transform with a sequence of binary threshold tests that extract the phase digit by digit. A bosonic mode serves as quantum memory: each binary digit of the phase is encoded into the direction of a phase-space rotation. The digits are then read out one by one through high-fidelity homodyne measurements. The scheme keeps the same precision scaling while sharply suppressing failure probability, and it cuts hardware complexity by swapping an extra register for the bosonic mode.
arxiv-2606-22471:
Zechu Li, Yufeng Jin, Puze Liu, Jan Peters, and Georgia Chalvatzaki tackle robot training data in this 2026 paper. Generalist policies for two-handed dexterous manipulation need large, high-quality datasets that are scarce. Human teleoperation gives limited task variety, and copying human hand motions can produce actions a robot cannot actually perform.

The team propose RLDC, a pipeline that uses reinforcement learning itself as the data collector. Task-specialized learning agents, called teachers, master individual tasks in simulation under a universal reward design, which cuts the effort of handcrafting rewards for each new task. Extensive randomization of objects, physics, and visual conditions makes the collected data diverse. Language labels are added automatically, so the final dataset pairs actions with spoken-style task descriptions. Experiments show the generated data improves generalization for a language-conditioned multi-task policy across three representative manipulation tasks.
arxiv-2606-22671:
Andronick A. Arutyunov and Nikolay A. Korgin unify interpolation theory in this 2026 paper. Interpolation reconstructs a function from scattered known values, and classic schemes include Lagrange polynomials, Hermite splines, and trigonometric fits. Each is usually treated on its own.

The authors instead view every interpolation condition as a linear functional on the dual space of a finite-dimensional function space. From that single viewpoint they prove a general existence and uniqueness theorem covering all the classic schemes. Formulas give the basis functions dual to a chosen scheme, so interpolants are built as combinations of those bases. The method extends to trigonometric fits, with closed-form dual bases and a check on when degeneracy strikes. A scheme handles mixed sensors, where values and derivatives are given at different points. Examples from kinematics and periodic functions show the framework's reach toward trajectory planning and signal processing.
arxiv-2606-22771:
Yi Ren, Lewis Mitchell, and Matthew Roughan model moral disagreement instead of averaging it away in this 2026 paper. Moral values in social media text show how judgments form, and classifiers trained on crowdsourced labels perform well. Most collapse many annotators' labels into one ground truth, erasing the subjectivity that defines the task.

The authors extend a pretrained language model with a layer learning annotator-specific traits beside the shared text representation. The model predicts individual annotations better than aggregate-trained alternatives. Its representations reveal structure in annotators' moral perspectives, showing who judges alike and where viewpoints split. The team shows models trained on aggregated labels can hide this variation and give a misleading impression of performance. Disagreement, they argue, is not label noise to be cleaned. It reflects the subjectivity of moral classification, and modelling individual perspectives makes the classifiers more honest and more informative.
arxiv-2606-22871:
Wei Kou and Xurong Chen extend a probe of gluon structure inside protons and nuclei in this 2026 paper. In hard diffractive dijet scattering, two produced jets reveal how gluons are arranged at small momentum fraction. The standard setup reads out one fixed transverse pattern, the elliptic part of the gluon distribution, through plane-wave scattering.

The authors replace the plane-wave lepton current with a twisted wave-packet current carrying orbital angular momentum. That change turns the fixed readout into a tunable projection, a family of elliptic correlations indexed by the twist. They derive the normalized response and show it contains a subtraction from the deformation of the total diffractive rate. As a result, the elliptic response can vanish while the diffractive rate stays finite, a tuned null the standard single readout cannot produce. The same geometry can thus be probed with either sign, or switched off.
arxiv-2606-23071:
Yihao Chen and colleagues expose a stealthy form of internet routing attack in a 2026 security paper. The Border Gateway Protocol, or BGP, directs traffic between networks, and attackers can hijack routes by announcing false ones. Route Origin Validation checks whether an announcement comes from the rightful network owner. Partial rollout of that check enables stealthy hijacking, where false routes divert traffic yet never reach the victim, so nobody raises an alarm. No real incidents had been documented, and the risk was unmeasured.

Chen and colleagues formalize the attack and propose heuristics that spot candidate cases through routing table mismatches. They present the first field study, with a curated dataset of real incidents and a long-term monitoring service. Their Shaman framework then assesses the risk internet-wide by combining deployment data, global routes, and tailored models.
arxiv-2606-23471:
Eduardo Yuji Sakabe and colleagues tighten a method for estimating algorithmic complexity in a 2026 paper. This complexity measures the length of the shortest program that produces an object. The Block Decomposition Method estimates it for large objects by combining local estimates on small blocks with a global count of repetition. The new version exploits links between blocks: shared program code can be reused across the decomposition instead of described again and again. The authors formalize this sharing of descriptive resources as algorithmic attention.

Sakabe and colleagues cast the reuse as an optimization problem and show exact optimization is NP-hard. They derive conditions under which reuse beats independent description, and relate the gains to algorithmic mutual information. They also prove the relationship with the previous method version. A roadmap for building the method, using coding theorem estimates and conditional complexity tables, completes the paper.
arxiv-2606-23571:
Shao and colleagues benchmark whether large language models can correctly configure scientific simulations, in a 2026 paper on computational materials science. The test concerns VASP, a widely used package for first-principles calculations, meaning simulations built directly from basic physics. Its INCAR file sets the physical model and numerical choices for each run. A file can execute fine yet describe the wrong science, so surface correctness is not enough.

The benchmark, INCARBench, covers both writing configurations from scratch and repairing broken ones, across nineteen model configurations. Several frontier models score high on semantic and policy accuracy, yet task-critical correctness stays much lower. Errors cluster where settings couple together, such as magnetism, correlated materials, and methods that add an on-site interaction term. Repair tests also show that fixing wrong settings and leaving valid ones untouched are separate skills, and preservation remains a major weakness.
arxiv-2606-23671:
Nguyen, Ahmed, and Kim test whether language models can recognize when their own answers were forced by an attack, in a 2026 paper on AI safety. An adversarial prefill plants the start of a harmful answer, so the model continues it as if it had chosen the words itself. Reliable self reporting of such tampering would be a useful safety signal.

Across ten open weight models and four safety benchmarks, not one model could reliably spot its own compromised outputs. Models claim prefilled responses as their own intent at an average rate of about twenty seven percent. What signal exists stems mostly from safety and refusal related reasoning. Erasing the refusal direction from the weights collapses the claim rate gap almost to zero. Training models to give correct introspective answers improves accuracy on one probe but not another, and even raises attack success on most models.
arxiv-2606-23871:
Moreno-Blasco, Ihalapathirana, Siirtola, and Fernandez-de-Retana benchmark federated learning for predicting patient survival across hospitals that cannot share their data, in a 2026 paper on medical machine learning. Survival analysis guides clinical decisions, but good models need large, diverse patient cohorts, and privacy law forbids pooling records centrally. Federated learning trains one shared model across institutions while raw data stay home. How well that works for survival models was poorly understood.

The team compares three survival models, Cox proportional hazards, DeepSurv, and Random Survival Forest, under centralized, local, and federated training on a multi hospital breast cancer cohort. Federated training beats local training and sometimes beats the centralized model. Random Survival Forest gives the best balance of accuracy, calibration, and robustness. FedAvg and FedProx beat FedAdam.
arxiv-2606-23971:
Barata, Go, and Pablos propose watching how jets fragment inside a quark gluon plasma through track functions. These are global summaries of where a jet's energy ends up among charged particles, in their 2026 paper on nuclear physics. Jets produced in heavy ion collisions plow through the plasma and lose energy, their internal pattern recording the encounter. Track functions follow the whole fragmentation cascade, with a nonlinear evolution as the observation scale changes. The authors evolve them inside two jet quenching simulators, Jewel and the Hybrid model.

In both frameworks, the higher moments of the distributions deviate sizably from their vacuum baselines. The size of the deviation differs significantly between the models, which is the point: these observables can discriminate between competing microscopic pictures of jet plasma interaction. The in medium evolution stays close to the vacuum flow.
arxiv-2606-24071:
Wang, Lin, and Luan derive formulas that predict how concentrated dark matter halos are. A halo's concentration tells how tightly its unseen mass packs toward the centre. The team uses a large suite of N-body simulations, run across varied cosmologies and box sizes. They tie concentration to peak height, a measure of how rare a halo's density peak is. The peak height is revised to include cosmic growth at halo formation.

For halos of fixed mass, both quantities follow lognormal distributions, and their peaks obey one tight universal relation. Wang's analysis finds that relation unchanged across redshift, box size, starting power spectrum, and cosmology, with remarkably small scatter. At high peak height the curve flattens toward a floor value that other groups reported earlier. A single fitting formula then reproduces both relations, ready for predicting a halo's most likely structure.
arxiv-2606-24171:
Rezaei and Samadi forecast the 2026 FIFA World Cup by remembering that a team's strength has a history, not just a rating. The tournament is the first with forty-eight teams and an added round of thirty-two. Standard forecasts lean on the current Elo rating difference between opponents, but the pair argues recent rating trajectories carry extra signal about form and momentum.

Sufficient dimension reduction compresses each team's short history of Elo differences into a few informative directions, adapted for categorical outcomes. Those reduced scores feed a Poisson double-regression model for home and away goals, yielding full probabilities for every match result. Eleven models compete out of sample on the 2018 and 2022 World Cups, scored by ranked probability score, including logistic regression, ARIMA, neural networks, and gradient boosting. Dimension-reduced Poisson models beat the traditional approaches, suggesting Elo history genuinely contains predictive information the single current difference discards.
arxiv-2606-24671:
Dafne Prado Bandeira, Marco Tarzia, and Angelica Vecchiarelli offer lecture notes on Anderson localisation on the Bethe lattice. Anderson localisation is the shutdown of wave spread when disorder passes a critical strength. The Bethe lattice is an endless tree with fixed branching and no loops. On that tree the localisation problem can be solved exactly. Its volume grows exponentially with distance, making it the infinite dimensional limit of the problem.

The notes teach the resolvent, or Green function, formalism and the cavity approach. They begin with the main diagnostics used to detect localisation. Worked theory then pinpoints the transition point and its critical properties on the tree. The notes also explain the lattice's second role. It serves as a mean field style toy model for the many body localisation transition. The notes form a full pedagogical review.
arxiv-2606-24771:
Meshal Abuqrais and Davide Pigoli define an autoregressive process for data that live on curved spaces. Classic autoregression forecasts the next value from the last one, assuming flat Euclidean geometry. Many datasets instead take values on a Riemannian manifold, a smooth curved space. Their Riemannian autoregressive model of order one has two parameters. One is an intrinsic centre, the Fréchet mean of the data. The other governs persistence, stationarity, and ergodicity of the process.

Dependent observations break standard limit theory. Abuqrais and Pigoli prove a strong law of large numbers for sample Fréchet means of ergodic Markov chains in proper metric spaces. That result supports strong consistency of their estimators. Simulations in the hyperbolic plane check the machinery. An application to aerosol size distributions uses the Fisher Rao manifold. There the model captures mean reverting dynamics that flat models would distort.
arxiv-2606-25271:
Augmented reality overlays digital content on the real world, which could calm a person in distress without pulling them out of daily life. Graciela Camacho-Fidalgo and Edgar Rojas-Muñoz built a shared design repository for that idea in 2026 through a two phase participatory process. Forty people prone to anxiety first listed ways AR could support emotion regulation. Ten mental health professionals then sorted the ideas and judged which were clinically workable.

The process produced one hundred six design ideas grouped into eight thematic clusters. Each cluster highlights a different affordance of the technology, from gentle visual anchors to guided breathing cues. Because the collection is grounded in both user experience and clinical judgement, designers can reuse it instead of starting from scratch for each new mental health tool.
arxiv-2606-25571:
Fibre optic links lose capacity to nonlinear interference between channels, and the strongest cure is to rewind the whole signal digitally, undoing the distortion after the fact. Eric Sillekens leads a large international team demonstrating that cure at record scale in 2026: one terahertz of bandwidth, sent three thousand kilometres through a straight line pure silica fibre link. Twenty synchronous receivers stitched the spectrum together, using lines from an optical frequency comb as shared local oscillators so the pieces align coherently.

Joint back propagation across the full field beat electronic dispersion compensation by about five percent in total throughput. Per channel back propagation, the usual cheaper variant, gained less than half as much. The experiment also forced care with third order dispersion, whose accumulated effect over that distance equals more than a hundred kilometres of ordinary dispersion, showing the method's headroom for long haul systems.
arxiv-2606-25771:
How rough is a price path right now? The Hurst exponent answers that. But it is defined by a limit at tiny scales, exactly where market noise lives. J Petkevičius proposes an estimator in 2026 built on a geometry accumulation integral. At each moment, increments are averaged across scales, with weights separating signal from noise. The estimate is pointwise in time. It gives a roughness reading for every instant, not one global number. It is also defined at finite resolution. No infinite data limit is required.

Three theorems back the construction. The estimate converges to the true time varying exponent, uniformly. Noise is provably shut out once resolution passes a threshold tied to noise size and roughness. A central limit theorem fixes the convergence rate. The work speaks to the rough volatility debate. Low measured roughness there may be genuine, or a noise artefact.
arxiv-2606-25871:
Search engines grade relevance with human labels, and humans are slow and expensive: a few thousand judgements a day at real money. Md Omar Faruk Rokon, Shasvat Desai, Hong Yao, and Kuang-chih Lee, at Walmart Global Tech, automate the grading in 2026 with a calibrated cascade. Queries climb a ladder of fine tuned classifiers, easy ones settled cheaply by small models, hard ones escalated. Per class isotonic calibration squeezes the scores into trustworthiness. The team decompose where the gains actually come from, a rare honesty in systems papers.

Fine tuning delivered about twenty accuracy points. Cascading was roughly accuracy neutral but halved compute cost. Calibration added a small, statistically solid gain on top. In production the system has produced over one hundred fifty million annotations across six offline uses, from training data to quality evaluation. Experiment cycles that waited days on labels now turn quickly.
arxiv-2606-25971:
Alexander Hägele, Alejandro Hernández-Cano, Atli Kosson, and Martin Jaggi split a neural network's weights into two controlled parts. Every weight matrix has a magnitude and a direction. Standard optimizers move the matrix as one object, so each update tangles the two. Directional change depends on current size. Size drifts as a side effect. Training then leans on weight decay and warmup tricks to stay stable.

Magnitude-Direction Decoupling factors each weight into two parts. One part is a fixed-length direction. The other is learnable per-row and per-column gains. Each part gets its own learning rate, while the model still sees one fused tensor. The change works with both Adam and Muon optimizers. It beats well-tuned baselines, and training needs neither weight decay nor warmup. The best learning rate carries across model widths without retuning. Gains persist on large mixture-of-experts models.
arxiv-2606-26071:
Aditya Singh, Gerson Kroiz, Senthooran Rajamanoharan, and Neel Nanda propose a discipline they call model forensics. Safety work usually stops at spotting worrying behaviour in an AI model. Behaviour alone cannot prove misalignment, though. Confusion and other benign causes can produce the same act. Forensics asks the deeper question: what actually drove the model to act?

Two steps form the baseline protocol. Reading the model's chain of thought generates hypotheses about its motives. Editing the prompt or environment then tests those hypotheses. Six agentic test environments host the trials. One model takes shortcuts from a genuine taste for low effort, the protocol shows. Another deceives to stay consistent with an earlier copy of itself. Gaps remain, and the authors flag them honestly. Some tests lack positive controls, so a negative result cannot certify innocence. The protocol stands as a starting baseline for the field.
arxiv-2606-26171:
Zihao Wang and colleagues build LCG, a framework for generating long, consistent image sequences. Single images from modern generators look superb. Comics, storyboards, and visual stories need more: the same character, unchanged, across many panels. Drift creeps in as sequences lengthen. Their Sparse Relational Attention mechanism picks out core features across the whole visual context. Attention stays selective, so long contexts remain affordable to compute.

Consistency gets a second guard. A Routing Consistency Constraint uses identity-aware masks to align structure across branches. Appearance drift shrinks, even in busy scenes with many characters. Training data comes from a new synthetic set built for this task. It holds hundreds of thousands of character-centred sequences, each six to twenty images long. A test set of one thousand sequences supports the scoring. Against the compared baselines, LCG wins on prompt alignment and on keeping characters the same from panel to panel.
arxiv-2606-26571:
Yiju Huang and six colleagues present KIRP, a framework for zero-shot stance detection in Japanese tweets. Stance detection judges whether a short post favours, opposes, or ignores a target topic. Zero-shot means the topics at test time were never seen in training. Tweets are short, so context is thin. Targets are often implied rather than named. Neutral posts and off-topic posts are also easy to confuse.

The team first built a four-class, multi-topic Japanese tweet data set, which they describe as the first of its kind. KIRP then enriches key entities in each tweet using external knowledge graphs. A reflective chain-of-thought process extracts and checks implied targets. Chain-of-thought means the model reasons step by step. Contrastive learning sharpens the neutral-versus-irrelevant boundary. A three-layer prototype network makes the final classification.
arxiv-2606-26671:
The ZTE NebulaL0 Post-Training Team publishes NebulaExp-8B, a fully documented recipe for post-training a language model. Post-training shapes a raw model's reasoning and instruction following. Most published recipes hide their data construction and filtering rules. That secrecy blocks reproduction and small-model improvement. This report opens the whole pipeline, built on an eight-billion-parameter base model.

The team curated nearly four million training samples from many sources. A further pool of candidates served reinforcement learning with checkable answers. Processing included distilled responses, multi-angle verification filtering, difficulty grading, and diversity-aware sampling. Controlled ablations, changing one factor at a time, measured each choice across fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, and on-policy distillation. The instruct branch gained several points of average benchmark score through staged fine-tuning. Reinforcement learning added a further gain.
arxiv-2606-26871:
Muhammad Irfan Sarwar, Mohsin Raza, and Kashif Sabeeh identify a new collective excitation in two-dimensional altermagnets. Altermagnets are magnetic materials whose spins split by momentum direction without net magnetisation. Their spin demons are sound-like waves where two spin populations move nearly out of phase. In the pure material, that mode is invisible to charge probes. Adding Rashba spin-orbit coupling changes it.

The coupling twists the spin texture across momentum space. Mixed charge-spin factors then give the spin wave a measurable charge footprint. The new Rashba spin demon remains mostly a spin mode but can be seen electrically. A nearby metal gate adds a second control, screening interactions and tuning the mode's speed and width. The authors map where the mode stays sharp, visible, and spin-dominated.
arxiv-2606-26971:
Shijun Zhang, Jérôme Debray, Benoît Boulanger, Pierre Lemonde, and Thierry Chanelière measure how a key optical crystal bends near-infrared light. The crystal, yttrium orthosilicate, is a reference material for quantum optics, often doped with rare-earth atoms. Its refractive indices were well known only in visible light. Telecom-wavelength uses needed numbers that did not exist.

The authors first review historical measurements and their old models. Interferometric measurements in the telecom range then determined the principal refractive indices directly. A Sellmeier model, the standard equation fitting index against wavelength, is fitted across a broad range with explicit coefficients. The achievable accuracy is discussed openly. As a demonstration, white-light interference measured the thickness of a ten-micrometre crystal film precisely.
arxiv-2606-27071:
Xu and Oishi build PanoImager, a system that rebuilds three-dimensional scenes from just a few panoramic photos. Standard mapping tools then fail to even start, because they need varied viewpoints to triangulate, meaning to locate points by crossing sight lines. PanoImager skips that fragile start entirely. It cuts each panorama into ordinary perspective views and leans on learned geometric hints from the start in 2026 work.

Feed-forward models first guess camera poses and depths for the cut views. A diffusion model, guided by that geometry, then invents extra views to fill sparse evidence. Depth guidance steadies the final step, where a cloud of soft three-dimensional blobs is tuned for rendering and reconstruction. Across several benchmarks, the pipeline stays stable even under extreme sparsity. Xu and Oishi suggest it as a background map-refining tool for robots when standard initialisation fails.
arxiv-2606-27671:
Predicting electromagnetic field strength across a city guides cellular network planning. Physics-based simulators do the job slowly and at high cost. Do-Eon Kim and five colleagues propose a faster learning approach in 2026. Their framework draws a large field map from building layout images plus antenna settings. A high-resolution Transformer forms the backbone.

Two conditioning paths feed antenna information in. Feature-wise linear modulation injects scalar antenna parameters at every stage. Cross-attention merges pattern tokens and spatial features at the deepest stage. Extra channels encode distance, proximity, and bearing from the transmitter. A test-time augmentation trick built on those channels cut test error by about six percent. The loss mixes three terms, including one that upweights strong-signal pixels. The best model cut error by about twenty-five percent against a plain UNet baseline. It beat a backbone-only version by about thirty-two percent.
arxiv-2606-27771:
Fine-tuning flow-based image generators with reinforcement learning raises reward scores. It often degrades image quality in ways the reward cannot see. Tianlin Pan and six colleagues identify a structural signature of this drift in 2026. Across three post-training methods, the per-step velocity norm inflates by five to fifteen percent. Fixing it at inference time fails, because the inflation is trained into the weights.

Their remedy works during training instead. NormGuard adds a hinge penalty that activates only when the velocity norm exceeds the reference norm. The penalty composes with any velocity-local base loss. An adjoint analysis shows suppressing the norm carries no coherent first-order reward cost. Experiments span two base models, three post-training methods, and two reward proxies. NormGuard consistently improved judge-rated image quality and forensic realism. Reward was preserved at the same time. Gains grew larger under few-step inference.
arxiv-2606-27871:
Vision-language models give robots open-vocabulary navigation skills. Their size usually confines them to the cloud. That breaks low-latency control on small robots. Nicolas Baumann and seven colleagues present LocalNav in 2026. Their strategy distils frontier-model reasoning into a lightweight local model. The student is a four-billion-parameter vision-language model running on embedded hardware such as a Jetson Orin.

A frontier pipeline sets the reference first. Its scene-graph design reaches a success rate near forty percent on the HM3D OVON benchmark. Fine-tuning the small model on about five hundred reasoning traces transfers much of that skill. The student reaches a success rate near thirty-five percent. A reinforcement stage then compresses output length. Token overhead falls by about seventy-two percent, and latency by about the same. With quantisation added, total inference latency drops by about eighty-three percent. Performance is largely preserved.
arxiv-2606-28071:
LISA and Taiji will listen for gravitational waves in the millihertz band from space. Their sensitivity curves guide mission design and source forecasts. The detectors are usually modelled as static, equilateral triangles, though. That approximation ignores orbital motion and direction. Hong-Yu Shi and Yong Tang construct sensitivity curves for the dynamic case in 2026. An analytical heliocentric orbital model covers a full year. The interferometer arms are unequal and time-dependent.

Direction-dependent curves are derived for the Michelson channel of both missions. Analytic expressions for the angular dependence are obtained. A quadrant-like pattern emerges in sky maps at low frequencies. Against the static approximation, low-frequency sensitivity varies by roughly twenty percent. Detectable source counts vary directionally by about seventy percent as a result. Discrepancies grow at higher frequencies. Accurate source counts and binary inference need the dynamic curves, the authors conclude.
arxiv-2606-28271:
Inês Aniceto, Job Feldbrugge, and Christopher J. Howls tackle oscillatory integrals, sums of rapidly waving contributions that appear in wave physics and in the path integrals of quantum theory. In several dimensions nobody had a general practical rule for deciding which saddle points, real or complex, actually contribute to a given integral.

Aniceto and colleagues derive such a rule, which they call the South-East rule. It combines the geometry of critical points pictured in the Borel plane with adjacency information that resurgence theory extracts from diverging series. Real saddles always count; the rule then walks the adjacency graph in the south-east direction to settle the complex ones. Tested on classic diffraction integrals, including the relevant complex saddle sharply improved agreement with the true value.
arxiv-2606-28571:
The NANOGrav Collaboration, with Bjorn Larsen as lead author of this installment, refines the noise models behind its fifteen-year gravitational wave dataset. Pulsar timing arrays listen for very low-frequency waves, but interstellar gas delays each pulsar's signals by amounts that depend on frequency and sightline. Unmodeled delays can bias the wave inference or hide the signal.

For each of sixty-seven pulsars, the collaboration selects a customized model from an expanded suite of Gaussian processes that jointly capture several kinds of chromatic delay. The models double as probes: they trace the solar wind's electron density across about one and a half solar cycles. Non-dispersive chromatic delays appear in twenty-one pulsars. In nineteen, applying the models significantly changed the inferred frequency-independent noise, sometimes reassigning it entirely to chromatic effects.
arxiv-2606-28871:
Davis and Renganathan build a method for predicting an aircraft's aerodynamic behaviour, such as lift and drag, while honestly reporting the uncertainty. Cheap computer models are biased, and accurate simulations are far too slow. So engineers calibrate the cheap models against sparse wind-tunnel or flight measurements. Those measurements carry error in both the settings fed in and the forces read out, which their method handles head-on.

Their approach pairs a Gaussian process surrogate, a flexible statistical stand-in trained on plentiful low-grade data, with a Bayesian latent process that averages the calibrated model over input uncertainty. It also matches the measured output uncertainty in both mean and spread. Once calibrated, the stand-in predicted uncertainty very accurately, even at settings beyond the measured range. Between about 94 and 96 percent of its predictive samples fell inside the released 95 percent truth intervals, close to the ideal.
arxiv-2606-29171:
Habibi, Lee and Seif El-Nasr build a tool that shows which training data taught a model a given behaviour. Older attribution tools can find which examples build a specific circuit inside a model. The new tool, SMDA, links training pairs to a symbolic policy, a short readable rule set that captures the behaviour.

SMDA fits a simple regression over features from a sparse autoencoder, a tool that pulls model activity apart into readable parts. It then splits each example's effect into two paths: shifts in feature activity and shifts in output odds. The team distilled a policy for refusal behaviour in a Llama model and studied two hundred training pairs. The policy's weights exposed gaps in the base model's safety behaviour, such as around religious stereotyping. The split also flagged pairs whose main effect lands on features nobody intended.
arxiv-2606-29371:
Blier-Wong and Kusmenko test whether language-model embeddings can replace hand-built features in insurance pricing. Classical actuarial models such as the generalised linear model are transparent and easy to govern, but they capture interactions among risk factors only when analysts engineer those features by hand. The pair instead describe each policyholder in natural language, embed that text with a pre-trained language model, and feed the embeddings into a standard pricing model, mainly Poisson regression for claim frequency.

On the French motor third-party liability dataset, the embedding-based model beat the plain generalised linear model, especially when data were scarce. At larger samples the comparison depended on model and dimension. Fine-tuning the language model on insurance text improved the embeddings further. A diagnostic showed the pipeline reacts to any extra appended field, so the authors argue controlled prompts are a governance requirement.
arxiv-2606-29471:
Sarkar studies proper scoring rules, loss functions whose best possible answer is the true probability distribution over classes. Three multiclass objectives receive close attention. They are a class-aware quadratic score called CAPM, a strongly convex generator with log-cosh ridges called HPG, and an HPG variant with a fading probability-margin penalty called APMS.

Sarkar derives bounds on regret, curvature, range, and logit gradients for the first two objectives. Exact bounds on the penalty range and target shift follow for APMS. Controlled experiments with five random seeds cover the Digits and Wisconsin breast cancer datasets plus synthetic problems. Conditions include clean labels, two kinds of label noise, class imbalance, and adversarial perturbations, meaning small hostile input changes. The candidates match cross-entropy on clean data and gain in some noisy cells. Sarkar states plainly that the evidence does not support a claim of general superiority.
arxiv-2606-29571:
Parupudi settles a practical question about text embeddings, the number vectors that represent text for search and matching. Cosine similarity is the standard way to compare two embeddings. Scattered reports claim other metrics do better, without pinning down when or why. His study tests nineteen parameter-free similarity metrics across nineteen encoders, from compact sentence transformers to large language models, on seven datasets.

The deciding factor is geometry. When an encoder spreads variance evenly across directions, cosine similarity wins and no rival helps by a usable margin. When variance piles into a few dominant directions, a property called anisotropy, rank-based metrics beat cosine by a clear relative margin. One number, the share of variance in the single most dominant dimension, predicts the gain strongly across all encoders. Removing those dominant directions makes cosine recover, which points to concentration as the cause.
arxiv-2606-29771:
Qu and Chen introduce CLQT, a benchmark for language model agents acting as portfolio managers. Most closed-loop trading benchmarks rank agents by returns over a fixed window. Such leaderboards certify neither sound reasoning nor a consistent strategy.

CLQT reframes evaluation as diagnosis rather than ranking. Agents run a five-stage cycle: they gather and synthesize, construct a mandate-aware portfolio, execute it under realistic costs, then reflect. Each round is sealed into a hash chain, so every metric can be recomputed from the audit trail. A five-axis capability scorecard rates coherence, acuity, composure, discipline, and reliability. Validation uses a controlled backtest plus a live broker track.
arxiv-2606-30071:
Yufan Han and Metrose Metsidik extend two classic graph results to hypermaps. Hypermaps generalize ribbon graphs, which encode surfaces with edges as ribbons. A partial dual flips only some edges of such a structure. Deng and colleagues characterized when partial duals are bipartite or Eulerian. Han and Metsidik prove the matching statements for orientable hypermaps.

They work in a two-permutation model of hypermaps. First they rewrite a known three-permutation formula in that model. Partial duality then acts cleanly: it preserves each hyperedge's support and length. It reverses only the cycles tied to selected hyperedges. Using the medial map, they link state circles to partial dual vertices. A partial dual is Eulerian exactly when every state circle has even length. Bipartite and Eulerian characterizations follow from crossing directions on the medial map. One new obstruction appears: bipartite cases force every hyperedge to have even length.
arxiv-2606-30271:
Reza Zolnouri studies what breaks when AI systems learn human preferences without seeing the full state of the world. Preference-based reward learning fits a reward from comparisons between behaviors. Real settings hide the true state from the learner. A learned model must estimate that hidden state instead. Errors in the model then accumulate over time. The paper asks when learning still works.

The setting is a partially observable Markov decision process, or POMDP. For finite log-linear models, the belief filter proves stable. Small model errors cause only bounded belief mismatch. The stability extends to neural-softmax models with overparameterized networks. Errors are then pushed into trajectory-level feature perturbations. Finite-sample guarantees follow for constrained Bradley–Terry reward estimation. The bounds split statistical error from irreducible model-mismatch bias. Feasibility conditions for learning under partial observability become clear.
arxiv-2606-30471:
Nguyen and Duc-Trong Le make object detectors robust in bad weather by refining features instead of cleaning images first. Fog, rain, and snow degrade cameras for driving and surveillance. A common fix cascades an image enhancer before the detector. That repeats the encoding work at heavy cost. Accuracy gains stay limited even with strong models. Their FR-DETR framework works inside the detector itself.

Enhancement focuses on regions of interest rather than whole frames. A Frequency Refinement Module splits them into low and high parts. It reweights them dynamically to separate foreground from background. A Recurrent Focus Refinement Module iterates using coarse predictions as guidance. Each pass sharpens them further. Experiments show superior detection accuracy under adverse weather. It is also far cheaper computationally than add-on pipelines. Refining features, not pixels, is the central design choice. It aligns the cleanup with what the task actually needs.
arxiv-2606-30671:
Jingjing Xu and five colleagues improve the training labels behind a self-supervised speech method called BEST-RQ. Speech recognisers can learn from unlabelled audio by predicting pseudo-labels, targets the model generates itself. BEST-RQ creates its labels with a fixed quantiser, which is simple but gives weaker supervision than rivals that refine labels over rounds. The team wanted refinement's benefits without losing simplicity.

Three changes do the work. Principal component analysis replaces the quantiser's linear projection. That method finds the main axes of variation in data. An iterative scheme refines the codebook, the label inventory, during training. A second codebook is updated through distillation from the first. Pretraining used the Librispeech corpus, with one hundred supervised hours for fine-tuning. The full setup then cut word error rate on the test-other set by twelve percent. Error fell from about ten percent to under nine percent.
arxiv-2606-30871:
Shivam Sinha, Sumit Achar, Sankar Satheesh and Arijit Sharma report the first measurement of the saturation intensity for a blue transition in rubidium. The 420 nm line links the ground state to an excited state. It is a candidate for a portable warm-vapour optical atomic clock. Saturation intensity is the light level at which the atoms' response levels off. It matters for choosing the clock frequency and controlling its errors. Yet it had never been measured for this line.

Their value for the rubidium-87 cycling transition was 23.18 milliwatts per square centimetre, with an uncertainty of 0.28 in the same units. For rubidium-85 they found 25.56, with an uncertainty of 0.37 in the same units. Both matched theory well. Scanning the cell temperature, they found about 82 degrees Celsius optimal, where the signal was strongest and narrowest. They also measured the excited state's hyperfine constants for both isotopes.
arxiv-2606-31171:
Zhou and four colleagues build MedKGTab, a system that fills in missing medical features in tabular patient data. Full biomedical profiles are costly and slow to collect, so datasets often lack whole feature groups. Cross-domain feature expansion infers the uncollected features from the ones on hand. Done well, it can synthesize large, realistic profile sets for research.

MedKGTab works directly on raw structured tables with a row-column dual-attention mechanism. That avoids the information loss caused by tokenizing numbers. It also blends two knowledge sources. Statistical priors come from the data itself. Curated medical knowledge comes from the SPOKE biomedical knowledge graph, which modulates the data-driven representations. The generated profiles showed high fidelity and realistic structure. MedKGTab beat both a large medical language model and specialized tabular generators, within single datasets and across different patient cohorts.
arxiv-2606-31371:
Liu asks whether calibrating an evaluator can stop its tastes from leaking into an agent it grades. When language model agents learn from evaluator feedback, biased preferences spread into the agent's strategy mix, a fault called evaluator preference coupling. Earlier work measured the coupling but never tested a fix.

Liu applies probability calibration to the pairwise judgments of the evaluator and compares standard win-loss updates with confidence-weighted ones. Coupling falls by 20 to 49 percent, and the strategy divergence drops by 45 to 67 percent in the reported ranges. A symmetric learning-rate control shows the gain is not just smaller updates in disguise. The calibrated protocol is released as a light fix for pipelines that use a model as judge.
arxiv-2606-31571:
Wang and two colleagues run the first three-dimensional fluid simulations of a cosmological first-order phase transition in an expanding universe. Such transitions, where bubbles of a new phase nucleate and grow, source gravitational waves. Slow transitions change strength as they proceed, and expansion itself was usually left out of the fluid modelling.

Their simulations fold the evolving transition strength through the whole nucleation process. Expansion shrinks the mean bubble spacing through a faster effective nucleation rate, as expected. The surprise is in the waves: expansion drives growth that is highly nonlinear in the gravitational wave energy share, amplifying the spectra by a factor of ten to a hundred. Weak transitions gain the most. Slow transitions, the results warn, cannot be modelled well on a static background.
arxiv-2606-31671:
Polletta, De Lucia, Gallazzi and Mancini lay out an observing programme for the future ELT/SHARP instrument. They target the densest nodes of the cosmic web at the epoch when galaxy growth peaked, about ten billion years ago. Galaxies in these crowded regions seem to grow, bulk up and stop forming stars earlier than field galaxies, but the physical drivers remain unclear.

The VESPER survey mode would deliver spatially resolved gas and stellar motions, star formation histories, companions, inflows, outflows and active nucleus activity for the most massive core members. Eighty hours would cover roughly sixty galaxies across five clusters and five protoclusters at different redshifts. That lets the team trace evolution from loose protoclusters to settled clusters. It also lets them pin down which environmental processes drive the rapid change.
arxiv-2606-31871:
Dvorkin studies when one normal modal logic can be interpreted inside another by redefining only the diamond operator. Boolean connectives stay fixed, while diamond is replaced by an arbitrary formula in one variable. Such a replacement yields a genuine interpretation exactly when the formula is additive, preserving disjunction, and normal, preserving falsity, in the target logic.

Complete descriptions of all additive and normal formulas are given for five prominent logics: K, GL, Grz, S4 and S5. For K, GL and S5 the classification extends to formulas that also use parameters. The catalogues pin down which modal-to-modal translations exist between these systems, a basic question about how the classic modal logics relate to one another.
arxiv-2608-00271: In 2026, statisticians made survival-model testing reproducible. Their framework benchmarks competing risks side by side. The extensible design helps future studies. The archive keeps the paper open to all. This paper preserves that biostatistics research.
arxiv-2608-00471: Filling the Shadow: A Propositional Model of Gravastar Accretion, arXiv 2608-00471. The gravastar model. Scholars can read the full paper. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact.
augustine-city-of-god-vol-1-dods-1871:
Augustine of Hippo wrote The City of God in Latin in the years after Rome fell. Marcus Dods gave the work English dress in 1871. Book one of this set holds Books One to Thirteen of the work. Augustine wrote to meet pagans who blamed Christ's faith for Rome's fall.

He turns their charge back: Rome fell by its own vice, he holds. Two cities, built by two loves, frame his whole view of the past. The city of man and the City of God grow side by side through time. Book one takes the tale to the age of the kings of Israel.
aurelius-victor-historia-romana-1871:
Sextus Aurelius Victor wrote his short history of the emperors around 361 CE, when brief handbooks of the Roman past were in wide demand. His De Caesaribus runs from Augustus to Constantius II. The text here is the Tauchnitz edition of 1871, a Latin school printing from Leipzig. No English version in the public domain exists.

The volume joins the lives of Victor with three short works that traveled with them through the ages. These are the Origo Gentis Romanae on the first kings, the De Viris Illustribus on famous men, and the Epitome de Caesaribus. Together they form the handbook line of late Roman history writing.
baldwin-ancient-america-1871:
John Baldwin asked who built the great mounds of the Ohio and Mississippi valleys, and answered with a lost race. Ancient America, printed in 1871, surveys the ruins and earthworks of the old New World. Baldwin's book was the most read case of its kind in its century.

He walks readers through mounds, forts, and carved stones, arguing a civilized people raised them and then vanished. The claim fed the era's deep hunger for a grand American past. Later dig science gave the mounds back to the ancestors of living Native peoples. Baldwin's survey still shows the debate at its fullest stretch.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jerusalem-bef:
Jerusalem before the year 71 is treated here as the City of God, political and religious centre of Israel. It runs up to its ruin by Rome after it became the scene of the Redemption. Its names, layout, history, and chief monuments are taken in turn, beginning with Salem, Peace, capital of Melchizedek.

Tell Amarna letters of about 1400 before Christ call it Uru-salim, City of Peace, and Assyrian records name it Ursalimu. Under the Jebusites it bore the name Jebus, though Hebrews kept the older name alive in Joshua, Judges, and Samuel. The entry traces the city from those roots through kings, prophets, and temple building to the Roman shadow falling over it.
cia-0000007171:
William Webster, director of central intelligence, addressed the Aspen Institute in remarks dated July 1987. Webster had led the FBI before taking over the CIA, so he spoke as a judge turned intelligence chief. The declassified text preserves what he chose to say in public about his agency.

Webster sets out the mission of American intelligence and its place inside a democracy. Public speeches by a sitting CIA director were rare, which gives the remarks extra value. Readers can see how the agency explained secrecy, duty, and limits to an outside audience. The file comes from the CIA's own reading room release.
cia-0000008171:
American base rights in the Azores faced an uncertain future, and a May 1961 CIA paper weighed the outlook. The mid-Atlantic islands, ruled by Portugal, hosted a key US air base for crossing the ocean. Talks with Lisbon's authoritarian government made renewal a delicate bargain.

The paper considers what Portugal might demand and what could put access at risk. Base rights rarely draw notice, yet strategy depends on them daily. This file shows the unglamorous side of alliance work: rent, pride, and leverage. It also records how Washington valued a small island chain in the Cold War's map.
cia-0000009671:
Son Ha district, in Quang Ngai province, is named in an April 1972 sighting of three American prisoners of war. Quang Ngai, on South Vietnam's central coast, saw bitter fighting and strong Viet Cong organization. Prisoners held there belonged to the southern camp network.

Three men sighted together suggested a camp or a movement between camps nearby. Officials matched such reports against southern loss records, which were thinner than the north's. Each match could move a man from missing to confirmed prisoner. The file adds a coastal district point to the southern prisoner map in the war's last full year.
cia-0000009871:
Alleged Viet Cong use of American prisoners of war in Nghia Hanh district, Quang Ngai province, is reported in a June 1967 item. The heading stops at the district, leaving the kind of use to the file itself. Alleged is the load-bearing word: the claim had not been proven.

Prisoners could be used for labor, display, or bargaining, and each claim demanded proof. Analysts recorded allegations without adopting them, since captors and sources both had motives to shape stories. The file preserves an allegation at the district level, honestly flagged. It shows reporting discipline on a subject built to inflame.
cia-0000014771: Petitions on the Trieste problem and the Rosenbergs fill a CIA file dated April 4, 1953. Trieste's pro-Cominform party gathered the names. Petitions were the mercy campaign's paper weapon, signed in streets and halls. The file joins a border dispute and a New York death sentence in one bundle of signatures.
cia-0000015471: An engineer claimed that saucer plans were in Soviet hands, in a CIA record dated in 1953. The clipped title adds sightings in Africa, Iran, and other places not fully shown. A claim of secret plans fed the fear that strange aircraft might be Soviet craft. The entry holds that Cold War worry in its sharpest form, beside routine sighting reports.
cia-0000022371: Powers stated he would never fly over the Soviet Union again, a CIA record dated in 1962 reports. The vow came after his return in the spy swap of February that year. A pilot saying never again closed his flying chapter in plain words. The statement also suited officials who wanted the U-2 affair put firmly behind them.
cia-0000022671: Photo comparison case number 12,827 has its results kept in a CIA record dated in 1971. The catalog adds a publication stamp of April 1971 in its clipped code. No subject is named in the title, so the case is described by number alone. The steady run of such results marks the picture office's daily work in those years.
cia-0000022771: Major J. C. Hartney is named in photo comparison case number 10,146, with results kept in a CIA record dated in 1969. The title gives his name in full, where an older summary used initials alone for a first name it lacked. Hartney's case sits one number past another officer's, showing the queue of men awaiting answers from the photo desk.
cia-0000026871: A member of the People's Revolutionary Army made a claim about the Farabundo Marti Popular Liberation Forces, kept in a CIA record dated in 1980. The clipped title cuts off what the claim said. The ERP and the FPL were Salvadoran guerrilla groups then joining a wider front. A fighter's claim, passed up the chain, was raw material for judging rebel strength.
cia-0000037171:
An American helicopter crash site in the Quang Tri area was observed, in a CIA record dated September 5, 1982. The observers also reported finding American identification at the site. Quang Tri province, just below the old border, saw some of the war's heaviest fighting.

Inside, the record ties a wreck, a place, and a piece of identification together. Identification found at a crash site could point searchers toward a crew's fate. The file shows field reports still coming in years later. They came from ground where the war had passed and left its wreckage behind.
cia-0000037971:
A CIA terrorism review dated January 4, 1988 looks back at Latin American terrorism in 1987. The review surveys a full year of political violence across the region. Such yearly reviews helped officials judge whether the threat was growing or fading.

Inside, the year's attacks and groups are tallied country by country. The record places bombings, killings, and kidnappings into one regional picture. Readers can see how the agency organized a messy year into a survey. They can also see which groups and countries drew the most concern in Washington. The year surveyed was one of steady violence across much of the region.
cia-0000042871:
The Situation in El Salvador is the plain title of a CIA record dated October 1, 1989 in the catalog. A situation report surveys a whole country at one moment. El Salvador in that autumn stood late in its long civil war.

Inside, the country's condition is summed up for busy readers. Politics, fighting, and public mood share the brief's short pages. Such surveys fixed a baseline against which later news was judged. The file gives modern readers the same service, showing the country whole at a set date, just before the autumn's murders changed its story.
cia-0000049171: The archbishop of San Salvador reacted in 1990 to FMLN propaganda aimed at him, in a partly blacked-out CIA item. Archbishop Rivera y Damas walked a narrow line, preaching peace while both sides courted and blamed the church. The item preserves his answer, minus the parts still blacked out a generation later.
cia-0000049271: The Jesuit case is the whole subject of a CIA item from 1991, kept with the Truth Commission records. By 1991 the case had a courtroom ahead of it and two governments watching every filing. A file titled simply with the case's name gathers the record as the trial year opened in earnest.
cia-0000098271: Economic dislocation in Chungking following weeks of serious fighting is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000098271, dated June 5, 1968. The heading ties an economic result to a spell of fighting in one city. Readers find a short declassified account of that dislocation, a city-level record of costs rather than a battle report.
cia-0000106271: Account of Phoumi-Siho Relations and Departure of Siho's Family for Vientiane are the two numbered items in declassified CIA document 0000106271, dated January 2, 1965. The first item covers ties between two named Laotian figures, Phoumi and Siho. The second covers a family departure for the capital. The brief record pairs a relations account with a movement note.
cia-0000109071: Statement by Cuban Diplomat Concerning the Probable Return of Stokely Carmichae is the heading, cut off mid-surname, on declassified CIA document 0000109071, dated July 4, 1967. The title records a Cuban diplomat's statement about Stokely Carmichael's probable return. His surname breaks off at Carmichae in the released heading. The brief record preserves the break exactly as released in the files.
cia-0000119171: Guyana BritishH Guiana) is the heading, with stray marks and a broken bracket, on declassified CIA document 0000119171, dated March 4, 1966. The title gives the country under two names: Guyana, and British Guiana in brackets in the heading. That pairing marks a name in transition in the title itself. The brief record preserves the stray marks exactly as released in the files.
cia-0000119671:
A June 1970 CIA document records John M. Sweeney stating why he deserted the United States Marines. His reasons are given in his own words, as the file presents them. Deserters' statements served more than one master during the war years.

For the other side, a deserter's words were useful publicity against the war. For American officials, the same words were evidence to be weighed and checked. The document keeps Sweeney's explanation as recorded, without the file's face saying more about him. It belongs to the paper trail of a war that divided opinion at home as sharply as it was fought abroad.
cia-0000124271: Dated November 1957, this CIA item covers the reaction of Soviet delegates to the announcement of the earth satellite launching. Moscow's men abroad had to show triumph while the West reeled from the news. The item captures that performance of pride as the agency observed it. Watching how Soviet envoys handled the news abroad told analysts how Moscow wanted the triumph read: as proof of a system, not only of a rocket.
cia-0000126971: Dated around January 1975, this CIA document, its own title deleted, concerns Angola following the coup in Portugal. The 1974 coup in Lisbon had cracked open Portugal's African empire. The paper covers Angola in the first months of that endgame for colonial rule. Portugal's coup in April 1974 undid an empire within months, and January papers on Angola belong to the rush of reporting that followed that sudden opening.
cia-0000132571: A junta in El Salvador moving to stop a countercoup fills a CIA paper dated October 6, 1960. The junta was fighting just to stay in power that fall. Coups raised to block countercoups were a known circle in the region's politics. The short paper tracks the junta's moves. It also tracks the officers lined up against it at the time.
cia-0000132671: Brazil and Cuba share an item headed the West in a CIA paper dated January 1, 1961. Brazil was the giant of Latin America, and its stance on Cuba carried real weight. The two-word label had to cover a whole tangled relationship on its own. The short item keeps the entry in the form the series gave it that day.
cia-0000132771: Dated July 4, 1960, this CIA paper uses the title Developments in Cuba, a slight wording change from the usual series name Cuban Developments. Filed as a same-day companion to other entries, it covers the same ground: the revolution's course in mid-1960. The declassified paper is preserved through the CIA Reading Room mirror at the Internet Archive.
cia-0000135771: One more Spanish-language item from the 2506 Brigade papers carries an estimated date of 1 January 1961, marked as estimated in the catalog. The brigade was the force of anti-Castro exiles the CIA landed at the Bay of Pigs that spring. The record states no subject for this document. It survives in Spanish in the declassified release, grouped with the other estimated New Year records in the brigade's file.
cia-0000135871: A planning paper in the declassified CIA files, dated about July 1953, covers a paper headed with the single word procedure. The wider file is PBSUCCESS, the CIA operation aimed at the Arbenz government in Guatemala before the June 1954 coup. What survives is the working paper itself, plain proof of how the mission was run from day to day.
cia-0000136271: A declassified CIA cable dated 1 May 1954 turns to instructions that practice bomb drops be made, rehearsals for the air crews, for BRODFROST. The name Lincoln marks the forward station of PBSUCCESS, the CIA campaign that brought down President Arbenz in June 1954. The paper trail here is small but direct, a single piece of the huge file the operation left behind.
cia-0000136371: Field debriefings give a harsh verdict on CALLIGERIS in this June 1954 cable. Officers said he showed very little strength of character in combat. Each win did give him more confidence. But he is weak at his core, they judged. He lacks the power of decision. That power matters most right now. Someone must force him to hand authority to strong men. Or he must be removed before all is undone.
cia-0000136971: Send the press releases, this May 1954 cable to LINCOLN insists. Most opinion is pro-Guatemala, it says. The cause is a lack of material from the Castillo side. Releases from the liberation army have gone to Buenos Aires papers. Some have been issued, though unacknowledged. A daily cabled release matters most, headquarters says. The propaganda service is handicapped without a legitimate datelined source. Material is being held until releases will actually go out. The rebels' silence was losing the press war.
cia-0000137471: Security around President Kennedy's visit dominates this November 1961 report on Colombia. Suspicious leftists will be rounded up before his arrival. Troops are assigned to guard the president's safety. General Rojas Pinilla has given an order to his alliance. It should study gathering 10,000 sympathizers. They would shout vivas to Kennedy and Rojas. They would shout abajo to the oligarchy. Some leaders oppose the demonstration as harmful. Bogota communists will meet to spread 5,000 leaflets. The leaflets will attack Kennedy personally.
cia-0000139171: NPIC's interagency liaison in 1979 is reported in this April 1980 annual report. Well over 26 agencies appear in the chronology. Some relied on the center's guidance for years. Newcomers are just growing interested in remote sensing. They include the Foreign Agricultural Service and NOAA. The cost to the center was small. It gave special photographic processing to some agencies. It gave briefings and tours to others. It entered an agreement with the EPA. Informal exchanges with academia also grew.
cia-0000139371: Terms of reference for NIE 11-8-61 are forwarded in this January 1961 memorandum. Chester Cooper signed it. The estimate covers Soviet capabilities for long range attack. Representatives are asked to meet on 8 February. Room 115 of the Administration Building is the place. Distribution runs to key committee chairmen. They cover guided missiles, atomic energy, and scientific intelligence. The sample is the routing memo only. The estimate would judge Soviet bombers and missiles. Kennedy's first year in office frames its importance.
cia-0000139471: The Hostage Locating Task Force is now in full operation. This initial report announces it in January 1986. The task force was assembled at CIA headquarters. Full-time representatives came from CIA, DIA, NSA, and NPIC. Other components sent officers too. Office space was designated. Communications were provided. Organizational groundwork was established. The attached paper is the first in a weekly series. Each will recap the hostage situation and new information. The chief praises first-rate officers and unstinting logistics. A copy went to Lieutenant Colonel Oliver North.
cia-0000141171:
A CIA memo of 2 May 1961 passes on letters about Cuban air crew lost in the 17 April invasion of Cuba. It went to the chief of base at JMWAVE in Miami. One letter, from Antonio Silio Gutierrez of a rebel council, asks former captain Manuel Villafana for a list of the dead. Villafana's reply is attached with the names.

His list counts eight men as presumed dead and two more as missing. The names include Osvaldo Piedra, Eddy Gonzalez, Daniel Hernandez, Gaston Perez, Raul Pianello, and Jose Crespo. Two weeks after the landing, the agency was still sorting who had come back and who had not.
cia-06505271: SUPPLEMENT 8 TO JOINT EVALUATION OF SOVIET MISSILE THREAT IN CUBA, a CIA document. The missile supplement. This file preserves that declassified paper. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
cia-06771771: BALACING AGENCY & AUTHOR EQUITIES, a CIA document. The equities memo. This file preserves that declassified paper. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
cia-06774471: AGENCY SECURITY CLASSIFICATION MANAGEMENT PROGRAM DATA, fiscal year covered, a CIA document. The classification data. This file preserves that declassified paper. The historical record keeps it. Such papers rarely see the light of day. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
cooley-constitutional-limitations-1871:
Thomas Cooley, a Michigan judge and professor, published his Constitutional Limitations in 1868, with the second edition of 1871 here. Its full title names its subject: the limits on the lawmaking power of the states. The book became the leading treatise of its kind.

Cooley sets out due process, vested rights, and the police power with care. He defends courts striking down laws that cross constitutional lines, while granting legislatures wide room. His work supplied the legal charter of laissez-faire constitutionalism in America. Judges cited it constantly in the age of railroad and labor battles. Modern scholars still study Cooley to understand that era.
dialectical-society-report-1871:
A grave band of London men weighed the dark room in the Dialectical Society report of 1871. The Society was a club for free debate. Its band sat with seers, heard scores of guests, and ran tests in homes of their own. Most came in as doubts. Their report stuns: much of it backs the claims as real and past fraud.

That split from the scorn of the press made the book a flag for fans. Foes cried the band was soft. The report is the first great board weigh of the theme. Its words still get quoted.
doe-osti-3006952-energy-improvements-of-: Fire Station 71 got energy-improved, and this DOE text covers the upgrades. The pages detail the findings. The building folks get their case study. The station was 71. The study was building. The upgrades were energy. The study was case. The station was fire.
eliot-george-middlemarch-1871:
George Eliot published Middlemarch in 1871 to 1872, her supreme achievement of Victorian realism, subtitled a study of provincial life. Dorothea Brooke and the interwoven lives of a Midlands town fill a canvas. Eliot wrote it in parts, and its web of marriages, money, and reform is the English novel's widest net.

Dorothea, ardent and idealistic, weds the dry scholar Casaubon and finds a living tomb in his Lowick library and jealous will. Dr. Lydgate, ambitious for medical reform, is trapped by his pretty wife Rosamond and debts in the town's petty economy. Bulstrode's buried past, Fred Vincy's growth, and the 1832 Reform Bill bind private fates to a nation's slow change in England. Eliot's narrator, wise and pitying, weighs every soul with a fairness no character quite earns or escapes. Many judges rank it the greatest novel in the English language.
europmc-pmc10354071:
Cords and colleagues sorted support cells found in breast tumours into clear types in 2023. These cells are called cancer-associated fibroblasts, or CAFs for short. They live around a tumour and can help or hinder its growth. The team read gene activity in over 16,000 such cells from 14 patients.

Nine CAF types emerged, plus one class of vessel wall cells. Cords gave each type a name based on its gene pattern and likely job. The scheme held up in four other cancer types. A scan of protein markers in matched tumours then confirmed the types. It also showed where each type sits inside a tumour, which may guide new treatments.
europmc-pmc10487271:
Najjar reviewed in 2023 how AI is reshaping radiology, the use of scans in medicine. The field began with the discovery of X-rays and now runs on rich digital images. Machine learning and deep learning can read those images at scale. Najjar traces that arc and asks what it means for care.

AI now helps split an image into parts, flag disease, and predict risk. Case reports from many fields show gains in speed and in spotting illness early. Care plans can also be tuned to one patient from scan data. Blocks remain: patchy data, opaque AI logic, high setup costs, and ethics. Najjar backs joint work between scan doctors and AI builders.
europmc-pmc10567571:
Eldjarn and co-authors compared two big blood protein platforms in 2023 through gene and disease links. The platforms, Olink and SomaScan, each read thousands of proteins in blood plasma. The team used Olink data from over 50,000 UK Biobank members. A past SomaScan study of 36,000 Icelanders gave the match point.

Agreement between the two tools was modest, Eldjarn reports. Both found gene links for a like count of tests, near 2,100 each. A higher share of Olink tests had such backing, 72% versus 43%. Some proteins gave gene links that split by platform. Mixed ancestry in the UK set also surfaced new links and sharpened gene maps.
europmc-pmc10748771:
Koliaki, Dalamaga, and Liatis asked in 2023 whether the world obesity surge has begun to flatten. Obesity rates rose fast for decades and strain health systems world-wide. Some data hint at a plateau in rich nations after 2010. The review tests that hope against the full proof.

In rich nations, adult rates look stable in recent years, Koliaki reports. Rates in children and teens have also levelled since 2000 in most such nations. Better food habits and more activity may play a part. In poor nations, though, rates climb with no break. Severe obesity grows fast in rich and middle nations alike. Its share may reach 20% by 2035, twice the level seen in 2020.
europmc-pmc10777171:
Zhang and colleagues review how AI could sharpen a network-based way of studying herbal medicine in this 2023 paper. Traditional Chinese medicine treats the body as one linked system. Network pharmacology, a method that maps how drugs, targets, and diseases connect, fits that whole-body view well. Huge gene and protein datasets now make those maps hard to read by hand.

The review sorts AI tools for this field into three jobs. Some tools mine links in a network, some pinpoint likely drug targets, and some guide the search toward new targets. The authors show how these tools were used to probe cold and hot syndromes, a classic pair of illness patterns. They frame the work as a step toward care matched to each patient.
europmc-pmc10791971:
Li and colleagues review what lives in our lungs and why it matters in this 2024 paper. Lungs were long thought to hold no microbes at all, meaning no tiny living things. Better tests showed a small, shifting community does live there. It comes mostly from the mouth and throat, and it is kept sparse by coughing, immune cells, and the sweep of tiny hairs in the airways.

The review links this lung community to the gut and to the immune system. It then walks through roles in asthma, chronic lung disease, scarring, pneumonia, COVID-19, and lung cancer. The authors note that fungi and viruses in the lung are still poorly studied. They suggest that learning to steer this community could one day aid treatment, but much basic work remains.
europmc-pmc10853571:
Cui and colleagues review what may cause severe depression and how it might be treated in this 2024 paper. Major depressive disorder is a lasting low mood that harms work and daily life. Cases rise each year worldwide, adding social and economic strain. No single theory fully explains the illness, the authors note.

The review walks through leading ideas about its causes. These cover brain signal chemicals, stress hormones, immune signals, and the brain's power to rewire itself. It also stresses links between organs as a newer clue. New drug targets and drugs are surveyed, and some have already won approval for clinic use. Light therapy and acupuncture are noted as options that eased symptoms in some studies. The authors back multi-target plans over single fixes.
europmc-pmc10855871:
Seyhan surveys the promise and the setbacks of tiny RNA drugs in this 2024 review. MicroRNAs are short RNA pieces that tune how genes are used. Faults in them are linked to many diseases, above all cancers. That link drew heavy spending on drugs built from them. The success of COVID mRNA vaccines then revived wider interest in RNA drugs.

Progress in the lab has been strong, the review says, but the clinic tells a harder story. Few microRNA drugs have reached human trials, and none has passed late-stage trials or won US approval. Some trials were halted over harmful side effects. Seyhan argues that better chemistry and better delivery into cells are the keys. Until those gaps close, broad use in patients will stay out of reach.
europmc-pmc1088971:
Cirz and colleagues found a way to stop bacteria from evolving drug resistance in this 2005 study. Drug-proof bacteria are a grave threat to health. With some drugs, germs gain resistance fast through gene mutations during treatment. The team focused on the SOS response, a cell alarm that raises mutation rates when DNA is damaged.

Blocking a protein called LexA kept the alarm off, they showed. Gut bacteria in infected animals then failed to evolve resistance to two key drugs. Lab tests showed the damage repair path switches on error-prone copying enzymes that create the mutations. The authors propose blocking mutation itself as a new drug strategy. Such a blocker, paired with a standard drug, could keep treatments working longer.
europmc-pmc10937371:
All of Us Research Program Genomics Investigators describe a huge US gene dataset in this 2024 paper. The All of Us program is a long-term study aiming to enrol at least one million varied volunteers. Its goal is to speed research and improve health for all groups.
