Patients whose pneumonia began in the community and who gained a second infection died at far higher rates, near forty six versus eighteen percent, on the edge of statistical certainty. Their blood showed lowered activity of a key immune receptor gene. Early immune dulling may flag who needs extra infection guarding, pending larger proof.
plos-pone-0350071:
Guoqiang Sun and co-authors built a forecasting model for power generation and load in 2026. Grid operators must predict demand closely to keep supply steady, yet power data has long patterns that simple recurrent networks lose, and big attention models cost too much.

Their model stacks gated memory layers with attention placed inside the stack, letting it stress the time steps that matter without ballooning in size. On three real energy data sets it beat ten rival models, cutting errors sharply against plain recurrent networks. It matched leading attention models on accuracy while training faster, a practical gain for daily grid planning.
plos-pone-0350271:
Brenna Ellison and co-authors surveyed American consumers in 2026 about government rules for ultra-processed foods. Six possible policies were tested, from defining the category to taxing it, as debate over such foods heats up.

Nearly a thousand adults answered. Information policies, a clear definition and dietary guidance, won the most support, while a tax won the least. Views split by beliefs about the foods, self rated knowledge, and personal traits. The pattern tells policymakers that the public will accept being informed and protected in schools long before it accepts paying more at the till.
plos-pone-0350571: Chang and five co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on hard-to-treat cervical cancer. The cancer had come back or spread to other parts of the body. The team tested the safety and effect of pairing immune checkpoint inhibitors with a class of drugs called TKIs. All patients carried a gene change named PIK3CA. Pairing drug types is a common hope when single drugs stop working.
plos-pone-0350671:
Dongwook Kim and colleagues reviewed emergency patients whose only complaint was spinning or dizziness, with no other clear stroke signs. A hidden stroke in the back of the brain can still be the cause, so doctors checked brain scans for fresh damage. Records covered four straight years at one emergency service, sorted by blood thinning and clot preventing drug use.

Patients fell into groups taking no such drugs, taking platelet drugs like aspirin, or taking stronger blood thinners. Finer sorting split aspirin alone, a second platelet drug alone, and both together. The study weighs whether prior drug use links with more or fewer hidden strokes once other illnesses are taken into account. For front line care, even isolated dizziness deserves careful stroke checks.
plos-pone-0350771:
Jan Turra and colleagues measure what a charcoal filter does to stress hormones during a specialized liver cancer treatment that floods the liver with chemotherapy while shielding the rest of the body. Blood from the liver is cleaned outside the body before returning, and patients often become unstable during the process. In fifteen procedures, blood was sampled at set points before and after the filter to track hormone levels and doses given.

The filter stripped out nearly all of one key stress hormone, noradrenaline, even as doctors kept infusing it at high doses to hold blood pressure. Two sister hormones passed through barely touched. After the circuit stopped, hormone levels rebounded sharply. Turra and colleagues say teams must plan dosing around this hidden drain.
plos-pone-0350971:
Yunnuo Zhu and colleagues used a long running United States military cohort to test whether how service members rate their own health forecasts later readiness. More than fifty thousand active duty members answered health and habit surveys, then were tracked three to five years later for care use, lost work days, weight, satisfaction, and staying in service.

Self rated physical and mental health predicted all five readiness outcomes, even after habits like smoking and poor sleep were counted. Members in the top band for physical health kept healthier weight, lost fewer days, used less care, and stayed longer. Low scores warned of the reverse. A short survey, the work suggests, can flag readiness risk early.
plos-pone-0351171:
Max Carlos Ramírez-Soto and four colleagues published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It follows pneumonia in Peru through health records. The authors compare how often pneumonia occurred, how often it sent people to hospital, and how often it killed. The comparison spans the years before COVID-19 and the pandemic years.

During the pandemic, masks, distancing, and overwhelmed hospitals all changed how pneumonia appeared in statistics. Separating real change from disrupted counting is the hard part of such comparisons. Health authorities in Peru, and researchers of pandemic side effects on other diseases, are the readers who need this careful before-and-during picture.
plos-pone-0351471:
Jinyang Dong and co-authors study a plant called cocklebur across China in this 2026 paper. Cocklebur is both a useful medicinal plant and an aggressive invader, so knowing where it will thrive matters. The team combined computer models of suitable habitat with analysis of the bacteria living around the plant's roots.

Their models show that human activity, elevation, and slope shape where cocklebur grows today, and that warmer future climates could expand its suitable habitat considerably. High-risk zones cluster in provinces such as Yunnan, Guangdong, and Inner Mongolia. Around its roots, bacteria tied to nitrogen cycling dominate, and these microbes seem to help the plant cope with stress and settle into disturbed ground. The authors argue that managing such two-sided species means watching both the climate and the microbes.
plos-pone-0351571:
Yi Chen, Xing Wang, and Wang Shaohua published a 2026 methods paper in PLOS ONE on using artificial intelligence to repair images of damaged cultural heritage objects. Their system, called YOLO-WSR, first detects damaged areas in a photograph, then restores them with a diffusion model guided by the object's structure and fine wavelet details. A quality-check module scores each restored image and feeds the result back so the output can be refined again.

On several public datasets, the combined system beat existing approaches at finding damage and produced restorations that scored better on standard image-quality measures. Removing individual parts of the system in turn showed that each piece contributed to the gains. The authors frame the method as practical support for digital preservation work: spotting damage accurately, restoring images automatically, and keeping visual records of fragile heritage objects in usable shape.
plos-pone-0351671:
Hafeez Ahmad and colleagues shrank the brain needed to sort fashion photos into their ten clothing classes, a standard test problem for image software. Top models for the task carry tens of millions of settings and need graphics processors, shutting out cheap devices. Their design pairs a small convolutional network with a lean form of self-attention, keeping under half a million settings in total.

The small model trained on an ordinary processor and sorted the Fashion-MNIST benchmark with accuracy a little above ninety-one percent. The team also added several ways to picture where the model looks when it decides, so users can audit its attention. For shops and apps running on phones or shop-floor hardware, the message is that respectable image sorting no longer requires a data center, and the reasoning can be shown, not just trusted.
plos-pone-0351971:
Anni Byman and colleagues studied five hundred seventeen Finnish primary school children, asking how the social weather of a classroom connects with movement, sitting, and grades. Wrist- and hip-worn motion trackers measured activity during school hours, children rated their peer relations, and grade averages came from school records. The team analyzed girls and boys separately, since their school days can differ.

Among girls, warmer peer relations went with less vigorous in-school activity, and more sitting went with higher grades. Among boys, more vigorous activity went with higher grades. Formal tests could not confirm the boy-girl split, so the authors treat the patterns as leads, not law. Still, the study argues that adding activity to the school day works through friendship and peer norms, not around them.
plos-pone-0352171:
Farah Seedat and seven co-authors set out this 2026 PLOS One protocol. It will check a set of survey tools that map how well migrants fit into a country's health system. The three tools list migrant health data sources, policies, and service provision. Tunisia is the test case. Forty to fifty national experts will each complete one tool matched to their skills.

As a protocol, the paper describes the plan, not results. Experts will rate each item for relevance and clarity. A follow-up survey will judge the tools as a whole. Focus groups will add depth. The team will measure how much the raters agree. They will also study the themes in the group talks. The aim is to confirm the tools capture what they claim. Only then should other countries adopt them.
plos-pone-0352671:
Mwalukunga, Moshi, and Kibusi asked young women students in Tanzania how they prefer to get sexual health information and care in a 2026 study. Early sex, limited contraception, and infection risk affect many students, while cultural and policy limits restrict services. Interviews explored what channels and settings young women would actually trust and use.

Knowing preferences matters because services that feel unsafe or judgmental go unused, whatever their quality. Young women can describe which sources feel private, accurate, and reachable from campus life. Their answers can guide colleges and health programs to offer information in forms students will accept, helping prevent infection and unplanned pregnancy.
plos-pone-0352771:
Aaron Eisen and four colleagues published this 2026 PLOS One study on how hardships faced early in life change the health effects of living near greenery. Their starting idea was that people raised with more stress may react more strongly to their surroundings, for better or worse. They tested this using health records from a group of nursing students.

Greenness around each student's home showed no simple straight-line link to fasting blood sugar. Instead, students with either heavy or light early-life stress had lower blood sugar when they lived in greener areas, while those in the middle showed no link at all. The authors argue that adding green space in poorer neighborhoods could lower diabetes risk for the people most shaped by early stress.
plos-pone-0352871:
Zepeng Chen and three colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One single-cell study of how colon tumors handle tryptophan, an amino acid whose breakdown can dampen immune attack. Working from single-cell sequencing data, the team scored metabolic activity cell by cell using several algorithms, then applied four machine learning methods to pinpoint the genes most consistently tied to that activity.

Immune cells called macrophages and gut-lining Paneth cells showed the highest tryptophan activity. Two genes, CYP1A1 and its partner regulator AHR, stood out as raised in the cancer and were selected by every algorithm, marking them as consensus findings. The authors propose both as candidate markers and treatment targets, while noting the analysis is computational and awaits experimental tests.
plos-pone-0353071:
Monowar Hossain and Mohammed Aman Ullah build a mathematical model of rotavirus spread in this 2026 PLOS ONE paper. Rotavirus causes severe diarrhoea that still kills many children under five, mostly in poorer countries. Their model sorts people into susceptible, vaccinated, infected, and recovered groups, using a fractional form of calculus that lets past states keep influencing the present.

They work out when the disease dies out and when it settles in, and derive a vaccination threshold number that separates the two fates. Approximate solutions come from a Laplace-based decomposition technique, checked for stability and accuracy. Models of this kind help officials judge how much vaccination coverage a community needs.
plos-pone-0353171:
Abdul Karim and three colleagues explore how first-year university students experienced learning persuasive essay writing online, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. During the pandemic the university taught its English foundation course through its own platform, with sequenced materials guiding students through outlining, drafting, editing, and revising. Eight students described the experience in interviews and questionnaires, and the team interpreted their accounts using phenomenological analysis.

Students said the step-by-step structure kept them engaged rather than lost. Writing collaboratively and giving each other feedback guided by a rubric stood out as especially meaningful. The authors draw a practical lesson for online teaching: sequence the work clearly, build in peer review, and students will lean into a skill many find intimidating.
plos-pone-0353271:
Kun Zhang and five colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One imaging study on telling harmless lung nodules from cancerous ones without surgery. Their method uses a tracer scan taken at two time points, producing simple uptake ratios for each nodule. Records from more than one hundred thirty patients, most with malignant nodules, were used to build and test machine learning classifiers on those ratios plus clinical variables.

Cancerous nodules took up more tracer early and held onto less of it over time. A blood tumor marker and one retention measure independently predicted malignancy. The best machine learning model separated the groups almost perfectly on its training data, with others close behind. The authors pitch the approach as an interpretable option for hospitals where advanced image analysis is unavailable, though outside validation is still needed.
plos-pone-0353571:
Wen Yu and Robert Langer report this 2026 PLOS One study on turning sandwich composite panels into portable outdoor tabletops that factories can mass-produce. Such panels, a light core bonded between stiff outer skins, are common in aircraft and transport but rare in consumer furniture. The authors built five panel designs that differed in core material, surface finish, edge sealing, and fasteners.

Testing the designs against customer needs and product standards showed that no single property decided success. What mattered was how materials, surface durability, moisture-proof edges, fasteners, and cost worked together. Blind rivets proved a practical fastening choice, and finishes behaved differently depending on the surface beneath them. The authors map out design routes that could bring these panels to the mass market.
plos-pone-0353671: Olorunmoteni and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE review on teen sleep health in Africa. As a scoping review, it maps patterns of sleep, what drives them, and what outcomes they link to. Teens need much sleep, yet school, work, and screens cut it short. A map of African evidence helps health planners see where research exists and where whole regions are missing.
plos-pone-0353871:
Vinh and Yen, in a 2026 study in Danang, Vietnam, build a phone app that screens high school students for color vision deficiency and then advises them on study and career choices. Weak color vision can quietly steer students away from fields where it matters, and paper tests are slow and rarely linked to guidance. Five hundred twenty-seven students took part.

The app uses a digital version of the classic dot-plate test. It agreed closely with the standard paper test, and it picked out seventeen students with some form of color deficiency, including rare complete color blindness. Students rated the app much the same whether or not they had the deficiency, and the feedback questionnaire held together well. The authors present the tool as a cheap, scalable way for schools, including poor ones, to screen early and counsel honestly about careers where color matters.
plos-pone-0353971:
Lina Wang and colleagues build in 2026 a new way to map disease clusters. Colour maps first show the broad pattern on a map. A flexible scan then tests which clusters are not due to chance. A dot map next shows detail inside the top cluster. That last step adjusts for how people are spread out.

Trials used made up data and real measles cases. The joined method found clusters more truly than single steps did. It also located hot cores inside the clusters. Each stage checks the stage before it. The flow moves from search to proof to fine detail. Health teams could aim control work with more care.
plos-pone-0354271:
Kim and Shin, in a 2026 study, use a decade of national health insurance claims to show how long-term care hospitals in South Korea have become places where many older people die. Patient numbers rose, and deaths involving these hospitals climbed sharply. The authors trace yearly trends and each person's path from entry to death.

New patients arrived in their early eighties, most often women, and people on medical aid or with disabilities were overrepresented. After admission, stays varied hugely: many died within a month, while more than a fifth stayed a year or longer. Most who died did so inside the hospital. The final phase of life often shifted from slow frailty to sudden infection, such as pneumonia or sepsis. The authors argue policy should build in palliative care, advance planning, and staff training to match that role.
plos-pone-0354371:
Houn Kim and co-authors surveyed parent runners to learn whether pushing a stroller changes injury risk. Stroller running keeps new parents active, but its effect on overuse injuries was unstudied. Their 2026 survey recruited parents online and compared two hundred stroller runners with a smaller group who ran without one.

Overuse injuries were reported by about three in ten non-stroller runners, against about two in ten stroller runners. Per distance run, the stroller group's injury rate was less than half the control rate. Injury types looked similar in both groups, with heel pain notably common in each. Kim and colleagues conclude stroller running appears safe and may help parents sustain activity in early parenthood.
plos-pone-0354471:
Deborah Ekusai-Sebatta and co-authors review in 2026 how human gene data are shared in joint research that involves lower income countries. Funders now often require sharing plans, yet sharing raises hard questions about consent, control, and fairness. Their review screened thousands of reports and kept a small set that dealt directly with practice on the ground.

Consent, misuse fears, unequal benefit, stigma, and unclear ownership all appeared as concerns. Mistrust and over strict rules slowed sharing. Trust and consent processes that fit local culture stood out as vital. The authors call for balance between open science and protecting the people whose data are shared.
plos-pone-0354671:
Heba H Mostafa and colleagues tested whether a commercial automated HPV test can find viral DNA floating in the blood of patients with HPV-driven disease. Such a test could be a shortcut for detecting and monitoring these cancers. Their 2026 pilot study ran the test on blood from cervical and throat cancer patients. It then re-tested the same samples with a custom, more sensitive three-primer laboratory assay.

The commercial test caught the virus in advanced cervical cancers and most throat cancers. It missed early disease and precancer entirely. The custom assay proved sharper, finding low viral levels in some early cases. Its sporadic signals in treated, disease-free patients complicate interpretation, though. The work maps both the promise and the current sensitivity ceiling of blood-based HPV monitoring.
plos-pone-0354871:
Sayaka Sato and co-authors test in 2026 whether gender fair wording in French changes how teenagers picture jobs typed as male or female. French uses a masculine form as the default for mixed groups, and paired forms name both genders. Two preregistered experiments asked adolescents to rate jobs described in either form for warmth, skill, and whether they could belong there.

Paired forms did not make views more inclusive among teenagers, unlike earlier adult findings. The job's own gender stereotype drove representation most, especially for girls, and age and gender shaped the effects. Language reform alone may not shift career pictures at this age, the authors suggest.
plos-pone-0354971:
Elizabeth Grylls and colleagues evaluate in 2026 a high performance training programme for sports officials run by a sport institute in Australia's Northern Territory. Five officials and their mentors gave measures before and after, covering confidence, resilience, how demands were judged, preparation, and assertiveness. Written reflections added depth to the numbers, and changes were checked for reliability rather than chance.

Three of the five officials showed reliable gains in confidence and resilience, with varied shifts in narrower skills such as decision making and communication. Interview material backed the positive picture. With such a small group, the authors present the work as insight into how elite officials grow, not proof for all.
plos-pone-0355371: Pointon and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE plan for a trial called ACTIVATE, aimed at medical students. The program under test is Thumos, a talking-therapy course based on cognitive-behavioral methods. The trial will assign students at random to judge whether it helps. Medical training is stressful, and a tested program could be offered before distress turns into illness.
plos-pone-0355471:
Cheng-Ru Wu, Ming-Han Chiang, Bao-Hui Huang, Hung-Lung Lin, and Yanran Huang published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It studies how tourists who meet Zhangjiajie online feel about the place, a Chinese scenic area famous for its towering stone pillars. The tools are text mining of online writing and a combined LDA-FDEMATEL analysis.

Online reviews and posts carry visitors' feelings in their own words, and text mining turns thousands of them into patterns. Understanding what moves online tourists helps scenic areas design for people who experience the place partly through screens. Tourism managers and researchers of digital travel behavior share the audience.
plos-pone-0356071: Fora and three co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on how partners' faces move in step. Facial synchrony means two people's expressions rise and fall together during interaction. The team described this matching across several dimensions at once. They tested whether the patterns can reveal the quality of a relationship. If faces betray how well two people connect, such measures could aid therapy and social research.
plos-pone-0356171:
Li Quan Warrick Tan, James Barkell, and Donna O'Connor map the research on how youth sport coaches learn their craft, in this 2026 scoping review. Coaching children in participation-focused sport, as opposed to elite pathways, has drawn growing interest, yet little is known about how those coaches actually develop. Searching sports and education databases for empirical studies since 2010, the team found just eleven articles that fit, and charted them by focus, setting, and findings.

Most studies tested coach education programs about autonomy-supportive coaching in team sports, and nearly all came from Western countries. Four themes organized the evidence: what enables coach learning, what blocks it, what coaches gain, and what determines whether training changes their practice. The authors recommend research beyond the West, across more sports, with bigger and more varied samples, and above all studies that follow learning into real coaching behavior.
plos-pone-0356371:
Mason Clay Mathews and Alexandria J Drake published a study of working partnerships in PLOS ONE in 2026. Partnerships often fail when the people in them want different things without knowing it. Mathews and Drake asked participants what they believe makes a partnership succeed, then measured how much those beliefs matched.

Their agreement scores show whether partners truly share a view of why they work together. Low agreement can be an early warning, flagged before stress cracks the alliance. Groups, firms, and community projects could use such a check the way they use a budget review: a simple way to spot hidden gaps in shared purpose before they grow costly.
plos-pone-0356471: Freimuth and two co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study that rethinks a small dinosaur from Early Cretaceous North America. The fossil, named Geminiraptor suarezarum, had been classed as a troodontid, a type of small meat-eater. The team argues it fits better with the plant-eating therizinosaurs. They also trace how upper jaw bones evolved across a wider dinosaur group. Reclassifying a fossil can shift ideas about diet and kinship.
plos-pone-0356771:
Kaida Jia, Yang Chai, Baozhou Chen, and Zunhai Gao present DOLD-Net, a vision model built for one of farming's hardest counting problems. The problem is animals packed body to body, hiding each other. Their 2026 paper assembles a two-branch backbone. It reads both fine edges and overall herd layout. A mechanism pushes context into hidden regions. Other modules sharpen blurred boundaries between overlapping animals.

Across four public livestock datasets, the model posted strong accuracy scores. It stayed efficient enough for farm deployment. It beat the usual trade-off between precision and speed. Reliable animal detection underpins counting, health checks, and welfare monitoring in smart barns. Occlusion is precisely where simpler detectors fall apart. The authors have released their code publicly.
plos-pone-0356871:
Sarah Al safi leads a team of eight validating a prediction tool for chemotherapy response in a common breast cancer, in PLOS ONE in 2026. For luminal cancers, which feed on hormones, doctors want to know before surgery whether chemotherapy will erase the tumor. Complete disappearance is the outcome most tied to survival. The tool is a scoring chart, a nomogram, built partly on a seventy gene test. The team checked it on fifteen hundred patients treated at a Seoul hospital between 2008 and 2021.

The chart did predict complete response, roughly doubling the odds for high scorers. Its overall accuracy was modest rather than sharp. Hormone receptor status, tumor and node stage, and a cell growth index each predicted response independently. The authors present the validated chart as one input among several for a hard decision, useful for sparing likely non responders a toxic course, not decisive alone.
plos-pone-0357171:
Michael Ekholuenetale, writing alone, analyzes gaps in COVID-19 vaccination among Nigerian women in a 2026 PLOS ONE paper. Overall uptake was low, and wealth gaps in uptake may mirror wider social unfairness. Data came from the two thousand and twenty-four Nigeria Demographic and Health Survey.

The sample covered over thirty-six thousand women of reproductive age. About one third of the richest women reported vaccination, against about one fifth of the poorest. A breakdown analysis credited schooling, media exposure, jobs, and health cover among the factors behind the gap. Targeted strategies for poor women, the author argues, are needed for fair coverage.
plos-pone-0357271:
Denial Aias and an international team dope a champion piezoelectric ceramic with two extra elements to see whether its light and electric behavior can be tuned without killing its strength. The base ceramic converts pressure to charge superbly, a gift for sensors and energy harvesters. Adding samarium and nickel shifted the material's transition points, light absorption, and how charge carriers get trapped, the authors report.

Nickel behaved differently inside this ceramic than it does in a related alkaline family, which surprised the team. Even so, the doped ceramic kept a reasonable share of its energy harvesting performance while gaining new optical tricks. Aias and colleagues say the trade gives designers a wider palette for devices that sense, harvest, and respond to light at once.
plos-pone-0357371:
Triono Bagus Saputro led a team of six authors studying pomegranate peels in Indonesia, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Peels are usually thrown away, yet they are rich in plant chemicals. The team profiled three Indonesian pomegranate peel varieties and tested their extracts for antioxidant and antibacterial effects, plus effects on cells grown in the lab.

Saputro's results argue for turning farm waste into wellness products, if further testing supports safety and effect. Comparing varieties matters because chemistry differs, and the best variety for products may not be the best for eating. Work like this adds value to crops farmers already grow. It also models a wider idea: the most useful part of a harvest is sometimes the part now discarded.
plos-pone-0357571:
Bibhuti Bhusan Mishra, K. Abhimanyu Kumar Patro, and Sudhakar Das published a 2026 paper in PLOS ONE proposing a new way to encrypt several images at once. Most schemes handle either gray or color pictures, not a mix, which limits real-world use. Their method, ECPD-MIE, first joins multiple images of any size into one composite. It then scrambles and diffuses the pixel values using chaotic maps, with keys seeded from a hash of the image itself.

An entropy control step adjusts the diffusion so randomness stays high across both gray levels and color channels. In the authors' tests, encrypted images showed flat histograms, almost no correlation between neighboring pixels, and entropy close to the ideal value. Standard attack measures also looked strong, and the outputs passed national randomness tests. The scheme aims at secure image sharing where mixed gray and color files must travel together under one lock.
plos-pone-0357671:
Fevzi Necati Avsar, Nihat Kılıcaslan, and Tuncay Sahutoglu compare two immune-calming drugs given to critically ill COVID patients in one hospital's intensive care unit. Both drugs were used widely against the runaway inflammation of severe disease, but head-to-head real-world evidence stayed thin. The team rebuilt each hospital day as a decision point and weighted the groups to balance patient traits before comparing deaths in hospital.

Neither drug's start was clearly tied to lower death at four weeks or across the whole stay; results sat almost exactly at no difference. Estimates for one drug stayed wide because few patients started it. Avsar and colleagues treat the finding as absence of a clear signal, not proof the drugs never help, and call for stronger designs.
plos-pone-0357771:
Rundase Gebeyehu and coauthors published a 2026 cross-sectional study in PLOS ONE on high-risk human papillomavirus among women living with HIV in Nekemte town, Ethiopia. These viruses cause most cervical cancer, and HIV's immune damage raises the danger, so women on antiretroviral therapy are a screening priority. Just over three hundred women attending therapy clinics gave cervical samples, tested with a commercial DNA assay, alongside questionnaire and record data.

About one woman in three carried a high-risk virus type, the authors found, with single-genotype infections from the two most dangerous types and from the pooled other types all represented. Regression analysis then identified which personal and clinical factors traveled with infection, though the abstract details the prevalence more fully than the individual risk factors. That one-in-three figure, they argue, justifies routine HPV testing built into HIV care in the region.
plos-pone-0357971:
Anzhen Xu leads a team of eight hunting a gene at the crossroads of metabolism and heart failure, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Failing hearts burn fuel abnormally, and lactate, long dismissed as waste, appears to tag proteins in a process called lactylation that may drive harmful remodeling. Merging single cell data from failing and healthy hearts, the team scored lactylation activity cell by cell, then let four machine learning methods nominate the genes in charge.

Support and smooth muscle cells in the vessel walls carried the strongest lactylation signal, and failing hearts ran hotter than healthy ones. Seven candidate genes survived the machine learning gauntlet. Of three that rose in failing hearts, one, HMGN2, proved the most consistent marker across datasets, and its network pointed toward immune inflammation and protein housekeeping gone wrong. The authors nominate it as a biomarker and a handle on the disease's metabolic wiring.
plos-pone-0358271:
Xiaoliang Zhao led a team of eight authors improving forecasts of fine air pollution, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. PM2.5 particles harm lungs and hearts, and timely forecasts let cities warn people and cut emissions on bad days. Their deep learning method combines an improved way of breaking the signal into parts with a tuning algorithm called FATA.

Zhao's hybrid model aims for sharper smog forecasts than standard tools give. Accuracy matters because false alarms erode trust, while missed peaks leave people unprotected. Cities choking on fine particles gain lead time for protective action, from school guidance to traffic limits. The method work here is technical, but its payoff is measured in breaths.
plos-pone-0358371:
Marco Angrisani, Vincenzo Atella, Wändi Bruine de Bruin, and Joanna Kopinska published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It asks how personality traits shape who suffers mental distress in a crisis. The evidence comes from the COVID-19 pandemic, which stressed whole populations at once.

Personality may explain why the same lockdown or job loss crushed some people and left others coping. Knowing which traits raise risk helps services aim support at those most likely to struggle in the next crisis. Mental health planners and researchers of resilience are the audience for this link between character and crisis response.
plos-pone-0358571: Burns and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE plan for shared global guidance on music therapy for children. The condition is paediatric posterior fossa syndrome, a speech and movement disorder that can follow brain surgery in children. Experts from many countries will build the guidance together. Shared rules could bring music therapy to more of the children who might benefit.
plos-pone-0358771:
Lilia Crew, Alyssa Seerley, Serena McElroy, and Andrea Grindeland Panter wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article. It sets out neurological tissue dissection techniques for mouse models, aiming at reproducible scientific results. Four materials are covered: the sciatic nerve, the spinal cord, the brain, and the fluid that cushions them.

Reproducibility fails when each lab harvests tissue a slightly different way, so shared techniques matter. A clear protocol for taking these delicate samples helps new researchers match the quality of experienced ones. Neuroscience labs running mouse experiments are the direct audience, and journals increasingly ask for exactly this kind of methods detail.
plos-pone-0359271: Kyvernitakis and six co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on a device used in pregnancy. A cervical pessary is a soft ring placed to support the cervix in women at risk of early birth. The team tracked the stiffness of the cervix after placement and how it settled over time. Steady stiffness data could show whether the device is helping hold the pregnancy.
pmc-13188971:
Deiviane Aparecida Calegar is first author on a 2026 article on chronic Giardia infections and health system gaps. Giardia lamblia is a gut parasite that impairs nutrient absorption and, even without diarrhea, contributes to growth and development delays and malnutrition in children. Spread runs through poor sanitation, contaminated water and food, and contact with animals.

Despite its impact, the disease is underdiagnosed, and the authors urge diagnostic tools that do not rely on microscopy and can scale up. Effective single-dose treatments exist but are not used at community level. Because exposure is continuous, reinfection is frequent. Strengthening primary care access to diagnosis and mass single-dose treatment in vulnerable communities is their central prescription.
pmc-13197571:
Seong-Mok Jeong and colleagues tested insect larvae as fish feed protein in a 2026 feeding study. Fish farming needs cheap new protein sources. Black soldier fly larvae can turn food waste into protein, and what larvae eat shapes their nutrient value.

Larvae grew for twelve days on food waste alone or waste enriched with soybean meal or fish meal. Enriched larvae carried more protein, though plain-waste larvae grew fastest. The larvae then fed olive flounder, a flatfish, for eight weeks. Flounder growth held steady on larva diets versus control feed. Fat profiles shifted: one protective fat rose while a key brain-healthy fat fell. Enrichment trades yield against nutrient gain, the authors conclude.
pmc-13198471:
Cibelle C L Brandão and colleagues measured toxic hydrocarbons in Amazon mangrove mud in a 2026 study. PAHs are pollutants from fuel burning and oil that can harm water life and people. Mangroves shelter fisheries and oyster beds, so the team sampled mud near ports, markets, and oyster areas in three towns.

Levels ranged from low to moderate overall. One town with oyster banks and a fish market ran far higher than the others. Source tracing blamed mostly biomass and coal burning, then fossil fuel burning. One compound topped risk guides in two towns, though a standard cancer-risk measure stayed below limits. Oysters may pick up the pollutants from stirred mud, a food safety watch point.
pmc-13201971:
Choosing the route to a deep brain lesion depends on the veins in the way, and a 2026 illustrative case led by Mizuto Sato shows that reasoning in action. The article describes a 69-year-old man with vertigo, nausea, and unsteady balance from bleeding of a cavernous malformation in the upper cerebellar vermis.

Scans over five days showed the blood collection growing, while vein imaging revealed an unusual drainage pattern with dominant occipital and marginal sinuses. The surgical team chose an occipital approach through the tentorium that avoided those veins and reached the lesion directly. Removal was complete, with no vein injury, stroke, or visual field loss afterward.
pmc-13202071:
Stent procedures stir inflammation in the arteries they treat, and a 2026 pilot study led by Reina Nagasaka checks that response in white blood cells. The research article studies how percutaneous coronary intervention changes neutrophil activation and maturity markers in blood from the coronary circulation and the wider body.

Twenty-nine patients gave paired blood samples just before and just after their procedures at an urban academic medical center. Immature neutrophils rose in coronary blood after intervention, and a surface marker tied to activation fell in both circulations during the same window. Degranulation and migration markers did not change, so the authors call for larger studies of long-term effects.
pmc-13202471:
Brightness and durability trade off in glowing nanoparticles, and a 2026 study headed by Eleonore Kurek checks that balance one particle at a time. The research article profiles dye-based organic nanoparticles built for two-photon fluorescence imaging, a method used for deep-tissue microscopy.

The team set two nanoparticle designs side by side tuned to the same two-photon brightness but different light stability. Single-particle saturation readings matched ensemble estimates once a local-field correction was applied to the data. Time-resolved tests then showed the particles with the strongest absorption bleached fastest under illumination. The authors draw design principles for engineering probes that balance signal strength against working lifetime in nonlinear microscopy.
pmc-13213171:
Shan Ding and colleagues hunt in 2026 for blood markers that can stage scarring in fatty liver disease without a biopsy. Liver sampling remains the standard for judging advanced scarring, yet patients dislike it and doctors need a gentler option.

The team combined liver gene-activity data with blood protein data, screened candidates with three machine-learning methods, and checked four finalists in 119 biopsy-confirmed patients. Together the four proteins separated advanced scarring from earlier stages with strong accuracy, matching established non-invasive scores. Levels of three rose steadily in mice fed a fatty diet. Single-cell and genetic analyses added clues about where the markers act and whether they might help cause disease.
pmc-13214171:
Chenjiao Ran, Xinyu Chen, Yong Huang, and Derui Kong build in 2026 a scan-based model to predict which stomach cancers will shrink under chemotherapy plus immunotherapy before surgery. Guessing wrong wastes months and exposes patients to needless toxicity.

Using pre-treatment CT scans from 281 patients at two centres, they divided each tumour into sub-regions with similar imaging character and measured texture inside and just around it. A combined model mixing those features with clinical data predicted response best, holding up across training, internal, and external patient groups. Region-aware imaging beat simpler tumour-only models. Such a tool could steer personalised choices before treatment starts, the authors propose.
pmc-13214371: Xinzhi Xu and seven co-authors issued this 2026 notice for their study of immune patterns in dermatomyositis. That disease inflames muscle and skin. The notice is a correction only. One figure panel used the wrong stain images for two cell groups. The data access note was also changed. It now says datasets can be had from the lead contact author on request. The authors say the error does not change the paper's findings or methods. The journal has updated the article itself.
pmc-13214571:
Susanne Stoll and colleagues map in 2026 the fine layout of touch sensation for the index fingertip inside the human brain. Using an ultra-powerful scanner, they tracked responses while rows of vibrating pins swept across the fingertip in different directions.

Their first model of each brain spot's receptive patch gave implausible answers, and simulations showed why: the patches are larger than the fingertip area they stimulated, so edges stayed unmapped. Holding patch size fixed rescued the position estimates. The fingertip's side-to-side axis mapped onto a top-to-bottom axis in the touch area, matching receptive properties measured in monkeys. The work gives the first detailed picture of human fingertip map architecture.
pmc-13215171:
Matthew B. Phillips and colleagues ask in 2026 why two drugs that block the same brain receptor feel so unlike in patients. Both memantine, used for Alzheimer's disease, and ketamine plug a channel that lets calcium into nerve cells. Too much calcium harms cells, yet memantine is gentle while ketamine has strong side effects.

In lab tests on made and native receptors, memantine's block grew as calcium inside the cell rose. Ketamine's block did not. High calcium locks the receptor in a rest state, and memantine holds it there. The effect shifts with receptor subtype. In harm tests, memantine shut down receptors most where calcium ran high and damage loomed. Aiming at sick circuits, not all circuits, may explain its kinder profile.
pmc-13215371:
Afeef Vehra and colleagues review in 2026 augmented reality training for balance in older adults, where falls cause injury and loss of independence. Overlaying digital cues on the real world may make rehabilitation more engaging and targeted than conventional exercises.

Ten studies with 235 participants met their criteria, mixing six trials with four observational reports. Programmes ran one to five sessions weekly for up to twelve weeks, with adherence between about eighty-three and one hundred percent. Gait stability and anticipatory posture control were the systems most often tested and improved. Randomised trials showed significant balance gains, while observational work mostly showed trends. One study covered every balance system, a gap the authors flag.
pmc-13218171:
Elie Bou Sanayeh and co-authors measure burnout among healthcare workers in Lebanon in a 2026 multicentre study. Lebanon has endured overlapping crises since 2020, and its health workforce has carried much of that strain, yet national data on burnout were missing. The study asked about financial well-being, which is rarely examined beside burnout.

The survey covered 907 workers, including medical students, nurses, physicians, and postgraduate trainees, using the Copenhagen Burnout Inventory and a financial distress scale. Nearly seven in ten respondents sat at moderate or high risk of burnout, with personal burnout the most common, followed by work-related and patient-related burnout. Risk fell with age over fifty, higher income, and better financial well-being, and rose with long hours, stressful workplaces, plans to emigrate, psychiatric history, and public sector employment. The authors call on health authorities to act on workplace conditions and financial stress to protect the workforce.
pmc-13218471:
Md. Habib Ullah Masum and co-authors design a vaccine against La Crosse virus entirely by computer in a 2026 immunoinformatics study. La Crosse virus, spread by mosquitoes whose range expands with climate change, can cause brain inflammation, mainly in children, and no vaccine or antiviral exists. A multi-epitope vaccine stitches together short viral fragments that provoke immune responses.

The candidate, named LACV-mVax01, targets the viral proteins G1, G2, and N. Computer checks suggested stability, with a low instability score and a structure rich in alpha helices, and a refined three-dimensional model passed quality metrics. Docking simulations showed the candidate binding to sensors TLR4 and TLR2, with the TLR4 pairing stronger, and molecular dynamics runs kept both complexes stable. Codon optimization predicted efficient production, and immune responses included antibody and memory cell formation. The authors stress laboratory, animal, and clinical testing must still prove the design works.
pmc-13219171:
Ana Julia Chaves Gomes and colleagues survey circoviruses in wild birds and mammals along the Paraná coast of Brazil in a 2026 study. Circoviruses are DNA viruses that infect many species and cause disease in some, but they are studied mainly in parrots, leaving their circulation in other wildlife murky. Migratory birds can carry viruses distances, which makes them valuable sentinels.

Nested PCR testing found one positive animal, a South American tern carrying a gull circovirus. Examination of that bird showed damage, including shrinkage of immune tissue in the spleen, kidney tubule injury, and congestion, and wasting. Sequencing showed the virus's code was eighty-three percent identical to gull circoviruses reported from the US, and sequencing plus analysis of its replication protein agreed. The authors present the finding as a step toward understanding how diverse these viruses are, which hosts they use, and how far along the coast they travel.
pmc-13221471:
Jillian L. Seiler and co-authors test a dual-acting obesity drug candidate in male primates, in a 2026 study of the melanocortin hunger system. Drugs hitting only the MC4R receptor have disappointed in general obesity. The team asked whether activating MC3R alongside MC4R would engage the pathway more fully.

Their oral peptide, called 710GO, produced clear weight loss in primates with diet-induced obesity, with limited rebound after stopping. Selective MC3R activation changed food intake depending on state, supporting a cooperative role for the two receptors. The candidate also paired compatibly with GLP-1 therapies and showed a favorable early safety profile, marking a fresh direction for obesity treatment.
pmc-13222771:
Mohamed Abubakar Ahmed, Abdullahi Abdirahman Omar, and Ahmed Omar Siyad examine why families refuse mechanical ventilation in Somali intensive care, in a 2026 essay. Many families read the ventilator as a sign that death is certain, not as short-term support. Refusal, pressure to stop support, and self-discharge all grow from that belief, the authors argue.

Fatalism mixes with out-of-pocket cost anxiety, limited knowledge of intensive care, and gaps in trust and talk about sedation and prognosis. The authors reframe some refusals as changeable rather than rejection, without blaming strained families. Proposed steps include family briefings, structured daily updates, early cost clarity tied to support, and a documented, non-coercive follow-up path.
pmc-13223071:
Rachel Hyzny and co-authors assemble an artificial intelligence pipeline that diagnoses carpal tunnel syndrome from wrist ultrasound, in a 2026 pilot study. Patients screened by a hand surgeon contributed 121 wrist images, seventy-three with the syndrome and forty-eight without. Three models work in sequence: one finds the median nerve, one outlines it, and one classifies disease status.

The localization model scored high on precision and sensitivity, and the outlining model overlapped expert marks well. The classifier reached about ninety-four percent accuracy, catching every true case in validation. Examiner experience currently makes ultrasound accuracy uneven, so the authors see decision support value. Larger multicenter datasets and better interpretability must come before clinical use.
pmc-13226171:
Ke and colleagues study what happens when the DNA-repair enzyme PARP2 is removed from T cells in mice already lacking PARP1. Blocking PARP enzymes, earlier work showed, can calm experimental gut inflammation. Yet patients with inflammatory bowel disease were reported to have lower PARP1 in the gut, a puzzle the team set out to probe.

Instead of protection, the double loss triggered spontaneous colitis, inflammation of the colon, with a distinct patchy pattern along its length. The result warns that PARP enzymes also guard gut health, and that wiping them out in immune cells can backfire. It refines where future PARP-based gut treatments might safely aim.
pmc-13226971:
Mohammad I Idris and co-authors test a 2026 orthodontic idea in a randomised trial: whether injecting platelet-rich fibrin, a concentrate of the patient's own blood, can protect tooth roots during braces treatment. Moving teeth sometimes shortens their roots, a side effect called apical root resorption. Thirty-six adults with moderate lower-front crowding received either four fibrin injections during treatment or none.

Three-dimensional scans measured root length once treatment ended. Roots shortened significantly in both groups, by about half a millimetre on average. The injected group fared no better than controls, with a negligible difference between them. The authors conclude plainly that repeated fibrin injections did not reduce root resorption in this setting.
pmc-13230271:
Maite E Houwing and colleagues check in 2026 whether a standard set of health questionnaires works well for Dutch children with sickle cell disease. Children aged five to seventeen and their caregivers filled in PROMIS forms covering anger, worry, mood, tiredness, pain, movement, friendships, and thinking. Scores were compared with an older quality of life measure to test validity.

One hundred two children and the same number of caregivers took part, including seventy-one matched pairs. Each form measured one clear topic and lined up well with the older measure, with sound reliability throughout. Parents and children agreed fairly well on most topics, though agreement was weaker for friendships and overall health. Caregiver reports look usable when a child cannot answer alone.
pmc-13231071:
Muhammad Ma ruf and colleagues use in 2026 public genetic databases to shortlist variants that may drive colorectal cancer risk. The cancer arises in the colon and rectum and ranks among the most common cancers worldwide. Variants tied to the disease were pulled from a genome study catalog, then annotated and checked in other public resources.

Gene activity data from human tissues showed how the shortlisted variants might change nearby gene behavior. Three variants stood out as high priority, linked to four genes involved in cell growth and immune signaling. Their frequencies differed markedly between world populations, which matters for fair screening. Such markers could support risk checks that reflect the ancestry of the people being tested.
pmc-13232571:
Le Wang and colleagues uncover in 2026 an odd origin story for the master male sex gene of Mozambique tilapia. A shortened copy of a female pathway gene, carried on the Y chromosome, now decides maleness in these fish. Jumping DNA elements helped copy, trim, and rewire that gene in an ancestral cichlid.

The male copy works by sabotage, blocking the normal female protein pair from switching on an egg shell gene. Ovary formation stalls while testis development proceeds. The borrowed gene then spread across several cichlid lines through past cross-breeding. Sex genes, the case shows, can defect from one sex pathway to run the other.
pmc-13232771:
Yuan-Shun Lo and colleagues show in 2026 that a growth factor called FGF9 slows osteoarthritis by switching on an antioxidant defense line. No current drug truly modifies the disease, which wears down joints in hundreds of millions of people. Gene profiles from nearly two hundred patient cartilage samples showed FGF9 running low compared with healthy cartilage.

Silencing FGF9 in cartilage cells raised harmful oxygen byproducts and sped cell aging by muting the defense line. Adding the factor back, or sending it inside tiny cell bubbles, reversed much of that aging in dishes. Gene therapy shots of FGF9 into mouse knees with induced joint damage slowed disease progress. The factor also nudged stem cells toward making fresh cartilage.
pmc-13233971:
Xiang-Shen Liu and colleagues published a 2026 brain imaging study mapping the functional organization of the hippocampus-amygdala complex, two deep structures central to memory and emotion. The team used connectopic mapping, a technique that charts smooth gradients in how each spot connects to the rest of the brain. Resting brain scans came from 410 healthy people and a separate psychiatric cohort of 367.

Six distinct gradient maps appeared in both datasets. One gradient family consistently resembled the distribution of the serotonin 5-HT1A receptor, measured from standard brain templates, with further matches in the dopamine system. People whose gradient pattern aligned more closely with that receptor map reported worse depression and anxiety sensitivity. The authors present the method as a bridge between wiring diagrams and the brain's chemical landscape.
pmc-13234271:
Franz Kanngießer and Stephanie Fiedler studied in 2026 how to rebuild the map of a Saharan dust plume hidden partly by clouds. Their case was the intense plume that reached Europe on 15 March 2022 during an atmospheric river event. Satellite pictures alone missed areas covered by cloud, which is common for dust events over Europe. The authors tested whether ground observations could fill those gaps.

Satellite images were paired with different sets of ground data using a nearest neighbour method. Data came from lidars that probe the air, sun photometers, weather reports, and particle measurements. Adding ceilometer and photometer records helped most in restoring the plume's full extent. The authors recommend that combination for future reconstructions of cloud-covered dust plumes.
pmc-13234371:
Ribal Aby Hadeer and co-authors presented in 2026 two cases of stones forming inside the pancreas during long-standing inflammation of the gland. Such stones can block the pancreatic duct, raise pressure, and cause the severe belly pain that dominates care. Both patients were men with chronic pancreatitis whose stones obstructed the duct. Pain relief was the central goal of their treatment.

Each man was treated by removing the tail portion of the pancreas, an operation called distal pancreatectomy. The authors report that both cases were managed successfully with surgery. Their review notes that choices among surgery, endoscopy, and other options depend on stone location, duct shape, and patient factors. Decisions should be made by a multidisciplinary team. Selected patients may gain lasting relief from the combined surgical approach described.
pmc-13235171:
Laura-Jayne Watson and a mixed stakeholder group described in 2026 making accessible information materials about life after voice box removal. Laryngectomy, usually done for advanced throat cancer, permanently changes breathing, speech, and swallowing. About four hundred sixty people undergo the operation each year in England. Community health workers often lack specialist skills or clear training material for supporting these patients at home.

Patients, clinicians, a designer, and a creative agency built an animation and infographic together through repeated rounds of feedback. Stakeholders reflect on what the collaboration taught them in the report. The materials will anchor workshops that design a fuller training package for community professionals. Wider sharing with patients and the public is planned afterward. The group aims for clearer information, more confident workers, and more compassionate care.
pmc-13236671:
Guorui Liu and co-authors measured in 2026 drawings of trees made by people with depression, people in remission, and healthy controls. Tree drawing is a projective test sometimes used in psychological assessment, usually judged by eye. Computer image recognition extracted fourteen size and proportion measures from each drawing. Groups held more than one hundred people each in the comparison.

Seven measures separated the three groups clearly, including canopy area, canopy height, trunk width, and total drawing area. The other seven measures, mostly with roots and height ratios, showed no reliable group differences. Recovered patients' drawings differed from currently depressed patients on the same seven measures. Remission drawings matched healthy controls across every measure taken in the study. The authors say quantified drawing features could support assessment of depression state and recovery.
pmc-13236871:
Gael Garcia-Valdez and colleagues reviewed in 2026 how cancer cells depend on L-arginine, an amino acid that feeds growth, energy balance, and defense against damage. Many tumors lose the ability to make their own arginine and must import it. That rewiring touches several classic traits of cancer, from rapid growth to hiding from the immune system.

The review explains how arginine sensing, through pathways such as mTORC1, links nutrient supply to tumor behavior and to immune cells around the tumor. Treatments that starve tumors of arginine or block its handling are surveyed, along with the escape routes cancers use against them. The authors present the pathway as a promising but contested target for new drug design.
pmc-13236971:
M Ibrahim and colleagues tested an upgraded spherical solar still in 2026 that turns sunlight into fresh water more productively than the classic design. Their version stacks four improvements: a vertical absorber, a two-axis tracker that follows the sun, a corrugated surface, and a heat-storing wax boosted with silver nanoparticles. Each change was also measured on its own.

The full system produced about 13.3 liters of water per square meter per day, more than four times the plain still's output. Tracking and the vertical absorber each added the largest single gains. The stored heat also smoothed output across the day. Production cost fell to about one cent per liter, which the authors say suits scattered communities short of fresh water.
pmc-13239071:
Elif Ersahin Telli and colleagues optimized a gelatin-free marshmallow in 2026, swapping the animal-derived gelling agent for aquafaba, the chickpea cooking liquid that whips into foam, plus gellan gum. Statistical optimization balanced density and taster preference, settling on small inclusion rates for both substitutes. Molecular docking then checked how the two ingredients interact.

The plant-based marshmallow came out denser, more viscous, and more heat-resistant than the gelatin control, with a higher water activity and visibly different color despite no added colorants. Microscopy showed smaller, less prominent granules than in the control. Docking predicted a favorable, stable interaction between the substitutes. The authors present the recipe as a workable vegan alternative that holds its foam without gelatin.
pmc-13239871:
Al-Hatem JihanYahya and colleagues optimise feeding for basil grown in aquaponics in a 2026 plant study. Aquaponic systems raise fish and plants together in circulating water, and spraying leaves rather than dosing the water keeps fish safe while still feeding the crop.

Using a compact nine-run experimental design, the team varied silicon, a nano-fertiliser, and a chelated micronutrient spray at three levels each. Every combination beat the untreated controls on growth, pigments, and nutrient content. The strongest recipe combined the highest level of all three sprays, maximising plant height, fresh weight, chlorophyll, and essential oil yield. Antioxidant activity fell at high inputs, suggesting better-fed plants faced less stress.
pmc-13240371:
Dandan Gao, Yuxuan Zhang, and Hongxin Ma prepare antioxidant peptides from quinoa protein and test them in ageing mice in a 2026 study. Quinoa is prized as a complete protein, and breaking it into small peptides with digestive enzymes can release fragments that fight oxidative damage linked to ageing.

Six enzymes were tried, and pepsin produced the most active preparation in laboratory assays, with over half its amino acids being essential types. Fed to mice aged artificially with a sugar treatment, the peptides protected liver, kidney, and lung tissue and restored antioxidant enzyme activity in blood and liver. Damage markers fell while the genes and proteins for protective enzymes rose.
pmc-13240871:
Song and colleagues at Anhui Medical University linked pulse pressure in the arm and ankle to coronary artery narrowing. The cross-sectional study enrolled two hundred eighteen patients at a tertiary hospital. Stenosis severity and the number of diseased branches came from clinical workups. Measurements were taken at both arms and both ankles.

Pulse pressure at all four sites ran higher in patients with severe stenosis. Left-arm pulse pressure stayed independently tied to severe disease after adjustment. Its discrimination reached about 0.86 in men and was nearly as high in women. Ankle readings flipped by sex, which the authors say argues for site-specific risk checks.
pmc-13241671:
Miquel and colleagues in Barcelona audited what becomes of registered rotator cuff trials across four registries. One hundred fifty-two trials that finished recruiting before 2022 qualified. The team hunted indexed publications and contacted authors of the missing ones. Discontinuation reasons were catalogued alongside funding and topic.

About forty percent of the trials never reached an indexed journal. Nearly a quarter of them were discontinued outright. Trials of biological treatments abandoned ship far more often than other topics. Even published trials often conflicted with their registry entries on major design points.
pmc-13242671:
Boyan Liu, Yuan Jiang, and Bihuan Zhao reviewed how long-read sequencing is changing the study of blood cancers, highlighting work from the 2025 American Society of Hematology meeting. Their article appeared in Biomarker Research in 2026. Long reads span tangled, repetitive stretches of DNA that short reads cannot cross. Studies at the meeting applied the method across many leukemia, lymphoma, and related disorders.

Rapid whole-genome long-read runs now assign cancer subtypes in near real time and catch mutations, copy changes, and gene fusions in one pass. Targeted sampling and methylation patterns add further classification power. Full-length RNA reads resolve transcript variants and fusion messages inside their exact cell clones. The authors say these gains expose structural variants that standard testing misses and refine risk grouping for treatment choices. With accuracy rising and costs falling, they expect long-read testing to enter routine diagnosis.
pmc-13242771:
Hui Yan and co-authors publish a 2026 population analysis of the antidepressant mirtazapine in Chinese inpatients with depression. Finding the right starting dose is tricky because other medicines and body weight change how fast the drug clears. The team built a mathematical model from blood level measurements.

One-compartment modeling described the data well, checked against extra clinical and literature data. Body mass index and two companion drugs stood out as clearance changers. Obesity slowed clearance notably, one companion drug slowed it somewhat, and another companion drug cut it by about half. Simulations supported the standard mid-range dose for typical patients, with step-downs for the affected subgroups. The authors offer the model as a dosing reference.
pmc-13243171:

pmc-13243871:

pmc-13245571:

pmc-13246471:

pmc-13246771:

pmc-13247671:
Kouadio D Ekra and co-authors forecast measles in Côte d'Ivoire through 2030 in a 2026 modeling study. The World Health Organization aims to eliminate measles in most African countries by 2030. The team asked whether current trends put their country on that path.

pmc-13248571:

pmc-13248971:

pmc-13250471:
Iraj Golikhatir and co-authors study ultrasound signs of body fluid levels in this 2026 paper. Emergency doctors must judge quickly whether a patient needs fluids, since only about half of patients actually respond to a fluid boost.

pmc-13250871:
Hoogstad and colleagues test a storytelling form of trauma therapy in adults with severe intellectual disability. pmc-13251171:

pmc-13251271:

pmc-13251671:

pmc-13251871:

pmc-13253771:

pmc-13254371:

pmc-13256771:

pmc-13257071:

pmc-13264271:

pmc-13264871:

pmc-13266371:

pmc-13266571:

pmc-13266871:

pmc-13267571:

pmc-13269571:

pmc-13269671:

pmc-13270071:

pmc-13271071:
Xinyu Wang is lead author of a 2026 review article on nanomedicine, treatments built at tiny scale, for colorectal cancer, tested in patient-derived xenograft models. pmc-13272071:

pmc-13272371:
Siyin Li and coauthors profile in 2026 a broad panel of antiphospholipid antibodies in pregnant women whose babies grew too slowly in the womb. pmc-13272571:

pmc-13272771:

pmc-13273471:

pmc-13273871:

pmc-13274071:

pmc-13274471:

pmc-13274571:

pmc-13274871:

pmc-13275771:

pmc-13276571:

pmc-13276771:

pmc-13276871:

pmc-13276971:

pmc-13277771:

pmc-13278971:

pmc-13279171:

pmc-13279871:

pmc-13279971:

pmc-13282171:

pmc-13282271:

pmc-13282871:

pmc-13283171:

pmc-13283371:

pmc-13284171:

pmc-13284471:

pmc-13284571:

pmc-13284871:

pmc-13285671:

pmc-13286071:

Kidney trouble, gut complaints, nerve damage, and plasma cell disorders showed up far more often before the light chain form. Heart failure, thickened heart muscle, rhythm faults, and carpal tunnel syndrome marked the path toward the age-related form instead. pmc-13286271:
Md Al Saber leads a 2026 computer-designed vaccine effort against monkeypox virus strains circulating since the 2022 outbreak. With global cases near ninety-nine thousand by mid-2024 and no vaccine built for this virus alone, the team took a build-from-genome route. Sixteen viral genomes went through a shared-gene screen to find stable targets worth aiming shots at.

Eighty core genes survived the screen, and proteins from four of them yielded the immune bait pieces. Four candidate vaccines were assembled from those pieces with boosters and linkers glued in. Shape checks, docking against an immune receptor, and motion runs all judged the builds stable and likely to provoke both arms of immunity. pmc-13286971:
Rabab Batool surveys the history and future of vaccine science in a 2026 perspective that runs from Jenner's cowpox experiments to genomic design. Genetics, computing, and immunology now allow vaccines tailored to individuals and built at speed. Emerging tools and platforms for personal immunization close the piece, which frames vaccinology as a field still accelerating after two centuries.
pmc-13287471:
Felicity K Hunter and co-authors fed mice in 2026 on a schedule that spread food evenly across the whole day, removing the usual feast and fast rhythm. They then tracked daily cycles in colon gene activity, gut microbes, and a protective antibody in the gut.

The colon cell clock kept ticking without feeding cues, yet a set of key genes lost their daily rhythm. Rhythms in the protective antibody faded almost completely. Microbe composition and their fatty acid products also flattened across the day. The authors conclude that when animals eat matters, not only what they eat, for keeping gut, immune, and metabolic rhythms in step.
pmc-13288271:
Haolei Wei and colleagues report a case linking a fungal allergy flare to a heart event, published in 2026. Kounis syndrome is a heart attack pattern triggered by allergic reactions. The patient was a 77-year-old woman with asthma, chronic lung disease, and a known Aspergillus allergy condition of the airways. She arrived with chest tightness and breathlessness as that allergy condition relapsed.

The authors urge heart checks when severe allergic airway disease flares, since the two systems can fail together.
pmc-13288371:
Jone Vencloviene and co-authors linked ambulance records in 2026 from Kaunas in Lithuania with space weather records. Records covered 2016 to 2021. They asked whether magnetic storms on the Sun change the odds that a stopped heart restarts at the scene. The set held 1,507 resuscitation attempts.

For those with a shockable rhythm, high activity days instead favoured restart. Storm start days showed no clear rhythm effect. Patterns ran stronger in men and in presumed heart causes. The authors treat the links as early, puzzling signals.
pmc-13288871:
Lateef Akanni and colleagues link child growth paths to teen worklessness in 2026. The UK Millennium Cohort supplied the data. Thinking and social paths ran from age three to fourteen. In all, 8,368 children were modeled. Teen status was read at seventeen.

At seventeen, 3.5 percent sat outside school and work. Lasting woes in both domains meant fourfold risk. Late social-emotional trouble tripled risk. Early woes that cleared showed no link. About twenty-eight percent of cases traced to child woes. Policy should back early social skills. School support should also start early.
pmc-13289071:
Simon Fabry and colleagues track aid money for surgery in poor nations in 2026. Their review spans 2014 to 2022. Data came from two large aid databases. Surgery gets a small slice of health aid. The team mapped who gave funds and who got them.

In all, 2.73 billion US dollars were spent. The share of health aid fell over time. It slid from 2.13 percent at the start of the period. It reached 1.32 percent by the end of it. Canada and the US led the donor list. Birth and womb care drew the most funds. Aid groups ran 51.4 percent of projects. Sub-Saharan Africa drew 55.17 percent of funds. The authors fear bypassing state systems weakens care.
pmc-13289171:
Pramod Chandru and colleagues frame a 2026 trial plan on lab tests in Australian ERs. Tests make up over half of non-labor costs there. Up to one fifth of tests are not needed. The UNTIE study will test audit and feedback. Five city ERs in New South Wales will join.

Sites will start the plan in staggered steps. Local champions and teaching will drive it. Dashboards and prompts will back it up. Two scores will be built for each visit. One counts tests done but not advised. One counts advised tests that were done. Change in the first score is the main check.
pmc-13289371:

Frontline staff saw the method as basic skills training for medics, while hospital staff saw a finishing school for rare, high-risk steps. Most viewed the training favorably overall.
pmc-13289671:
Yanran Zhang, Zahari Ishak, and Bicheng Diao map psychological capital as a network in teachers, in a 2026 study. Psychological capital bundles self-efficacy, hope, resilience, and optimism. Studies often lump the four into one score, hiding how parts interact. The team surveyed 1,271 junior high school teachers in China. Hope served as the main bridge toward career commitment, while optimism bridged little. The network's strength pattern held up well under resampling checks. The authors advise support programs that grow hope and resilience in culturally fitting ways. They argue that part-level dynamics, not total scores, should guide teacher support policy.
pmc-13289771:
Chengyi Han and co-authors review drying methods in endoscope reprocessing in a 2026 systematic review. The team searched three databases for studies of drying methods and their effects. Sixteen articles passed the quality checks for inclusion.

Six studies tracked residual droplets, six tracked microbial growth, and four tracked both. Manual drying alone left more moisture and growth behind. Pairing automated drying with standard steps cut residual fluid and contamination further. Drying cabinets stood out as the most effective automated option in the gathered reports. The authors recommend writing automated drying into standard reprocessing protocols. They note that consistent drying may be as important as the disinfection step itself. Hospitals can audit channel dryness as a simple quality target.
pmc-13290471:
Jeffrey Pea and co-authors build a screening assay for non-hormonal contraceptive leads in a 2026 study. The assay watches mouse egg cells mature in a dish, a process a drug could pause. Blocking that maturation without hormones is a long-sought contraceptive strategy. Eggs were matured for about fourteen to sixteen hours with single doses of test compounds. The team screened 818 compounds chosen from a bioactive library.

A hit had to block maturation by at least eighty percent. Twenty-nine compounds cleared that bar in the first pass. Fresh supplies and dose curves confirmed eighteen of them. Five froze eggs at the earliest stage, though four worked through a known enzyme route the team wanted to avoid. Thirteen let maturation resume but stopped the final polar body step. The authors value the assay for sorting blockers by stage and reversibility. Confirmed hits offer starting points for contraceptive chemistry.
pmc-13290871: A short correction notice from 2026 by Weilin Qi and colleagues fixes two figures in their study of preoperative phase angle and complications after ileocolic resection for Crohn's disease. The notice supplies only replacement ROC figures: in the male subgroup of 86, phase angle predicted complications with an AUC of 0.748 at a 4.5° cutoff, and in the female subgroup of 33, an AUC of 0.864 at 3.9°. No further text or methods are given.
pmc-13290971:
Short upper arms in achondroplasia, and whether lengthening the humerus helps, are examined in a 2026 questionnaire study led by Cristina Giuli. Care at one center was studied in 27 patients grouped by whether they had surgery, had not had it, or were children who might consider it later.

Those who had lengthening described better daily function and gave satisfaction scores of 4 out of 5 in most cases. Among untreated adults, 2 of 5 voiced regret over lasting limits. In the child group, 9 of 14 wanted future surgery, which supports earlier discussion of timing in care plans.
pmc-13291271:

Defense enzyme levels rose in young plants. Starch and protein breaking enzymes climbed at high pulse rates. One stress gene quieted across all treated lots. Field tuning still needs care by dose. pmc-13291371:

Swelling cells and harsh signals fell in lungs. Protective enzymes rose while damage marks fell. Two pathways drove the effect, one calming and one guarding. Blocking the guard pathway removed the benefit in cells. Stool chemistry shifted with treatment too.
pmc-13291671:

Such multi-partner shields are common in nature. Pest control with fungi must reckon with these guards. Ignoring inner microbes can doom a biocontrol plan. Ecology here spans plant, insect, and microbe alike.
pmc-13291771:

Rubber resists decay and piles up as waste, yet it feeds more than 4,000 commercial products. Mass loss stayed small, between about 0.77 and 1.24 percent of the disc weight, but staining and microscopy showed oxidation, cracking, and erosion. pmc-13291971:

Joining carbon groups onto aromatic rings usually needs separate systems for different partner types. Light-born holes turn surface hydroxyl groups into hydroxyl radicals, which pry hydrogen from the ring. pmc-13292471:
Pablo José Rufino-Moya and a large team catalog a 2026 parasite community inside the booted eagle in southern Spain. pmc-13292671:

pmc-13293271:

pmc-13294071:

pmc-13294171:

pmc-13294271:

pmc-13294771:

pmc-13294871:

pmc-13294971:

pmc-13295071:

pmc-13295171:
Lili Zhou and colleagues review nanomedicine aimed at tumour-associated macrophages in a 2026 article. pmc-13295771:

pmc-13295871:
Edwin Egbe Atem and colleagues assess two food fish stocks in the Central Gulf of Guinea in 2026, where catch records are too thin for standard methods. Bonga shad and lesser African threadfin both feed coastal towns and support local incomes.

pmc-13295971:

pmc-13296171:

pmc-13296271:

pmc-13296371:

pmc-13296571:
Sima Shajari and colleagues test, in 2026, natural coatings for keeping peaches fresh after harvest. Fruit loses market quality fast in storage, so the team combine salicylic acid at three strengths with aloe gel and clove extract at varied doses and track weight, firmness and chemistry.

pmc-13297071:

pmc-13297371:

pmc-13297671:
Jiangmei Cao and colleagues review gelatin-based gels that carry several functions at once for sports injury repair, in a 2026 article. pmc-13297871:
Parasitic cysts returned across a young farmer's liver, chest, and heart lining in an unusual case reported by Silviu Gabriel Vlăsceanu and colleagues in 2026. The 26-year-old, who worked around dogs and horses, had several abdominal hydatid cysts removed back in 2016.

pmc-13298971:
A chatbot that talks patients through a standard depression questionnaire earned users' trust in a 2026 feasibility study by Zhijun Guo and co-authors. Of those asked to compare, 71% felt more confident in the chatbot-assisted score, praising its structure and supportive tone. Comfort rated 8.4 out of 10. pmc-13299271:

pmc-13299571:
Duoduo Lv, Heyu Tang, and Lingyun Zhou review evidence linking air pollution to fatty liver disease tied to metabolic dysfunction, in a 2026 survey. It also interacts additively with lifestyle and social factors. The authors discuss responses from personal habits through global cooperation, arguing pollution checks and control belong inside liver disease prevention and treatment plans.
pmc-13299671:

The author calls for structural reform on legal, financial, and digital fronts, plus trust-based care shaped by patients' own cultures.
pmc-13300071:

pmc-13300471:

The authors call the acceleration concerning and ask for work on the sex and regional drivers so interventions can be targeted.
pmc-13300671:
