The team asked whether the phytocytokine receptors PEPR1 and PEPR2 help carry that signal.

Treatment with the fungal protein SsNLP1 switched PEPR genes on strongly. Plants missing both receptors responded weakly, with less oxidant burst, fewer defense genes, and poorer resistance to the fungus. Plants overproducing PEPR1 answered more strongly on every count. The results show plant cytokine signaling reinforcing pathogen-pattern immunity against a broad-host-range rot.
pmc-13300871:
Julia Zuzanna Bura and co-authors relate physical activity to everyday functioning in people living on long-term left ventricular assist devices, in a 2026 study. The pumps restore circulation, yet many recipients still struggle with daily tasks. The study enrolled 262 adults sorted into four groups by device status and self-declared activity, then scored function and quality of life with two standard questionnaires.

Active patients on device support earned the best scores, reporting stronger function and lighter symptom burden, while inactive patients fared worst. Activity levels tracked with concrete abilities such as walking, climbing stairs, doing housework, and carrying groceries. The pattern held across both questionnaires. The authors argue that regular movement belongs inside long-term device care and rehabilitation planning, not as an optional extra. How patients live day to day may matter as much as how the pump performs.
pmc-13301071:
Tian Ran and co-authors use eye tracking to watch Chinese learners resolve ambiguous pronouns in Russian in a 2026 study. Russian leans on gender and case agreement to settle who a pronoun means, while Chinese offers no such crutch, so the two cue systems collide for these learners. Readers at two proficiency levels worked through sentences where reference could stay ambiguous or be settled by grammar alone.

Both groups slowed down at ambiguous pronouns, proof that ambiguity itself costs effort online. Stronger learners read faster overall, while weaker learners clung harder to the first mentioned character as the likely referent. Even the advanced group did not fully trust Russian gender agreement to disambiguate, suggesting that wiring grammar cues into split second comprehension stays effortful late into learning. The authors offer the results as evidence on how cue weighting shifts with proficiency.
pmc-13301571:
G Pontes Saad and co-authors stretch pulsed field ablation beyond the veins without X ray guidance in a 2026 workflow study. Fifty-nine patients, forty-five paroxysmal and fourteen persistent, were treated fluorolessly, steering by three dimensional mapping and an ultrasound catheter inside the left atrium watching tissue contact. Because pulsed fields spare the esophagus and phrenic nerve, the team added back wall isolation in twenty-nine patients and vena cava isolation in fifteen.

Every targeted structure was isolated, procedures averaged about seventy-eight minutes, and no major complications occurred; one patient's kidney numbers rose and recovered on their own. Two cases needed a remap to finish, after which the workflow ran clean. Over a mean eight months, only two patients, about three percent, saw their arrhythmia return. The authors argue the lesion sets buy substrate control without thermal injury's collateral risks, keeping a safety profile while steadying rhythm.
pmc-13301671:
Heart ultrasounds in long COVID turn up oddities whose meaning stays murky, Jana Khawandi and a large team report in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis. Sixteen studies compared echocardiogram findings between people with post-COVID-19 condition and those without it. The work feeds into Canadian guideline development for the syndrome.

Patients with the condition were more likely to show structural or functional deviations on their scans, especially if their acute infection had put them in hospital. How much those deviations matter clinically remains unclear, though. Bias, indirectness, and imprecision dragged the certainty of evidence down to very low on the GRADE scale. Better accuracy studies come next, the authors say.
pmc-13301771:
Mattia Corianò and co-authors revisit heart transplant outcomes in a 2026 study built around the newer 2022 definition of pulmonary hypertension. High pressure in the lung arteries before transplant is linked to graft failure and early death. European guidance lowered the resistance cut-off that separates two forms of the condition, and the team tested whether the new grouping predicts one-year survival better.

The single-centre review covered 357 recipients transplanted between 1985 and 2020 who had pressure measurements before surgery. Survival at one year was best in patients without lung hypertension, while the two reclassified groups looked similar. Reclassification did not sharpen prediction, and only average pulmonary artery pressure above the threshold independently signalled risk. The result may prompt a rethink of pre-transplant testing routines.
pmc-13301971:
A leaner object detector hunts circuit-board flaws without losing its eye, Zhenling Wang and colleagues present in a 2026 methods study. Starting from YOLOv8, they swapped in a RepGhostBottleNeck backbone to cut parameters, added an attention module and a small-object detection head, and reworked the loss function. The target defects ranged from open circuits and shorts to mouse bites and stray copper.

On the team's assembled dataset, the tuned model reached a mean average precision of 0.976 at the standard overlap threshold. The authors frame lightweight as relative to the bulky YOLOv8L baseline, prizing balance over extremes. Such detectors could fit factory inspection lines where speed, accuracy, and deployment cost all bind at once.
pmc-13302071:
Aleksandra Stańska and co-authors describe, in a 2026 Polish cohort study, how a structured psychosocial score guides lung transplant preparation rather than blocking candidates. The SIPAT tool rates readiness, support, mental health, and substance risks. Their programme uses the results to target help at fixable problems before listing.

Records covered 491 consecutive candidates assessed between late 2021 and late 2025, whose average risk burden was low. Total scores, domain scores, and candidate categories showed no meaningful link to who eventually got listed. Even a higher-risk cluster identified by the analysis was no less likely to be listed. The authors argue the tool works best as a roadmap for support, not a pass-or-fail gate.
pmc-13302671:
Lina Zhu and co-authors build, in a 2026 modelling study, a machine learning route to predict density in laser-printed parts made from a nickel superalloy used in jet engines. Dense, defect-free parts are essential, yet only fourteen experiments were available, far too few for ordinary modelling. The team tested ways to stretch that small dataset safely.

Three augmentation methods were compared under physical rules, and eight physics-based input features were constructed from the printing settings. A neural network predicted density most accurately, well ahead of a simple physics formula, with support vector and forest models close behind. Energy density per volume supplied over half the predictive power. The authors present the framework as an interpretable aid for process tuning.
pmc-13302871:
River mud makes 3D-printed concrete tougher against winter, Lu Yin and colleagues demonstrate in a 2026 freeze-thaw study. Yellow River sediment replaced quartz sand at up to full substitution in engineered cementitious composites, both cast and printed. Samples endured 150 freeze-thaw cycles while strength, stiffness, and pore structure were tracked with imaging and microscopy.

Moderate replacement, a quarter to a half, packed particles better and refined pores, improving frost resistance. The fifty-percent mix kept about eighty-two to eighty-four percent of its compressive strength after all 150 cycles. Printed layers still suffered at their interfaces under cross-layer bending, confirming that print seams remain the weak direction for cold-region construction.
pmc-13303071:
Cooling, not chemistry, may be green hydrogen's biggest water problem, Bernhard Wortmann and colleagues calculate in a 2026 global modeling study. Electrolyzers shed waste heat, and evaporative cooling can multiply a plant's water demand several times beyond the roughly nine liters each kilogram of hydrogen consumes directly. The team layered a thermodynamic cooling model over climate, water-stress, and renewable-resource maps, season by season.

Sun-blessed regions, prime solar territory, repeatedly coincided with scarce water and fierce cooling demand. Wind-rich regions skewed cooler and wetter. Their composite Water Risk Index flags where desalination, reclaimed water, or dry or hybrid cooling must enter project plans from the start.
pmc-13303871: Giorgia Salerno and co-authors issue a 2026 author correction to a study on dye and deep eutectic solvent pairs for dye-sensitized solar cells used indoors. Chemical structures in Scheme 1 had presentation errors and were replaced. The scheme caption wording was updated, and one compound label in the results was corrected from 3a to 3b. The notice states that the errors do not affect the experimental results, data interpretation, or conclusions. The scheme and text were updated in both HTML and PDF versions.
pmc-13303971:
Chang Guo and Zizhi Tang examine a liver enzyme called malic enzyme 1 in painkiller overdose injury in a 2026 mouse study. Acetaminophen overdose is a leading cause of sudden liver failure, and the standard antidote works best when given early.

Mice lacking the enzyme in liver cells suffered far worse injury after overdose, with more fat oxidation damage, weaker cell power units, and stalled cleanup systems. Raising enzyme levels or restoring them protected the liver, and a disabled enzyme version failed to help. The enzyme guards the liver by sustaining reducing power and energy balance.
pmc-13305171:
Li Wei, Chengjia Xie, and co-authors investigate, in a 2026 study, why some strains of the gum-disease bacterium Porphyromonas gingivalis produce more indole, a metabolite behind bad breath. Indole comes from the enzyme encoded by tnaA, yet strains differ in output. Data from a periodontitis cohort linked saliva indole signatures to disease severity and to this bacterium's abundance.

Comparing thirty-six complete genomes showed the enzyme itself barely varies. What differs is the mobile DNA element sitting beside its gene: high-virulence strains carry one transposase family, milder strains another. In patient saliva, the high-virulence element's activity tracked with the enzyme's activity and with clinical measures of gum damage. The authors stress association, not proven cause, and call for functional experiments on the neighboring element's role.
pmc-13305371:
Xiaoyang Wang and co-authors pool studies of bedside ultrasound for skull fractures in children in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis. Head injuries are common in childhood, but CT scans expose young brains to radiation that doctors prefer to avoid.

Four databases were searched through September 2025, and nine emergency department studies qualified. Pooled results showed the sound test caught most fractures while rarely flagging healthy skulls, giving a strong overall accuracy score. The authors place ultrasound as a helper beside clinical judgment, not a stand-in for CT when inner brain injury is feared.
pmc-13305471:
Camille Lapeyre leads a 2026 pilot study teaching French family doctors about lower-carbon inhaler choices. Pressurized puffers for asthma and lung disease emit many times more greenhouse gas than powder or mist devices, yet they dominate reliever prescribing in France.

Thirty-four doctors from ten health centers attended one short face-to-face session in 2023. Surveys with two patient cases, one asthma and one lung disease, were taken before and three months after. Answers were sorted by whether choices included the high-emission puffer. Early shifts in awareness and intended prescribing are the focus of this pre-post pilot.
pmc-13305671:
Eunkyo Ha analysed twelve years of hospital data from South Korea in a 2026 study of childhood breathing viruses before and after COVID-19. Records covered children admitted with respiratory infections from January 2012 to December 2023 at one large centre.

Of 12,306 children, most fell in the earlier period, and median age rose from 20.0 to 27.0 months after the pandemic years. Rhinovirus and human metapneumovirus became more common while flu fell, seasons shifted toward summer and autumn, and infections with three or more viruses rose. Weather alone did not explain the changes, pointing to a need for flexible surveillance.
pmc-13305871:
Asmaa T Alenazi and co-authors investigate in 2026 how the K5 capsule of a probiotic Escherichia coli strain affects its contest with Salmonella in the gut. Resistant Salmonella strains are narrowing treatment options, so probiotic competition interests the team. They removed capsule export genes from the probiotic strain Nissle 1917.

Mutants lacking capsule parts were checked with staining and growth tests in rich and minimal media. Competition was measured in direct co-culture and in assays using only conditioned medium. Losing the capsule lowered the probiotic strain's fitness in cell-free fluid and let Salmonella grow more. The findings link a surface structure to colonization resistance, and they may inform how probiotic strains are selected or improved.
pmc-13305971:
Jacksaint Saintila modelled links between habits and mental strain in 684 adults in Peru in a 2026 survey study. The team looked at sport, sleep length, meat free diet and faith in food choice skill.

Models took in age, sex, school, home life and body mass. Low faith in food skill went with high strain in the reported scores. Sport linked to low strain through that faith path, and sleep and diet showed like paths. The team says food skill faith is a self control point worth care in adult mental health work.
pmc-13306071:
Christopher F. Sharpley updated evidence on brain wave patterns in melancholia, a severe form of depression, in a 2026 systematic review. Brain imaging work has grown, yet records of electrical activity remain sparse despite promise for guiding brain stimulation care.

Findings linked melancholia to many electrical measures in complex and uneven ways, with several aspects barely studied at all in the authors' summary. Gaps cover which signals are stable, how they relate to symptoms, and whether they can guide targeted treatment. The review closes with concrete directions for tighter future studies in this neglected area.
pmc-13306771:
Dominik Zaborniak scheduled driverless factory vehicles with a fault-tolerant predictive search in a 2026 study. A max-plus model captures robot timing and switching choices, while a tree search explores assignments whose count grows fast with horizon length.

Delay estimates update live so the plan adapts when transport slows unexpectedly, and a cost rule punishes long or uneven trips. Dispatch runs through internet-linked operator stations tied to a central controller by live message streams. Blender simulations showed tighter spread of completion times under faults in reported results. The linked dispatch desk lets staff step in when plans must change on the floor.
pmc-13307371:
Alok Jindal and co-authors report a 2026 pilot case series on partial unilateral lentiginosis, a rare pattern of one sided dark spots that has no standard care. Six patients, four female and two male, aged from 10 to 32 years, received Q-switched Nd:YAG laser care at 532 nm.

Dose began low and rose in steps, with visits spaced two to three weeks apart. One patient cleared fully, and the other five each gained more than 70 percent fading, while harm stayed mild and brief. Scores from patients were high, and the authors see the laser as a safe option worth wider study.
pmc-13308371:
Susanna Esposito and a global consensus panel review vaccination against meningococcal serogroup B disease in 2026. The illness is rare but kills quickly and leaves those who live through it with serious after-effects. Protein-based shots beat the failure of sugar-based routes for this group, and the panel weighs real-world results.

England's infant programme cut disease in babies given the shots by three quarters within three years of launch. Cover still varies because strains in the wild differ in their surface markers, and antibodies fade over time. The shot barely reduces throat carriage, so herd cover stays limited. Open questions include preschool and adolescent booster timing, which plans have not settled. Possible cross-cover against gonorrhoea remains mixed across studies. The panel urges age-based boosting and stronger genome tracking of strains in the wild.
pmc-13308571:
Khaled Abubaker and colleagues report in 2026 a seventy-two-year-old man whose routine testosterone injection seeded a stubborn thigh abscess with Mycobacterium abscessus. This fast-growing soil-and-water germ resists many drugs and usually attacks people with weak defences, yet this patient had none. Standard drugs failed first.

Wound cultures at last named the germ, and long multi-drug treatment came next. His stay grew harder when acute breathing failure needed ICU care and a breathing machine. Injection sites that refuse to heal deserve doubt for unusual mycobacteria, the authors argue, even in healthy hosts. The germ lives through cleaning fluids and forms biofilms on gear, which explains outbreaks after shots. Early aimed cultures could shorten the naming drift this case shows.
pmc-13309371:
Hatice Çavdarcı and colleagues present a 2026 animal study on floor design for fast-growing broiler chickens. Farms often use litter on the floor, but partly slatted floors may keep birds cleaner. The team tested whether mixing slats with litter changes welfare and daily behavior.

Six hundred young Ross-308 chickens were split into five groups, from full litter to full slats. Birds on more slats stayed cleaner and kept better breast feathers, yet they showed more hock and breast burns and weaker walking. Birds on litter foraged and moved more, while slatted birds rested and preened more. The authors weigh cleaner housing against poorer leg health and less natural behavior.
pmc-13309571:
Xile Han and co-authors place a fiber-optic sensor inside working sodium-ion batteries in a 2026 study. What happens in the thin layer where electrode meets fluid governs charging, yet watching that layer live is hard. Sodium-ion cells draw interest as a cheaper storage option for large grids.

The grating sensor tracked ion movement without disturbing the cell and revealed a middle stage between ions settling on the surface and ions spreading inward. Cells whose middle stage ran shorter charged faster. Adding up the sensor light signal over time also gave charge level with accuracy above 98 percent in the reported tests. The authors offer the tool for battery checks and design.
pmc-13309671:
Muriel Elhai introduces a special collection on precision medicine in systemic sclerosis in a 2026 editorial overview. The disease hardens skin and can scar inner organs, yet its course varies sharply from person to person. Standard grouping by skin spread and antibody type captures only part of that variety.

Four articles in the collection take up overlooked drivers of difference, starting with sex. Women develop the disease more often, while men more often face widespread skin disease, lung scarring, and worse survival. Other pieces address further patient traits that shape outlook and treatment response. The author argues for care plans sorted by deeper biology, brought back to bedside decisions.
pmc-13310671:
Wen Sun and co-authors pool results across PD-1 immune drugs for returned throat-area cancer in a 2026 review. Nasopharyngeal carcinoma that returns or spreads carries a poor outlook, and PD-1 blockers plus chemotherapy now lead first-line care. Which blocker performs best was unsettled.

Nineteen studies with 1,459 patients entered the pooled analysis, covering response, control, survival, and severe side effects. Overall response reached 64 percent and disease control 94 percent across regimens in the combined data. Toripalimab pairs led on response and time without growth, at a median of 21.4 months without progression in its subgroup. Tislelizumab pairs led on total survival, at a median of 45.3 months in the subgroup figures.
pmc-13310971:
Weijie Yao and colleagues build an early warning model for severe pancreatitis tied to high blood fats in a 2026 study. Fat driven pancreas swelling is now the second top cause in China and turns severe more often than other types. Early sorting would guide intensive care.

A build group of 478 patients came from 36 hospitals, and a fresh group of 145 patients tested the model. Seven signs from the first day, including calcium, pulse, and breathing rate, fed a boosting model. Scores sorted severe cases well in both groups and beat older scoring systems. Visual tools show how each sign moves the risk.
pmc-13311171:
Augustin Demain and Etienne Willemart report a black knee found during joint replacement in a 2026 case and review. A woman aged 54 years had knee surgery, and the joint showed dark pigment that revealed ochronosis, the tissue form of a rare metabolic disease. The disease ruins large joints fast, yet it is often missed until surgery.

Past reports, though weak in design, suggest knee replacement eases pain and restores function well in this disease. Implant survival looks much like that in the general group. Known pigment buildup harms cartilage and tendons over decades, so joint checks should watch for dark tissue clues.
pmc-13311371:
Ahmed Ibrahim AbdElneam and co-authors map the gene landscape of alopecia areata in a 2026 data study. In this autoimmune illness, the immune system attacks hair roots and causes patchy hair loss.

Gene data from a public set comparing patients and healthy controls yielded 5134 genes with changed activity. Network tools picked out ten hub genes, among them CCL5, CCR7, and CXCL9, plus leading control factors such as FOXP3. Chemokine signaling and cytokine pathways stood out. The study also predicts 49 small RNAs that may steer these genes. The map points to targets that future drugs for hair regrowth could aim at.
pmc-13311771:
Timothy C Hardcastle, Charles Mock, and Christine Gaarder comment on updated WHO guidelines for essential trauma care in a 2026 article. The new guidance updates a 2004 document that shaped trauma systems in many countries.

The guidelines sort needs into structure, supplies, and process, with tables that fit recommendations to facility level. Items are marked core or extended, so poorer regions can pick the steps with the biggest payoff first. The commentary reads the document beside prehospital and quality guidance and stresses integration with other WHO policy. The hard part now is turning paper standards into staffed, stocked services everywhere.
pmc-13311971:
Chun-Min Wang and co-authors compare three stroke transfer models in a 2026 study from Taiwan. A new integrated drip-and-ship system uses a transfer platform to tighten coordination between hospitals.

The study covered 1063 patients with suspected large vessel blockage: 814 sent straight to the full stroke center, 185 by standard transfer, and 64 by the integrated system. The integrated group matched the direct group on scan timing and beat standard transfer clearly. It also had the highest rates of clot drug and clot removal treatment, and the shortest door-to-puncture times among treated patients in this study.
pmc-13312071:
Maha Alkhaldi, Laura Lindsey, and Charlotte Lucy Richardson explore, in a 2026 qualitative study, how unpaid carers manage medicines for people with long-term conditions and what help community pharmacies give them. Carers often collect prescriptions and field medication questions, yet their own support needs are rarely examined. The researchers interviewed carers who helped a relative or friend with at least one long-term condition, then analyzed the transcripts thematically.

Twenty-four carers took part, all caring for family, with 17 looking after one or both parents. Three themes emerged: caring itself is multifaceted, carers must wade through confusing medication information and systems, and pharmacy staff can leave carers feeling empowered when communication works well. The authors argue that pharmacies should tailor support to each carer's situation and communicate more directly, and they call for research from the pharmacy staff side as well.
pmc-13312371:
Masashi Soga, Kevin J Gaston, and colleagues examine, in a 2026 perspective article, why people's everyday contact with nature keeps shrinking across generations. They call the pattern the extinction of experience. As environments degrade, each generation grows up with a thinner personal ecology of direct encounters with the natural world. Borrowing ideas from behavioural genetics, the authors ask how such impoverished experience gets passed down inside families and households.

Two reinforcing routes emerge. Children can inherit an already reduced ecology from their parents. Rich experience can also fail to transmit when surroundings remove the chance, motivation, or ability to engage with nature. Either way the loss compounds, deepening disconnection and making recovery harder. The authors argue the cycle can also run in reverse. Policy, urban planning, education, and public health can jointly support engagement. Decline then turns into a self-reinforcing recovery that serves both biodiversity and human well-being.
pmc-13312971:
Ting Shen and colleagues pool, in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis, the randomized trial evidence on cardiac rehabilitation for patients with atrial fibrillation. Structured exercise programs clearly help such patients move better, yet whether rehabilitation also stops the rhythm disorder itself from returning, the outcome patients care about most, had looked inconsistent across trials.

Eleven trials covering 1,550 patients met the entry rules. Rehabilitation cut the risk of fibrillation recurrence overall, with a risk ratio of 0.77 against controls, but the benefit faded to non-significance in the smaller subgroup treated after ablation. Walking capacity improved meaningfully, by roughly 32 meters on the six-minute test in the pooled figure. Deaths and hospitalizations, though, showed no difference between groups. The authors support rehabilitation for recurrence and fitness while noting survival effects remain unproven.
pmc-13315071:
Veeral S Sheth and co-workers give a plain summary of four-year results for faricimab in diabetic macular edema, published in 2026. The summary covers the RHONE-X trial, a two-year open extension of the YOSEMITE and RHINE studies of this eye drug.

In the extension, patients who had gotten faricimab every 8 weeks, faricimab on a flexible plan, or aflibercept every 8 weeks all moved to faricimab at a dose of 6.0 mg on a treat-and-extend plan stretched up to every 16 weeks, as the design states. The drug stayed well tolerated over the two added years, with side effects matching its known profile. Vision and anatomy gains from the parent trials held through the extension. The summary brings long-term proof to patients and clinicians in clear terms.
pmc-13315171:
Serina S Applebaum and co-authors report a small retrospective comparison from 2026 on glaucoma surgery with the XEN45 gel stent. Adults over 40 with open-angle glaucoma and high eye pressure had the stent placed through an open conjunctival route, some with removal of Tenon tissue and some without, at one academic center.

Forty eyes were matched and followed for one year. Success rates, eye pressure, drug burden, and vision were similar in both groups, with mean pressure near 14.83 in the tissue-removal group and 16.88 in the other group at one year. Early problems were slightly more common with removal, while later added procedures were fewer.
pmc-13315671:
Reshed Abohalaka and colleagues examine, in a 2026 population study, whether two markers of type 2 inflammation in asthma tell the same story or different ones. Blood eosinophil count and fractional exhaled nitric oxide may reflect different pathways, and their links to lung function, allergy, and nasal polyps were unclear. Among treated participants, eosinophils alone tracked with reduced lung function, more nasal polyps, and more clinical allergy, and joined with nitric oxide in bronchodilator responsiveness. Among untreated participants, neither marker acted alone; only their combined effect tracked with lower lung function and more allergy. The authors conclude the markers capture distinct yet complementary aspects of inflammation, and support using both when phenotyping obstructive airway disease.
pmc-13315771:
Jin-long Liu and a large team built in 2026 a combined lab and modeling method to predict lung exposure for inhaled protein drugs. Breathing in therapy acts fast and skips first-pass breakdown, yet aerosol traits and lung shape make exposure hard to forecast across species.

Using recombinant human interferon-alpha1b as the test drug, they measured aerosol behavior at several strengths and with mouthpiece versus facemask devices, then modeled particle settling in lungs. A lung-focused body model for mice and healthy adults was built and checked against drug level studies. Delivery efficiency changed with setup, informing human dose prediction.
pmc-13315971:
Ivan Camilo Sanchez-Rojas and a large team report in 2026 on yellow fever cases in Nariño, Colombia, during 2024 and 2025 that looked like dengue or leptospirosis. A focal outbreak centered on Ipiales, near the Ecuador border, touching rural and Indigenous communities exposed to forest transmission cycles.

The affected zone lies in a low Andean to Amazon transition area, unlike the high-altitude town itself, which may hide yellow fever risk. Regionally, yellow fever had caused 486 cases and 209 deaths across seven countries by late May 2026 in the authors' count. Careful case review can sharpen local detection where diseases mimic each other.
pmc-13316271:
Yong A Yu and co-authors studied in 2026 an oncolytic vaccinia virus therapy, Olvi-Vec, that may restore platinum sensitivity in ovarian cancer. In mice with platinum-resistant disease, pairing the virus with cisplatin gave a durable anti-tumor effect, setting up human testing in the VIRO-15 trial.

Patients in that phase 1b and 2 study were heavily pretreated with resistant or refractory disease. Fluid from the abdomen showed viral infection and clearing of tumor cells, and paired biopsies tracked gene and immune changes by multiplex staining and RNA profiling. Phase 2 survival without progression was compared with each patient's last platinum course.
pmc-13316371:
Julia Sgrott and co-authors report a 2026 study of a short revision course, led by fellow students, for international medical students in Germany. The course covered medical psychology and medical sociology, subjects where newcomers often struggle with both language and local expectations.

Thirty students took tests before and after the course, with two test versions swapped between groups to keep the check fair. Scores rose clearly after the revision days, a gain the statistical test marked as strong. The authors read the result as proof that fellow students can teach effectively, not just staff. They urge medical faculties to spread such peer programs, which also help newcomers settle socially into their new country.
pmc-13316471:
Anika Wijewardane and Mark Holland review, in a 2026 article, how acute medicine can ease the urgent care crisis in British hospitals. The specialty was built to give early expert checks within the first 72 hours of a stay, yet patchy access has diluted its units and same-day services.

Drawing on published proof and national benchmark data, they add a case study of one large district hospital that rebuilt its acute unit. Stronger leadership, clear entry paths, joined-up team work, and firm targets tied to early discharge cut stays, raised direct discharges, and sped flow from the emergency department. Restoring the model's core job, they argue, is a practical fix that other hospitals can scale.
pmc-13316571:
Sungjin Ju and co-authors present, in 2026, a virus-like particle system that delivers CRISPR editing machinery into cancer cells without using DNA. Delivery remains a major barrier for genome and epigenome editing as therapy. Particles that carry the editor as a protein and RNA complex act briefly and then disappear.

Editing worked efficiently across several cancer types. Particles could target mutant cancer alleles selectively, harming cancer cells while sparing normal ones. Delivering an epigenome editor silenced genes in a stable way for more than 120 days and helped overcome escape from gene knockout. Compared with DNA vectors, particles showed fewer off-target effects. In mice they appeared safe for the liver and slowed tumour growth in a xenograft model.
pmc-13316671:
Maria Pârlea and colleagues publish a 2026 standardized protocol for dating zircon crystals and reading their trace elements with a laser linked to a mass spectrometer, tuned at the PetroChron laboratory. Zircon is geology's favorite clock, since it traps uranium while shutting out lead at birth.

The write-up fixes settings for gas flow, pulse rates, and laser strength across two workflows: dating alone, and dating plus element reads in one pass. Test runs gave ages within five percent of true values and element accuracy better than ten percent for most targets, while using little material. Labs studying river, volcanic, or heat-changed zircons gain a ready recipe that keeps fine detail and high throughput together.
pmc-13317671:
Xian Lin and co-authors identify, in 2026, a gene that links sugar metabolism to DNA repair in lung adenocarcinoma, a common lung cancer. Tumour cells often burn sugar quickly and repair drug damage efficiently, both of which blunt chemotherapy. How those traits connect was not fully understood.

Multi-layer data analysis singled out a gene called SGO2, which was raised in tumours and predicted poor survival across three patient groups. SGO2 protected the repair protein BRCA1 from breakdown, strengthening repair and reducing sensitivity to cisplatin in cells and animals. A dietary compound, oxamic acid, slowed sugar use, lowered chemical marks that open the gene, and switched SGO2 down. Treated tumours progressed less, with no obvious toxicity in animals.
pmc-13317771:
Zengtao Wang and a large team hunt, in a 2026 study, for immune signs that predict death after patients successfully come off VA-ECMO, the heart-lung support machine. Many deaths happen after weaning, yet few markers sort who stays in danger.

Blood profiling covered 125 adults: 70 survivors, 33 who died on support, and 22 who died after weaning. Plain T cell counts did not separate the groups, but two CD4 subsets did: a PD-1 negative, TIGIT positive group ran high in those who later died, and its mirror ran low. Day-one readings sorted risk into bands where death rates ran from 10.53 to 70.59 percent across the scale. The signature could guide closer watching after weaning.
pmc-13318571:
Mao Chen and colleagues present a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of enteral immunonutrition, tube feeding enriched with immune-supporting nutrients, for people having stomach cancer surgery. Standard tube feeding served as the comparison.

Nineteen randomised trials with 1,653 patients were pooled from searches running to December 2025. The enriched feeding cut infectious complications, with an odds ratio of 0.48 reported for that outcome, and also lowered total complications and gut intolerance. Hospital stay shortened by about a day and a quarter, antibody levels improved, and inflammation markers fell. Benefits looked strongest when feeding spanned the operation and lasted seven to ten days, though the authors rate the certainty of evidence as only moderate.
pmc-13318771:
Xiushen Dong leads a 2026 study linking visual skills to serve reception in elite men's volleyball. Outside hitters have to judge fast jump serves in a split second. Twenty-four elite players were tested on ten visual skills with a sensor station. Their season-long reception records came from match data software.

Perfect reception rate was the performance measure. It correlated strongly with eye-hand coordination, at r = −0.778 in their analysis. Near-far quickness and reaction time also linked strongly to success. A small regression model kept all three as independent links. The authors suggest vision testing adds useful information about reception skill. They caution that the design is cross-sectional and the sample small, so cause cannot be claimed.
pmc-13318871:
Anbalagan Sanjana and Pragasam Viswanathan review, in 2026, how gut microbe products connect imbalance in the gut to cancer formation. Microbes make small molecules that talk to the host body. When the community is disturbed, those outputs change. The shifts can affect barriers, inflammation, gene control, and genome stability.

Compounds covered include short-chain fatty acids, secondary bile acids, polyamines, and indole derivatives. Many are measurable in stool, blood, or urine. That makes them candidates for low-burden cancer screening and prognosis markers. New sequencing and metabolite profiling tools now map these networks in depth. The authors also discuss treatments that reshape the microbiome. Method problems still block clinical use, they note.
pmc-13318971:
Wei Zhang, Weike Tian, and Chao Zhang report a 2026 cell and animal study of granzyme B in rheumatoid arthritis. Joint-lining fibroblasts drive much of the damage in this disease. The team lowered granzyme B in cultured MH7A cells. They also treated arthritic rats with a granzyme B inhibitor.

In dishes, knockdown slowed cell growth, migration, and invasion. More cells died, and more paused in later cycle phases. In rats, blocking the enzyme left cartilage smoother. Joint lining overgrowth and inflammatory cell entry both fell. The PI3K/AKT pathway changed in step with treatment in both settings. The authors suggest silencing granzyme B could slow rheumatoid progression through that pathway.
pmc-13319071:
Fatih Cebeci and colleagues present a 2026 survey study of digital addiction and climate anxiety among Turkish high school students. The sample held 3,561 students, 56.4 percent of them female. Teenagers completed scales for digital addiction, eco-anxiety, and hopelessness. Mediation analysis tested whether hopelessness carried the link.

Digital addiction showed only a weak direct tie to eco-anxiety. Its link with hopelessness was stronger, and hopelessness related clearly to eco-anxiety. Once hopelessness entered the model, the direct path to eco-anxiety lost significance. The indirect path through hopelessness stayed significant, indicating full mediation. The authors argue heavy digital use feeds climate worry mainly through future pessimism and lost control. Programmes should build media literacy and coping resources alongside.
pmc-13319371:
Paula Henríquez Miranda leads a team that reviews trial proof on blood pressure care during surgery in a 2026 article. Swings in pressure while a patient is under sedation may cut blood flow to the brain. Such swings have been tied to confusion and thinking problems after surgery, but trial results so far do not agree.

Thirteen trials in adults were found across three large databases and checked for flaws by two readers working apart. Set dose drips, personal pressure targets, and breathing or sedation tweaks mostly kept pressure steadier and helped some early outcomes. In one trial, a personal target cut clouded awareness by a wide margin. Wide gaps in methods blocked a pooled count.
pmc-13319671:
Nicole A Withrow and co-authors run, in 2026, a small pilot of a plant-based high-protein shake for people taking GLP-1 weight management drugs. Such drugs often cause gut side effects and reduced appetite, which can cut protein intake and raise the risk of muscle loss during weight reduction.

Twenty adults who had used the drugs for at least four weeks drank one to two shakes daily for seven days. Nobody dropped out, and participants rated the shakes as likable. Bloating and constipation eased significantly two hours after the first serving, though symptom change across the week was not significant. Protein and fibre intake rose significantly over the intervention. The authors call for larger studies to confirm the benefit.
pmc-13320271:
Yining Xie and co-authors study how planned feed limits shape sheep meat flavor in a 2026 study of Gangba sheep on high land farms. Farmers often hold feed back for a spell then feed freely again, a cycle that can lift growth, yet its effect on meat taste was unclear at the chemical level. Graded feed cuts followed by free feeding were tracked with deep chemical scans of muscle.

A mild cut, to 85 percent of free intake in the plan tested, lifted taste active building blocks and rich fats and gave the strongest scent in tool checks. Deeper cuts pushed muscle toward burn and stress paths and blunted flavor gains. Mild limits plus refeeding may thus be a precise way to lift meat quality where feed runs short.
pmc-13321371:
Mirko Micovic and colleagues describe global inequality in brain surgery as a postcode lottery in a 2026 article written for EANS committees. Where a patient lives and what they earn strongly shape access to lifesaving neurosurgery. Two opening stories contrast a tourist flown to elite care within an hour with a farmworker who reached surgery too late.

More than five billion people lack ready access, about five million needed operations go undone each year, and no neurosurgeon practises at all in 33 countries in the cited data. North America and Western Europe hold four to eight surgeons per 100,000 people, against fewer than 0.1 across sub-Saharan Africa. Fair financing and workforce growth are urged.
pmc-13322071:
Rhea Amatya and colleagues describe, in 2026, using a four-question climate survey inside their veterinary hospital to shape client communication about climate and animal health. Many American veterinary clients worry about environmental issues, yet beliefs differ sharply by region and clinic, so national findings translate poorly to a single practice.

The instrument, called SASSY, sorts people into six climate belief groups and is already validated. The team applied it locally while developing educational resources for clients. Heat, air pollution and disasters increasingly affect pets, making tailored guidance valuable. The authors found the tool feasible and informative in daily practice. They encourage other clinics to try it as a practical first step toward communication matched to their own clients.
pmc-13322571:
Magalli Diaz Bravo reviews, in 2026, how artificial intelligence paired with virtual reality could reshape physical rehabilitation. Recovery needs intensive, personalised practice sustained at home, yet services suffer staff shortages, distance barriers, cost and poor adherence to home exercise. Supervision between clinic visits is the missing piece, the author argues.

Systems that estimate body pose from cameras, combine several sensors and give low-latency feedback can guide exercise in real time and adapt difficulty. Learning science explains why immersion alone fails without teaching and motivation. Across muscle, nerve, heart, cancer and chronic pain groups, virtual programmes improved engagement, capacity, movement quality and satisfaction when coaching and home monitoring were included. The author frames the technology as a clinician-governed co-pilot that widens fair access.
pmc-13322871:
Syahrul Sazliyana Shaharir, Adli Ali and Fahd Adeeb introduce a journal collection on genes, microbiomes and environment in autoimmune disease, in a 2026 editorial. Loss of immune tolerance sits behind these varied disorders, shaped by inherited risk, infections and changes in gut microbes.

Five articles in the collection cover shared genetic patterns, single gene variants and viral triggers. One study traced the global burden of rheumatoid arthritis and juvenile idiopathic arthritis in people aged 0 to 19 years, finding rising rates over three decades. Genetic analyses in that work pointed to immune traits that may help cause both conditions. The editors frame the set as a move from lab findings toward patient care.
pmc-13322971:
Anthony Ransford leads a large Quantinuum team reporting a 98-qubit trapped-ion quantum computer called Helios, in a 2026 paper. Trapped ions hold the best gate accuracy of any approach, yet growing qubit counts without losing that accuracy has stayed hard.

Helios uses barium ions in a charge-coupled layout, with a rotating storage ring that links two working zones and gives all-to-all connections between qubits. A new software stack compiles changing programs in real time, and parallel work speeds operations. Error rates for single and paired gates and for state readout stayed very low across zones in their tests. The team argues the design can grow further without hitting a basic limit.
pmc-13323071:
Hee Jeong Cho and a large Korean team write to the editor in 2026 on how fast patients respond to treatment in multiple myeloma. Most risk tools use fixed measures taken at diagnosis, which miss how disease behaves once therapy starts.

Their retrospective study covered people with relapsed or refractory myeloma treated at 17 centres in South Korea between January 2015 and June 2021, using carfilzomib or ixazomib based regimens as second-line care. Response kinetics, meaning the timing of reaching a response, forms the focus, alongside clinical and disease factors tied to it. The letter argues that such timing adds prognostic value beyond depth of response, early relapse and treatment resistance.
pmc-13323171:
Anna Condella and Nicholas J Johnson comment on machine learning for selecting patients for extracorporeal resuscitation, in a 2026 editorial. This rescue method can lift survival after refractory cardiac arrest, yet choosing candidates and running the logistics remain hard, and most scoring tools lack validation.

They discuss work by Chen and others in the same journal issue, covering 1,953 adults with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest across four Taiwanese centres over nine years. A causal forest model estimated each patient's survival gain with or without the treatment, moving past fixed entry rules. The editorial weighs that shift toward personal benefit estimates and the care needed before such models guide real-time decisions.
pmc-13323371:
Junseok Jang, Minseo Gwak and Hyunggee Kim review, in 2026, how cancer stem cells trade metabolic favours with the ordinary cells around them. These rare self-renewing tumour cells drive relapse and drug resistance, partly by flexibly rewiring how they make energy. Their metabolism was long treated as a private, cell-internal trait.

The review gathers evidence that support cells and organ-resident cells actively sculpt the metabolic niches these stem cells live in, and receive signals back. That two-way traffic helps explain why tumours differ between organs and why the same drug can succeed in one site and fail in another. The authors close by discussing repurposed drugs aimed at the supportive niches, arguing that context-aware metabolic treatment could undercut stem-cell-driven resistance.
pmc-13323571:
Ran Yan and a large team study a GNB3 gene variant and stroke recurrence in China, in a 2026 registry analysis. Their group held 1,233 patients with large-artery ischaemic stroke. All joined the registry within 72 hours of stroke onset. Whole-genome sequencing found the C825T variant, which affects G protein signals tied to platelets and inflammation.

Carriers of the 825T allele made up about 72.7 percent of the cohort. They had a lower one-year recurrence risk than non-carriers after adjustment. The link appeared in the aspirin-only subgroup, though the interaction test was not significant. Higher interleukin-6 partly weakened the genetic protection in mediation checks. The authors propose the variant as a recurrence marker worth testing in treatment choice.
pmc-13323671:
Khayreddine Bouabida and Margarieta Okang describe a child's chronic belly pain that drew escalating procedures, in a 2026 case report. An eleven-year-old boy had lasting upper abdominal pain after an injury, and repeated tests found no structural cause.

His picture fitted functional abdominal pain under Rome IV rules, a gut-brain interaction disorder. The family, convinced a blood vessel was at fault, pushed toward a celiac plexus block and then surgery to release the median arcuate ligament. Pain returned after surgery, matching the gut-brain account. The authors argue for early, clear explanation that validates symptoms and answers caregiver fears, to stop harmful escalation and support recovery.
pmc-13325371:
Miori Nogamida and Hirotoshi Mori trace the first reaction steps when ionic liquid fuels meet hydrogen peroxide in a 2026 study. Such fuels ignite on contact yet stay safer to store than hydrazine, a classic but toxic propellant.

Automated path searches and orbital analysis covered four candidate anions. The borohydride anion showed the lowest ignition barrier, at 20.6 kcal per mol, and the largest heat release, at minus 105.4 kcal per mol. Adding cyano groups steadily dulled reactivity, and two anions failed to ignite at all. Ignition hinged on how well the anion donates electrons into the peroxide bond. The rule gives designers a molecular compass for greener rocket fuels.
pmc-13326071:
Chiara Anna Giordani and colleagues track cefazolin use in joint replacement patients carrying penicillin allergy labels in a 2026 study. Wrong allergy labels steer doctors away from the best preventive antibiotic.

Records covered 172 primary joint replacements from 130 patients between 2013 and 2024 at three hospitals. After 2022 guidance sorted patients by reaction risk, cefazolin use in low-risk patients rose from 64 to 88 percent of cases. Moderate-risk use rose from 40 to 64 percent without reaching firm proof. No allergic reactions occurred with any antibiotic. Vancomycin plus clindamycin remained the main fallback. Hesitancy persisted despite the perfect safety record.
pmc-13326571: Aidé Martínez-Cuenca and co-authors issued this brief 2026 item. It is only a correction notice. It serves their article on sleep traits and thinking problems in bipolar disorder across age groups. The notice adds the funding details that were missing. Support came from the Carlos III Healthcare Institute and Spanish science ministries. European regional funds and the Government of the Principality of Asturias also gave support, under file IDE/2024/00774. The sponsors had no role in design, analysis, or publication choices. The article has been updated.
pmc-13327171:
Yijiao Xue and team built stretchy plastic rubbers that are at once strong, tough, fire-safe, and self-mending. Their 2026 paper takes on a design clash: these traits run on distinct workings, so joining them is hard, though soft robots, bendy sensors, and electronics want them. The team built a phosphorus- and nitrogen-rich, biphenyl-bearing diol as hard blocks with side arms, using chain pi-pi stacking for strength and mending.

The finished rubber stretched to about 2500% before it broke, with toughness near 379 megajoules per cubic meter and pull strength of 46 megapascals. Mending hit 95% for pull strength and 99% for break stretch, and the stuff put its own flames out, with a limiting oxygen index of 38.6. The team showed sensitive multi-mode tattoo sensors made from it. The team puts the molecular build plan forward as opening new paths for strong, bendy, tough rubbers with many built-in jobs.
pmc-13328271:
K A Werner and a large team pair bench culture with genomics to find a priority pathogen in wastewater in a 2026 study. Carbapenemase-producing Klebsiella pneumoniae resists last-line drugs, and sewage monitoring could warn hospitals early, but targeted methods were scarce. Their workflow filtered raw inflow from four treatment plants in north-eastern Germany and grew bacteria on selective plates.

All 33 samples tested positive, at counts between 102 and 104 colony-forming units per 100 mL across the set. A total of 253 isolates were verified as the target producer, most carrying blaOXA-48 type genes. A culture confirmation step plus gene checks gives surveillance a reliable recipe, the authors argue, beyond simple DNA presence.
pmc-13328371:
Francis Barchi, Helen Apps, and Peggie Ramaphane study condom knowledge among adolescent girls in Botswana in a 2026 analysis. Girls in Sub-Saharan Africa still carry a heavy HIV burden, so the team surveyed 306 schoolgirls aged 14 to 19 in the northwest in 2021. Only 15 percent reported having had sex, and risk behaviors such as smoking or drinking were rare.

Girls who had not had sex had 70 percent lower odds of reporting correct condom knowledge than experienced peers. Those unsure of their HIV status had about 80 percent lower odds of feeling able to insist on condoms. Knowing AIDS has no cure tripled the odds of correct use knowledge. Confidence and knowledge travel separately, the results warn.
pmc-13328471:
Yu Chen and Dongfan Chen review vowel sound measures in autistic children's speech in a 2026 narrative review. Speaking trouble varies across the spectrum, but minimally verbal children and those with speech-motor difficulty may show unusual vowel patterns. Measures such as formant frequencies, vowel space size, duration, and wobble can be read objectively from recordings.

Some subgroups show flatter vowel contrasts, more variable sounds, and odd timing, though no single profile fits all autistic children, and the literature searched ran to September 2025. Direct therapy evidence stays thin and small, centered on auditory-motor mapping training. Vowel measures look best as candidate gauges for planning therapy in selected children, the authors conclude.
pmc-13329871:
Sreeram V Ramagopalan and Michael L Ryan examine United States drug price policy and its spillover to Europe in a 2026 article. After legislative backing fell short, an executive order told health officials to test most-favoured-nation pricing, which ties United States prices to prices abroad. Three pilot schemes followed, covering Medicaid and parts of Medicare.

The pilots differ: one is voluntary, while two are mandatory drafts with set patient shares. Price can be set by the lowest country price or by a weighted average across 19 reference countries, as the authors lay out. Set against Europe's joint clinical assessment, the authors argue that launch pressure on firms is compounding. Early signs and limits of that pressure form the core of their case.
pmc-13330671:
Wenjie Xu and team found that ginkgolide A boosts cardiomyocyte differentiation from stem cells. Their 2026 study, using a CRISPR-Cas9-built TNNT2-mCherry marker stem cell line and a defined cardiac protocol, screened ginkgolides for effects on heart cell output. Ginkgolide A much raised heart cell output and sped spontaneous beating, while blocking cell death during turning. RNA sequencing found stage-wise rises in antiapoptotic genes such as MCL1 and XIAP with cardiogenic factors NKX2-5 and GATA4. Molecular docking showed strong binding potential between ginkgolide A and cytochrome c, hinting it blocks intrinsic mitochondrial cell death by interfering with cytochrome c binding to APAF-1. The team presents it as a safe culture additive to raise cell survival and yield for biomanufacturing and tissue building.
pmc-13332371:
Annika Kreienbrinck and co-authors set out a 2026 plan for a pilot study on translation apps in mental health care. When patients and clinicians share no language and no interpreter is free, judgment quality and trust suffer, yet phone-based translation has barely been tested in this setting.

The single-arm practice study will enroll 12 German-speaking mental health providers and 2 Turkish-speaking trained patients. Each provider will run a practice session of up to 30 minutes using the Mabel app, which translates speech in real time. Sessions will be recorded and followed by surveys and follow-up talks, covering ease of use, translation quality, communication quality, and nonverbal behavior. Practical measures such as sign-up, timekeeping, and how well the setup is received will shape a larger trial. As of March 2026 no one had enrolled, with sign-up planned from May 2026.
pmc-13332471:
Fatumastar O Adan and colleagues set out 2026 technical principles for custom antibiotic spacers in complex shoulder revision surgery. Shoulder replacement use keeps rising, and revisions are expected to rise with it. When infection, instability, loosening, or fracture forces implant removal, a staged rebuild is often needed. Ready-made spacers are simple and repeatable, but their fixed shape fails in severe bone loss, wide canals, narrow canals, or fracture.

The paper explains how surgeons shape a custom humeral spacer to fit the damaged bone, restore length and stability, and deliver antibiotics locally. Case illustrations show the principles applied to varied complex anatomy. The value is practical: a spacer tailored to the defect can hold the joint space and fight infection while the patient awaits final reconstruction. Surgeons facing anatomy that no catalog device fits gain a worked, step-by-step alternative.
pmc-13333071:
Qinsi Liu and colleagues report a 2026 real-world assessment of raising the baricitinib dose in severe alopecia areata that had answered poorly to standard care. The approved 4 mg dose leaves roughly 60 percent of severe patients short of a meaningful response in trials.

Four women, averaging 26.5 years old with a mean starting severity score of 64.5 on the SALT scale, took 6 mg daily between January 2023 and June 2025 after weaker results on conventional therapy. Three of the four, 75 percent, gained clinically meaningful hair improvement on repeated SALT scoring. Laboratory wobbles appeared in three patients, including mild platelet rises, brief mild anemia, and a symptom-free creatinine rise, all settling, and no severe events occurred. The authors support testing step-up dosing properly in randomized trials.
pmc-13333371:
Catherine Sulca and colleagues followed tuberculosis patients through treatment in a 2026 longitudinal study, hunting for immune signs that show the drugs are working. Sputum tests monitor cure poorly, and antibody behavior during therapy has been little studied compared with T cell responses.

The team measured antibodies against the bacterial protein Ag85A, sorted by subclass, and tested their power to direct natural killer cells to kill infected targets, alongside perforin-making NK cell counts. As treatment finished, cytotoxic antibody activity rose significantly and matched higher perforin output. One subclass moved the other way: Ag85A-specific IgG3 fell steadily over treatment, a pattern the authors read as a fingerprint of bacterial clearance and settling inflammation. They propose the pairing of stronger killer activity with fading IgG3 as a monitoring biomarker for TB therapy.
pmc-13333471:

By week 48, 64.63 percent had cleared virus below the response threshold and 39.02 percent had seroconverted. Both genes climbed differently in responders than non-responders, and their week-12 rises foreshadowed the steeper virus and antigen declines seen by week 24. At week 24 the pair predicted responses with AUC values reaching 0.8549 for SAMD4A on viral response and 0.8717 on serological response. The authors propose both genes as practical mid-treatment checkpoints for deciding whether interferon is worth continuing.
pmc-13333671:
Wenling Ding and Renchang Liu present a 2026 case report and literature review about gallbladder inflammation without stones in a young child. The case involves a 7-year-old boy infected with both Epstein-Barr virus and cytomegalovirus.

The boy arrived with fever, swollen neck glands, abdominal pain, abnormal liver tests, and a thickened gallbladder wall but no gallstones, during infectious mononucleosis from the two viruses. Once doctors clarified the diagnosis, they stopped antibiotics and treated him conservatively, and he improved without surgery. Gallbladder inflammation is rare in children and easy to mistake for other illness. The authors urge clinicians to consider this viral cause when a child with mononucleosis develops right-sided upper abdominal pain.
pmc-13335471:
Stefania Boccia and colleagues present a 2026 strategic research agenda for custom prevention toward a EU rollout roadmap. The rapid growth of omics technologies, combined with digital health resources, has ushered in a new era of medicine. This precision revolution has created new opportunities for custom care by identifying individual risk profiles from multiple sources of health-related data.

This matters most for chronic diseases, whose complex nature and major burden on health care systems may benefit from more accurate risk grouping in wide care. Tailored prevention aims to refine existing strategies, including cancer screening, prevention drugs, and lifestyle programs, beyond traditional risk grouping based primarily on age and sex. The document gives EU policy leaders a shared roadmap for bringing custom care into practice.
pmc-13336371:
Geunhye Kim and colleagues study 2026 surface protein rewiring of stem sacs promoting lung cancer targeting via potentiated receptor-ligand interactions. Non-small-cell lung cancer death rate remains high because mutation-matched treatments target only small patient subsets and always face drug pushback. In this regard, multi-pathway stem sacs offer a hopeful broad platform for beating unmet needs of lung cancer treatments, especially for patients lacking known cancer drivers.

Nano-bits made by fusing drug-primed stem sacs with liposomes exhibit greatly improved treatment effects. According to gene-reading and siRNA knockdown tests, this enhanced tumor aiming of tumor cells is driven by drug-induced rise of key cell stick proteins, specifically ephrin type-A receptor 2.
pmc-13336471:
Yichen Zhai and co-authors built a causal method to judge a Wolbachia mosquito suppression program in a 2026 study. Releasing Wolbachia-carrying males sterilizes wild Aedes aegypti matings, but field effects vary across places and times, while standard checks report only averages.

Their framework uses distribution-based synthetic controls on trap-level counts, building full what-if distributions for treated areas rather than a single average. That allows detailed comparison of what happened against what would have happened, measuring how suppression varied with time and with the past abundance of mosquitoes before release. The analysis concerns the joined incompatible and sterile insect technique. Richer effect figures help program managers see where and when releases work, instead of trusting a pooled number.
pmc-13336971:
Eduardo Sergio Oliveros-Mata and co-authors print magnetic sensors directly into shaped parts in a 2026 study. Their 3D-printed magnetic field sensor shows a magnetoimpedance effect above 300% at low frequencies and can rebuild a full three-axis field reading from one point using Hall measurements. Sensor shape itself tunes response, range, and working frequency.

Flexible spring and cross-shaped sensors demo the design freedom. Uses shown include magnetic toggle switches for smart homes, smooth joysticks for robots, three-axis magnetometers, and 4D-printed actuators that sense their own motion. Folding sensing into printed structures lets each part know its surroundings and user input, a step toward self-aware machines.
pmc-13337371:
Seung-Ji Kim and Kang-Seuk Choi examine how vaccination itself shapes a poultry coronavirus in a 2026 review of Korea's experience. Infectious bronchitis virus changes fast through mutation and gene swapping, eroding vaccine protection. Korea's dense, connected farms, wide vaccine use, and long tracking form a telling test case since the virus was first found there in 1986.

Virus families rose, split, and replaced each other in waves, ending with kidney-harming GI-19 types in front, including KM91 and QX-like variants. Vaccines remain a must, yet steady immune pressure plus vaccine and field strains mixing together foster escape variants. The authors frame a vaccination-driven cycle with lessons for controlling other coronaviruses.
pmc-13339171:
Jiale Li, Yancai Kang, Fan Zhou, and Junsheng Mu review care when heart disease and lung cancer occur together in a 2026 article. Both diseases share risks such as smoking, and patient numbers grow with aging. Cancer surgery strains the heart, while heart drugs raise bleeding risk.

Recent decade literature guides staged choices. Early cancer with mild heart disease and good function may allow combined surgery. Advanced cancer or complex heart disease favors staged care with smaller incisions. Radiation dose and clot prevention need balancing in non-surgical care. Low inflammation, heavy calcium, high SYNTAX scores, and diabetes flag poorer outlooks as reviewed.
pmc-13340071:
Jiaji Wang and colleagues map microbes across sterile drug cleanrooms with geographic software in a 2026 study. Finding contamination sources in pharma plants is hard from lists alone. Isolates collected from 2022 to 2025 were tied to exact workshop locations.

A total of 1,117 isolates were identified by gene sequencing as reported. Staphylococcus and Micrococcus dominated clean areas, while diversity ran highest in loosely controlled zones and lowest in top-grade areas. Maps revealed clumping and spread paths clearly. Targeted fixes followed in a case example, showing spatial tracking can turn routine monitoring into source hunting.
pmc-13340871:
Sleep apnea that worsens on the back gets a full review from Avneesh Prabakar and colleagues in 2026. In positional obstructive sleep apnea, breathing disturbance scores run much higher lying face-up than in other positions, and the pattern may affect over half of all sleep apnea patients.

Gravity pulls the tongue and soft palate backward when supine, narrowing the airway, and the repeated oxygen drops tie into sharp blood pressure surges. The review gathers evidence on mechanisms, frequency, and treatments that target position-specific causes rather than defaulting to standard CPAP alone. Racial and ethnic gaps in both occurrence and treatment adherence argue for care fitted to each patient.
pmc-13341371:
Gemma A Lewis and colleagues tested how much type 2 education is enough in 2026 in a randomised feasibility trial. The trial enrolled 120 UK adults due to attend a type 2 self management education programme. Volunteers were randomised to receive full, 60 percent, 10 percent, or 0 percent delayed education. Main outcomes were self management skills. Quality of life and diabetes distress were secondary outcomes.

Mean age was 61 years and mean HbA1c was about 8 percent at baseline. The trial asks whether minimal attendance at 10 percent yields real gains. It also weighs 60 percent, the globally adopted completion mark, against full attendance. The findings could reshape education targets for busy patients and services.
pmc-13342171:
An AI pain-check app is tested for usability in Portuguese care homes by Isa Brito Félix and co-investigators in a 2026 study. Pain in advanced dementia often goes unseen, and the PainChek app reads facial muscle movements to score pain in people who cannot speak for themselves.

Nineteen caregivers, after training, performed nine tasks while thinking aloud under international usability standards. Eight tasks passed with over 95% success, but an interrupted assessment task managed only 42%, flagging a design weak point. Seventeen distinct error types were catalogued. Satisfaction scores were benchmarked against normative datasets to judge whether the Portuguese version is ready for wards.
pmc-13345971:
Andy G. X. Zeng and co-authors asked in 2026 how human blood stem cells recall past inflammation. It drives ageing and cancer risk. Stem cells must make blood for decades through a life of infections. Yet how they adapt after inflammation in people was largely unknown.

The team built graft models in which human stem cells faced inflammation and then healed. They profiled single cells in depth. Two gene programmes stood out, marking distinct adaptive states. The study shows a lasting stress memory in the stem cell pool. Repeat infections may thus tilt later blood making toward ageing and cancer. The work also points to spots where that memory might be reset.
pmc-13347371:
Murugesan Panneerselvam and co-authors design ten phenothiazine dyes on a computer and rank them for solar use, in a modelling study from 2026. Each molecule pairs a donor with an acceptor across a bridge, and aryl swaps tune flatness, energy levels. Charge flow under quantum calculations that also track solvent effects and excited states.

Later members of the set showed smaller energy gaps, stronger charge shift, and deeper colour shifts toward visible light in the reported runs. Small singlet-triplet gaps hinted at good exciton use, and transport checks split the set, with two members favouring holes, two favouring electrons, and several balanced. One member, PTZ10, led on light capture and charge split, marking it for lab follow-up.
pmc-13347671:
Tianqi Liu and Fengshuo Leng track blast air and toxic gases from coal dust explosions in a vertical shaft, in a safety study from 2026. Noncaking coal dust was ignited in a tall pipe. Sensors followed impact airflow speed plus carbon monoxide and dioxide spread over height and time to map the danger zone as the blast grew.

Airflow speed rose then fell, peaking after 45 milliseconds of reaction time in the reported run. While heat and fast air carried carbon monoxide outward and widened its toxic reach. Carbon dioxide passed 0.08 percent by mass near the ignition zone early on. Wall zones held more dioxide than the pipe centre at some heights, an uneven pattern that matters for rescue planning.
pmc-13348071:
Paolo Federico Garducci and colleagues test glue embolisation for bleeding outside the gut organs after injury or medical harm, in a study from 2026. Records covered 54 patients treated from 2021 to 2025 whose scans showed active bleeding or a false aneurysm, each blocked through a leg artery with a cyanoacrylate glue mix at varied dilution.

Technical success reached 100 percent, and lasting bleeding control held in 46 patients, a share of 85.2 percent, within thirty days. Injury caused 83.3 percent of cases, most needed only one vessel blocked. Six patients needed a second session for new bleeding nearby, supporting glue as a fast first option in emergencies.
pmc-13348171:
Bo Li, Jae Whan Park, and Han Woong Yeom film kink defects moving inside a layered crystal in real time, in a study from 2026. Kinks along domain walls in tantalum sulfide can carry protected information, yet their hopping rules were murky. So a scanning tunnelling microscope tracked several kinks over long spans while calculations priced each hop.

Two hop styles appeared, tiny one-cell steps and larger few-cell jumps, with atom-level paths matched by the energy models in the reported work. Firing the microscope current raised hop rates markedly, giving a handle to push kinks on demand, a needed step toward soliton-based computing without wasted motion.
pmc-13349771:
Lei Hua and colleagues review how artificial intelligence could sharpen care for membranous kidney disease, in a review from 2026. The disease is the top cause of primary nephrotic syndrome in adults yet swings from quiet remission to kidney failure. While biopsy and a single antibody marker poorly forecast each path, pushing doctors toward trial-and-error immune drugs.

Uses span automated tissue measuring, scan-plus-blood models that may skip biopsy, drug choice models pitting rituximab against cyclophosphamide, and living patient models fed by multi-omics in the survey. Siloed data, opaque models, and thin global testing are flagged as brakes, with the tools framed as aids that sharpen, not replace, clinician calls.
pmc-13349871:
M H Albert and co-authors updated in 2026 European rules for stem cell transplant in inborn errors of immunity and metabolism. They build on the 2021 consensus from the joint working party of the transplant and immunodeficiency societies. Over five hundred single-gene immune errors are now known. New gene finds and treatment gains outpaced the older rules.

The update adds advice where knowledge has grown. It extends cover to inborn errors of metabolism, better matching the working party's scope. For clinicians worldwide, the consensus gives current criteria on who should get transplant, when, and with what conditioning and donor plans. The rules aim to harmonise care for rare ills where single-centre experience is of necessity thin.
pmc-13350471:
Srikant Manchiraju authored a comprehensive 2026 review of self-concept clarity, how clearly and steadily people know who they are. The concept covers self-beliefs that are well defined, consistent, and stable over time.

The review treats clarity as a judgement about the shape of self-knowledge rather than its content or positivity, separating terms the field often mixes. It organises research into clarity as an outcome of upbringing, culture, and digital life; as a predictor of wellbeing and relationships; and as a buffer under stress. Heavy reliance on self-report questionnaires is questioned. The map shows where a secure sense of self protects mental health.
pmc-13351171:
Jose Lucar and colleagues reported a sharp rise in invasive disease from nontypeable Haemophilus influenzae at a Washington, DC hospital in a 2026 case study. Nine adults arrived over nine months with severe illness from this bacterium, now the main cause of invasive H. influenzae disease since vaccination tamed the type b strain.

Genome sequencing showed some illnesses came from one shared strain and others from unrelated ones, hinting at mixed spread patterns rather than a single outbreak. The authors call for wider surveillance of a germ that increasingly strikes adults, including people with HIV, as vaccine success reshapes which strains circulate.
pmc-13351571:
Adidsuda Fuengfoo and co-authors report a 2026 randomised trial of parent training for Thai preschool children at risk of ADHD. Families often face unclear diagnosis and care models imported from Western settings. Caregivers of children aged 3 to 5 years, screened with Thai scales, joined either group training or a group given written materials.

Outcomes were checked at baseline, 2 weeks, and 6 weeks with caregiver reports. The training group showed large falls in ADHD symptoms, with gains in both inattention and hyperactivity that held at 6 weeks. Positive parenting rose at 2 weeks, no harms occurred, and every family stayed in the trial. The authors present the short group format as a workable model for low-resource services.
pmc-13351871:
Jung Chun Kim and colleagues build a 2026 deep learning model to predict lung function loss after radiotherapy for lung cancer. Standard dose measures give weak personal forecasts and ignore uneven lung health visible on scans. Records for 276 patients with stage I to II disease who had breathing tests before and after treatment were analysed.

A pre-trained 3D ResNet-18 drew features from chest scans taken before treatment, joined with age, sex, baseline breathing, and dose data. A weighted loss handled uneven class sizes. Agreement scores reached 0.65 for vital capacity, 0.72 for one-second volume, and 0.83 for their ratio. The model also flags patients likely to cross into a high-risk breathing state.
pmc-13352171:
Elisha B Are and co-authors compare ways to estimate the time-varying reproduction number of an epidemic in 2026. The number, called Rt, shows whether spread is growing or shrinking and helps judge control steps. Two common tools were tested: the Birth-Death Skyline model in BEAST 2.5, which uses genome data, and EpiEstim, which uses case data.

A simulation platform built fake outbreaks with both sequence data and case lists, mimicking past epidemics. Varied sampling setups revealed where each method drifts and where each holds up. When case data grew sparse and unreliable, genome data still gave reasonable Rt values, even with uneven sampling. Guidance follows on matching method to data conditions.
pmc-13352471:
Hisashi Takahashi leads a 2026 brain scan study of diet variety, moving history, and brain volume in rural Japan. Participants came from the Tango longevity cohort in rural Kyoto and had brain MRI after cognitive screening. A total of 235 middle-aged and older adults were analysed, with brain volume measured from T1 scans by SIENAX software.

After age and sex adjustment, each added diet diversity point linked to 925 cubic millimetres more brain volume, with a P value of 0.016. Having moved during life linked to 18,294 cubic millimetres more volume, with a P value of 0.048. Both links held in fuller models. Diet pattern checks and sensitivity tests supported the main findings.
pmc-13353171:
David Shaholli and colleagues validate an Italian version of the Perception of Aggression Scale in 2026. Aggression toward health staff is a lasting workplace hazard that shapes staff welfare and care quality. The short scale was given to 475 health professionals across hospital departments and teaching settings.

Internal consistency was strong, at 0.82 for viewing aggression as dysfunctional and 0.76 for viewing it as functional. Scores held steady on retest. Harmful readings of aggression dominated overall, while meaning-based readings were commoner among men and physicians. A strong inverse link joined the two views. A trusted Italian tool now supports safety planning and training design.
pmc-13353571:
Pamela G. Jones studied how the absence of the germ protein FIS changes Escherichia coli at low heat, in 2026. At thirty-seven degrees the bacterium grows as ordinary rods, but just above its minimum growth heat it forms small rods. FIS is a nucleoid-linked protein that helps arrange the germ genome, and its role in that cold-adapted shape was unclear.

Growth and nucleoid staining showed that a fis null mutant grew poorly at twelve degrees. It first formed threads with loose genomes, hinting FIS helps produce small rods with compact genomes in the cold. The mutant later adapted, with two-phase growth pointing to a make-up response. The study shows how genome packing supports germ living near the edge of growth.
pmc-13354371:
Yeganeh Pakbaz led a 2026 study of incomplete op removal of non-melanoma skin cancers at a single centre. Basal cell and squamous cell cancers are among the most common cancers worldwide, and complete excision is key to prevent recurrence. When margins are unclear, people face further surgery, higher costs, and worse results.

The look-back snapshot study studied 448 lesions removed from 413 people between 2017 and 2022, testing how patient traits, lesion traits, and anatomical site related to incomplete excision.
