The study names the situations where surgeons most often leave tumour behind. Op teams can use those patterns to plan wider margins or closer follow-up for high-risk lesions.
pmc-13355171:
Isabel Pemjean and co-authors ran a 2026 pilot in Santiago, Chile, testing a phone app subsidy for fruit and vegetables in low-income families. The program, Bolsillo Saludable, gave 30 families monthly funds to buy fresh produce at an open-air market. Over eight weeks, the team tracked app use, sales, and views from families and vendors.

Every family used the benefit each month, and both families and vendors rated the program highly. Spending on fruit and vegetables rose by about 38 percent, and over half of families felt their diet improved. Problems with few vendors and billing steps must be fixed before the program can grow.
pmc-13355371:
Abdulmajeed Alajlan and others surveyed tofacitinib use across two pregnancies in alopecia universalis, ran the case report and papers review in 2026. Alopecia areata causes unpredictable, non-scarring hair loss with a heavy psychosocial burden, and Janus kinase blockers have transformed care for moderate-to-severe disease. Expecting and breastfeeding, however, raise special safety questions for these small-unit drugs.

The report follows a patient exposed to tofacitinib through two pregnancies, set against issued evidence on Janus kinase blockers in pregnancy. Results for mother and infants are weighed with disease control. Doctors gain rare, useful evidence for advice people who face the hard choice between effective care and pregnancy safety.
pmc-13356671:
Richard B Witkov and Dorian Alexander examine the ethics in 2026 of doing extracorporeal CPR before a patient reaches hospital. This rescue method uses a heart-lung machine during cardiac arrest, and field use is spreading worldwide. The field setting raises distinct questions on place, timing, consent, patient choice, and fair access that hospital use does not.

Starting too early could weaken standard CPR, while delay cuts the chance of survival with good brain function. Moving patients carries its own risks, and many moved patients are later denied the procedure. The authors urge programs to weigh risks and gains for all affected parties, using the four classic ethics principles, before launch.
pmc-13357071:
Yamen Ahmad Muad and co-authors searched in 2026 for a useful marker gene in esophageal squamous cell carcinoma, a cancer of the food pipe lining with few reliable markers. They combined five gene datasets, used selection tools to narrow candidates, and checked the winner in patient tissue and cancer cells. The gene DDR1 stood out as a lead candidate.

DDR1 ran high in tumors across all datasets, and a model using it alone sorted tumor from normal samples well. In forty paired patient samples, DDR1 was high and a small regulator RNA was low. Blocking that regulator raised DDR1 and switched on spread-linked signals, pointing to a target chain.
pmc-13358571:
Fan Gao and Xiaokang Gong chart a research field in a 2026 study on esophageal cancer. After proteins are built, cells can tag them with chemical changes that alter how they act. These tags, called post-translational modifications, help drive this cancer's growth and drug resistance. The authors counted and mapped the papers on the topic from 2000 to 2026.

Using a large science database and mapping software, they traced who publishes most, which tags draw the most work, and where the gaps lie. They also flagged genes that might predict patient outcomes. Such a map helps new studies aim at the open questions instead of repeating ground already covered.
pmc-13358771:
Prasad Shirke and co-authors compare spit tests across three groups in a 2026 study. Gum disease and mouth cancer both involve long-term inflammation and tissue breakdown. The team measured two substances in saliva: chemerin, a signal that draws immune cells, and MMP-9, an enzyme that chews through tissue.

They tested 90 people: healthy volunteers, patients with gum disease, and patients with oral squamous cell cancer, 30 in each group. They also recorded standard gum health measures for comparison. If spit levels track disease well, a painless saliva test could one day help dentists spot mouth cancer earlier.
pmc-13359371:
Bartłomiej Fliszkiewicz and co-authors tackle a stubborn chemistry problem in a 2026 paper. Nucleophilicity measures how eagerly a molecule donates electrons to a partner, a key guide for predicting reactions. Existing formulas based on quantum theory work on small test sets but drift from real behavior on wider ones. The team set out to build a better index from data.

They ran a symbolic regression, letting the computer search for a formula that mixes orbital energies, charge data, and solvent traits. The new index matched the standard experimental scale far better than older ones, and refining it by molecule family improved it further. The work shows both the promise and the limits of global reactivity formulas.
pmc-13359571:
Klemen Krašovec and co-authors study awake brain surgery for gliomas in a 2026 paper. When a tumor sits in the brain's language zone, surgeons keep the patient awake and map function during the operation. That allows the widest removal while sparing speech. The team asked what predicts worse language after surgery, and what predicts survival.

They reviewed 37 patients with malignant gliomas in the speech-dominant half of the brain, treated at several centers. Language worsened in six patients, about one in six, and older age raised the odds. Knowing the risk factors helps surgeons counsel patients and plan how boldly to cut near vital tissue.
pmc-13361271:
Philipp Wiesener and others raised carbon dioxide cut by coating step edges with N-ring carbenes, in 2026. Atomic step edges on metal faces are highly active speeding sites due to reduced linking and changed electric structure, yet organic ligand coating had aimed flat flats, leaving step edges untouched.

Decorating atomically defined step edges of gold(788) with carbenes increased speeding action toward carbon dioxide cut matched with undecorated edges. High-clearing scanning probe studies shown site-given coating. Speeding teams gain a plan for tuning the most active surface sites, rather than the average surface, for carbon conversion.
pmc-13362071:
Jun-Tong Wang and co-authors review smart ways to predict and remove bitterness in health peptides in a 2026 paper. Peptides from digested proteins can benefit health, but many taste intensely bitter, which blocks their use in foods and supplements. The team builds a framework joining three parts: predicting bitterness by computer, removing it on target, and judging the result from several angles.

Deep learning tools, including structure-activity models and graph networks, can flag bitter peptides fast and show how they grip taste receptors. Computer help also improves classic debittering, such as wrapping peptides in composite wall materials for delivery. The review weighs how these methods track the metabolic fate of the peptides. A joined-up system could open the food market to more health peptides.
pmc-13362471:
Yushan Liu and colleagues report a 2026 genome-wide study of Hsp20 genes in sunflower, a crop hurt by heat waves. These genes make small guard proteins that protect plant cells when temperatures spike. The team scanned the whole sunflower genome, traced how the gene family grew, and tested which genes switch on under heat in the lab.

They found 65 Hsp20 genes, most of them turned on by heat stress. Seven rose more than a thousand-fold after ten hours of high heat, and two rose over four thousand-fold. Those two stand out as prime picks for breeding or engineering sunflowers that cope better with hot weather, a growing need as summers warm.
pmc-13363171:
Ozgun Yetkin and colleagues present a 2026 sleep study on teens with juvenile myoclonic epilepsy, a seizure type that strikes most often near waking. Eleven patients and ten matched healthy teens wore wrist motion trackers for two weeks. The team read both standard sleep measures and the day-to-day steadiness of rest and activity rhythms, plus morning-evening preference surveys.

Standard sleep measures looked the same in both groups, which hides the real gap. The patients' daily rhythms were far less steady from day to day and more broken within each day, with lower peak daytime activity. Teens who leaned morning-type kept stronger rhythms. The authors argue that rhythm care, not just sleep length, deserves a place in managing this epilepsy.
pmc-13364171:
Le Wang and colleagues present a 2026 study on catching runs of bad readings in underwater long-baseline positioning, the acoustic system that tracks submersibles by timing signals from seabed beacons. In rough seas, outliers arrive in streaks and can drag a Kalman filter off course. Their robust filter checks each new fix against how fast the vehicle can physically move and against recent history, using a mask that blocks suspect data from updates the moment it appears.

Simulations showed the design spots and suppresses streak outliers better than standard positioning, single-outlier checks, and a leading robust filter variant, with the clearest gains under consecutive faults. The authors aim the method at maneuvering targets in cluttered, real-world water.
pmc-13366571:
Matthew Vasuta and co-workers show in 2026 a fast spin coat route that grows stack films of unlike plastics in less than three minutes. A film's top skin sets how it meets the world, for use as coat, sense, or guard skin. Their route lays one germ coat, then grows new monomers on it in turn.

The films reach huge chain weights with tight spread. Top skins can run from a hair thin to three times the base depth. Test stacks shun all drops, love water to an edge, or block protein stick. Small solvent use adds to the draw.
pmc-13369771:
Minh Tri Truong and colleagues map toxic metals in road dust across seven mid-size cities in the eastern United States in a 2026 study. Dust was tested for eleven potentially toxic elements, including copper, zinc, arsenic, cadmium, and lead. Statistical methods were used to trace each element to likely sources and to judge health risk.

About one third of the hazardous load was linked to coal burning and past pesticide use, while two thirds came from city sources such as vehicle wear, waste burning, and industry. The most hazardous metals tended to cluster in lower-income areas, even where their overall levels were modest. The study gives city officials a source-by-source picture for street cleaning, traffic control, and soil safety work.
pmc-13370071:
Meiya Okano and colleagues report artery disease in two Japanese bantams infected with Marek disease virus in a 2026 case study. The virus usually causes nerve damage and lymph cancers, while vessel disease is rare. Both birds showed hardened, narrowed arteries through the body, and both were examined after death.

In the first bird, cancer-like lymph cells had spread in the spleen and liver. In the second, no such spread was seen, yet viral proteins were still found in artery walls and in smooth muscle cells there. The authors argue that infected lymph cells may carry the virus into vessel walls. The cases widen the known harm of this poultry virus and may help vets recognise vessel disease in infected flocks.
pmc-13371671:
Pakeezah Tabasum and colleagues report a rare skin disease in a teenager with suspected bowel disease in a 2026 case study. Pyodermatitis vegetans is a chronic inflammatory skin condition linked to inflammatory bowel disease, especially ulcerative colitis, and it is rarely reported in children in Pakistan. A 17-year-old boy had suffered recurrent vegetative skin lesions for ten years.

Lesions began behind the left ear and spread to the face, armpits, back, chest, buttocks, and genitals, alongside gut symptoms including painful bowel movements and fresh rectal bleeding. Skin biopsy showed features diagnostic of the condition, and blood tests showed anaemia and very high IgE. The case urges clinicians to look for bowel disease when a child presents with such stubborn, warty skin plaques.
pmc-13374071:
Samaneh Rokhgireh and others describe surgical problems during gender-affirming hysterectomy in transgender men on testosterone in a 2026 case series. Laparoscopic hysterectomy is central to gender-affirming care, yet long-term testosterone can thin cervical tissue, narrow the cervix, and reduce vaginal stretch, complicating pelvic surgery. Four patients at a tertiary centre, each with at least two and a half years of testosterone therapy, were reviewed.

Complications included one posterior cul-de-sac perforation, one cervical avulsion requiring open surgery, one bladder dome injury, and deep vaginal tears in all four patients. Two cases needed help from urology or vascular surgery. All patients recovered without lasting sequelae, though one was unhappy with abdominal scarring. The series urges surgeons to plan for testosterone-related tissue changes in advance.
pmc-13377371:
Olivia Carere and co-authors scored web help pages on heavy monthly flow in a 2026 study. Pages were drawn from top web search hits and from expert picks. A total of 63 pages in English made the cut from 353 found.

Scores weighed trust, looks, read ease, and truth and depth on six care points. The mean trust score sat well short of the top mark, and just a few pages hit a high bar. Gaps in drug and surgery facts were among the flaws logged. The team gives page makers a clear list of what to fix so sick folk get sound facts fast.
pmc-13377871:
Esther Paulo and co-authors cut a power part in brown fat in a 2026 mouse study. Brown fat burns fuel to make heat, and that burn needs cell power parts. Mice bred with the part off in brown fat alone were the test bed.

Their brown fat lost its heat craft, and a back-up heat path failed too since cell stress cut all protein make. Yet on rich food the mice stayed slim and sugar-sound at plain and warm room heats. Fat that can't burn may still talk to the body in a way that guards it. That twist reframes what brown fat is for.
pmc-13378071:
Çiğdem Öztürk and colleagues test whether TROP-2 expression predicts chemotherapy response in luminal B breast cancer in a 2026 study. TROP-2 is a cell surface glycoprotein overexpressed in many epithelial cancers and targeted by antibody-drug conjugates. Expression was scored by immunohistochemistry in 211 invasive breast cancers, with H-scores above 200 classed as high.

High TROP-2 tracked with HER2 negativity, lymph node spread, and poor response to neoadjuvant chemotherapy, classed as residual cancer burden II or III. In multivariable models, molecular subtype, stromal immune infiltration, and high TROP-2 independently predicted chemotherapy response. The work presents TROP-2 as both a prognostic marker and a possible target for antibody-drug therapy in luminal B disease.
pmc-13378471:
Hoang Yen Vo and colleagues present a 2026 study of tiny polymer particles designed to carry material into cells through a sugar gateway. Each particle is a single folded polymer chain, shaped somewhat like a tadpole, with a head and a tail. One part was based on a common polymer called PEG, and the other carried the sugar fructose.

Particles with the fructose part on the outside were taken up by cells far more than those with it tucked inside. Uptake was highest in the cells that carry the most sugar gateways, and blocking one gateway, GLUT1, largely stopped it. The work shows that surface placement matters as much as content when designing such carriers.
pmc-13379671:
Mangabeira and colleagues compare two pain-control methods for cats having spay surgery, in a 2026 randomized, blinded animal anesthesia trial. Twenty female cats received a lumbosacral epidural, numbing drug injected near the spinal cord, or quadratus lumborum blocks, ultrasound shots into a muscle layer, using levobupivacaine. Heart and breathing measures were recorded at seven time points. Pain was scored for 6 hours afterward on a pain scale, with methadone on hand as rescue relief.

No real differences appeared in any heart-lung variable between the two methods during surgery. Anesthetic infusion rates were similar, at 0.36 against 0.39 milligrams per kilogram per minute for the epidural and block groups. Pain scores after surgery did not differ, and no cat needed rescue analgesia. Only one cat, in the block group, needed methadone, at the 6-hour check. Mangabeira concludes the ultrasound block matches the epidural, a useful alternative when a spinal shot is impractical.
pmc-13379871:
Ruhi Sanvordekar and co-authors published a 2026 study checking how reliable a chatbot's answers are when parents ask about children's dental injuries. Knocked or broken teeth are common in childhood, and quick, correct first aid strongly affects the outcome. Many parents now turn to artificial intelligence tools for urgent advice.

The team put fifteen realistic parent questions to the chatbot and asked 29 experts to grade each answer. They scored relevance, correctness, logic, clarity, and completeness on a five-point scale. The study was run at a dental college hospital in Goa, India. Its results show where chatbot advice can be trusted and where it may mislead worried parents.
pmc-13379971:
Rui Guan and co-authors published a 2026 study on how nursing students in China feel during conflicts with patients, and what softens the blow. Conflict is a common strain during clinical training. The study asked whether support given and received, together with mental resilience, protects students' emotional responses.

The survey covered 423 interns who had faced such conflict, recruited from six hospitals in Henan between August and October 2025. Students completed three standard questionnaires. Both two-way support and resilience were strongly linked with calmer emotional responses. The results suggest that training schools and hospitals can help by building support networks and resilience, not only by teaching conflict skills.
pmc-13382171:
Edoardo Raposio and Elisa Bertulla published a 2026 paper linking an eighteenth-century art idea to modern ideals of the female buttock profile. The artist William Hogarth proposed an S-shaped serpentine curve, the line of beauty, as the most pleasing form. Interest has revived as buttock augmentation procedures grow more popular.

The authors examine how that particular S-curve relates to the curve of the lower back and buttocks in western aesthetic ideals. Such reference lines, they note, are increasingly sought to make surgical planning and outcome assessment more objective. The paper bridges art theory and cosmetic practice, asking whether a classic curve can guide modern body contouring.
pmc-13382271:
Kyrah S Goeree and colleagues present a 2026 systematic review on whether the body site where fat is taken affects how much survives when it is moved to the breast. Fat transfer is now used for full breast reconstruction, but survival of the moved fat is unpredictable. Donor site might explain part of that variation.

Seven studies covering 291 patients were included, with fat taken from the abdomen or the thighs. Average survival differed between the pooled groups, though follow-up times also differed. Every study carried a serious or critical risk of bias, and no study addressed full breast reconstruction directly. The authors conclude that firm guidance on donor site is not yet possible.
pmc-13382671:
Karla D Torres-Muñoz and co-authors report a 2026 study synthesising a family of ring-shaped molecules with anti-inflammatory activity. The target structures combine two fused rings sharing one atom, a shape prized in drug design for being rigid yet flexible. A catalyst-guided reaction set two key stereocentres in the first step.

Through a short sequence needing only one full purification, the team made eighteen variants differing in their side groups and fused rings. Tested in a mouse ear swelling model, the compounds matched or slightly beat a standard anti-inflammatory drug. Further tests showed reduced white cell entry into tissue, and three compounds selectively blocked one of the two main inflammation enzymes.
pmc-13382771:
Alvarez-Sola and colleagues build LiRNA, an interactive atlas unifying liver datasets, in 2026 hepatology research. Mouse liver findings fail to translate to humans, and checking them against human data was hampered by fragmented, inconsistently described datasets. The team identified 17 RNA-sequencing datasets covering over 3,000 human liver biopsies and reprocessed them the same way. They packaged them in a web application where researchers can test gene links without coding skill or fetching files.

The atlas reproduced established liver biology, including fibrosis-linked genes, sex-dimorphic patterns, and hepatitis C response patterns, confirming the cleanup. The team then re-tested 64 published gene findings from journals against the atlas's independent cohorts. Fewer than half of those findings generalized consistently across the assembled datasets. Alvarez-Sola presents that sobering rate as the atlas's value: a reality check on whether a mouse or single-cohort claim survives contact with the breadth of liver data.
pmc-13382871:
David Spanswick's team presents LanCL1 as a fresh drug target for neuropathic pain, in a 2026 paper. LanCL1 is widely expressed in the nervous system and, unlike its bacterial namesakes, does not make lanthionine. Instead it attaches glutathione to damaged protein residues, a repair-like chemistry that may turn harmful in disease states.

The paper weighs evidence that tuning LanCL1 activity could ease nerve pain by a route distinct from opioids and gabapentinoids. LanCL1 sits mainly inside cells but may reach the cell surface in pathology, opening drug access questions. The piece maps what is known and what must be proven before LanCL1 modulators reach patients.
pmc-13382971:
John Senanu and fellow participants review a 2024 training school on brain drug research held in Harare, Zimbabwe, in a 2026 meeting report. Thirteen participants from eight African countries spent one week building skills in drug action, study design, and drug testing. The school aimed to grow local capacity as brain and mental disorders rise across sub-Saharan Africa.

Reflections from all participants showed the school met its main goals for core knowledge and networking. Cultural exchange and joint work across fields also ranked high in their accounts. The group recommends longer hands-on sessions and planned follow-up after the program to strengthen future editions.
pmc-13383471:
Zhina Ebrahimi's team tested a planned-behavior curriculum for eco-friendly habits in lower secondary students, in a 2026 quasi-experimental study. The team randomized schools in Piranshahr, Iran, assigning 50 students to intervention and 50 to control. The program ran three 45-minute sessions built on attitude, norms, perceived control, and intention.

After the program, the intervention group scored significantly higher on every planned-behavior construct, plus environmental knowledge and responsible behaviors, versus pre-test and control. The gains support brief theory-based lessons as a lever for youth environmental action. Schools gain a tested template for turning green attitudes into habits.
pmc-13383671:
Kelty and colleagues chart how endurance exercise remodels liver metabolism over time, differently in males and females, in 2026 exercise biology research from the MoTrPAC consortium. Rats trained for 1, 2, 4, or 8 weeks, and their livers underwent multi-omics profiling: joint measurement of proteins, chemical changes, and metabolites. The liver matters because it manages fuel for the body during training, yet its adaptation sequence, and how sex shapes it, had not been mapped before.

Female livers progressively increased oxidative phosphorylation protein complexes, the machinery that burns fuel with oxygen. Male livers instead raised acetylation, a chemical tagging, on energy enzymes, through the enzyme carnitine acetyltransferase. Exercise boosted cholesterol and bile acid synthesis in both sexes, while males excreted more of it and cholic acid in feces and cleared liver lipids by week 8. Markers of liver scarring activity fell in both sexes. Kelty frames these dimorphic signatures as the route to exercise's liver protection.
pmc-13384371:
Shi and colleagues meta-analyze whether simple skin perfusion signs predict death in sepsis, in 2026 critical care research. Sepsis kills through microcirculatory failure, and the skin shows it as mottling, slow capillary refill, and a low peripheral perfusion index from a fingertip sensor. Searching seven databases to January 2026, the team pooled cohort and case-control studies linking these bedside signs to 28-day, 14-day, and in-hospital mortality. They screened quality with a bias scale before combining results across studies.

The analysis included 22 articles covering 2,727 sepsis patients. A higher mottling score was associated with 28-day mortality, at an odds ratio of 2.27 in the pooled estimate. It predicted 14-day mortality, at an odds ratio of 1.96 across the studies reporting that endpoint. Prolonged capillary refill time likewise carried prognostic association. Shi argues these zero-cost bedside signs, requiring no laboratory, deserve a place in sepsis risk assessment, especially where monitoring technology is scarce.
pmc-13389171:
Daniel Tehrani's team worked out how cells build the backbone of chondroitin sulfate, a long sugar chain that decorates cell surfaces and the matrix between cells and is later heavily sulfated. Four related proteins were known to cooperate, with paired complexes apparently required for activity.

Sequence analysis and modelling showed each protein carries two transferase domains joined by a cystatin-like linker, and only paired CHSY-CHPF combinations formed working enzymes. Cryo-electron microscopy proved the CHSY3-CHPF1 complex, and mutant tests proved only the CHSY domains add sugars, while CHPF domains stabilise their partners.
pmc-13390271:
Lin Yang's team surveyed 7,850 secondary school students in China to measure depressive and anxiety symptoms and to weigh maternal mental health among the risk factors. Self-found depression affected 11.6 percent and anxiety 18.1 percent, with female sex, suburban residence, parental discord, academic stress, inactivity, screen time, and maternal symptoms all contributing.

Academic pressure carried the largest group attributable share for both results, near thirty-five percent for depression and forty-six percent for anxiety, followed by suburban residence and excess screen time. The authors argue that school pressure and family mental health deserve joint focus in prevention programs.
pmc-13390371:
Mingyao Huang's team reviews CD155, the polio virus sensor, and its sensors as immune checkpoint targets in glioma, a fast-moving brain cancer with a strongly damping immune setting and poor treatment response. CD155 is often run high in glioma and tunes defences through blocking sensors TIGIT and CD96 plus the switching-on sensor CD226.

Those links blunt killer T cell and natural killer cell activity while fostering control forms, helping tumours escape destruction. Immune drugs, dual-target immune drugs, and CAR-built immune cells targeting the CD155 axis are in testing. The review weighs their promise against the hurdles of breaking glioma immune damping.
pmc-13391671:
Allison Brandt Anbari and colleagues systematically review, in 2026, clinical practice guidelines for breast cancer survivorship care. Care after treatment is complex and often falls short of standards, while existing programmes invoke guidelines unevenly compared with other conditions.

The review lists which guides hold advice of use to women who have had breast cancer. It asks if the pile of guides can merge into a short set of topics that a clinic can use. Staff gain a neat map of where guides agree and where they clash. The aim is care that clinics can give in the same way each time, not a shelf of books no one reads in full.
pmc-13392171:
Petit and colleagues test whether singing in a mixed-neurotype choir changes how neurotypical adults think about autism, in a 2026 psychology study. Twelve choristers sang for 6 months alongside eight autistic adolescents and three specialists, completing questionnaires before and after about their representations of autism and their willingness to mix. The study is framed by the double empathy problem: difficulty between autistic and non-autistic people as misunderstanding, not one-sided deficit, an idea the choir puts into practice.

After the season, participants' views of autism became richer and more accurate, aligning with a difference model of the condition. Choristers reported more able and inclined to mix with neurodivergent people beyond the choir. Petit calls the findings preliminary, given the chosen group, but argues they support the neurodiversity paradigm with evidence. Inclusive spaces around a craft, the authors suggest, teach what awareness campaigns cannot: competence and comfort across types.
pmc-13392671:
Łukasz Jach and three colleagues showed two hundred twenty-five young Polish adults internet memes about mental struggles such as depression, anxiety, delaying tasks, and hiding feelings. Participants then rated how funny each seemed and how much it felt like their own lives. Ratings were set against measures of dwelling, reflective thought, self-regard, and humour styles. The study is the first to cover such a wide spread of problem themes.

Depression memes drew the highest funniness scores, while procrastination memes felt most personally familiar. People prone to dwelling linked memes to themselves more, while reflective thinkers rated them funnier. Stronger self-regard went with finding the memes less funny and less personal. Cheerful bonding humour predicted less personal linking, while mocking and self-putting-down humour predicted more.
pmc-13393071:
Kalliopi Megari and Kremena Dinkova Genova review how trauma in early childhood bends cognitive development, the growth of attention, memory, language, and self-control. Their narrative review traces the pathways from frightening or neglectful early experiences through changes in brain structure and function to the learning difficulties that can follow children into school and beyond. It also separates sudden trauma from grinding chronic stress, while noting the two often arrive together.

The stated aim is practical: giving teachers, psychologists, and health workers a theoretical base for targeted strategies that support healthy development after adversity. Quality of life runs through the argument as the outcome that matters most. By organising mechanisms, outcomes, and interventions in one account, the authors hope services can spot affected children earlier and respond with help matched to how trauma reshapes the developing mind.
pmc-13393271:
Yiling Yang and coauthors survey viruses carried by mosquitoes and biting midges along the western Yunnan border of China in a 2026 study. This subtropical border region holds many insect species and serves as a key entry point for imported viruses, yet midge-borne viruses with animal-to-human spillover risk have been little studied there.

In July 2018 the team collected insects from Mangshi, Yingjiang, Lushui, and Tengchong, sorted them, and tried to isolate viruses in cell cultures. The work maps which viruses circulate in each insect group and where spillover risk may be highest. Public health readers gain a baseline for watching this border for new outbreaks.
pmc-13393471:
Hu and colleagues report a 2026 genomic investigation of a cutaneous anthrax case in Hinggan League, Inner Mongolia. The event began in November 2023, when a herder slaughtered and skinned a dying sheep and developed skin anthrax. Investigators collected 18 samples from the patient, leftover mutton and sheepskin, and the environment, then combined field epidemiology with whole-genome sequencing of the bacteria.

Four of the 18 samples tested positive, and anthrax bacteria were cultured from the patient, the mutton, the sheepskin, and a transport vehicle. The four isolates all belonged to the A.Br.001/002 lineage and shared more than 99 percent genome-wide identity by average nucleotide comparison. That near-identical genetic match, alongside the exposure history, supports a single-source event running from the infected sheep through contaminated products to the patient. The authors argue routine genome typing can link cases to animal sources in pastoral regions.
pmc-13393771:
Tori Millsteed and colleagues probe whether wheat grain uses a C4-style photosynthesis pathway in a 2026 spatial transcriptomics study. Wheat is a C3 plant central to food security, and C4 biochemistry could help it endure heat and drought, so engineers have long sought to add that pathway.

Using spatial gene-expression mapping of developing grain, the team found most suspected C4 genes in their predicted tissues. The enzyme PEPC appeared in photosynthetic pericarp cells, while the endosperm hosted other pathway steps. The paper sharpens the debate over grain photosynthesis and guides future crop engineering.
pmc-13393871:
Yang Liu, Steffen Kottackal, and Wenlin Hao tested a hands-on training module in spinal fluid diagnostics for fourth-year medical students. The skill mixes theory, microscope work, and clinical judgement. Undergraduate courses rarely teach it in structured form. Eighty-four students in a mandatory neurology practical took a pre-test, sat a theory session, examined real cerebrospinal fluid samples at the microscope, then retook the test in the same sitting.

Median scores doubled, from three to six correct answers, with the strongest gains in procedural knowledge, diagnostic interpretation, cell findings, and microscope-based diagnosis. Knowledge of when to perform a spinal tap started high and stayed put, leaving little room to grow. Students rated the blend of theory and practice positively. The authors conclude that a single structured, practical session lifts short-term diagnostic knowledge measurably.
pmc-13394371:
Paul West Okojie and Linnaya Graf review, in 2026, what blocks tuberculosis care for people displaced inside India and Nigeria. Both nations carry heavy loads of the lung disease, yet displaced people draw little research. The authors compare the two settings and sort the barriers they find. They also gather local steps that have tried to close the gaps.

Poverty, stigma, weak clinics, and poor coordination all limit care, the review finds. India, unlike Nigeria, lacks a clear plan to protect the health of displaced people. The authors call for fairer policy, stronger basic clinics, and joint work across sectors. Their aim is care that reaches people forced from home.
pmc-13395371:
Evgeny Pokushalov leads a 2026 trial of group therapy aimed at lowering the stress hormone cortisol. Sixty adults were split between an eight-week group program and a matched active control. The program mixed social-emotional skills, slow breathing with heart feedback, and new ways to frame hard thoughts. Spit samples over three days and hair samples tracked hormone output.

Daily cortisol output fell more in the program group, and the drop held at six months. Hair cortisol, a month-scale record, also ran lower in the program group. A lab stress test showed no group gap, though. Side effects were rare and alike. The authors back group work for lasting hormone calm.
pmc-13396471:
García-Marín and team assemble, in 2026, complete genomes of Mycobacterium tuberculosis from clinical isolates in Spain's Valencia Region, exposing diversity that standard short-read sequencing misses. Roughly 5 to 10 percent of the tuberculosis genome resists short-read mapping. Of 266 culture-positive isolates from 2016, they sequenced 216 with long-read PacBio HiFi tools, mostly lineage 4 strains, and checked the complete genomes against short-read results.

Complete genomes uncovered a median of 312 extra single-letter differences per pairwise comparison, implying a rate of change 1.44 times higher than short-read studies estimated for the bacterium. The extra changes concentrated in hotspots, especially the pe/ppe gene family, where gene conversion, copying between similar genes, drives variation. Some vaccine candidate epitopes sit in those hotspots, a finding with design implications. Complete genomes also sharpened transmission networks and, at the within-host level, removed false variant calls that patient-specific references exposed.
pmc-13396671:
Liang Zhang and others lift crystal trait guesses with a multi-view shape graph net in a 2026 study. True crystal shape and web reads are key to machine craft in big crystal sims, yet most nets catch just part of that shape.

Their MGT net learns still scalar reads and turn-aware direction reads at once, fused by a pro-router that weighs each view per task. Multi-task self-taught pretraining cut mean miss by up to 14 percent on past best crystal tests. Stuff labs gain a truer crystal read for trait guesses.
pmc-13396871:
Evelyn K. Ansah and co-authors surveyed Ghanaian patients with high blood pressure on how they view checking their own readings at home, and whether phone-based tools could help. Their 2026 study notes that clinic visits in Ghana are spaced two to three months apart, leaving long blind stretches in blood pressure control.

The authors gathered patients' knowledge, habits, and beliefs about their condition and about self-monitoring, alongside their readiness to use mobile health apps. An app that returns feedback on home readings could tighten control between visits, they argue, but only if it is designed around what patients already understand and do. The survey supplies that groundwork.
pmc-13397471:
Mona Dabbas and fellow authors compare two ways of removing the lingual tonsils in children whose sleep apnea came back after standard tonsil and adenoid surgery. Their 2026 review weighs robotic surgery through the mouth against the older direct approach. The question matters because leftover tissue at the tongue base can keep blocking the airway at night.

Searching four large databases through January 2026 yielded 17 studies covering 470 children, most treated the traditional way. Robotic cases cut the apnea score by far more on average, a mean drop of 16.20 events per hour against 3.64 for the older method. The trade-off was harm: robotic patients had much higher rates of swallowing trouble, infection and bleeding, so careful case choice is urged.
pmc-13397671:
Xueyan Cao and co-authors are named on a 2026 editorial notice flagging image problems in their 2023 gallbladder cancer paper in BMC Cancer. Editors warn readers that panels in two figures appear to overlap. The paper had claimed the anti-nausea drug aprepitant slows gallbladder cancer growth and spread through reactive oxygen species and MAPK signalling.

In figure 2B, panels labelled for different drug doses and times seem to share image content, and the same concern is raised for figure 3B. Readers are told to treat the results with caution while the record stands unresolved. All ten listed authors agreed to the notice, which the journal issued as an Expression of Concern rather than a retraction.
pmc-13397971:
Li-Chong Lai and a large team ranked the factors behind work-related muscle and bone disorders among shift-working nurses. Their 2026 study compares seven machine-learning models to predict these disorders, which are highly common in nursing and may worsen when rotating shifts disturb body clocks. Managers need a validated tool that points to the strongest, changeable risks rather than a long list of suspects.

Among 1,080 shift nurses, 85.19 percent reported a disorder at some body site. Perceived control, social support, sleep quality, chronotype, frequent bending, and night-shift nap length ranked near the top, and a random forest model predicted best with a median AUC of 0.919. The paper supports targeted fixes for sleep, schedules, posture, and support, while its cross-sectional design limits causal claims.
pmc-13398071:
Anjali Shenoy, Daniel J Falconer and Adam W Barb engineer antibody tail pieces that keep working after their sugar coat is removed. Their 2026 study tackles a known snag: the sugar chain on IgG antibodies steadies their grip on immune receptors, but its varied forms make each drug batch uneven. Removing the sugar normally wrecks the grip on the CD16a receptor that drives protective responses.

Added disulfide bonds, tiny chemical staples, hold the tail's binding surface in shape without any sugar at all. The rebuilt pieces came out uniform in makeup yet still bound the receptor as needed. The design opens a cleaner starting point for yeast-display tuning of future antibody drugs, free of sugar-driven variation.
pmc-13399571:
Keiichi Ikeda investigated an unexpected route by which glowing marker proteins entered cell nuclei during a control experiment. His 2026 paper began when red fluorescent mCherry protein appeared in nuclei of HeLa cells built as controls. Fluorescent proteins are routine lab markers, so an unexplained nuclear route could mislead imaging studies.

Ikeda found that fluorescent proteins were taken up by autophagosomes, moved into lysosomes, and then reached nuclei. Blocking autophagosome-lysosome fusion or lowering syntaxin 17 reduced nuclear entry for HeLa cells, with no such drop for HepG2 cells. Electron microscopy showed autolysosomes fusing with the nuclear envelope in HeLa cells, while a direct pore route also existed. The paper warns researchers to check marker location, since cell type changes the route.
pmc-13399671:
Kaiyong Chen and colleagues tested a blood protein called soluble B7-H6 as a non-invasive flag for liver cirrhosis following hepatitis B, in a 2026 prospective study. The standard blood scores, FIB-4 and APRI, were built on hepatitis C patients and perform unevenly in hepatitis B. The team measured soluble B7-H6 by ELISA in 159 patients with hepatitis B-related liver disease: 77 with chronic hepatitis and 82 with cirrhosis.

Marker levels climbed with disease severity. On its own, soluble B7-H6 separated cirrhosis from chronic hepatitis with an area under the ROC curve of 0.87 in that analysis. That beat APRI at 0.75 and FIB-4 at 0.79 in the head-to-head analysis. Combining the new marker with FIB-4 did better still, reaching an area of 0.92 with sensitivity of 85.4 percent and specificity of 88.0 percent. They position the combined model as a practical tool for spotting cirrhosis early without a biopsy needle.
pmc-13400271:
Tisya Banerjee and co-authors examine in 2026 how one chemical mark on the folding helper protein Hsp90 changes its work. Hsp90 helps many other proteins fold and mature. Most marks are shared by its two human forms, but the mark studied here, at a spot called threonine 446, occurs only on the Hsp90 beta form.

The team links that mark to kinases, enzymes tied to the cell stress response. Once marked, Hsp90 beta no longer responds to helper proteins that tune its energy use. Its client proteins then mature in a simpler, less controlled way. The result reshapes how the cell checks protein quality.
pmc-13400471:
Jaqueline Loaeza-Loaeza and co-authors study, in 2026, how added DNA methylation silences glutamate transporters in glial cells. Glutamate is the main excitatory signal in the brain, and glial transporters clear it to prevent toxic buildup. In tumors and degenerative disease, that clearing system often fails.

The team forced retinal glial cells and a tumor cell line to overproduce DNMT3B, an enzyme that adds methyl marks to DNA. Global methylation rose within two days. Uptake tests then showed the transporters working less, and their gene expression fell in both cell types. Checking one transporter gene promoter confirmed heavier methylation. The results tie a methylation shift directly to lost glutamate control.
pmc-13400671:
Marie Kebke, Emmy Adolfsson, Joakim Strömberg and Mats Dehlin follow, in 2026, rheumatoid arthritis patients day by day after steroid injections into inflamed finger joints. Such injections are common, yet few studies track how quickly finger pain eases and how long relief lasts from the patient point of view.

Patients rated pain and mobility daily for 14 days after injection into a knuckle or middle finger joint. Three quarters reached the low-pain target, most within four days, and two thirds reported better mobility by two weeks. Middle finger joints responded better than knuckles. The only clear predictor was the volume of steroid injected, with larger volumes doing better. Among responders, relief held for at least three months.
pmc-13401471:
Ahmed Y Bukannan and Deema S Al Abdrabbuh carried out a 2026 national survey of topical corticosteroid misuse among adults in Saudi Arabia. These skin creams are mainstays for inflammatory skin disease. Unsupervised and cosmetic use can cause steroid-induced skin damage, and local data on public awareness were scarce.

Between January and March 2026, adults across the country completed a structured online questionnaire covering their steroid use, knowledge, awareness of steroid-caused skin conditions, side effects, and misuse habits. The analysis included 1,248 members. Misuse was counted when a respondent reported at least one risky behaviour. The list ran from non-prescription use, cosmetic use, and social-media-driven use to sharing medication, long unsupervised use, reusing old prescriptions, and applying steroids to fungal infections. Regression modelling then found independent predictors of misuse.
pmc-13401571:
Mounika Vattigunta and colleagues assessed how accurately ChatGPT-4o translates laser tattoo removal patient instructions into German, in a 2026 letter-style study. Patients increasingly use accessible AI tools to translate medical guidance, so the safety of those translations needs checking before people act on them.

The team gathered fourteen patient instruction documents from Google, mixing private practice and academic sources, and uploaded them as PDFs to ChatGPT-4o with a translation prompt. German-speaking patients were the audience in mind, building on earlier work that tested AI translation into Spanish. Their goal was to judge whether the translated procedural instructions are accurate enough for patients deciding about tattoo removal care. The study adds a German data point to the growing checks on AI translation in medicine.
pmc-13401671:
Pratik Sahu and co-authors surveyed medical and paramedical students in a 2026 cross-sectional study in Vidisha, Madhya Pradesh. It measured awareness about child sexual abuse and India's POCSO Act, the law protecting children from sexual offences. Health workers are central to spotting abuse early, reporting it, and meeting legal duties.

A tested questionnaire with two sections went to 278 students at a government medical college, scoring awareness of abuse and knowledge of the Act into set levels. Awareness of abuse proved weak across both groups, and not one member showed complete awareness. Most medical students were rated low on awareness, while a large share of paramedical students were simply unaware. Knowledge of the law showed its own gaps, underlining a training problem for future front-line workers.
pmc-13401871:
Mauricio Sarmiento and a large binational team compared frozen and fresh stem cell grafts for autologous transplantation in multiple myeloma, in a 2026 study run in Santiago, Chile, and Seville, Spain. Freezing grafts gives scheduling flexibility, but it may add toxicity and cost.

The non-randomized study ran in two phases. The retrospective phase covered 284 patients given cryopreserved grafts and 148 given fresh grafts between 2018 and 2023. A prospective phase in 2023 to 2025 added 16 frozen and 25 fresh graft recipients, tracked for clinical endpoints and inflammatory biomarkers. Fresh grafts took hold faster: neutrophil recovery arrived at a median of eleven days, against fourteen to fifteen days for frozen grafts, and hospital stays ran shorter as the results continue.
pmc-13402071:
Sakue Masuda and fellow authors argue, in a 2026 editorial, that choosing antibiotics for acute cholangitis should turn on patient risk rather than a simple broad versus narrow label. Acute cholangitis is infection of the bile ducts, and draining the bile often controls the source fast, so needlessly wide drug cover adds harm without helping. A large Japanese claims study found broad first treatment did not lower deaths compared with narrower cover.

What counts as broad, they note, depends on likely germs, local resistance patterns, and each patient history, not drug class alone. Common gut germs dominate mild community cases, while resistant Gram-negative germs, Pseudomonas, and Enterococcus drive harder ones. Their plea is risk-adapted first treatment: reserve the widest drugs for patients whose risk of resistant infection is genuinely high.
pmc-13403371:
Joseph H. Breeyear and a large team ran a 2026 gene study on how men and women with type 2 diabetes respond to sulfonylurea drugs. They split results by sex in a trial group of 871 people. Blood sugar change after treatment was the main measure, and two other groups were used to check the signals.

Gene regions with sex-linked effects turned up in both sexes, in men alone, and in women alone. One region near TMEM64 and NECAB1 held up in a second male group. A variant there also tied to lower peak insulin in men after a single dose. The results argue for sex-aware dosing research.
pmc-13403571:
Syed Al Jawad Sayem and colleagues compared three ways in 2026 to measure an antibiotic in pig blood. Labs need exact drug levels to set doses, yet the top lab method costs a lot. They tested the standard method against a microbe growth test and an antibody test in healthy and sick piglets.

All three methods passed standard checks for exactness and range. The two cheaper tests matched the standard closely, with matching drug curves over time. Sickness shifted how the drug spread in the body. Cheap tests plus free software could help farms in poor areas set doses with care.
pmc-13405071:
Noha Alnazzawi builds a model that reads doctors' free-text notes to flag heart disease, reporting in 2026. High blood pressure and diabetes raise heart risk, but much of that information sits in narrative records rather than tidy fields. Automatic extraction could help doctors act earlier.

Narrative data from the PrevComp corpus were combined with the structured UCI heart disease dataset. Extracted risk factors fed a LightGBM classifier, a fast tree-based learning method. The model reached 83 percent accuracy for predicting whether heart disease was present in the reported testing. The author presents structured mapping of notes as a practical route to personalised prevention, while noting the work rests on existing datasets.
pmc-13405571:
Andressa Fernanda Paza Miguel and co-authors examine tumour features and immune cells in mouth cancer, in a 2026 study of 31 samples. Oral squamous cell carcinoma varies in how it grows and spreads, and those patterns may forecast survival. Staining methods reveal both tumour shape and the immune cells inside it.

Features scored include tumour budding, invasion depth and thickness, and spread along nerves or vessels. Neutrophils and killer lymphocytes were counted at the tumour core and its growing edge. Heavy budding travelled with nerve and vessel invasion and thicker tumours. More neutrophils, loose growth patterns and spread-out tumours all tracked with shorter survival in the reported curves.
pmc-13405671:
Michael Simon and team tested whether obesity changes the acute blood vessel response to maximal aerobic exercise. Their 2026 work weighs vessel markers CTRP9, total nitric oxide, and flow-mediated dilation in 11 obese and 9 normal-weight young men. Readings were taken before, right after, and one and two hours after a maximal treadmill test. Obesity is tied to arterial stiffness and vessel dysfunction, yet acute exercise responses by weight status had been unclear.

CTRP9 fell from right after exercise to one hour later, mainly in normal-weight men, then returned to baseline. Nitric oxide rose mainly in obese men right after exercise before settling back. Flow-mediated dilation did not change in either group, though obese men showed lower dilation across time. The authors conclude that maximal exercise briefly shifts vessel biomarkers regardless of obesity, with no acute dilation edge for either group.
pmc-13405871:
Anthony J Gifford and colleagues evaluate a ten-week stand-up comedy course for LGBTQ+ adults, in a 2026 qualitative study. Stigma and minority stress drive high rates of mental distress in this group. The programme, LGBTQteehee, teaches participants to turn lived experience into stage material.

Six participants shared their experience in a focus group and interviews after the course. Two themes emerged: standing up together as a queer ensemble, and comedy as catharsis. Belonging, diversity and a feeling of safety underpinned the first. Reframing painful stories as jokes built confidence and a sense of owning the moment in the second. The authors present comedy as community care, not just entertainment.
pmc-13407471:
Josef Finsterer argues, in a 2026 letter, that brain-wave reactivity tests cannot cleanly predict recovery after traumatic brain injury. The letter discusses a study of 40 patients. Reactivity of the brain-wave test to sound and pain was present in 45 percent. Its absence tracked poor outcome scores at three and six months.

The objection is dependence: a reactivity reading only means something if the pathways carrying sound and pain signals to the brain are intact. Head trauma patients may also carry spinal cord or nerve damage. A flat response might then reflect a broken wire, not a hopeless brain. The reverse error is possible too. Finsterer asks how many study patients had such accompanying injuries, and notes that traumatic brain injury itself lumps together very different kinds of damage, complicating any single predictor.
pmc-13408371:
Zilong Ye, Haoyu Huang, and colleagues build in 2026 a light sensor designed for wireless links that resist eavesdropping. Ordinary broadband detectors pick up everything, inviting crosstalk and interception. Their organic device instead answers only two narrow colour bands, one visible and one in the near infrared, and powers itself.

A built-in optical cavity with a carefully chosen spacer layer creates that selectivity, and the sensor reacts in well under a microsecond. Pairing the hardware filtering with chaotic encryption produced an error rate below one in ten thousand at megabit speeds in their tests. Retuning the cavity pushed the second band into the short-wave infrared. The work sketches a route toward private light-based communication, spectroscopy, and photonic networks.
pmc-13408471:
Qi Yang, Xiaojun Huang, Chunling Wu, Yan Zeng, and Xinzheng Zhang describe in 2026 a way to collect cryo-electron microscopy images far faster by simply never stopping the camera. Cryo-EM reconstructions need huge image sets, and ordinary acquisition wastes time while the camera idles between shifted beam positions. Their method records continuously throughout the beam-image shift routine.

On two common direct detectors the approach captured roughly thirty-four thousand micrographs per day for single-particle work and about a thousand tilt series per day for tomography. Reconstructions from the rushed data kept their quality. Because the trick is implemented in software scripts and needs no hardware changes, existing facilities can adopt it directly. Structural biology laboratories gain a route to cheaper, higher-throughput data collection.
pmc-13408671:
Marija Karadzovska-Kotevska and a Swedish team test in 2026 whether the tiny tissue snippets taken during lung cancer diagnosis can support full molecular profiling if they are preserved in a stabilising solution. Treatment choices now hinge on histology plus mutations, fusions, and protein patterns, yet bronchoscopic samples are small. Biopsies and needle aspirates went straight into the preservative during routine work-up.

Every tumour yielded good-quality DNA, RNA, and protein. Gene fusion testing succeeded in nearly all cases, expression-based subtype calls mostly agreed with the clinical pathology diagnosis, and mutation results matched routine testing completely. Mass spectrometry added proteomic subtypes on top. The proof-of-concept suggests one small preserved specimen can feed the whole modern work-up, sparing patients repeat procedures when tissue runs short.
pmc-13408971:
Iva Bačić, Michael Schaub, Jürgen Kurths, and Dirk Witthaut extend the mathematics of synchronisation in 2026 to networks where interactions involve whole faces and volumes, not just links. The topological Kuramoto model describes oscillators coupled across the cells of a geometric complex, a setting fit for brain tissue and power grids alike. The question was which locked patterns such systems can hold.

The team introduces topological Kirchhoff conditions that characterise every phase-locked state, each labelled by winding numbers that count how phases twist around independent cycles. Worked examples on rings, Platonic solids, and simplices exposed a clean rule: a boundary needs at least five elements before multiple stable states can exist. Winding numbers at different dimensions then stack into cascades of multistability. The framework ties a network's shape directly to its repertoire of collective rhythms.
pmc-13412371:
Jae Hun Oh and co-authors build in 2026 a prediction model for a grim path some cardiac arrest survivors follow toward brain death. Standard outcome scales lump these patients into a broad poor-outcome class, hiding a distinct trajectory. Using a Korean registry of comatose patients treated with targeted temperature control, the team combined brain scan measures, a blood marker at 48 hours, and clinical details.

Of 376 patients analysed, 74 met their working definition of progression toward brain death. Younger age, a non-shockable first rhythm, a low grey-to-white matter ratio on scans, and higher marker levels each predicted that path. The combined model scored an area under the curve of 0.895 in the full group, with internal checks holding up well.
pmc-13412871:
Filippo Messina and co-authors describe in 2026 the MRI patterns and three-month course of a painful foot condition marked by bone marrow swelling. The presumed algodystrophic pattern resists simple painkillers and is hard to classify, so its imaging map mattered. Their retrospective series covered nineteen consecutive patients at one centre, all treated with a combined protocol built around neridronate injections and vitamin D, some adding physiotherapy and magnetotherapy.

Swelling concentrated in the midfoot, hitting the navicular and third cuneiform bones most often in the scans reviewed. Median pain scores dropped from 8.0 to 3.0 over three months, and a function index improved from 80.0 to 41.0 in the same window. Daily painkiller use fell from 78.9 percent to zero, though no control group lets them credit the drug alone.
pmc-13413471:
Faroug Ismael and colleagues experiment in 2026 with adding ultrasound to the diamond wire saws that slice sapphire crystal. Sapphire's hardness and optical clarity make it prized for engineering parts, and slicing sets the final surface quality. Vibration may keep the abrasive sharp, hammer away debris, and help lubricant reach the cut, yet its influence was under-studied. Single-factor and combined tests varied vibration strength, horn position, feed speed, and wire speed within industrial ranges.

Surface roughness and waviness served as the scorecards, and the team fitted prediction formulas to both. Faster feeding and faster wire each weakened the ultrasound benefit in their runs, while horn placement barely mattered. Ranked influence ran feed speed first, then wire speed, then vibration strength. The authors say controlling the two speeds matters most for finish quality.
pmc-13415871:
Süleyman Korkusuz and Büşra Seçkinoğulları Korkusuz compare arm muscle, strength, dexterity, and thinking in older adults by living setting, in 2026. Eighty-five adults aged sixty-five to eighty took part: thirty-nine in nursing homes and forty-six living in the community. Ultrasound measured muscle thickness, dynamometers measured grip and pinch, and pegboard plus Stroop tasks tested dexterity and cognition.

Nursing home residents showed thinner forearm and upper arm muscles on every site measured. Grip, pinch, pegboard scores, and cognitive scores all ran lower in that group too. Living conditions, social resources, and environment likely explain part of the gap, the authors suggest, pointing to targeted activity programs.
pmc-13416071:
Shuangshuang Chen and colleagues built an AI writer in 2026 for traditional cultural art design texts, a field where text generation lagged behind image work. The team gathered feature-text pairs for classic crafts, then added a cultural-meaning attention layer and a style-constraint module to a Transformer model, plus a checker.

The new model scored 0.72 on a standard text-match measure, with 92.5 percent correct cultural terms and 89.3 percent style match, best on ceramics, and held up within 5 percent across craft domains. Design researchers gain a tested tool for drafting culturally faithful art-design prose.
pmc-13416371:
Regina Matey Sánchez, Mónica Riaza Gómez, and Miguel A. Reina adapt a neonatal intensive care parent stress scale for Spain, in 2026. Parents of babies in intensive care face helplessness and anxiety that affect bonding and outcomes. Translation, back translation, expert review, and a pilot with fifteen parents preceded testing in 160 parents, split evenly between mothers and fathers.

Reliability was excellent, with a total consistency score near 0.97 in the reported alpha values. The original four factor structure fit poorly in Spanish data. A five factor structure under one general stress factor fit better, though still below standard thresholds. Larger independent samples must confirm the structure before wide clinical use.
pmc-13417371:
Laura Botto and co-authors expose lung cells to diesel exhaust particles and watch membrane changes tied to virus entry, in a 2026 laboratory study. Street level pollution had tracked with worse COVID outcomes, and fatty membrane zones called lipid rafts help the coronavirus enter cells. The A549 lung cell line served as the test system.

After exposure, the viral entry receptor ACE2 shifted into lipid rafts, and one ganglioside, GM2, rose while two relatives fell. A stress signal, IL-6, also increased. Other inflammation proteins stayed flat. Actual viral entry was not tested, so relevance to infection remains a hypothesis for follow up work.
pmc-13417471: Evidence-Based Complementary and Alternative Medicine retracted a 2018 article by Hossen and colleagues in 2026, acting with publisher John Wiley & Sons Ltd. The article had claimed that two mushrooms protect rats from harm caused by the pesticide carbofuran. The journal found repeated image elements across several figure panels, with parts of Figures 6 and 7 matching panels in other articles, or matching each other after stretching or rotation. Because the figure record could not be trusted, the article was withdrawn in full.
pmc-13418471:
Martin Hřivňacký and colleagues show that a classic anaesthetic stops plant seedlings bending toward light, in a 2026 study on Arabidopsis. Diethyl ether vapour blocked the bending response to weak blue light from one side. Bending needs the hormone auxin to gather on the shaded side, driving uneven growth. Early light sensing steps were checked separately from later hormone movement.

The light receptor's activation mark was untouched by ether, so sensing stayed intact. Auxin redistribution failed, though, and a key auxin transporter no longer moved to its working position. The result is first proof that anaesthetics can block hormone driven growth responses in plants.
pmc-13418871:
Wu and colleagues report a 2026 brain scan study of depression after stroke. The team scanned 84 patients with acute stroke at rest: 35 with poststroke depression and 49 without. They measured degree centrality, a count of how strongly each brain area connects with the rest, across three speed bands of brain activity.

Patients with depression showed lower centrality in the right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, an area for control and planning, in every band tested. The matching area on the left was lower in one band only. Some other regions showed raised centrality in that same band, and the shifts tracked depression scores. A control hub that loses influence across all activity speeds is a strong lead for why mood falls after stroke, and a possible target for stimulation therapies.
pmc-13419071:
Drew Cooper and colleagues study sleep in people with diabetes who use automated insulin delivery, systems that adjust dosing around the clock. Poor sleep is common in diabetes, yet its links to device use and blood sugar results were little mapped at scale. Their cross-sectional study drew 529 adults from the OPEN Project, covering the years 2020 to 2023.

Participants rated their sleep quality and their fear of low blood sugar on standard surveys. Users of open-source and store-bought systems were both included, along with people not using automation at all. Continuous glucose data supplied real-world sugar measures to set beside the survey scores. The mixed picture helps device teams and clinics see where night-time worries and poor sleep may call for added support.
pmc-13419171:
Koki Takeda and colleagues mine a national drug safety database in Japan for reports of macular swelling tied to a common cancer drug. Their set held 585,738 adverse event reports in total, of which 123 involved swelling at the center of the retina.

Diabetes and use of certain glaucoma eye drops also carried raised signals in the same data. Such database studies cannot prove cause, yet the strength of the gap marks eye checks as worth weighing for patients on this drug.
pmc-13419671:
Samuel Lloyd-White and colleagues review five years of inpatient psychiatric care for autistic children and teenagers in England's Thames Valley. Many autistic adolescents land in wards that are poorly set up for neurodivergent needs. The study covers referrals from 2019 to 2024 through one provider network in the south of England.

Routine service data described who was referred, their clinical picture, and how their stays ended. Autistic patients were set beside their non-autistic peers on the same measures. Routine scores hinted at slower progress during care and greater difficulty at both entry and discharge for the autistic group. Clear gaps like these give services a base for redesigning wards, staffing, and discharge plans around autistic young people.
pmc-13419871:
Eisuke Nakao and colleagues judge an AI reading aid during nose-passed stomach endoscopy at a hospital in Japan. The thin scope route is gentler for patients, yet small lesions stay easy to miss. Their study ran from May 2024 to October 2024 at Tane General Hospital with the aid watching every exam.

In total, 392 patients enrolled, and 98 tissue samples from 87 patients went through the final analysis. Biopsy was taken for every suspect spot no matter what the AI said, and lab diagnosis of the tissue served as the truth standard. That design keeps the AI honest, since its calls face tissue proof each time. Results tell clinics whether the aid earns a place in daily lists or adds noise.
pmc-13421671:
Shreedevi Kumar leads a nine-author team testing, in a 2026 study, a slow-release form of CD200 — a 'stand down' signal for the immune system — as a treatment idea for osteoarthritis. In arthritic joints, inflammatory macrophages release factors that drive cartilage cells to break down their own matrix, and CD200 can quiet those macrophages through its receptor.

Fluid from treated macrophages then lowered the cartilage-digesting gene activity of cartilage cells in culture. pmc-13422271:

Its surface effects are familiar. The endothelium was less charted: a single layer that keeps the cornea clear and cannot regrow.

The affected eyes held significantly fewer cells per square millimetre than their healthy partners, roughly twenty-five hundred against twenty-nine hundred. Cell size varied more in infected eyes as well. Central corneal thickness was also recorded. The authors warn that the layer's silent loss adds to this infection's long-term cost.
pmc-13424171:
Wenbin He and six colleagues build a framework for the lifelong learning ability of college nursing teachers, guided by Ecological Systems Theory, which nests a person inside widening circles of influence. Ability, in their model, renews itself in a loop rather than rising in a straight line. The framework aims to steer teacher development programmes.
pmc-13424571:
Fuyuki Ishida and four colleagues present a faster way to build up metal parts layer by layer without melting anything. Their ring-jig method grows from friction surfacing. A rotating metal bar rubs directly on a base plate. It deposits a uniform layer by friction alone, avoiding the costly powders and heavy energy input of fusion printing.

The numbers are striking. The method deposits up to 8,000 cubic centimetres per hour, against a maximum of 800 for fusion-based printing and 2,400 for other solid-state approaches. Layers bond soundly at the interface, the authors report. For large structural parts made in small runs, they argue, that speed and simplicity could make additive manufacturing practical where it currently is not.
pmc-13424771:
Kerstin Kremeike and nine colleagues distil a three-day international symposium, held in July 2025, on building death and grief literacy as an answer to loneliness at life's end. Experts from social work, volunteering, palliative care, migration studies, LGBTQ+ advocacy, caring communities, and psychosocial support met to compare how communities can respond better to dying and bereavement.

Sessions traced how literacy about death and grief is relational and practical, not just factual. They also traced how grief itself breeds loneliness. That risk falls hardest on marginalised people, who face poorer outcomes. The entanglement of loneliness with the wish to die in severe illness drew particular attention. Concrete recommendations for policy, practice, and education close the essay.
pmc-13425071:
Byonggu An and colleagues describe a 2026 case in which a combined laparoscopic and endoscopic operation made stomach cancer treatment possible. An older woman had early gastric cancer in the antrum, yet most of her stomach had herniated into her chest through a large type III hiatal hernia. A first attempt at endoscopic submucosal dissection failed because the displaced stomach could not be maneuvered safely.

Surgeons reduced the hernia laparoscopically and then completed the dissection endoscopically in a single-stage hybrid procedure. The report shows how correcting anatomy first can rescue a standard organ-preserving cancer treatment that anatomy alone had ruled out.
pmc-13425871:
Fuady and colleagues co-developed in 2026 a framework to help research findings shape health policy in Indonesia, built with the researchers, officials, and civil society groups who would use it. Many countries struggle to turn evidence into policy, and Indonesia had no formal framework of its own. The team combined a literature review with expert consultations and a round of interviews testing the draft for clarity.

Seventeen participants shaped the framework. The review confirmed barriers such as weak infrastructure, split governance, thin research capacity outside big centers, and studies that miss what policy makers need. Supports included political commitment and broker units. The final framework links two domains, producing evidence and the policy process, with steady two-way collaboration among academics, officials, and communities. The authors say its principles could travel to other health systems.
pmc-13425971:
Sied Kebir and a multicenter group report early safety results for tumor treating fields started around radiotherapy in newly diagnosed glioblastoma in 2026. Electric field therapy improves survival when begun after chemoradiation, but starting before and during radiation was untested. Arm A of the PriCoTTF phase I/II trial enrolled adults aged 18 to 70 with IDH-wildtype glioblastoma or gliosarcoma, performance status of at least 60, and planned focal radiation.

The feasibility cohort asks whether patients can actually wear the device through radiation without excess harm. Positive feasibility would open a randomized test of earlier field therapy in this aggressive brain tumor. The first phase asks a plain, key point: can sick men and women wear the cap each day through weeks of rays with no new harm?
pmc-13426871:
Van Woudenberg and colleagues published a 2026 study on checking fetal stress during labor. For 60 years, doctors have tested fetal scalp blood for acid levels. A lactate test promises the same signal with fewer failed samples. The team compared both measures across 263 samples at one hospital.

Lactate and acid levels moved together, though the link was only moderate overall. The lactate test still flagged abnormal acid results with good accuracy. A cutoff at 5.6 gave the best balance of catches and false alarms. Sensitivity and specificity both landed near four in five cases. Doctors at the center now back a switch to lactate testing. Lactate testing also fails less often at the bedside, they note.
pmc-13427071:
Wenche Ryberg and colleagues tracked suicidal thoughts in patients during the first ten days after leaving psychiatric hospital. Suicidal ideation means thoughts about ending one's own life, and the days right after discharge carry known high risk.

Thirty-six adults used a phone app to rate their thoughts five times a day for ten days after discharge. Thoughts appeared in about half of the 1,073 completed check-ins, and women reported them more often than men. Nothing measured before discharge separated patients who later reported thoughts from those who did not. Long-standing hopelessness, self-hate, and mental pain scores did predict how strong the later thoughts became, Ryberg reports.
pmc-13430171:
Alexander Chaverri-Carvajal and colleagues analyze, in a 2026 study, the social roots of memory and thinking decline among older Dominicans. The team used a national intake registry of older adults, covering 4,408 people aged 60 and over assessed between late 2022 and late 2025. A standard mental test with a cutoff score defined impairment.

About 53 percent of participants scored in the impaired range, a striking share. Dependence in daily activities carried the strongest links, roughly doubling the odds. Loneliness doubled them as well, and depressive symptoms added a further lift. People outside the capital region showed far higher rates than city residents. Being able to read, holding private insurance, and living in the metro area each protected. The findings feed a young national care system its first hard numbers.
pmc-13431771:
Lona-Durazo and colleagues test whether immune proteins in blood can cause brain diseases, and whether effects differ by sex. They cover Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and a motor nerve disease called ALS. Sex gaps in how often these diseases strike hint at sex-linked biology.

The team used Mendelian randomization, a gene-based method that mimics a trial in nature. It checks if gene-tied protein levels push disease risk up or down. Some protein links differed between women and men for Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease. Other proteins, such as TREM2 in Alzheimer's disease, held up in both sexes. No strong causal proof came out for the motor nerve disease. Some flagged proteins may suit tests as future drug targets.
pmc-13431871:
Szatkowski and Mastalerz review NSAID exacerbated respiratory disease, a condition in which common painkillers such as aspirin trigger breathing attacks in people who already have asthma and nasal polyps. Their 2026 review pulls together gene studies, cell profiling, and new biomarker work to give a single integrated picture of immune, lining, and lipid pathways.

A proposed diagnostic index mixes urine levels of two fat signals with sinus scan scores, offering a test that avoids a risky drug challenge.
