Biologic drugs aimed at the allergy type pathway now anchor treatment, while aspirin desensitization, slow dose building, suits select cases.
pmc-13433171:
Andrea Fernandez-Gutierrez and co-authors reviewed in 2026 how legume crops bear drought, the top growth brake for farm yield and a sharp threat to food supply. Legumes feed people and stock with rich protein and fiber, and they stock soils with nitrogen through partner germs. Breeding tougher kinds needs a firm grasp of how the plants sense and meet dry spells.

The review walks through drought hits at each growth stage and the signal webs that fire in reply. It weighs the test setups scholars use to grade toughness, with their strong and weak points laid side by side. Fast, high-volume trait reads earn a close look as a tool that could speed exact breeding. The authors aim the survey at breeders who face hotter, drier fields.
pmc-13433471:
Alun R C Jones and co-authors read the genomes of three roaches and five termites in 2026 to trace how gene switch proteins shifted as group life rose in this insect order. Caste gaps in group kinds call for rich gene control. Bee and ant shifts are well mapped, while roach and termite shifts stayed dim.

Some marks match the bee path: looser grip on some switch families, tighter grip on others, plus termite-only family growth. Key gaps part the orders too. Termite switch families shrank in spots, with no payback shift in the grip codes or their start zones. Richer group life did track with wider mix in the switch parts that fire genes, while grip parts held still. Switch growth alone cannot tell the tale, the authors say.
pmc-13433771:
Guowei Zeng and co-authors mapped force-sense channels in 2026 in mouse hearts squeezed by a tightened main artery, then traced how the heart's outer skin talks to scar cells under load. Scar growth under pressure load is a shared root of heart failure, yet drugs aimed square at scars stay rare. A time-line atlas of sense channels led the hunt.

One channel topped the list and sat thickest in outer skin cells. Mice bred to lack it in that skin grew less scar and kept better heart work. Its reach split: one path feeds scars near the skin, while a scent signal passed to deep scar cells does the wide work. Blocking the signal's port with a drug eased scars and heart strain in mice. Human samples backed the chain.
pmc-13434271:
Changrui Hu and colleagues build a camera-based tool for gauging how hard fish feed in factory fish farms that reuse water. Right feeding cuts waste and cost, yet dense stocks, rippled water, and shifting group acts make camera reads hard.

Their hybrid tool joins a convolutional net for local detail with a vision transformer for whole-scene context, side by side. A memory module then tracks feeding acts over time, giving a steady read of feeding strength from video. Farm staff can feed to hunger, not to clock, saving feed and keeping water clean.
pmc-13434371:
Sedtawut Kwanboon and coauthors give a mayfly a valid name in 2026, more than twenty years after it was first listed. The earlier name rested only on an unpublished thesis, so it never counted in formal terms. Specimens now come from Yunnan in China plus two provinces in northern Thailand.

Form traits and a DNA barcode both support the insect as its own species. The egg is described for the first time, with drawings of each life stage. Keys help readers sort young and adult forms of all Thai species in the genus. River survey teams gain a firmer name for their lists.
pmc-13434571:
Foster and collaborators followed 232 Kenyan infants from 9 to 23 months of age. About half were exposed to HIV but uninfected. The team tested whether early dietary diversity protects against stunting in the second year. Diets were captured by food frequency questionnaires. Growth was converted to World Health Organization scores. Children entered the analysis with scores above the malnutrition cutoff.

At 9 months, 42 percent of infants met minimum dietary diversity. That means foods from at least five groups in the scoring used. Meeting that bar at 9 months was associated with a hazard ratio of 0.51 for stunting through 23 months. That roughly halved the risk in this cohort. Diversity showed no significant association with wasting or underweight. The signal pointed specifically at linear growth protection during infancy. Diverse diets were also linked with 86 percent lower risk of low subscapular skinfolds, a trunk fat measure. Similar trends appeared for flesh food intake.
pmc-13434771:
Qian Yu's team studied 194 IVF patients in China in 2026, linking information overload to pregnancy chances through distress. Patients rated overload, fear that illness would worsen, and felt stress at moderate to high levels, and the three scores rose together. After adjusting for clinical factors, higher scores on each measure went with lower odds of clinical pregnancy, a pattern the authors read as distress bridging overload and outcome.

The paper urges routine mood checks and steps to cut the information burden during long, complex fertility treatment. Readers should keep the design in mind: one center, one time slice, and links, not proof that overload itself causes failure. Clinics get a humane, testable idea for support that may help patients cope and, perhaps, conceive.
pmc-13435471:
Oguzhan Begik's team presented FIRST-seq in 2026, a nanopore method for reading RNA modifications and structure from cDNA. RNA chemical marks bend reverse transcription in enzyme-specific ways, leaving error fingerprints that can map marks across the transcriptome and probe folding. FIRST-seq skips second-strand making and PCR, works with any reverse transcriptase, and reads signatures at single-base resolution.

Testing enzymes and buffers cut early stops and sharpened error detection. Pairing the method with DMS probing picked up two marks at unpaired sites, matching known structures in test tubes and living cells. RNA teams get a flexible, low-cost platform for mark and structure work. Its value will grow as groups test it on diverse RNAs and enzymes.
pmc-13435571:
Li Huang's team studied OTULIN in 2026 in newborn mice harmed by excess oxygen, a model of bronchopulmonary dysplasia. The enzyme OTULIN edits ubiquitin tags and has been tied to lung injury, but its role in oxygen-linked newborn lung harm was unclear. Mice raised in high oxygen showed lung injury with higher OTULIN, fewer mitochondria, and more fusion and recycling of these powerhouses in lung tissue.

Boosting OTULIN in lung lining cells cut reactive oxygen, steadied membrane charge, and restored mitochondrial balance. The team linked OTULIN directly to OPA1, a mitochondrial protein, and named RNF31 as a regulator of OPA1 stability. Neonatal teams get a detailed protective mechanism, still at the animal stage, for a disease with few targeted options.
pmc-13436071:
Shaofeng Chen and coauthors learn why making a fat cutting enzyme poisons E coli in 2026. The enzyme, phospholipase D, is prized for making rare lipids, yet cells that make it sicken. Shape, charge, and ion checks trace the harm step by step.

Its product, phosphatidic acid, piles up and drives potassium out of the cell nonstop. Ion chaos then sparks a burst of toxic oxygen radicals that wreck the cell. Gene reads suggest fixes: burn the acid faster into fresh lipids and calm membrane mix ups. Those fixes may lift enzyme yields for factory use. The work doubles as a case study in enzyme toxicity.
pmc-13436571:
Zhao and colleagues wrote a 2026 review on tiny particles built from lanthanide metals. These metals can both make and mop up reactive oxygen, a cell-damaging chemical family. That two-way control suits diseases driven by oxygen damage in tissue. The review covers design rules, working routes, and medical uses of the particles.

The particles can shield healthy tissue from oxygen damage and calm swelling. Aimed at tumors, they can boost treatments that kill cancer through oxygen bursts. Designs now span glow-in-the-dark builds, multi-metal mixes, and single-atom catalysts. Computer-guided design is speeding the search for better particle recipes. The authors still flag open questions on how bodies clear these particles. Safer dosing and better targeting must come before wide clinical use.
pmc-13436971:
Sana Almutairi and co-authors reply to a critic of their study on immune patterns in people who live with both rheumatoid arthritis and asthma. In the 2026 letter, they answer points about drug effects, steroids, and missing detail on disease activity. They explain that patients with a recent flare of either condition were kept out, and that extra checks by treatment group showed no clear differences.

Several gaps are openly granted. Asthma subtypes, such as allergy-driven or weight-linked forms, were not sorted, though the authors argue their readings argue against a hidden weight-linked group. Only seven signaling proteins were measured, blood was drawn once, and the group was small even if it met power needs. The writers call their study a first step and say larger groups, wider protein panels, and repeat measures over time should test the picture.
pmc-13437171:
Toru Yamamoto and co-authors warn dentists that the recovery stretch after intravenous sedation deserves the same watchfulness as the procedure itself. Their 2026 letter draws on a Japanese case in which a 29-year-old man with intellectual disability seemed fine during treatment, then coughed, produced heavy secretions, and saw his oxygen level fall sharply. He needed pressure support, and chest imaging showed fluid in both lungs.

The airway stays unprotected and shares space with the work field, so saliva, blood, and rinse fluid can block breathing or trigger spasm. Staff attention also drifts toward notes, cleaning, and discharge once treatment ends. Negative pressure lung injury is rare, yet blocked airways during recovery can cause it. The letter urges teams to keep airway watch, suction, and rescue skills ready until each patient leaves.
pmc-13437271:

The measure, called the stress hyperglycemia ratio, compares blood sugar during illness with a person's usual level. Their 2026 study pooled 16,440 patients from four centers plus a large intensive care database. The team tracked gut bleeding after surgery and deaths in hospital, two outcomes that matter after bypass work.

Gut bleeding struck 1,158 patients, just over seven percent, and 214 patients died during their stay. The link between the sugar ratio and both harms formed a U shape: risk ran lowest in a middle band and rose at both low and high values. The authors suggest that both extremes deserve attention when teams judge risk. A patient whose stress sugar stays flat may be in as much danger as one whose sugar soars, and either pattern can flag who needs closer watch.
pmc-13437571:

Their 2026 study grew four varieties each of barley, faba bean, potato, and sweet potato in three European soils. Fluids around the roots were gathered with a hybrid soil and water method.

Soil type and plant variety both shaped what came out, though their weight differed by crop. Across most crops, faster-growing plants leaked less, a trade-off the authors highlight: carbon spent feeding the root zone cannot also build body mass. Root shape traits explained part of the leakage in some crops but never all, and no single rule fit every species. It also warns breeders: selecting for richer root leakage may quietly tax yield.
pmc-13437971:

Their 2026 paper examines three such proteins in depth: their shapes, jobs, and known links to illness.

Changes in these proteins ripple outward: energy output falls, corrosive oxygen byproducts rise, and quality control for worn mitochondria falters. Neurons, with their huge energy bills and long lives, suffer earliest and worst. Their pitch is that a neglected corner of cell biology, the mitochondrial ribosome, may hold fresh entry points for treating degenerative brain disease.
pmc-13438671:

A feature once dismissed as junk turns out to be load-bearing, inviting a second look at other repeats.
pmc-13439271:

The model captures electrons that repel each other on a grid and may explain high-temperature superconductors, materials that carry current without loss when fairly warm. Exact answers are out of reach, so computer methods compete on accuracy. Their method reached leading accuracy for the doped two-dimensional model. Curiously, distinct attention heads inside the network each picked up correlations at a different scale, helping the state capture long-range order. Results backed a striped ground state at half filling when a diagonal hopping term was added, matching patterns seen in real cuprate materials.
pmc-13440171:

Overall anemia hit about forty-six percent, mostly mild to moderate. Malaria infection nearly doubled odds, and an age-sex interaction stood out: boys aged fifteen to sixteen had nearly triple the odds of girls the same age. School health programs get a large, current burden map with malaria control and older-boy targeting as priorities.
pmc-13440771:
Sato and colleagues reported in 2026 two cases of burst aneurysms on small collateral arteries in moyamoya disease. In that condition, blocked brain arteries force the growth of a fragile web of backup vessels. Aneurysms on those vessels are common and their rupture carries a grim outlook. Reaching them by catheter is hard because the vessels are tiny and winding.

In the first case, the aneurysm bled again before treatment, and sealing it through a catheter was marred by a rupture during the procedure and fluid buildup in the brain afterward. The second patient had the parent vessel closed off by catheter without complications. The authors weigh the promise and the peril of the approach. Success depends on whether the lesion can be reached safely, so careful mapping of the collateral network must come first.
pmc-13441271:
Wolff and colleagues described in 2026 a 75-year-old woman whose scattered bleeding turned out to be acquired hemophilia A, a rare disorder where the immune system attacks a clotting protein. Her factor VIII activity was very low, and the inhibitor was confirmed. Treatment paired a bypassing clotting drug to stop bleeding with steroids and weekly rituximab to wipe out the inhibitor. Within four weeks her clotting tests normalized fully, and the authors stress quick recognition of this rare disorder.
pmc-13441771:

Only women with normal function and no thyroid antibodies stayed in the reference group.

Four hundred eighty-two pregnancies appeared over eighteen months, and 182 women qualified for the clean reference set. Early thyrotropin ran lower than pre-pregnancy values, then rose slightly later in pregnancy. Standard intervals for thyrotropin and total thyroxine are reported for both trimesters. pmc-13442371:

pmc-13442671:

People who later grew side effects showed a distinct cell mix up front, with fewer memory B cells among the shifts. The team hopes such marks can guide care that calms side effects without dulling the anti-tumor push, a balance steroid care now risks.
pmc-13442871:

pmc-13443171:

pmc-13444371:

One path through ease, views, and intent gave the largest solo share. Sport confidence thus feeds tool habits through how tools feel to use, step by step. The authors urge PE programs to build sport belief and tool ease in tandem for lasting uptake.
pmc-13444471:

Layer views showed a tight sheet build in the best extract.
pmc-13445671:

pmc-13448971:

pmc-13449571:

pmc-13449771:

pmc-13453071:

pmc-13462671:

Proof of its worth has grown across the whole arc of care, from screen to last days. The alliance, formed by a top United States cancer charity, sets shared marks for lasting use.

The call asks health systems to fund guides as core staff, not side perks. In the United States, guide work can now be billed to state health plans. Some lands have passed laws or ministry plans to spread it. The authors put the voice of lived patients first in each plan. Equity is the test: guides must reach the poor, the rural, and the shut out first.
pmc-13463971:
Toshiki Tezuka and nine co-authors sort pain types in Parkinson's disease using a shared classification system. Pain burdens over half of patients, yet its kinds blur together in clinic notes. The system splits pain tied to the disease into tissue, nerve, and nociplastic types, the last arising from altered pain processing.

In a first pass over 192 patients, tissue pain was most common, then nociplastic, then nerve pain. A deeper check of forty patients found nerve pain scored far harsher than nociplastic pain on shared scales. Nerve pain also paired with stronger motor ups and downs and with brain wiring changes on scans. Nociplastic pain showed no such marks, though it hurt quality of life just as much.
pmc-13464071:
Kai Huang and ten co-authors show how a plant compound, Bruceine A, turns a DNA repair protein into an immune alarm for colorectal cancer. The protein, Ku70, normally guards DNA inside the cell nucleus. Bruceine A drags Ku70 out into the cell body, away from its repair post.

pmc-13464271:
Nouman Ahmad and colleagues report a 2026 single-stage repair of tangled congenital aortic arch disease in a 42-year-old man. Bleeding needed a second look and a lung infection followed, but both were managed and recovery proceeded. pmc-13464971:
Xinyu Li and four co-authors frame how microglia, the brain's resident immune cells, may rebuild blood vessel networks after ischemic stroke. Reperfusion saves some patients, yet repair in the weeks after stroke lacks good treatments. Vessel regrowth around the dead zone supports barrier healing and recovery, and microglia help steer it.

Herbal compounds, vesicle therapies, and nano-carriers all enter the discussion, with strict identity checks demanded first.
pmc-13465171:
Khajamohiddin Syed surveys four decades of cytochrome P450 research by African scientists, from 1987 to 2025. These enzymes break down drugs, build hormones, and clear poisons in nearly all life. No one had tallied the continent's share of the field before this count.

Strong suits include drug response, hormone building, insecticide resistance in malaria mosquitoes, and enzyme sensors. Work with partners abroad ran deep throughout the period. Precision medicine, heavy data work, and industrial uses remain thin spots the author flags for investment.
pmc-13465371:
Yang and colleagues score food supply security across Gansu Province in this 2026 evaluation study, applying China's broader food security concept that looks beyond grain tonnage alone. Growth was strongest in the central and eastern Hexi Corridor and the Longdong region, while parts of Longzhong and Longnan lagged behind. Supply quality and safety scored highest of the five dimensions, and economic security acted as the strongest driver of improvement. The authors recommend consolidating those strengths while directing investment at the lagging regions to close the imbalance.
pmc-13465671:
Xu and co-authors measured how flexibly brain networks rewire themselves after stroke in 2026, hunting for signs that predict arm recovery. Their tool was temporal variability, how much a brain region's connection pattern reshuffles over time during rest scans. The study enrolled 33 patients with left-sided and 30 with right-sided deep stroke damage. Fifty-six healthy volunteers served as controls. Arm motor scores were taken twice.

Other spots, including a left movement area and the cerebellar network, reshuffled more than in controls. Right-sided patients showed extra losses in vision and default-mode areas. pmc-13465871:

A simple protein crash step recovered more than 92 percent of the drug from plasma. The drug held up almost perfectly, above 99 percent stability, at room temperature, in the autosampler, and through freezing cycles. Each run took just four minutes. The authors present the method as ready for pharmacokinetic studies.
pmc-13466271:
Yang Shi and colleagues strengthened graphite sealing rings for hot, high-pressure valves by weaving in surface-treated carbon fibres. Plain graphite rings seal well but creep, wear unevenly, and lack strength under the extreme loads inside industrial valves.

The team varied fibre content from zero to 7 percent and measured strength, friction, and endurance under load. Five percent fibre proved best, lifting compressive strength by about 58 percent over plain graphite. Friction held steady at 0.15 to 0.18 across sliding, and creep resistance improved as well. After 1,000 hours under sustained load, the best rings kept over 78 percent of their starting strength. Shi credits fibres anchoring into the expanded graphite, bridging cracks and carrying load across the ring.
pmc-13466471:
Altaf Kondkar and colleagues test two inherited variants in adrenaline receptor genes for links to the common form of glaucoma, in a 2026 Saudi case-control study. The group held 167 patients with primary open-angle glaucoma and 251 controls, genotyped with standard PCR assays. Complete data for both variants covered 412 people.

One variant form in the ADRB1 gene, the Gly49 version, appeared more often in patients and roughly doubled the odds of disease across several statistical models, surviving strict correction. The ADRB2 variant showed no link on its own. Neither variant tracked with eye pressure or optic nerve cupping measures, suggesting the effect works through routes other than pressure alone.
pmc-13466971:
Şimşek and co-authors reviewed a 2026 set of records from preterm babies in a Turkish neonatal intensive care unit who received their two-month combination vaccine. Fever and blood changes after vaccination can mimic sepsis, tempting doctors to start antibiotics unnecessarily. The team asked which factors actually drove that decision.

Babies given antibiotics stayed in hospital far longer, a median of ninety-nine versus seventy-eight days, Şimşek found. Their inflammation marker CRP and a white cell ratio both ran higher after vaccination. Only CRP independently predicted antibiotic use in adjusted models, yet just fifteen percent of treated babies had positive cultures. The authors warn these markers cannot separate infection from vaccine reaction alone.
pmc-13467571:
Ridwan R. Waliyuddin and co-authors review in 2026 pulsed field ablation, a newer non-thermal way to correct atrial fibrillation, in patients with obesity. Four cohort studies met the criteria, and their results on rhythm relapse were mixed. Relapse rates looked lower than with radiofrequency ablation, though the gap was not statistically firm. In one study using only the new method, success did not vary across weight categories. Against balloon freezing, one matched study favored the pulsed approach at one year while another did not.
pmc-13467671:
Helena C. Teixeira and colleagues tested two ways to toughen the plastic matrix of carbon fibre composites for freezing space conditions. Epoxy turns brittle in deep cold and cracks under thermal cycling, threatening the light structures spacecraft depend on.

One strategy swapped in a specialty resin; the other blended in rubbery core-shell particles at low doses suited to factory production. Two percent particles won: they raised the soaked-up impact energy of the plain resin by 125 percent in early tests. In full laminates, the toughened matrix kept tensile behaviour while more than doubling crack resistance between layers. Gains reached 102 percent at room temperature and 122 percent at cryogenic temperature, Teixeira reports.
pmc-13468271:
Amapola De Sales-Millan and colleagues follow in 2026 the gut microbes and symptoms of 25 Mexican children with autism spectrum disorder. Gut imbalance in autism has been tied to digestive trouble and to symptom severity. Stool was sampled at the start, at three months, and at six months for microbial sequencing, with deeper metagenome sequencing in a subset.

Gastrointestinal symptoms were scored with a standard index alongside the microbial work. The longitudinal design lets the authors connect shifts in microbial composition and diversity, and in the functional genes the community carries, to clinical change in the same children over time. Families and clinicians need longer, repeated-measures evidence like this before synbiotics can move from promise to recommendation, which is the gap the study addresses.
pmc-13468571:
Renato Cicchetti and colleagues develop in 2026 a 24 gigahertz radar that reads breathing and heartbeat without touching the body. They test whether circular polarization makes it robust against cluttered rooms. Radar vital-sign monitors fail when vibrating metal panels and furniture bounce back stronger signals than the chest itself. The system uses horn antennas with converters that switch the radar waves between linear and circular polarization modes.

An optics-based model, simulations, and bench experiments in a worst-case setup with vibrating metallic panels all pointed the same way. Circularly polarized radar separated the vital signals from the environmental disturbance more reliably than the linear mode. Contact-free monitoring is wanted in homes and hospital wards alike, for burn patients, newborns, and infection control. A radar that works in a real, rattling room rather than a quiet lab is the step this work supplies.
pmc-13468671:
Feng Xie and colleagues train radar anti-jamming strategies in 2026 by letting an intelligent jammer and a radar fight inside an AlphaZero-style game. Adaptive waveform choice is the radar core problem: it must keep sensing while a smart adversary tries to blind it. The authors model both sides as competing agents making sequential decisions, with Monte Carlo tree search steering the search toward the most valuable confrontations.

Learning in this duel improved the sampling efficiency of useful training situations and sped up convergence of the radar strategy. Crucially, the team did not stop at simulation: a semi-physical validation rig, mixing real hardware with simulated elements, checked that the evolved strategies survive contact with real electronics. That bridge from algorithm to hardware is where many anti-jamming ideas die, so demonstrating it is the paper main contribution.
pmc-13468871:
Dekha and co-authors mapped in 2026 where two control systems of lymphoma cells meet: chemical gene tags, called epigenetics, and signaling pathways relaying growth orders. B-cell lymphomas often return or resist treatment, so new targets are prized. The review focuses on protein kinases, enzymes passing signals along, including two lesser-known ones, CK1 and CK2. Signaling and tagging jointly shape the tumor's immune surroundings too. The authors argue for hitting both systems at once. Such paired attacks, they suggest, could break the resistance that single drugs meet.
pmc-13469171: Li and colleagues published a correction in 2026 to their earlier article reporting a CSNK2A1 gene variant as the cause of Okur-Chung syndrome, a rare developmental condition. The authors state they accidentally left out a citation. The missing paper, in Chinese, first described the patient and the main genetic findings, including several figures. The correction supplies the full reference. The later article had expanded on that report with 65 further cases. It also added analyses linking gene changes to symptoms. The authors apologize.
pmc-13469471:
Junyue Lin and a large team report an immunotherapy study, published in 2026, building engineered T cells against glioblastoma, the most aggressive brain tumour. Their cells carry a receptor fusion construct aimed at B7-H3, a protein on the tumour, and the team built in reporter switches so they could watch two activation pathways switch on.

The engineered cells suppressed glioblastoma growth in dishes and in animals. When the cells met their target, the NF-kappaB and NFAT pathway reporters lit up, showing both pathways participate in the killing response. The authors propose the reporters as an early readout of potency for judging such cell therapies before clinical use.
pmc-13469671:
Piotr Targowski and co-authors test in 2026 whether changing radio frequencies helps drone networks survive jamming and interference. Military and civilian drones alike can lose their links when an enemy jammer or stray signals crowd the channel in use. The team compared staying put, switching at once when quality drops, switching after a set outage, and hopping on a fixed schedule.

Frequency moves paid off only once radio conditions had degraded. Switching at once worked best against ordinary interference from the environment. Scheduled hopping delivered the most packets under deliberate jamming, gaining about twelve percentage points over a fixed channel. The authors warn that delivery rate alone should not pick the policy. Coverage gaps, delay, and jitter can point commanders toward different choices for each mission phase.
pmc-13470271:
Iris Groman-Yaroslavski and colleagues showed in 2026 that Natufian foragers cultivated cereals about 4.5 millennia before domestication. Microscopic wear on flint sickle blades from el-Wad Terrace and Salibiya I, dated roughly 15,000 to 11,700 years ago, recorded harvest of semi-ripe and ripe cereals by shattering. Stripping traces, replicated by experiment as threshing, removed spikelets and freed grains.

Harvest stretched from mid-spring semi-ripe stands to very late spring dry stems, targeting mixed stands of early, late, and non-shattering plants. Natufians planned around that mixture to limit seed loss and bank seed for next year's sowing. The intensive, organised harvest counts as early cultivation, pushing organised cereal farming far earlier than systematic domestication records suggest.
pmc-13470371:
Pineda and colleagues explore in this 2026 immunology paper what makes a cancer vaccine based on cDC1 cells work. Lab-grown versions of these cells had already controlled tumors in mice, but the reasons were not settled.

Both systems contributed to tumor control, and having both on the same vaccine cell was needed for a strong response. The lab-grown cells closely matched those found inside tumors, and mice lacking their own cDC1 cells responded poorly, showing the host's cells also help.
pmc-13470771:
Sihao Huang, Kunqing Jiang, Xin Chen, Wei Chen, and Xianbiao Bu model in 2026 a system that would store energy as compressed carbon dioxide inside basalt rock. Their simulations tested different basalt types and operating settings.

The system could repay its build cost within its lifetime, at an electricity cost near that of porous rock air storage. pmc-13470971:

Interpreting such data usually needs machine learning, but labeled examples are scarce and complex tasks defeat standard models.

Foundation models learn from huge unlabeled datasets. They then adapt to new tasks with few examples. In early studies cited here, this approach already beats older methods at naming chemicals and predicting molecular properties. The authors envision progress from larger curated sample and spectral libraries, privacy-preserving training, joint modeling of several data types at once, and clearer explanations of model decisions. They present this as the start of a new era rather than a finished shift.
pmc-13471171:

Five years of follow-up were available in the records.

Remission was common and front-loaded. About 60 percent of patients, 701 people, reached a first remission. Of those, about 93 percent did so within the first 24 months. Several traits stretched the wait. Men took about 12 percent longer than women to remit. Patients with other diseases also waited longer, as did older patients, those with a family history, and those with higher cholesterol. One hospital's patients remitted more slowly than the other's. The authors call the first two years a golden window and urge intensive early management to seize it.
pmc-13471271:

Extreme sweating, weakness, and headache topped the list. Results varied widely between studies, and no difference appeared between migrants within a country and those who crossed borders. The authors call the burden high and under addressed.
pmc-13471371:

The authors call clot removal safe and feasible here, but not proven better.
pmc-13471471:

pmc-13471571:

pmc-13471671:

pmc-13472571:

pmc-13474371:

pmc-13474571:

pmc-13474771:

pmc-13474871:

pmc-13474971:

pmc-13475271:

pmc-13476071:

pmc-13477271:

The authors say development checks and early support should reach every child with a heart defect, not only those who had early surgery.
pmc-13479571:

pmc-13479971:

pmc-13480071:

pmc-13480471:

pmc-13482371:

The catalyst particles came out uniform at about 50 nanometers across, and the tuned microelectrolysis alone removed 97 percent of the drug at its best settings in the optimization runs. Adding catalyst and ultraviolet light pushed removal to 98 percent even at a high starting concentration of 100 milligrams per liter within 55 minutes of treatment. That beat the plainer systems clearly, microelectrolysis alone at 62 percent, catalyst alone at 85 percent, and catalyst without light at 93 percent overall.
pmc-13482471:
Liu and colleagues profile 138 cases of classic adrenocortical carcinoma in 2026, a rare and aggressive adrenal gland cancer, treated at Peking Union Medical College Hospital across four decades. Chinese data on the disease are thin, so the team combined their 1984 to 2024 case records with gene expression profiles from 79 patients in an international cancer database. They charted who gets the disease, how it presents, and which markers track survival.

Women outnumbered men, most patients were diagnosed past 40, and tumors favored the right gland at 1.28 times the left side's rate in the cohort. The median tumor measured 9.05 centimeters across at diagnosis, and the growth marker Ki-67 ran high, with a median of 20 percent of cells staining positive. Advanced stage came with higher Ki-67, and higher Ki-67 in tissue or gene form predicted worse survival, with fast-growing tumors enriched for cell cycle and p53 pathway genes.
pmc-13482571:
Fariba Shohani and three colleagues tested in 2026 how salicylic acid and silicon help a medicinal plant, Scrophularia striata, endure drought. Drought curbs growth and reshapes secondary metabolism, especially in medicinal plants grown for their chemistry.

In a greenhouse trial with two ecotypes at 50 and 100 percent field capacity, drought cut chlorophyll, leaf water, protein, and vessel diameters while raising ion buildup. Silicon sprays boosted antioxidant activity, and silicon plus salicylic acid lifted chlorophyll b, carotenoids, leaf water, and protein under drought. Metabolite counts and diversity fell with drought alone but shifted in treatment- and ecotype-linked ways, showing elicitors rework plant chemistry rather than simply raising it.
pmc-13483471:
Puxian Fang and co-authors report a 2026 study pinning down which part of a host protein coronaviruses cannot do without. The protein, TMEM41B, aids many coronaviruses, yet deleting it outright kills mouse embryos, blocking plans for virus-proof farm animals. Working with a pig deltacoronavirus that can also infect people, the team cut the protein into pieces to find the vital stretch.

The virus needed the protein while copying itself, not while entering or leaving cells. One segment, the sixth membrane span, proved essential alongside a known core region. Mice bred without just that span resisted a mouse coronavirus, suffered less liver damage, and survived better. Trimming one small span may thus yield animals that shrug off coronaviruses while keeping the protein's day job intact.
pmc-13483571:
Zhicheng Ke leads a 2026 study asking whether a blood microRNA combined with bedside lung ultrasound can diagnose acute lung injury more accurately. Blood levels of miR-769-5p, a small regulatory RNA, were measured in patients alongside ultrasound scores of the lungs. Cell experiments with lung-type cells exposed to bacterial toxin tested how the marker affects inflammation signals.

Patients with lung injury showed lower blood levels of the marker than comparison groups. Pairing the blood test with the ultrasound score improved diagnostic accuracy beyond either measure alone, and both measures tracked with injury risk. In cells, raising the marker reduced inflammatory signaling, reactive oxygen output, and cell death. The combined approach may help clinicians confirm a dangerous and hard-to-pin-down lung condition sooner.
pmc-13483671:
Fanrou Zhang and colleagues design a nanoparticle treatment aimed at the mitochondrial stress that fuels gum disease. Their 2026 study builds ceria particles, a known antioxidant material, tuned with ruthenium in different arrangements. The goal combines two jobs, mopping up harmful reactive oxygen inside cells and capturing mitochondrial DNA that leaks out and triggers inflammation.

A middle arrangement using tiny ruthenium clusters beat both single-atom and larger-particle versions on enzyme-like activity and immune calming. The clusters also raised positive surface charge, which helped the particles bind the leaked DNA by electrical attraction. In rats with induced gum disease, local treatment eased gum inflammation and suppressed inflammatory activity. Size and structure tuning therefore decided how well one particle could do both jobs at once.
pmc-13486371:
Machado and colleagues published a 2026 study on what Brazilians know about sepsis across a decade. Sepsis, the body's runaway response to infection, kills hundreds of thousands in Brazil yearly. Early recognition by the public speeds care, yet awareness has lagged. The team compared three national surveys of lay people over time.

Awareness of sepsis improved substantially across the survey years in Brazil. Still, large knowledge gaps remained at the end of the period. Schooling and income shaped awareness more than almost any other trait. People who had met sepsis through family illness also knew more. The authors urge campaigns aimed squarely at lower-income audiences next. Brazil counts roughly 240,000 adult sepsis deaths in intensive care yearly.
pmc-13486471:
Emami-Karvani and co-authors isolated a bacterium from oil refinery sludge that both eats iron and desalts water inside a microbial fuel-cell device. The strain, Advenella faeciporci ZF1, tolerates heavy iron doses that would kill most microbes. Their 2026 study placed it in a three-chamber desalination cell fed with real refinery brine, where bacterial electricity nudges salt ions out of the middle chamber.

Over fifteen days the cell removed about 71 percent of sodium and about 79 percent of calcium from the brine tested. Chloride removal was weaker, at about 28 percent over the same run. At moderate salinity the device produced a peak voltage near 410 millivolts within 48 hours of operation. The bacterium also stored energy-rich granules and showed magnetic sensing behavior. Emami-Karvani proposes it for combined desalination and cleanup of metal-laden industrial wastewater.
pmc-13486671:
Matti Gärtner tests if a shift in dopamine signals changes blood flow in a brain reward hub in depression. Loss of joy is a core sign of major depression, and it ties to weak dopamine action. In this 2026 trial, 111 people took part: 57 with major depression and 54 healthy peers. Each got one low dose of amisulpride, a dopamine blocker, or a dummy pill. No one knew who got which.

The drug raised blood flow in the ventral striatum, the hub in focus, in both groups. No other reward area changed in a firm way. Flow in that hub tracked self-rated loss of joy. One right frontal gap seen on dummy pills faded on the drug. One dose can't treat depression, but the scan gives a clean target to aim at.
pmc-13487171:
Yun Zhang sorts dialysis patients by how tied in they feel with other people. No past study had mapped this spread for people on long-term dialysis. This 2026 study enrolled 365 patients at a large hospital in Anhui, China. In the end, 345 valid forms came back. Scales scored felt ties, social support, and bounce-back strength.

Three groups came out of the data. Low felt ties held 31.9 percent of patients. Mid ties held 42.3 percent, and high ties held 25.8 percent. School level, job state, and dialysis shift each helped set group place. Illness load, bounce-back strength, and support levels played parts too. Dialysis eats much of a patient's week for years. Early checks can point tie-building help to the third who start most cut off.
pmc-13487571:
Boyang Zhou pools trial evidence on a drug class used alone for adult eczema, separating skin-applied from swallowed versions. Published in 2026, the systematic review and meta-analysis gathers five studies of phosphodiesterase-4 inhibitor monotherapy in atopic dermatitis. Quality grading uses a standard observational scale, and pooling runs in dedicated review software.

Topical versions cut eczema severity scores significantly by four weeks and held the gain at twelve weeks, with fewer overall side effects than comparison care. Swallowed versions cut scores progressively more through sixteen weeks and beyond, yet raised systemic side effects significantly. Target lesion severity also fell quickly under topical treatment. Route therefore decides the trade, since creams offer gentler safety while pills offer deeper effect at higher cost to tolerability.
pmc-13487671:
Wong and the editors of Australian Prescriber prepared a short drug comment in 2026 on elafibranor, sold as Iqirvo. The drug treats primary biliary cholangitis, a slow liver disease that harms the small bile ducts. It is meant for adults who gain too little from the usual first drug, ursodeoxycholic acid, or who cannot take that drug at all.

Elafibranor turns on two cell switches, called PPAR-alpha and PPAR-delta, that help control bile acids, swelling, and scar growth in the liver. In the ELATIVE trial, about half of the treated patients met the blood test goal at one year. Very few on placebo did so, and gains showed within four weeks. Common side effects were gut pain, loose stools, and nausea, mostly mild in grade.
pmc-13488571:
Mohammad Alshaban and co-authors study sleep problems in autistic children in Jordan in a 2026 survey. Parents of more than five hundred children filled in a standard sleep form. The children were aged two to fourteen, and most were boys. Poor sleep was very common in this group. Many children fought bedtime, woke in the night, or slept too few hours.

Sleep was worse in children who also had epilepsy, a brain condition that causes seizures. Age and sex made little difference in the scores. The team adjusted the counts for these factors and still found the same pattern. They advise doctors to ask about sleep at each visit and to treat seizures with care, since both shape how well a child rests.
pmc-13491671:
Wenjing Ma and four co-authors gather in 2026 every known case of a rare intestinal cancer defined by loss of the SMARCA4 gene switch. The tumor grows as sheets of undifferentiated cells, lacks any standard treatment, and usually kills quickly. The team adds two new patients to eighteen published cases and summarizes the combined picture.

Four in five patients were men, with an average age of fifty-six, and tumors often showed dead tissue and rapid cell division under the microscope. Staining confirmed SMARCA4 loss in every case, and spread to distant organs was already present in about two of five patients at diagnosis. Median survival was eleven months, and chemotherapy helped little. Two patients, though, stayed in complete remission beyond eighteen months on the immune drug pembrolizumab.
pmc-13493771:
Tulyakanit and co-authors compare two operations for involutional entropion, an age-related condition where the lower eyelid turns inward and lashes rub the eye. Both operations add a lateral tarsal strip, a tightening step at the eyelid's outer corner, but differ in how they fix the muscles that hold the lid out. The 2026 review covers 155 patients treated at two Thai hospitals, with 184 eyes operated on and follow-up averaging just over three years.

Success rates were nearly identical, at just above nine in ten eyes for both procedures on the authors' figures. The Wies operation was quicker, taking about 68 minutes per eye against roughly 83 minutes for the Jones approach in the operating room data. Outcomes diverged by surgeon experience: trainees matched consultants with the Wies method but did notably worse with the Jones method. The authors suggest the quicker operation suits older patients and training settings.
pmc-13493871:
Wang Xin and four colleagues combine gene data and machine learning in 2026 to find the scaffolding genes that matter most in diabetic retinopathy. The disease thickens the retina's basement membranes early on, a remodeling of the extracellular matrix, the protein mesh between cells. Overlapping diabetes and eye-disease gene lists with a matrix database produced nine candidate genes.

Six learning algorithms raced to classify patients, and the Extra Trees model won. Five genes survived importance testing, including SFRP1, FN1, and ECM2, and their expression patterns shifted distinctly from healthy to diabetic to eye-diseased samples. The genes tied into nerve-related pathways and tracked with several immune cell types in the tissue. Regulatory networks and drug databases then connected the five to candidate medicines, sketching future treatment leads.
pmc-13493971:
Awj Twam leads a sixteen-author team testing in 2026 whether a computer can grade liver cancer risk from MRI scans with no human outlining at all. Clinicians normally trace tumors by hand before computing enhancement pattern maps, voxel level fingerprints of how contrast washes through tissue. A lightweight network called PocketNet took over the tracing, and its output fed the same risk analysis.

Human experts disagreeing with each other set the realistic accuracy ceiling, and the machine approached it for larger tumors while lagging on small ones. Reassuringly, risk predictions from machine outlines matched those from hand-drawn ones, because the enhancement fingerprints tolerate wobbly borders. A fully automated biomarker could slot into surveillance programs for high risk patients without adding radiologist hours.
pmc-13494071:
Bollemeijer and colleagues compare two ways of treating severely malnourished children in Jowhar, Somalia: standard facility-based feeding programmes versus village health workers treating children in their villages. World Health Organization guidance allows the village option, but solid evidence has been thin. Their 2026 study enrolled 1,183 children with uncomplicated severe malnutrition during the first months of 2024, split between two facility sites and eight villages, all receiving therapeutic food and weekly checks.

Recovery rates came out nearly equal, with the village group just a shade behind on raw proportions, and adjusted analyses found no difference in weight gain. Children reached by village workers arrived less severely depleted, suggesting earlier detection, and they finished treatment sooner, easing the burden on families. The facility children had started out worse on both arm circumference and weight-for-height measures. The authors back expanding the village model in hard-to-reach areas of Somalia.
pmc-13495171:
Marianne Richaud and colleagues report, in a 2026 study, that DNA floating free in blood carries a record of how it was wrapped in the cell, and that cancer changes the pattern. Such fragments come mostly from blood cells and survive because they ride on nucleosomes, the spools DNA winds around. The team pulled fragment maps from a public database for healthy people and cancer patients.

They found that how fully a spool site is occupied tracks with how tightly DNA binds there, shown by coding patterns and fragment sizes. Occupancy also split cleanly between healthy and cancer samples, and a learning model told seven cancer types from health with high scores on both sensitivity and specificity. Cancer shifted the pattern body-wide, yet each type kept its own marks. The authors offer the readout both as basic insight into blood DNA and as a base for blood-based cancer tests.
pmc-13495371:
Hermel and Saven reported the Scripps regimen in 2026, a low-dose pairing of vemurafenib with rituximab for hairy cell leukemia, a rare slow-growing blood cancer. Standard drugs cure many patients but crush blood counts and immunity, and the usual vemurafenib dose often forces dose cuts without lasting control. Their pilot used a quarter-strength vemurafenib dose for a fixed period alongside the antibody rituximab in fifteen patients, both newly diagnosed and relapsed.

Every patient reached a complete blood count recovery. The overall response rate was 87 percent, with about three in four reaching complete remission and just over half clearing measurable residual disease. Blood counts recovered over one to two months, and the lack of heavy marrow suppression contrasted well with older therapy. Results looked similar in new and previously treated patients. The authors call the regimen a lower-toxicity option that deserves testing in larger prospective studies.
pmc-13498571:
Linzhi Yin and colleagues present in 2026 a computer model that predicts how the inner structure of a common aluminium grade changes during cold rolling. Lab checks and a cost study accompany the model. Rolling thinner strengthens the metal through tiny crystal defects called dislocations, and tracking their density helps explain grain refinement, meaning the shrinking of metal crystals. The work also weighs use of this aluminium in lithium-ion battery parts.

Simulations covered thickness cuts from light to severe, run inside standard engineering software with a custom material routine. Heavier cuts raised plastic strain and refined grains most near surfaces and edges, while defect density rose fast then levelled off. X-ray checks at two mid-level cuts matched predictions closely. Their cost analysis favoured this grade over two rivals across a ten-year view.
pmc-13499271:
Elena Fonseca and others offer a seminar on holistic seizure illness care for adults with intellectual development disorders. In 2026, the review argues for multidisciplinary, person-centered management aligned with International League Against Seizure illness learning goals. Seizure illness is far more common in this group, yet spotting the illness is hampered by communication limits and reliance on caregiver reports.

The authors cover video EEG challenges, drug effects on cognition and quality of life, and personalized plans balancing seizure control against side effects. They also cover set transitions from child to adult care and from family to professional care. Two anonymized cases illustrate practice, with recommendations for reassessing causes, genetic testing, tailored assessments, and sleep and reproductive guidance.
pmc-13499671:
Thekrayat Joodi Jassim and others build a copper-nickel tiny compound and use it to build a sharp current sensor for idarubicin, a cancer-fighting drug. In 2026, the study maps the twin-center compound and its tiny-scale form, at about fifty-six billionths of a meter, then coats a screen-printed graphite probe with it. Tracking drug levels in blood and tissues matters for dosing.

The sensor read idarubicin in a straight line from 0.01 to 3.0 µM, with a finding limit of 0.003 µM, beating the bare probe for drug rusting. The compound also showed germ-killing action against both Gram-plus and Gram-minus germs. The work offers a quick, cheap, single-use sensor for drug and body samples.
pmc-13501571:
Hamza Jawad leads a six-author team reporting a 2026 genome study of sheep that resist the blood-feeding worm Haemonchus contortus, a parasite whose drug resistance is growing. The team infected 32 Rideau Arcott ewe lambs and counted worm eggs in their droppings at five time points. Sixteen animals showed consistent extreme responses: nine resistant and seven susceptible. Resistant lambs carried far fewer eggs, about 10.5-fold lower at day 21 and three- to fourteen-fold lower later. Combining three detection algorithms yielded 22,184 high-confidence variants grouped into 3,751 regions covering 2.63 percent of the genome. One 2.3 megabase duplication containing the mucus-related gene CLCA1 appeared only in resistant sheep, which also held many more gene gains overall. Susceptible sheep showed duplications tied to metabolic problems. The findings offer targets for breeding parasite-resistant flocks.
pmc-13501671:
Sopak Supakul leads a six-author team presenting a 2026 review of how human pluripotent stem cells are used to model the striatum, a brain region central to movement, reward, and habit. Animal models mislead here because cell makeup, timing, and wiring differ between species. The review covers methods for coaxing embryonic and induced pluripotent stem cells into striatal cell types, above all the medium spiny neurons that form the region's main output. Patterning with small molecules, direct transcription factor induction, and three-dimensional organoid and assembloid cultures all feature.

Human medium spiny neurons mature slowly, a trait the authors link to specifically human disease vulnerability. Most disease modelling so far concerns Huntington's disease, where the models exposed early developmental, synaptic, and network faults. Newer work extends to other conditions and to cortico-striatal assembloids that join two brain regions. Remaining gaps include incomplete maturation and missing non-neuronal cell types.
pmc-13501871:
Mohamed Suhail Mohamed Nabi leads a seven-author team with a 2026 narrative review of congenital heart disease in children, spanning early detection, treatment, and life after repair. The team searched PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar for work published from 2015 to 2026, including studies, reviews, and guidelines on diagnosis, survival, development, and quality of life. The conditions range from small septal holes that may close alone to blue, duct-dependent lesions needing treatment within hours of birth.

The review walks the care pathway: prenatal ultrasound and fetal heart scanning, newborn pulse screening, confirmatory heart ultrasound, steadying medicines, catheter procedures, open surgery, and intensive care, followed by structured lifelong follow-up. Survival has improved greatly, yet survivors still face leftover lesions, rhythm problems, lung pressure disease, growth and learning delays, and repeat procedures. The authors argue that early detection, fast referral, lesion-specific planning, and permanent team surveillance decide outcomes.
pmc-13501971:
Richard B. Yapi and six colleagues published this 2026 pilot study on teaching human and animal health workers together to fight brucellosis in Côte d'Ivoire, where the bacterial zoonosis is under-recognised in human medicine. First, a March 2024 survey of 54 professionals in the Hambol region measured baseline knowledge. Then the team designed a one-day interprofessional workshop and ran it in February 2025 with 22 participants from medical, veterinary and public health institutions, testing knowledge before and after.

At baseline, 91 percent of respondents knew of zoonoses, but only 39 percent could identify brucellosis, and nobody named it as a cause of fever or miscarriage. Veterinarians were far more aware, at about 81 percent, than human healthcare workers at about 23 percent. After training, overall knowledge scores rose from 34.5 to 37.0, and symptom recognition improved. Diagnosis and control knowledge did not budge. The authors call joint training feasible and promising, while asking for larger, longer studies.
pmc-13502771:
Meritxell Ventura-Cots and others test whether admission blood pressure predicts short-term death in severe alcohol-associated hepatitis. In 2026, the multi-site forward-looking cohort covers 323 hospitalized patients, checked in an independent cohort of 290, with lives modeled against liver disease gravity, age, and encephalopathy. Mean arterial pressure reflects tissue perfusion and systemic hemodynamics.

Patients below 80 mm of mercury faced twenty-eight-day mortality of 27.3 percent versus 8.0 percent above that threshold, and ninety-day mortality of 40.3 percent versus 15.6 percent, with more acute kidney injury but similar illness rates. Testing showed lower transplant-free lives below the threshold. The authors propose restoring hemodynamic hold as a healing target.
pmc-13503871:
Shengjian Liang leads a team that imaged how a childhood lung virus locks onto human cells, in a 2026 study. The virus, enterovirus D68, can cause severe chest illness and a polio-like weakness in children. A cell protein named MFSD6 serves as its main door into airway cells.

Sharp microscope images show the virus bound to a loop of that protein, for both an old strain and a current one. One part of the loop plugs into a single virus coat unit, while a sugar chain on the loop grips the next unit over. That sugar contact pops out a fatty plug inside the virus and loosens it, priming it to infect. The two-part grip may stop the virus from opening too early.
pmc-13504771:
Miguel A. Quiroz-Reyes leads a team reviewing how surgeons pick filler materials that hold the retina in place after eye surgery, in a 2026 paper. Choices include air, gases, silicone oils, and heavy liquids. Each floats or sinks and grips the eye wall in its own way.

The review ties those physical traits to where the retina tore and how complex the case is. Light fillers support the upper retina; heavy ones prop up the lower part. For simple detachments and many macular holes, air or a short-lived gas works well with less pressure trouble. Heavy oils and staged heavy liquids suit giant tears low in the eye, though proof is mostly observational. Gel-based stand-ins for the eye's natural jelly remain experimental.
pmc-13505171:

One type dissolves over time and the other does not. Working from records and paired three-dimensional scans taken before and after treatment, they measured ridge width, height, and shape at several depths.

Horizontal bone change did not differ clearly between the membrane types at any level measured. How the membrane was fixed in place, the starting ridge angle, and the thickness of the tongue-side bone plate did shape bone change near the crest. Starting concavity depth and top bone thickness also linked with bone gain, though each unit change mattered only slightly. The authors stress careful scan-based planning before surgery, and they ask for prospective studies with more even patient groups.
pmc-13505371:
Masaki Okamura and colleagues present a cheap handheld way to measure the average tilt of leaves across a whole crop canopy. Their tool is a small stereo depth camera held level above the crop, taking colour and depth pictures that simple geometry turns into an average angle.

Tests against a board set at known angles and against single leaves checked with a digital level confirmed the readings. The method's average angle also matched a similar trait from a far pricier canopy analyser. Field trials separated rice, barley, soybean, and wheat by variety, growth stage, and planting density. Because the kit is light, fast, and inexpensive, the authors expect field researchers without sensing expertise to adopt it readily.
pmc-13507271:
Weiqiu Liang leads a 2026 team that brings nickel catalysis into radiation chemistry to tame its wild radical mixtures. Borrowing from light-driven metal chemistry, the team let nickel corral those radicals into chosen pathways.

For carbon-hydrogen arylation, a reaction attaching ring groups to carbon skeletons, yields jumped from under five percent to as high as 82 percent. No light sensitizers were needed, and light-sensitive starting materials survived. Chiral ligands, handed helper molecules, even steered the reaction toward one mirror-image product with strong excess. Radiation-driven synthesis gains selectivity long thought out of reach.
pmc-13508271:
Balveer Saini and Dinesh Kumar Saini present a smart staffing system that adjusts hospital worker levels to live patient demand, in 2026 work. Hospitals face rising costs and demand with fixed rosters that cannot flex at busy hours. Their model blends fuzzy logic, which handles vague inputs like urgency grades, with a genetic algorithm that searches for better rosters. It was tested in simulations modeled on a multi-specialty hospital in Jaipur, India. The system watches queues across several service points at once.

Simulations showed peak-hour waiting times fell by nearly three quarters after the fuzzy logic changes. The genetic search then cut average waiting time by about half compared with fixed staffing. Stress tests showed the model coped well when sudden surges hit the system. The authors argue that live staffing control could trim waits and use scarce staff better, in place of rosters set once and left unchanged.
pmc-13508371:
Jakub Helvich and six co-authors study how teen activities change the web of links among mental health, substance use, and problem social media use, in 2026 work. Data came from a 2022 national school survey in Czechia covering 14,588 adolescents with an average age under fourteen. Network models mapped how heavy social media use, mood symptoms, drinking and smoking, and pastimes connect. Separate networks were built for each pastime type, from solo sports to arts and community groups, and then compared.

When solo sports entered the model, the link between drinking and problem social media use vanished. Community activities and solo sports each softened some conflict and escape links around social media. Only sports tied to less loss of interest in pastimes from social media, with solo sports strongest. Community activities, by contrast, linked to more deception and family conflict around use.
pmc-13511371:
Matera and colleagues published a 2026 survey on gut-microbe knowledge among Italian child-health workers. Gut microbes shape baby and child health, yet clinic routines lag the science. The survey drew 441 professionals in pediatric and perinatal care across Italy. It asked about training, know-how, attitudes, and daily practice habits.

Attitudes toward microbe science ran highly positive across the respondents overall. Self-rated knowledge, though, varied widely between professional groups surveyed. Past training in the topic tracked with both knowledge and practice use. Those without training integrated microbe ideas far less into care decisions. The authors call for structured, team-wide education pathways in the field. Clear clinic pathways for probiotics remain missing, respondents added. Testing habits for microbes in clinic also came under the survey.
pmc-13512371:
Nargis Sultana and Kathryn L. Braun review how the quality of city green space relates to physical activity in older adults, in a 2026 systematic review. Regular movement protects independence and health in later life, and parks may be a daily lever. The team searched three databases for quantitative studies from 2016 to 2024 and sorted green space quality into availability, ease of reach, and attractiveness.

Studies varied widely in how they defined older adults, measured movement, and captured social and geographic context, which blurred direct comparison. Green space features still showed links to activity worth taking seriously. The authors call for age-friendly design as a planning default, shared measurement standards, and more work that asks older people directly what draws them out. Inclusive planning with elder voices, they argue, is the missing piece in much current research.
pmc-13514271:
Chrysa Andrikopoulou and ten co-authors synthesize evidence on whether breathing in micro and nanoplastic particles can shape lung cancer development, in 2026 work. Plastic output keeps climbing, and tiny particles now float through air, water, and living tissue. Indoor and workplace air offer the most plausible lung exposure route. Cell and animal studies add DNA damage, chromosome instability, and disturbed growth signaling to the picture. Chronic redox imbalance, tired immune clean-up cells, and tissue transition programs echo known inflammation-driven cancer routes. Some data cast nanoplastics as promoters that help other airborne toxicants rather than lone starters. Human population evidence remains thin, and cause is not established. The authors frame the particles as plausible modifiers needing long, low-dose study.
pmc-13518871:
Guirong Su and four colleagues build a 2026 theory for predicting electron flow through single molecules sandwiched between unlike metal contacts. Screening 144 varied junctions, the team traced one-way conduction to two linked causes: uneven anchor groups polarize the molecule, and shifting adsorption states change coupling. A composite descriptor joining tunneling and thermal effects predicted behavior with over 93 percent accuracy. Their best configuration reached a rectification ratio of 19.25 at low voltage, far beyond conventional donor-acceptor designs.
pmc-13518971:
Peng Zhao and a large team run a randomized phase 2 trial in 2026 of low-dose baricitinib plus danazol for immune thrombocytopenia. In this disorder the immune system destroys platelets, and bleeding risk climbs. Enrolled patients had already failed steroids and at least one later-line treatment, a hard-to-help group. Each arm received 108 patients across multiple centers.

Six-month durable response, the main goal, reached 45.4 percent with the combination versus 20.4 percent on danazol alone. Side effect rates were similar between arms, near 48 and 45 percent, with two discontinuations and one severe event in each. Zhao and colleagues call the pairing a promising new option needing confirmation.
pmc-13519671:
Yan and colleagues tested a traditional Chinese herbal formula, Taohe Chengqi decoction, against sepsis-linked brain dysfunction in rats, in a 2026 preclinical study. Sepsis, the body's runaway response to infection, often clouds thinking and damages memory through barrier breakdown between blood, gut, and brain. The team induced sepsis surgically, gave the formula at several doses beforehand, and tracked survival, cognition, and tissue damage.

Yan found treated rats showed milder brain symptoms and less damage in the cortex and hippocampus, the memory center. Treated rats also had a tighter intestinal barrier and a preserved barrier around the brain's fluid spaces. The authors present the DUSP6 and FOXO1 pathway as the formula's protective mechanism and a candidate target for this condition.
pmc-13519771:
Kiera H Harwood leads a seven-author review in 2026 on how much intravenous tobramycin people with cystic fibrosis should receive. Clinicians disagree on which concentration target to chase.

Searching four databases yielded 26 eligible studies. Peak concentration and total daily exposure both tracked with lung function gains, with total exposure the steadier predictor. Trough levels and total exposure tracked with toxicity. Current peak and trough targets still look appropriate, the reviewers conclude, and exposure-guided dosing targeting a defined daily range looks promising. Evidence quality was mostly poor, so better trials are needed.
pmc-13519871:
Lenya de Brouwer leads a team building a kidney-liver organ-on-a-chip from human stem cells to model how the two organs talk to each other during drug handling. Liver and kidneys jointly metabolize and clear medicines, so testing organs separately misses interactions. Their chip co-cultures liver-like cell clusters with kidney tubule-like cells under flowing fluid.

Growing the tissues together changed gene activity on both sides. Kidney cells boosted signaling, polarity, and transport programs depending on the liver partner, while liver cells shifted metabolism, fat handling, and protein production. A companion spheroid model activated the prodrug ifosfamide into its toxic metabolite, though levels stayed too low to harm the kidney tissue in this setup.
pmc-13520171:
Martina Randazzo leads an eight-author comparison in 2026 of two developmental tools in toddlers at risk for autism or developmental delay. The Griffiths III scales profile development across domains, while the DAES is an interactive screening tool aimed at autism. Children aged 18 to 48 months were enrolled, 310 in total, including typically developing controls.

Griffiths profiles separated the groups most sharply in language and communication and in personal-social-emotional domains. DAES total scores also separated the groups, running highest in the autism cohort, and higher DAES scores tracked with greater autism severity on the standard ADOS-2 measure. Randazzo and colleagues argue pairing both tools in routine assessment sharpens early detection and guides tailored intervention.
pmc-13520271:
Seyed Ali Hashemi leads a five-author case report in 2026 on a liver fluke found somewhere it almost never goes: inside an abdominal wall muscle. Fasciola hepatica normally settles in the liver and bile ducts after people eat contaminated water plants. A 55-year-old Iranian woman arrived with five months of abdominal pain and major weight loss, no jaundice, and a mass in her right upper abdominal wall.

Stool tests found no eggs, and blood work was nearly normal. During admission a flatworm emerged from her rectus abdominis muscle, and tissue examination showed parasite-driven muscle inflammation with abscess. Morphology and antibody testing confirmed the fluke species. She received triclabendazole and stayed well across 90 days of follow-up.
pmc-13520371:
Iris Parés-Salomón and colleagues examine in 2026 how sitting, standing and moving through the day relate to muscle and joint symptoms in hybrid office workers who split time between home and office. Hybrid routines can raise total sitting time, with possible costs for comfort.

Questionnaires and thigh-worn activity monitors covered 163 workers in Ireland, Slovenia, Spain and the Netherlands. Symptoms in the past week were recorded with a standard Nordic questionnaire. Analysis treated the day as a fixed budget, so more sitting means less of something else, and swap calculations estimated effects of trading sitting for activity. Full pattern results guide employers planning healthier hybrid routines.
pmc-13520471:
Mohamed and colleagues reviewed in 2026 how well TheraCal LC, a light-set dental filling material, works for capping the soft pulp inside permanent teeth. Pulp capping aims to keep a tooth alive after deep decay is cleaned out, instead of removing the pulp. TheraCal is easy to handle and releases minerals, but firm proof of how well it works had been thin.

The team searched four databases and found 11 trials, run between 2015 and 2025, that tested TheraCal against older materials such as calcium hydroxide, Biodentine, and MTA. Across follow-up of six months to three years, TheraCal matched the rivals on success, kept pain low, and supported new dentin growth under the cap. Most trials carried some bias risk, mostly in patient assignment, but the authors judge TheraCal a sound choice.
pmc-13520671:
Jordan A. Smink and Robert W. Lamb share in 2026 a scalable routine for turning Muddiest Point notecards from large microbiology classes into one shared review video. Asking students to name their murkiest concept works well in small classes, yet hundreds of cards can bury an instructor.

Cards are grouped into recurring themes, ranked by frequency and teaching importance, then answered in a chaptered video with a worksheet. Pause-and-predict prompts, live sketching and fill-in tasks keep viewing active. Students can jump straight to their sticking point. Guidance covers accessibility, online variants and light-touch evaluation for busy teaching teams.
pmc-13521271:
Ruiz-Sola and co-workers in Spain put forth in 2026 a mutant green alga as a stopwatch for how plant cells build their solar panels. The alga, Chlamydomonas, is a one cell swimmer used in labs worldwide. Their mutant, called chIL, lacks a dark enzyme for making green pigment. Kept in the dark, its cells stay yellow, with a bare, unbuilt chloroplast, the cell part that runs sun based food making.

One flash of light starts the build at once. Pigments, sun proteins, and working food making all show within one to three hours, fed by starch the cells stored. A drug that blocks the chloroplast's own protein making froze the build and sent alarm words back to the cell core. The team says the mutant lets labs time each build step, and test how the chloroplast talks to the rest of the cell.
pmc-13523371:
Shivani Singh, Ruhani Singh, and Sunita Sharma review artificial intelligence tools for studying neglected protein families in a 2026 article. Many protein groups lack lab structures, and older modeling methods struggle with them. Modern deep learning systems can now predict structures at near-lab quality, model how proteins bend and their disordered regions, and tackle contacts between proteins and between proteins and drug-like compounds.

Two case studies, covering orphan receptors and disordered regions, illustrate what the new tools can do for systems once considered hopeless. The authors also compare older and AI pipelines, summarize key model lines, and offer practice guidelines. Remaining challenges include lab validation, modeling movement, and ethical questions around generated data. The review serves as a roadmap for lighting up the dark parts of the protein world.
pmc-13523471:
Emil Bečka and others report 2026 experiments on how damaged mitochondria trigger neutrophil traps, sticky webs of DNA that neutrophils cast out. After trauma, such debris can provoke these traps, harming tissue and raising infection risk. The team asked whether that harmful response could be quieted without weakening defense against bacteria.

Lab, animal, and patient blood work showed intact mitochondria drive trap formation through two receptors working together, with several signaling proteins at work. A lab-made activator of one receptor, named FPRA14, reduced mitochondria-driven trap formation while keeping phagocytosis, bacterial killing, and infection control in a mouse model that paired mitochondrial injection with staphylococcal pneumonia. Two signaling proteins pulled in opposite directions. The authors propose this receptor as a focused treatment target after trauma.
pmc-13524071:
Hannah Viola leads a large team in a 2026 study showing that empty nanoparticles can resolve lung fibrosis in mice by reprogramming immune cells. Fibrosis burdens many organs and has few treatments. Innate immune cells can drive scarring, yet they also help dissolve it, and the team tested whether degradable particles could switch monocytes toward repair.

Particles made of a biodegradable polymer, carrying no drug cargo, shifted profibrotic macrophages in culture toward antifibrotic activity, altered their energy use, and raised enzymes that break down collagen and related matrix. Given intravenously, the particles resolved established bleomycin-induced lung scarring and reversed the direction of over a thousand genes. Treated lungs showed less profibrotic signaling, more repair pathways, and greater monocyte recruitment, supporting materials-based immune therapy.
pmc-13524671:
Jeffrey Coombs and colleagues study, in a 2026 database analysis, outcomes after arthroscopic rotator cuff repair with or without tranexamic acid given around surgery. The drug limits bleeding and is used to improve visibility and shorten operating time in shoulder repair. Whether it changes later complications, pain, and opioid use was the question.

Using the TriNetX database for repairs between 2010 and 2024, the team matched 7,645 patients who received the drug with an equal matched group who did not. Patients given tranexamic acid filled fewer opioid prescriptions at one month and at one year. Readmission odds were lower at one year but not at thirty days. Rates of pulmonary embolism and superficial or deep surgical infections did not differ significantly between matched groups.
pmc-13524971:
Scagliola and co-authors linked a 2026 protein called eIF6 to epigenetic control in skeletal muscle, the body's largest metabolic organ. Histone acetylation, a chemical tag that loosens DNA packaging, helps set muscle gene activity. Whether eIF6, a translation factor, steers that tagging in muscle was unknown.

Lowering eIF6 in cultured muscle cells raised histone acetylation, and the same pattern appeared in cells from mice carrying one copy of the gene. Whole animals showed pronounced excess acetylation, strongest in younger mice, Scagliola found. Two deacetylase enzymes, HDAC4 and HDAC5, fell in step with the rise in acetylation marks. Experiments across cells, mice, and fruit flies pinned the drop on eIF6 controlling how those enzymes' messages are translated into protein.
pmc-13526071:
Sébastien Goutal and colleagues compared two PET tracers for imaging brain cholesterol turnover in animals. Published in 2026, the head-to-head study tested [18F]CHL-2205 against [18F]T008 in macaques, healthy rats, an Alzheimer rat model, and mice engineered to overproduce the enzyme cholesterol 24-hydroxylase. That enzyme clears cholesterol from the brain and is thought to shift in Alzheimer disease and other brain disorders.

Both tracers behaved well, with similar breakdown profiles and confirmed target binding under blocking. CHL-2205, however, showed higher brain uptake in macaques and rats, stronger binding potential, and greater sensitivity to modest enzyme increases in engineered mice. In Alzheimer-model rats, both tracers rose over controls, with CHL-2205 rising more. The authors favor CHL-2205 for future translational studies of brain cholesterol balance.
pmc-13526171:
Nisha Dua and colleagues report a study, published in 2026. It compares two diode laser methods for oral leukoplakia. These are white mouth patches. They are the most common mouth disorder with a risk of turning malignant. Sixty patients had confirmed uniform lesions. One group received laser ablation, which vaporises tissue. The other received laser excision, which cuts tissue out.

Patients were checked at one, three, and five weeks. They were checked again at six months. Ablation gave less pain, bleeding, and swelling. Early healing was faster too. But recurrence was substantially higher after ablation. This was especially true where biopsies showed mild abnormal cell change. The authors favour ablation for lesions without abnormal change. They favour excision where abnormal change is present.
pmc-13526471:
Balaban and colleagues present a 2026 case report of nerve injury blamed on a surgical tourniquet, the cuff used to drain and block blood in a limb during surgery. A 27-year-old construction worker had a spiral arm fracture fixed with a plate. A sterile exsanguination tourniquet sat high on the arm for seventy minutes, while the radial nerve was found and protected in the wound.

After surgery the patient showed weakness and sensory loss in the radial nerve's territory, the pattern called radial-dominant neuropathy, despite the nerve being visually safe. With the nerve protected in surgery, the cuff was the likely cause. The deficit was transient and recovered. A correctly placed cuff can still injure nerves, so time under pressure matters.
pmc-13526771:
Bonsang Koo and a large team report a neuroscience study, published in 2026. It concerns a chemical tag on messenger RNA. The tag is called m6A.
