It helps growing neurons move messages along their long fibres. Proteins read the tag. One reader is YTHDF2. The study asks what that reader does in young cortical neurons.

Removing the tag-writing protein Mettl14 impaired axon growth. This was in the developing brain. Many messages were left stranded in neurites. The team mapped tagged messages at single-letter resolution. The tags linked to synapse and axon genes. YTHDF2 works with motor proteins to carry tagged messages outward. The protein FMRP aids this transport.
pmc-13527271:
Rui Tian and Klaus Scheffler propose, in a 2026 MRI methods study, a compression scheme that makes highly accelerated scans using rapidly modulated magnetic fields computationally practical. Such field modulations enrich the signal but break ordinary reconstruction, creating a heavy data burden. Their group-patch approach compresses small data patches that share the same field patterns.

Because the modulations change slowly compared with the sampling rate, one compression matrix per field group can be computed once and reused across patches, mimicking extra virtual receiver channels. Tests on human brain scans at two field strengths achieved joint compression factors between eleven and twenty times with negligible encoding loss. Reconstruction times and memory use fell dramatically, with single slices finishing in seconds. The authors frame the method as removing a core bottleneck.
pmc-13527471:
Pate and colleagues published a 2026 case report on hives in a newborn given a heart drug. Prostaglandin E1 keeps a vital heart channel open in babies born with heart defects. Their patient, a nine-day-old boy, waited on the drug for heart surgery. On day nine, a spreading red rash covered his face, trunk, and limbs.

The patches moved and faded within hours, a classic hive pattern. No breathing trouble or other allergy signs appeared at any point. Such rashes stem from the drug's direct action, not true allergy. Mistaking them for allergy could stop a life-saving drip needlessly. The drug was able to continue while the rash was watched. Skin teams can help separate true allergy from drug effects early.
pmc-13528171:
Özgür Appak, Nilay Danis, and Sükran Köse audit missed hepatitis C confirmation testing at a Turkish hospital in a 2026 study. The records cover all antibody tests in 2025. Nearly twenty-eight thousand tests ran on about twenty-four thousand people. Antibodies showed in about 1.28 percent. A positive antibody needs a gene test to prove active infection.

That follow-up was never ordered for about a third of reactive patients. Stored blood from seventy-nine such patients was retested. About four percent carried active infection. Specialist clinics ordered confirmation far more often than general ones. Repeat antibody testing was common and wasteful, seen in about thirteen percent of patients. Nobody retested many times had newly turned positive. The authors push automatic reflex gene testing in the lab. It would close the gap and cut pointless repeats.
pmc-13529171:
Cao and Hai reported a 2026 case of a 25-year-old woman who survived a pulmonary embolism that caused cardiac arrest. A pulmonary embolism is a large blood clot blocking the lung arteries. Risk factors included estrogen-containing birth control pills and a leg injury that kept her immobile. Scans confirmed a saddle clot at the pulmonary artery split and a vein clot.

Cao describes treatment with veno-arterial ECMO as a bridge while clot-dissolving drug was delivered through two catheters placed at the clot. ECMO is a machine that pumps and oxygenates blood outside the body. During care she developed airway bleeding, the complication of blood thinners. The team controlled it with local measures and a vessel-tightening drug, continuing anticoagulation rather than stopping it. She came off ECMO after 73 hours and recovered, a result the authors offer as a template for balancing clot and bleeding risks.
pmc-13530171:
Sedigheh Ashkavandi and co-authors test in 2026 how a membrane lipid called GM1 affects brain cell firing when a key chemical messenger system is damaged. Loss of cholinergic signaling harms memory circuits in Alzheimer disease. Recordings came from single cells in the hippocampus of living anesthetized male rats.

Three GM1 doses each raised firing rates, with larger doses giving stronger lifts. Rats with lesions mimicking cholinergic loss responded more sharply than controls, even at the lowest dose. Firing stayed within normal ranges. The pattern suggests membrane-focused treatments may act differently depending on how damaged a circuit already is.
pmc-13531971:
Rushuang Yang and co-authors test in 2026 whether advanced MRI measures of squeezed lower-back nerves match patient symptoms. People with one-sided disc herniation pressing a nerve root underwent nerve-focused imaging plus a quantitative T2 mapping method that senses tissue water. Pain and disability scores came from standard questionnaires.

Visual nerve readings caught about 92 percent of symptomatic cases yet flagged half of painless sides too. Swelling values ran higher on the squeezed side, and the side-to-side gap tracked leg numbness scores. Combining pictures with numbers may guide treatment choices better than either alone.
pmc-13534671:
Guoqian Hao and colleagues assembled a full genome for apple of Peru, a medicinal nightshade with insect-repelling power. Published in 2026, the genome paper used long reads plus Hi-C linking for Nicandra physalodes, a South American herb now widespread in disturbed habitats. Its withanolides and alkaloids underpin both medicine and pest deterrence, yet genomic resources were thin.

The genome spans about 934 million bases, with nearly all sequence anchored to ten chromosome groups and a long contig N50 near 87 million bases. Repeats cover about seventy-three percent of the genome, and nearly 28,000 protein-coding genes were predicted, almost all given a known role. The resource opens study of special chemical production, insect resistance, and adaptation. Readers get a genome guide for a chemically rich non-crop nightshade.
pmc-13536571:
Sarah Wazlawik and Claudia Oppenauer run in 2026 a pilot study on drug side effects and pill taking in borderline personality disorder. Most patients take mood drugs even though talk therapy is the first-line care, and side effects are common. Records came from a special unit in Eggenburg with confirmed diagnoses.

Most patients reported side effects, led by low mood, tiredness, dizziness, and shaking, while forgetting doses drove most missed pills. Tests found no path from side effects to symptoms through pill taking in the small group. Larger clinic studies with direct dose checks are needed next.
pmc-13536671:
Ronnie Sebro leads a 2026 pilot imaging study of soft tissue sarcoma, a rare cancer that grows in muscle, fat, and other soft tissues. Five patients received two kinds of PET scans within two weeks, one using a tracer that marks low-oxygen areas inside tumors. Tumor tissue was also tested for three proteins linked to low oxygen and poor outcomes.

Larger tumors showed more of one protein, PLOD2, and higher-grade tumors showed stronger uptake of the low-oxygen tracer. The two scan types also tracked closely with each other. The authors stress that five patients are far too few for firm conclusions. They present the results only as early clues that justify a larger trial of the tracer as a noninvasive marker.
pmc-13536771:
Ramesh Kunwar and colleagues survey job satisfaction among local health workers after decentralization in Nepal in a 2026 study. Nepal shifted to a federal system a decade ago, moving health duties toward local levels. A total of 444 workers in Sudurpashchim Province rated satisfaction across work setting, staffing adjustment and policy, and local governance. Statistical models tested which roles and regions reported lower satisfaction.

Overall satisfaction was low, with fewer than one in six workers satisfied. Satisfaction was highest for work setting and lowest for adjustment processes and policies after federalization. Senior officers, highly educated staff, and Himalayan region staff reported lower satisfaction in key areas, while municipal health staff reported higher governance satisfaction. The authors urge direct engagement on adjustment rules and career growth in remote areas.
pmc-13539671:
Senguler Ciftci and Erman reframe how the cancer protein KRAS switches on, using a branch of mathematics that counts network configurations. KRAS flips between an active form bound to GTP and an inactive GDP form, and that switch drives a large share of human cancers, yet its logic stayed fuzzy in on-off models. Their 2026 generalisation of the Gaussian network model treats the protein's residue-contact map as a weighted network and computes its thermodynamics exactly, using a classic theorem about spanning trees.

The accounting revealed an entropy-driven bargain: the active state pays a systematic energy penalty. It buys it back with a marked gain in conformational entropy, the sheer number of ways its contact network can arrange itself. The balance tips at a defined effective temperature. One stretch, the Switch I region, emerged as the control locus where the nucleotide rewires the network.
pmc-13539971:
Petr Bureš leads a 2026 comparative study of genome architecture in ferns and flowering plants, the two great lineages of vascular plants. Ferns carry famously large genomes, yet how their chromosomes evolve beside the faster-changing flowering plants was unsettled.

The team built a dataset covering more than eleven hundred fern species, with genome size, chromosome counts, base composition, and pore sizes on leaves. Fern chromosomes changed far more slowly than those of flowering plants, and genome size stayed tied to chromosome number, hinting that ferns rarely slim down after genome doubling. Bigger leaf pores in ferns vanished once genome size was accounted for, pointing to cell size as the driver.
pmc-13540871:
Sofyan Sufri and Misbahul Jannah assess, in a 2026 qualitative study, how well North Aceh District in Indonesia runs its system for finding, reviewing, and answering maternal deaths. Aceh's maternal death rate sits above the national average despite the national policy being adopted.

Interviews with sixty policymakers, health workers, and community representatives, plus five programme documents, were judged against eight implementation measures. Work concentrated heavily on the first step, identifying deaths, while reporting, review, response, and monitoring lagged. Weak public communication, low community involvement, thin frontline skills, fuzzy accountability, and constant staff rotation held the cycle back. The authors call for fuller follow-through at every stage.
pmc-13542071:
Xiang Li and five colleagues analyse, in a 2026 study, what makes crowdsourced magnetic maps of roads accurate enough to use for positioning. Volunteers' phones can collect the Earth's magnetic fingerprints cheaply, yet device quality and collection habits vary wildly.

Trajectory data from many smartphone models were judged on both position accuracy and magnetic accuracy. High-performance mainstream phones gave the cleanest data. Repeating a route about ten times improved accuracy, after which extra passes bought little. Quiet periods such as night or early morning cut electromagnetic noise, and open ground beat tower-shadowed urban canyons. The authors turn these findings into a boundary-setting method for planning collection campaigns.
pmc-13542171:
Hossein Kadkhodayan and Taher Alizadeh build, in a 2026 materials study, a three-part photocatalyst meant to turn carbon dioxide into solar fuels using visible light, answering the climate pressure of rising emissions. Single photocatalysts convert slowly, so the design stacks complementary structures at different size scales.

Nickel and copper nanoparticles were loaded onto a double perovskite crystal grown with a carbon nitride partner, forming junctions that shepherd charges apart before they recombine uselessly. A battery of imaging and spectroscopy tools verified the structure. Performance was tuned with a Taguchi experimental design across temperature, stirring, reaction time, gas and catalyst doses, light intensity, lamp distance, and acidity. The authors report an optimised, reusable system.
pmc-13543371:
In a 2026 study, Yicang Wang's team asked whether blood magnesium levels track with diabetic retinopathy, the eye damage that diabetes can cause. Three groups of 150 people took part: one without diabetes, one with diabetes but spared eyes, and one with retinopathy. The team read metabolic and inflammatory markers, tested which factors pointed to eye disease, and checked magnesium in the blood and retinal tissue of diabetic mice.

Magnesium and sodium stepped down step by step from the healthy group to the retinopathy group, while blood sugar control grew worse along the same path. Models tied higher blood sugar and longer time with diabetes to greater retinopathy risk, with magnesium pointing the other way, toward lower risk. Adding magnesium to the standard sugar marker sharpened detection. Diabetic mice showed the same low magnesium in blood and retina, giving the human pattern a lab echo.
pmc-13543771:
Emirhan Atlayan, Berkay Berk, and Sevcan Unluturk published a 2026 proof-of-concept study estimating the pigment content of red wine from photographs, avoiding laboratory chemistry. Anthocyanins give red wine much of its colour and value, and their total amount is a quality yardstick. Wine was photographed at three depths and in three colour systems. Three modelling approaches, from a linear chemometric method to a neural network, learned to predict the pigment measure from image features.

The neural network won, explaining about ninety-seven percent of the variation in cross-validation, with the random forest close behind at ninety-six percent. The linear model trailed at about ninety percent and made the largest errors. A shallow two-millimetre sample photographed in the right colour space worked best. A camera and software, the authors argue, could give wineries a fast, non-destructive pigment check, at least under controlled conditions.
pmc-13544571:
Xun Li and colleagues published a 2026 retrospective study of complex chronic conditions in a children's intensive care unit in central-southern China, reviewing 9,589 admissions from 2020 to 2025. A standard paediatric classification sorted each child's long-term conditions by organ system. The team asked which condition types, and which combinations, carried the worst odds of bad outcomes such as organ failure and death.

Nearly half of admissions, forty-nine percent, involved at least one complex chronic condition. Yet those children accounted for about seventy percent of deaths and adverse outcomes and well over half of all bed days. Multiple conditions raised the odds further. Transplant-related and metabolic conditions were the riskiest single types, and the pairing of metabolic disease with cancer multiplied odds more than eightfold. Cancer with blood or immune disorders was the commonest pairing. Building the condition pattern into triage, the authors argue, sharpens risk prediction.
pmc-13545571:
Qi Pan and colleagues used three MRI-based measures in 2026 to probe subtle brain changes in primary insomnia, a sleep disorder linked with thinking problems. Thirty-two patients and 32 healthy adults of similar background had sleep, mood, and cognition assessed alongside detailed brain scans. The measures captured white matter damage, fluid movement along blood vessels, and enlarged spaces around vessels.

Patients showed more white matter heterogeneity than controls, while signs tied to the brain's waste-clearing system were weaker and less consistent. Across everyone, worse white matter scores went with poorer results on two standard cognition tests. The authors urge caution, given the small group and the fact that everyone was scanned only once.
pmc-13546571:
Qianlong Ling and colleagues studied in 2026 how sphingosine-1-phosphate, a fatty signaling molecule in blood, helps colorectal cancer grow blood vessels and spread. Tumors need new vessels to feed themselves, and this lipid is known to promote several cancers. Blood tests showed patients with colorectal cancer carried more of the molecule than expected, alongside higher levels of a vessel marker.

In cell experiments, the lipid made cancer cells behave more aggressively and raised output of VEGFA, a vessel growth factor, through the STAT3 signaling switch. Blocking that switch or the growth factor removed much of the effect, and mouse tumors confirmed the pathway in living tissue. The authors suggest the lipid could serve as a marker for how far the disease has progressed.
pmc-13547371:
Zheng and colleagues used Britain's postwar sugar rationing in 2026 as a natural experiment on how the first thousand days of life shape aging. Human proof that early nutrition steers lifelong health is scarce, since such trials cannot be run. Rationing ended in 1953, so people conceived just before and just after differ mainly in early sugar exposure. The study covered about sixty-five thousand UK Biobank participants.

Those exposed to rationing developed hallmark aging diseases about nine percent less often. Their risk of death from any cause ran about nineteen percent lower. By several biological age clocks they measured one to just over one year younger, with lungs, heart, and liver looking youngest. Blood protein patterns fit the picture. The authors say the results back current advice to limit added sugar in infancy.
pmc-13548471:
Eren Güzeloğlu and colleagues gauged Istanbul children's doctors' comfort with medical AI. Published in 2026, the snapshot study surveyed 130 child doctors at a major top-level hospital. AI now aids child spotting, handling, and decision support, yet uptake hinges on doctors' knowledge and views.

Doctors scored upbeat attitudes at 3.81 and downbeat at 2.83, with overall readiness at 74.97, a moderate-to-high level. Older age tracked lower upbeat views and readiness, and doctors with 21-plus years lagged younger peers. Positive attitudes strongly matched readiness scores, with ability and thinking as top drivers. The authors call for age-targeted training and workplace backup, most of all for senior doctors.
pmc-13548571:
Jinhui Xu and colleagues lay out a 2026 study protocol for spotting frailty in older adults hospitalized with tuberculosis in Guizhou Province, China. Frailty raises the risk of poor outcomes, yet it is rarely measured in this group, and machine learning has seldom been tried for the task. Enrollment runs from June 2026 to May 2027 across several hospitals.

Clinicians will record clinical, laboratory, and personal details, then train algorithms such as logistic regression, random forests, and gradient boosting to classify frailty within a week of admission. Repeated cross-checks inside the data and a separate external check are planned to guard against overfitting. Secondary measures include hospital stay length, delays in seeking care, and deaths within thirty days. The authors hope the models give busy wards a quick, reliable frailty screen that supports personal care plans.
pmc-13549971:
Shane M. Dunne and colleagues model how river floods and sea-level rise will ripple through Europe's regional economies by 2100, in a 2026 economic study. Europe is warming fastest among continents, and its regions are tightly traded together, so local damage can travel. Using a dynamic economy-wide model split into fine regional units, the team simulated both hazards together and tracked direct losses plus the indirect effects through supply chains and markets.

The combined hazards acted as a divergent force. Some regions faced devastating output declines of up to about half their economy, while others were lightly touched. Poorer regions lost proportionally the most, widening gaps both between and within countries. The authors argue that continent-level averages hide this splintering, and that regional detail should guide adaptation spending if cohesion policy is to keep regions from drifting apart.
pmc-13550571:
Özcan Öcük reported in 2026 on propeller flaps used to repair soft tissue defects in the lower part of the leg. In a retrospective review, 52 patients aged 23 to 58 received flaps sized from 8 by 4 to 18 by 7 centimeters. The study focused on perforator arteries and on what surgeons did when blood pooled in the flap, a frequent problem.

No patient lost a flap completely, while three developed partial tissue death. Ten patients had moderate venous congestion and received leech therapy, and 23 had an extra venous connection made during surgery. Larger artery diameter linked to more supercharging, while a greater rotation angle raised the risk of congestion, which the author presents as manageable with these salvage steps.
pmc-13551971:
Meng Xie and five colleagues analyzed a stomach germ and metabolic markers in central China in a 2026 study. The germ is Helicobacter pylori. It is best known for stomach harm, yet it may affect the whole body. The study held 83,054 adults at one health center, from 2021 to 2025. A breath test set each person's germ status. Models adjusted for age, sex, body mass, and many blood measures.

About a quarter of the group tested positive. Rates peaked in the early fifties. Raised LDL cholesterol was the strongest independent link to infection. Fasting glucose also linked to infection. Total cholesterol's link faded once LDL was counted. The team calls the germ a body-wide metabolic stressor and floats gains from curing it.
pmc-13552571:
Maria Fernanda de Almeida, with a large global team, published a 2026 survey of delivery room care for very preterm infants. Twelve neonatal networks took part. A pre-tested online survey went to 608 units. It asked how often set practices were used for infants born before twenty-nine weeks. Answers reflected practice in 2022 and 2023. Each practice was rated from very frequent to never.

Replies came from 382 units, with response rates varying by network. Active resuscitation at twenty-two weeks was frequent in only about a fifth of units. The share rose steeply by twenty-four weeks. Delayed cord clamping was common. Cord milking was less common, except in Japan, where most units reported it. Most units began breathing support with low oxygen levels. The team calls for studies that link these practice gaps to infant outcomes.
pmc-13554071:
Adesuwa S Erhunmwunse leads a five-author team studying how cover crops reshape soil life in citrus groves in a 2026 report. Cover crops are plants sown between trees to guard and feed the soil. The team compared seeded mixes with weedy ground in a young grove and an old one. Soil was sampled at three depths across two years.

Soil fungi answered to cover crops, while bacteria barely shifted in either grove. In the young grove, one mix changed fungal groups within three months, and both mixes stood apart after two years. In the old grove, depth shaped fungi most, with cover effects strongest near the surface. Helpful fungi that partner with roots grew richer under cover in both groves.
pmc-13554171:
Shahrina Akter, Tokey Sifullah Tanjil, and Md Golam Hafez study colliding sound-like waves in dusty plasma in a 2026 paper. Dusty plasma mixes electrons, ions, and heavy charged dust grains, found in space and in labs. Their waves move toward each other head-on through this mix, pulled by a drag force from flowing ions. Math methods drawn from wave theory yield the rules for these paired waves.

Solutions show both repeating wave trains and lone humps that hold their shape. The team built answers for one, two, and three humps meeting at once. Collisions shifted each wave's position, and plasma settings tuned how big that shift grew. The results guide lab and space studies of how such waves trade energy.
pmc-13555871:
Suli Guo leads an eight-author team tuning water flosser settings for plaque removal in a 2026 study. Water jets aid brushing, yet the best mix of nozzle size, distance, and pressure was unproven in real mouths. Twelve volunteers wore custom titanium guides, printed from their own mouth scans, holding the jet at exact settings. Nine setting combinations were tested in a structured grid.

Pressure mattered most, then distance, then nozzle size. The best mix paired a mid-size nozzle and mid distance with the highest pressure tried. Plaque was stained before and after thirty seconds of jetting, and removal was measured in three dimensions. The winning settings cleared about ninety percent of plaque in the target zone, giving designers firm numbers.
pmc-13555971:
Quan Zuo, Li Zhao, and Tao Ge test admission blood markers for predicting heart failure or shock during hospital care after major heart attacks in a 2026 research note. Their single-centre records held 509 attacks, with 140 patients having both key markers measured within a day. One marker, BNP, reflects heart wall strain, while D-dimer reflects clot breakdown. Nearly half the marker group developed failure or shock.

A combined burden score tied strongly to those complications after adjustment. BNP alone performed just as strongly, with slightly better sorting accuracy. Patients high on both markers fared worst, with four in five developing failure or shock. The authors label the work exploratory risk enrichment, not a validated prediction tool.
pmc-13557871:
Junyi Mo and ten colleagues profiled in 2026 a dangerous lung inflammation caused by cancer immunotherapy drugs, using patients who had undergone lung biopsy. Checkpoint inhibitor pneumonitis can kill, yet its symptoms and scans resemble infection or tumour growth, and its tissue patterns were poorly mapped. The team reviewed 217 suspected cases at a Guangzhou hospital between 2018 and 2022 and analysed the 44 patients with usable biopsy tissue.

Records, scans read by two radiologists, laboratory values, and slides read by lung pathologists were combined for each case. Biopsies came from needle sampling guided by ultrasound or other routes, and the study catalogued clinical features, scan patterns, and microscopic appearances side by side. Follow-up data fed an exploratory look at prognosis. The authors aim to give clinicians a firmer basis for recognising this side effect and telling it apart from its imitators.
pmc-13558571:
Akbar Hussain and seven colleagues assembled in 2026 a phone-based prototype that guesses diseases from combinations of symptoms and then offers lifestyle guidance. Predicting illness when several symptoms overlap is a recognised hard problem, and the authors are careful about the limits of such tools. Their experiments used a public dataset of about five thousand symptom records spanning 41 diseases, together with files of precautions, medicines, diets, and exercises.

Seven standard machine learning models were compared, and the strongest reached high accuracy under the study's testing protocol. An Android app backed by a web service turns the winning model's guess into matched advice drawn from the supporting files. The authors insist the prototype is a decision-support and teaching aid, not a validated diagnostic device, and they list outside clinical testing and clinician review as essential next steps.
pmc-13562271:
Elisabeth Hertenstein and colleagues measure how common insomnia disorder is among ward patients with mental illness, using full diagnostic interviews rather than survey forms. Their 2026 study covers 427 patients across four German and two Swiss mental-health hospitals, applying DSM-5 criteria for the disorder. Sleep complaints are famous in mental illness, yet a formal disorder label had never been counted ward by ward.

Nearly a third of patients, 30.4 percent in the interview results, met criteria for an added insomnia disorder. Another 38.4 percent had regular insomnia symptoms without reaching the disorder threshold, meaning over two thirds bore sleep complaints of some weight. Rates did not vary by age or psychiatric diagnosis group, though women were hit much more than men. The authors call for routine sleep checks on wards and for fitting cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia, the first-line treatment, to ward care.
pmc-13562771:
Mackenzie L. McKeown and Alexander M. Crizzle pilot a health profile of Canadian long-haul truck drivers, probing how obesity ties to productivity and test performance. Trucking logs Canada's highest rate of worker compensation claims, and drivers work long sedentary hours far from home. The 2026 study recruited 36 drivers through associations and companies nationwide. Each completed questionnaires on work and health, gave basic body and blood-pressure measures, and sat batteries of thinking, vision, and movement tests.

Nearly two-thirds of the group, 63.9 percent, met the obesity threshold. Drivers with obesity took more sick days, more often worked while sick or hurt, and reported more crashes than leaner peers. Their divided attention and concentration also scored worse on testing. Other measures showed no clear split. The authors call the productivity cost real but the cognition picture tangled, and they frame the small pilot as groundwork for a fuller national study.
pmc-13563571:
Fábio M. Svartman and six colleagues ask which face of chronic lung disease makes lung cancer screening scans come back positive in Brazil. People with COPD crowd screening programmes because entry rules rest on age and smoking. The 2026 analysis covered 1,034 eligible patients with chronic respiratory disease at a tertiary hospital, all screened with low-dose CT. COPD was defined four ways: a doctor's diagnosis, a breathing-test blockage ratio, both together, or emphysema seen on the scan itself.

Positive scans ran at 12.6 percent, the most worrying category at 5.6 percent, and cancer was found in 2.2 percent. Only scan-seen emphysema, present in 76.5 percent, independently raised the odds of a positive result, with a prevalence ratio of 1.74, and of the worst category, at 3.27. Diagnosis labels and airflow numbers showed no link. The authors say emphysema, not the COPD label, is the feature screening teams should watch.
pmc-13564071:
Sarah J. Miller and a large team build, in a 2026 study, a single-cell atlas of polycystic kidney disease. Data came from several mouse models that differ in faulty gene, age of onset, and speed of decline. The atlas maps which kidney cell types change, which genes switch on or off, and how cells signal to each other when cysts form.

One signal stood out across models: osteopontin, made by the gene Spp1, rose in disease-linked cell clusters. Deleting that gene in one model modestly reduced cyst severity and improved kidney function. The team also released a free searchable website so other researchers can mine the atlas for treatment targets.
pmc-13567871:
Vlatko Karanfilovski and colleagues survey kidney biopsy and glomerular disease care in North Macedonia, a country of about two million people. Glomerular diseases, which attack the kidney's filtering units, are an important cause of kidney failure there, and biopsy is the key to diagnosing them. This 2026 global perspective traces the field from the first biopsy in the 1970s to today's national centre at the University Hospital of Nephrology in Skopje.

Four trained nephrologists now perform ultrasound-guided biopsies, with complications in about 6 percent of 345 native kidney biopsies and no biopsy-related deaths. Immunofluorescence testing, routine for decades, speeds early diagnosis. The authors present the country's concentrated, high-volume model as a useful reference for other small health systems building glomerular disease care.
pmc-13568871:
Sungdo Kim and colleagues build, in a 2026 study, a solar water evaporator shaped like an insect compound eye and made from recycled PET plastic waste. Their graphite-filled foam has a spongy, moldable structure that moves water upward while a rounded multi-surface shape catches sunlight from many angles.

Under standard one-sun test light, the device evaporated water at a strong rate for its footprint, and an outdoor unit with a condenser produced fresh water across fourteen hours of natural sun. Side surfaces, heat spreading inside the foam, and steady capillary flow all contributed. The design offers a route to low-cost clean water gear built from plastic waste.
pmc-13568971:
Sehun Oh, Bridget Freisthler, and Devan Hawkins explore, in a 2026 analysis of a long-running United States youth survey, how construction work relates to binge drinking among adults in their early thirties. County construction job share and each person's own job were modeled together, along with work schedules, job insecurity, and psychological distress.

Living where construction employment was larger directly linked to less binge drinking, hinting at a protective community effect. Working construction itself raised exposure to demanding schedules, which raised drinking, yet it also lowered job insecurity and distress. The split findings point policy toward long hours and scarce vacation time rather than toward the industry alone.
pmc-13571371:
Juan Morales and Efraín Gil report a 45-year-old man with Rosenbaum syndrome, a rare fault in the heart's electrical wiring that risks total block. His heart tracing showed one main branch blocked plus alternating blocks in two smaller branches, a pattern that can hide between episodes.

The man felt short of breath on exertion but had no structural heart disease on checks. Fearing sudden complete block and death, doctors implanted a dual-chamber pacemaker wired into the left bundle branch area. That pacing style mimics the heart's own wiring, so the chambers squeeze in natural order. At follow-up his symptoms had resolved and the heart's activation pattern looked normal again.
pmc-13573371:
Jalal Al Khateeb, with four colleagues, reports a 2026 case of stomach infection by cytomegalovirus in a healthy young woman. This herpesvirus usually sleeps quietly in people with sound immune systems, and stomach disease from it is rare. Its signs mimic common gut trouble, so tissue proof is the key step.

The patient, aged 23, came in with stomach pain, vomiting, diarrhoea, and heavy leg swelling after a flu-like spell. Blood tests showed swelling markers up, anaemia, and very low albumin, the protein that later leaked from her gut. A scope showed a raw, sloughing stomach lining, and biopsy found the virus's owl-eye cell changes. Three weeks of an antiviral drug brought fast recovery, with swelling gone and labs near normal. At one month she was well, with no symptoms left.
pmc-13573471:
Shama Prasada Kabekkodu, with three colleagues, reports a 2026 study that hunts hub genes behind stem-like traits in cervical cancer. A small set of cancer stem cells can regrow the tumour, seed its return, and shrug off drugs. The full gene set that keeps those cells stem-like was not pinned down for this cancer.

The team mined past papers and a cell marker database to build a list of 1,345 stemness-linked genes. From that pool, they screened for hub genes, the well-connected few that may steer the rest. The work then weighs how those hubs tie to patient outlook, to immune patterns in the tumour, and to drug response. Lab checks back the computer findings. Hub genes that pass all filters could serve as markers or drug targets for a cancer that still kills many women.
pmc-13574771:
Hassan Gbran and Hendro Murtiono present a 2026 method for spotting early damage in tropical heritage buildings from laser scans. Old masonry in humid lands cracks and soaks long before the eye can tell, and shape-only scan tools miss the damp signal. The new descriptor joins shape with brightness at each point.

The team extended a standard shape histogram with local brightness histograms, then tested the mix across three detector types. Tests used 500 fake cases plus three real scan stretches, two bridge spans and a tunnel, with near 29 million points. The hybrid score more than doubled the shape-only score on the joint quality measure. Damp faults were caught at a high rate with far fewer false alarms from condensation. Even with contrast cut by two fifths, the lead held. Checks cover masonry and concrete in humid tropics only.
pmc-13576171:
Huan Tang leads a 2026 study of muscle loss in stroke patients staying in hospital. Sarcopenia, the loss of muscle mass and strength, is common after stroke and drags down recovery and quality of life. The team measured how widespread it was and what tracked with it, using Asian working group criteria.

Just over half the inpatients, 50.8 percent, met the criteria for sarcopenia. Older age, limb weakness, swallowing problems, lower daily-living scores, and worse nutrition scores each raised the odds on their own. Regular exercise linked to lower odds. Quality of life scores on a sarcopenia-specific survey ran clearly lower in the affected group, across movement, body composition, daily tasks, and fears. The authors call for early screening and support for stroke patients at risk.
pmc-13576571:
Sijia Liao and three colleagues propose a new statistical method for linking a single outcome to a whole image, in a 2026 paper. Such models estimate a surface over the image showing where the image matters. Common smoothing assumptions blur that picture, hiding which regions truly drive the outcome.

Their method, the Generalized Dantzig Selector, demands both sparsity and smoothness of the surface at once. Sparse patches mark regions with no effect, which makes the result readable, while smoothness keeps estimates stable. Simulations and real datasets showed clearer region finding and better accuracy than existing approaches. The team also proves error bounds for the estimator, giving users a sense of how far off it can be. Worked examples span health, brain, and environmental data.
pmc-13577971:
Jordan Gillespie leads a 2026 systematic review asking whether a dark skin thickening called acanthosis nigricans signals metabolic syndrome. The skin change, velvety dark patches in body folds, is a known flag for insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes. Metabolic syndrome is a cluster of risks that raises the odds of heart disease and early death, so an easy visual cue would help early detection.

Searches found 656 articles reporting the skin sign alongside at least one syndrome criterion. Insulin resistance showed the strongest overlap, present in 72.6 percent of reported cases on average. Two-thirds of reports met more than one criterion, with insulin resistance plus raised body mass the most common pairing. In studies where everyone had the skin sign, 67.4 percent met the full syndrome definition. The authors urge primary care to treat the sign as a prompt for metabolic checks.
pmc-13581471:
Anna Liss and colleagues compare the full costs of two non surgical gum disease care plans, in a 2026 study of six hundred fifteen patients in general dental practice. One plan is the classic route, cleaning roots across several visits. The other teaches the patient first, then does the deep clean in a single session. Costs counted the care itself, travel, and lost work time, alongside pocket healing and bleeding checks.

The classic plan cost more in fees by a clear margin and a bit more in lost work time, while travel costs nearly matched. Healing results at six months showed no real gap between the plans. The authors argue the leaner plan frees shared resources for other patients, and that policy should weigh price beside proof when picking a standard route.
pmc-13582071:
Ayaka Tsutsumi and colleagues show that how a study handles missing data can move its answers, in a 2026 audit of child appendix surgery research. A review of one year of papers found over half never mentioned missing data at all, and most of the rest simply dropped incomplete cases. The team then re-ran risk hunts in a national surgery database of over one hundred forty thousand operations, using five ways to treat the gaps.

Nearly four in ten records held holes, mostly height and race. Core risk factors, like illness class and operation length, stayed firm under every method. Others, like white cell counts and body measures, flickered in and out of significance by method. Dropping cases proved the most conservative route. The authors push for filling gaps by imputation and for journals to demand clear reporting.
pmc-13582771:
Kai Liao and colleagues report a 2026 study asking whether a brain scan for tau protein can be made much shorter without losing its value. Tau builds up in Alzheimer disease, and the scan with the tracer named 18F-MK6240 is often used to judge how far the disease has spread. The usual scan takes 20 minutes, which is hard for patients with memory loss who cannot lie still for long.

The group rebuilt scans from 69 memory clinic patients into 5, 10, 15, and 20 minute sets and compared them side by side. Fifty patients read as tau positive and 19 as negative at every length. Even the 5 minute images lost only a little quality, and the numbers for tau spread matched the full scans closely.
pmc-13585671:
Burnor and colleagues test in 2026 whether virus levels in wastewater track ordinary clinical surveillance for influenza A and respiratory syncytial virus in California. Wastewater monitoring promises a view of community transmission that does not depend on who seeks a test.

The team compared wastewater from eighteen treatment plants across ten counties, from July 2022 to March 2024, against data streams. The streams were sentinel laboratory results, mandatory electronic reports, and confirmed influenza hospitalizations. Correlations between wastewater concentrations and the clinical datasets were strong and positive, with a typical rank correlation in the low six tenths range across sites and datasets. Timing analysis, however, found no consistent lead for wastewater: it sometimes ran ahead of clinical data and sometimes behind, by up to a few weeks either way. The authors conclude wastewater best augments, rather than replaces, other surveillance.
pmc-13586771:
Joanne S. Carpenter and a large team ask whether sleep patterns can forecast which troubled young people will fall seriously ill. The study followed 250 people aged 12 to 30 who came to youth mental health services in Sydney, Australia. Each wore a wrist monitor for up to about three weeks to record sleep length, timing, and quality. The team then tracked their care for years as part of a long-running cohort.

Longer sleep at the start, not shorter, predicted a move into full bipolar or psychotic illness. It roughly doubled the odds of that shift and brought it sooner, even after mood and other warning signs were counted. A late sleep midpoint also pointed toward some full illness, though less firmly. The authors read long sleep as an early warning sign worth acting on in youth services.
pmc-13587271:
Saba Izeldin and colleagues quiz senior medical students in Sudan on diabetic eye disease in this study, run in 2022 and published in 2026. Diabetic retinopathy, damage to the retina from diabetes, is a leading cause of blindness that good screening can prevent. As future frontline doctors, students need to spot risk and refer on time. The team surveyed 166 fifth- and sixth-year students at the University of Khartoum with a scored questionnaire.

Average scores landed in the moderate band. Most students knew that years with diabetes drive the risk and that blood sugar control is central. Gaps showed on the disease's vessel nature, on when a first full eye exam should happen, and on laser treatment, which only a bit over half could name. Students who leaned on their college teaching, and those with a close relative with diabetes, scored higher. Stronger teaching is the authors' fix.
pmc-13587371:
Chen and colleagues reported a 2026 genetic study in newborns with congenital heart disease, meaning heart defects present at birth. Some of these babies develop high pressure in the lung arteries, a dangerous condition called pulmonary arterial hypertension. The team asked whether variants in the ACE2 gene change that risk.

Chen enrolled 321 Han Chinese newborns, including 208 with a left to right shunt defect and 113 healthy controls. Three ACE2 variants were typed with Sanger sequencing, a standard DNA reading method, and blood levels of related proteins were compared. No variant or combined pattern linked clearly to the heart defect or to lung pressure risk. One pattern in girls looked protective before statistical correction, but that signal faded once corrections were applied.
pmc-13587971:
Hamza H Cheema and colleagues grade water, sanitation, and hygiene services at two Pakistani hospitals with a World Health Organization tool. Clean water and working sanitation underpin safe care and infection control, yet local facility-level data were scarce. In December 2025, two assessor teams scored one hospital in Rawalpindi and one in Islamabad across close to a hundred shared indicators in seven domains.

The Rawalpindi hospital scored about three quarters of the available points, the Islamabad one about two thirds. Hand hygiene was the strongest domain at both, and sanitation the weakest. The widest gap sat in management and workforce rather than in pipes or buildings, and both sites scored far better on basic than on advanced items. Sixteen indicators failed at both hospitals, clustering in wastewater, laundry, and planning. The authors urge investment in governance alongside hardware.
pmc-13589071:
Sen Yu and five colleagues uncover a brake on pancreatic cancer hidden in a cell's sealing machinery. The protein in question, ZO-2, normally helps stitch cells together at tight junctions, and its behavior in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma was unknown. Their 2027 study linked patient tissue data with lab and mouse experiments to trace what happens when ZO-2 fades.

Tumors held less ZO-2 than healthy tissue, and low levels tracked aggressive disease and worse survival. Restoring ZO-2 slowed cancer cell growth and spread and shrank tumors in mice. It works by grabbing a mitochondrial protein, PGAM5, and holding it in the cell body. Without that grip, PGAM5 crowds the mitochondria and stokes their output, reactive oxygen, and energy supply, which fuels the cancer. ZO-2 levels also tracked immune cell presence. The authors nominate the pair as a drug target.
pmc-13593571:
Candice C. Bedford and a large team of co-authors use data from NASA's Perseverance rover to reconstruct how water changed the olivine-rich Margin unit in Jezero crater on Mars. Orbital images had suggested the unit might be an ancient lake shoreline, and the rover's SuperCam instrument let the team test that idea rock by rock.

Rocks at higher elevations look like slow-cooled crystals that barely met water, while lower exposures record several episodes of change. Carbon-rich fluids first moved through the bedrock and left carbonate behind, then lake or groundwater exposure shifted that carbonate and deposited silica in the pores. Later still, hot fluids ran through younger cracks and laid down fluorite-bearing veins. That layered history of water makes the unit a promising place to look for signs of ancient life.
pmc-13593971:
Lynn Jia Tay, Siew Chin Ong, and Lyn Xuan Tay set out the plan for a review. The review will gather health utility values for breast cancer patients in low- and middle-income countries. Utility values are single numbers summarizing quality of life for use in cost-effectiveness studies, and their 2026 protocol explains why borrowing such numbers from rich countries can mislead local decisions.

The review, registered in advance and following standard reporting guidance, will search four major databases for studies using the EQ-5D questionnaire in these settings. Results will be pooled with statistical models that suit proportion-style data, and separate analyses will compare questionnaire versions, country income levels, and cancer stages. The authors expect the finished review to give planners in resource-limited health systems numbers that reflect their own patients' lives rather than imported assumptions.
pmc-13595471:
Joyce Meijer and colleagues examined how reimbursement policy shaped gene-expression testing and chemotherapy decisions in Dutch breast cancer care. From the Netherlands Cancer Registry, 138,765 women aged eighteen to sixty-nine with early-stage cancer diagnosed between 2011 and 2024 were included. Testing rates and chemotherapy use were tracked across reimbursement periods and regions.

Among 17,525 patients with a testing indication, use rose from 9 percent without reimbursement to 25 percent under retrospective reimbursement and 37 percent under publicly known reimbursement. Low-risk test results usually meant no chemotherapy, while high-risk results usually meant chemotherapy. Yet only about a third of eligible patients received a test even when reimbursement was known, a gap the authors flag for follow-up.
pmc-13595771:
Elizabeth Palu and co-authors tested a weight loss challenge designed with, and for, a Samoan church community in Sydney, where Pacific Islander migrants face high rates of diabetes and obesity. Their 2026 feasibility study delivered twelve weekly lifestyle messages on activity and eating through peer supporters and volunteers, asking first whether the model could work at all.

Engagement was strong: dropout ran at only about five percent and the program cost little to run. Among the thirty-four participants with complete measurements, median weight fell by a few kilograms over twelve weeks, with body fat down and vigorous activity and sitting time both improved. Attending at least eight sessions predicted bigger gains. When the community reran the challenge a year later, average weight loss was larger still, suggesting the tailored, community-led design can sustain itself.
pmc-13598071:
Nicole A Perry-Hauser leads an eleven-author study of mice missing the Adgrl3 gene, a brain receptor genetically tied to ADHD and substance use, measuring how their striatum handles dopamine. Two complementary methods gave seemingly opposite answers in their 2026 experiments.

In brain slices, electrically triggered dopamine release ran higher than normal in both striatal regions. In living mice doing a timed reward task, a fluorescent dopamine sensor showed weaker cue-evoked signals in the reward region. The animals were also slower to press and collect rewards. That echoes task-switching difficulties in ADHD. A stimulant challenge showed the dopamine stores themselves were intact, able to release normally when pushed. The authors read the split as a wiring problem in how terminals are organized, and they call for work on the spatial layout of dopamine release sites.
pmc-13598871:
Xianping Huang and colleagues report a 72-year-old man with chest tightness, cough, and a history of coughing blood, against a background of thirty years of smoking and eight years of mine-dust exposure. Chest imaging showed diffuse silicosis and narrowing of a lower-lobe bronchus. Bronchoscopy revealed a swollen, tumour-like bump in the upper lobe.

Narrow-band imaging showed thick, tortuous vessels in dark bluish green, indicating a submucosal artery curving directly to the surface, the hallmark of bronchial Dieulafoy's disease. No biopsy was taken, to avoid life-threatening bleeding, and contrast imaging confirmed the diagnosis. Bronchial artery embolization stopped the bleeding, with no recurrence after two years.
pmc-13601471:
Dávid Jónás and three colleagues track an aging signal in dog DNA in 2026, testing blood as a window on body aging. With age, chemical methylation tags loosen their grip on repetitive DNA elements named LINE-1, which may disturb genome stability. Dogs age faster than humans and share our homes, making them a useful model. The team measured LINE-1 methylation in blood cell-free DNA and in brain prefrontal cortex.

They mapped 264 potentially active canine LINE-1 elements and chose a stable target site shared across copies. A digestion-based test, checked against a second method, measured methylation at that site. In healthy dogs, blood methylation fell steadily with age, following a curved pattern. Older dogs showed lower brain methylation too. The authors propose blood LINE-1 methylation as a candidate non-invasive aging marker in dogs, noting their groups were snapshots, not dogs followed across life.
pmc-13613771:
Arta Lamallari and colleagues test in 2026 how much load thin chewing-surface veneers can bear before they crack, and whether the material and the base beneath them change the answer. Veneers one millimetre thick were made from zirconia, two glass-ceramic materials, and a resin composite. Each type was bonded to one of three bases that mimic worn teeth: dentine ringed by enamel, plain dentine, or resin composite, with ten samples per group.

Before breaking them, the team aged the samples through 1.2 million chewing cycles with heat and cold swings between 5 and 50 degrees. Both the veneer material and the base type shaped the breaking load, and reliability analysis showed how the risk of failure spread. Dentists restoring worn back teeth can use the results to pair material and tooth base more wisely.
pmc-13614871:
Leila Kasraian and colleagues analyse six years of blood donor deferrals in Iran, from 2016 to 2021, in a 2026 study of the national donation database. Deferral means turning a willing donor away, for a short time or for good, and it shapes both blood supply and whether donors ever return. The records covered nearly thirteen million donation attempts across the country.

Of those attempts, 16.67 percent ended in deferral, split into 14.37 percent temporary and 2.30 percent permanent. First-time donors were turned away far more often, at 32.19 percent, against 8.98 percent for regular donors. Rates also varied by province and were high among women donors. Blood services can use such patterns to coach new donors better and to keep experienced ones from drifting away after a single refusal.
pmc-13616271:
Jae Yeong Jang, Hanchul Cho, and Young Jung present a bio-inspired way to grow tiny cracks inside a sensor film using swelling microspheres, instead of stretching or bending the film from outside. Crack-based strain sensors are prized in health monitors and robot skins because a crack that opens slightly changes resistance a lot, giving extreme sensitivity. External bending, though, offers poor control over where cracks land and how dense they are.

Expanding spheres build stress from within, and the stress gathers where the metal film is thin, splitting it in repeatable patterns. Their sensor reached a sensitivity figure of 24,320 at a stretch of just 1.6 percent. It stayed steady under both held and repeated loads. Built-in cracking gives designers a dial for crack shape and density, opening finer wearable and structural sensors.
pmc-13617271:
Yifan Li and three colleagues review additive manufacturing, better known as 3D printing, as a remedy for the production bottlenecks holding back tissue engineering and regenerative medicine. Building living tissue requires exact control of structure, cell placement, and reproducibility, which traditional fabrication struggles to deliver. Printing promises to translate digital designs into three-dimensional constructs with defined shape and internal architecture.

Working through examples of bone-cartilage units, skin, and vascular grafts, the review tests where printing truly helps: structural fidelity, spatial patterning, digital reproducibility, and tailoring to the patient. The authors also weigh stubborn limits, including bioink trade-offs, resolution limits, and regulatory barriers. Their verdict is that being printable does not guarantee biological function. Clinical success will hinge on proving tissue maturation, integration with the host, and compliance within real hospital workflows, helped by data-driven design.
pmc-13618371:
Guoqiang Zou and three colleagues mine public gene data for diagnostic markers of osteoarthritis tied to the RHO GTPase family, proteins involved in cell signaling and inflammation. They combined several expression datasets with a single-cell dataset, filtered differentially expressed genes through machine learning feature selection, and built an artificial neural network classifier. A final shortlist of genes was checked across datasets and explored for pathway and immune links.

From eight hundred one altered genes, three biomarkers survived: VAV1, STMN2, and RND1. The neural network separated patients from controls very strongly in its training data and well in validation data. Each gene connected to dozens of pathways, with five shared by all three, and one marker tracked with natural killer cell levels. In the single-cell data, fibroblasts emerged as the key population, communicating strongly with endothelial cells. The authors propose the trio as candidates for early detection research.
pmc-13618771:
Yunjian Li and four colleagues build a machine learning potential that lets computers simulate cement's binding glue, calcium silicate hydrate, with near-quantum accuracy. This disordered nanoscale gel decides concrete's strength and durability, yet its shifting chemistry defeats simple models. The team trained their potential on more than fifty thousand quantum-labeled cases drawn from nearly seven hundred distinct mixes spanning defects and hydration states.

The resulting model reproduced structural, dynamic, and mechanical properties close to full quantum calculations. It settled long-standing disagreements with high-pressure X-ray experiments, and transferred reliably to large, disordered, and nanoporous systems it had never seen. It also runs much faster than the standard reactive force field it replaces. The authors frame it as a foundation for cement modeling at many scales, a data-driven cement genome, and lower-carbon construction materials.
pmc-13619071:
Isabel Ericson led a 2026 study of insomnia symptoms in a Swiss cohort in Lausanne, asking how common they are, what they travel with, and how overnight sleep recordings differ. Insomnia is diagnosed from self-report, so its sleep signature remains murky. The team drew on 3,947 adults aged forty to eighty-two. Insomnia symptoms meant trouble starting or staying asleep at least three nights a week in the past month, or regular sleeping-pill use.

A third of participants met that definition. Older age, female sex, less education, blood fats, heavy drinking, depression, anxiety, sleeping-pill use, and daytime sleepiness each tracked with symptoms. Among 1,718 people who had overnight recordings, those with symptoms slept less and took longer to fall asleep. They woke more after sleep onset and slept less efficiently, all by small margins. Finer brain-wave measures, such as faster wake-like activity, showed more consistent links.
pmc-13619671:
Isabel Hoffmann and four colleagues ran a pilot study on two small RNA molecules in the blood of pregnant women with pre-eclampsia. Pre-eclampsia is a dangerous blood pressure disorder of pregnancy that can begin early or late. The team compared ten women with early-onset disease and eight with late-onset disease, each group against its own set of healthy controls, using a precise lab method to measure two microRNAs.

One molecule, miR-210-3p, ran higher in the early-onset group than in its controls, though a stricter check weakened that result. The second molecule showed only a numerical gap that did not reach significance. Late-onset cases looked much like their controls on both measures. With such small groups and overlap with fetal growth problems, the authors label everything here exploratory and ask for larger, cleaner studies.
pmc-13621771:
Tao Zhou and three co-authors examine how PFOA, a long-lasting industrial chemical, may harm male reproductive health. Their study links the chemical to three problems: erectile dysfunction, male infertility, and testicular dysfunction. Rather than testing patients, the team used a network approach that maps how a chemical, its protein targets, and disease genes connect.

The team gathered PFOA targets and disease genes from public databases, built interaction maps, and tested on a computer how strongly the chemical binds key proteins. Ten core genes were shared across all three conditions, touching hormone signals, nitric oxide pathways, cell death, and inflammation. Early cell experiments backed some of the predicted gene changes. The authors present the map as a working theory that still needs direct testing before firm risk claims can be made.
pmc-13626071:
Melissa C Osborne and co-authors build a virtual reality program that teaches parents to childproof their homes. Injury is the top killer of American children, and over 2,700 under-six deaths from accidents were counted in 2023, many at home. The team followed human-centered design, drafting content from research, then interviewing five parenting-program providers and seven parents in focus groups about limits, content, and appetite for headset learning.

The prototype trains three skills: spotting hazards, removing or softening them, and supervising children well. Parents then tried the prototype in a small pilot of five. Feedback shaped how the program could slot into existing evidence-based parenting services, which rarely teach home safety in a structured way. A safe virtual home, the authors hope, builds habits that hold in the real one.
pmc-13626371:
Minghai Huang and colleagues grade eye surgery by severity for Mooren's ulcer, a painful, cornea-eating disease that resists medicine. Their review covers twenty-four patients operated on between February 2016 and January 2024 after drugs failed, with follow-up averaging thirty months. The algorithm matched the tool to the damage: membrane grafts for shallower ulcers, partial-thickness corneal transplants for deep ones, and full transplants for large holes.

Healing after the first operation reached nearly ninety-six percent overall, and the eyeball survived in twenty-one of twenty-four patients. Vision results split by severity, with membrane graft patients most often keeping useful sight, while recurrence haunted the transplant groups and both full-transplant cases did poorly. A severity ladder, the authors conclude, saves globes even when sight stays fragile.
pmc-13626971:
Zahra Taheri-Ezbarami and colleagues interview Iranian health workers about the strain of nursing the dying. Fifteen participants, from bedside nurses and head nurses to supervisors, academics, a manager, and a critical care doctor, spoke in depth between October and December 2023. Their accounts were sorted by content analysis into four tangled themes that feed one another.

First came the emotional burden itself: fear, compassion fatigue, moral distress, and grief. Around it sat systemic neglect, with training gaps, no national standards, and no palliative care organization. Then came fractured teamwork in a doctor-centered system with blurry roles. Finally came missing support, from money to technology. The authors call for end-of-life care to be built into policy, protocols, and nursing education.
pmc-13629071:
Jeanne I. M. Parmentier and four colleagues taught computers to hear breathing in hard-working horses. They used plain microphone recordings. Their study appeared in 2026. Standardbred trotters make loud breath-out sounds at high effort. Tracking breath rate in training could flag welfare and performance trouble early.

The team compared a classic signal method with two deep learning designs. One network design performed best. It spotted breaths reliably and guessed breath rate with the smallest average error. It beat both the rival network and the classic method. The models also held up well on quieter, lower-effort recordings. The authors call the work a first step. Routine breath checks in training yards may follow.
pmc-13629271:
Hanna Järbrink and four colleagues reviewed the medical records of 270 patients aged sixty-five and over admitted with physical trauma to a Swedish level-one trauma centre between 2020 and 2024. Published in 2026, the study counted nurse-sensitive adverse events, harms closely tied to nursing care, using a modified trigger tool.

Just over a quarter of patients suffered at least one such event, giving an overall rate near thirty-eight events per hundred admissions. Hospital-acquired infections were the most common harm, followed by overfilled bladders and pressure injuries. Frailty raised the odds, and length of stay emerged as the strongest predictor of all. The authors urge earlier risk spotting and more reliable preventive nursing for this vulnerable group.
pmc-13630471:
Zhijun He and four colleagues report the rescue of a woman of seventy-one with a chronic rectal fistula. A fistula is an abnormal channel. Hers sat at the join left by rectal cancer surgery twelve years earlier. Imaging showed the tract plugged by a hard mass of stool. The mass was nearly three centimetres wide and lodged inside the fistula itself.

Working through a scope, the team widened the tract. They broke up the mass and pulled it out. Then they closed the opening in stages. Barbed stitches pulled the edges together without knots. Controlled burning stripped the tract's lining to spur fresh healing. A large clip sealed the hole. Checks three to four weeks later confirmed full healing with no leakage. The authors present the sequence as help for chronic fistulas. Such fistulas resist simple clipping.
pmc-13631771:
Marvah Hill Pierre-Louis and fourteen colleagues studied lung health in rural Uganda, where long-term lung data are scarce. Adults answered health questions and took breathing tests up to three times over four years. The team measured how much air people could blow out and how that ability changed with age, symptoms, smoking, and income.

Nine hundred two adults completed over fourteen hundred acceptable breathing tests. About one in seven had abnormal lung function at the start, more often women and people with lasting chest symptoms. Lung capacity fell each year even in this young group where most people had never smoked. Decline was faster among those whose first tests looked normal. Because risk persisted despite normal early results, the authors urge earlier detection and stronger local lung care.
pmc-13633071:
Thomas Langelet and six colleagues report a fatal complication of cosmetic fat transfer surgery. A forty-year-old woman suffered cardiac arrest during breast fat grafting, where fat taken by liposuction is injected elsewhere. Revived but unstable, she showed signs of an overloaded right heart and a mass inside it on ultrasound imaging. Doctors placed her on a heart-lung support machine at once.

Her course turned grim. A whole-body clotting disorder consumed her blood's clotting factors, demanding huge transfusion volumes within a day. Lung failure, repeated clotting problems with a stroke, and failing heart function followed, and care was eventually withdrawn. Autopsy found fat blocking her lung vessels and fat caught in the cords of a heart valve, matching the mass seen on imaging. The authors say spotting such trapped fat early may signal a heavy embolic load and a poor outlook.
pmc-13633171:
Anne-Claire Dupont and four colleagues published this 2026 case report on a cancer scan that disagreed with a tissue test. A forty-eight-year-old woman had been treated for hormone-sensitive breast cancer. Four years later, pain led to a suspicious spot on her breastbone. One scan type, which tracks sugar use, lit up strongly there. A second scan, designed to light up where estrogen receptors are active, showed nothing in the same spot.

A biopsy settled the question: the spot was metastatic cancer whose cells still carried estrogen receptors strongly. The second tracer reports whether receptors are free to bind, not whether they exist. Leftover drug effects, changed receptors, or uneven tumor biology can all hide uptake. The authors warn that a blank scan must never be read as missing receptors, since that mistake could steer patients away from hormone therapy that might help.
pmc-13633571:
Alexandre Meurant and four colleagues tested whether one joint training hour could sharpen anesthesiologists' pain decisions for older surgical patients. Older adults react more strongly to pain drugs, and their pain is harder to judge when thinking is impaired. A geriatrician and a clinical pharmacist taught the session together. Seventeen anesthesiologists answered twenty case vignettes before and after, and their answers were scored against a panel of thirteen geriatric experts.

Scores rose by nearly a third after training. The biggest gains came in choosing pain medicines and in managing side effects. Pain assessment scores did not improve, which hints that this skill needs a different teaching approach. Most participants had never been trained in prescribing pain relief for older adults, and most did not know the guidelines. The authors see team teaching between specialties as a practical way to close that gap.
pmc-13635471:
Wakako Kawarazaki and six colleagues studied why aging kidneys let potassium build up in the blood. High potassium is common in older people and can disturb the heart's rhythm. Klotho, a protein tied to slower aging, falls with age. The team used mice born with reduced Klotho to trace how the kidney's final urine segment handles potassium. They measured the channels that secrete potassium, the salt channel powering them, and the hormone that coordinates both.

The low-Klotho mice developed high blood potassium and excreted too little in urine. A growth signaling hub, mTORC1, ran overactive and pulled the main potassium channel off the cell surface. The salt channel and its hormone ramped up in compensation, which masked the problem until a blocking drug unmasked it dangerously. Blocking mTORC1, or topping up Klotho, restored the channel and normalized blood potassium. The authors name this axis a treatment target.
pmc-13639671:
Atsushi Araki wrote a 2026 editorial on bladder dysfunction as an overlooked complication of diabetes. The piece responds to a study by Chawla and colleagues linking bladder problems with poor sleep among clinic patients who have type 2 diabetes.

Araki notes that lower urinary tract symptoms affect an estimated half to four fifths of people with diabetes, spanning urgency, incontinence, and incomplete emptying. Poor sleep and bladder trouble each lowered quality of life in the cited study. The editorial urges clinicians to ask about bladder function routinely, treating it as a core part of diabetes and geriatric care rather than a side issue.
pmc-13641971:
Débora Costa Ruiz led a 2026 lab study of image quality from a stationary intraoral tomosynthesis system, which takes conventional two-dimensional dental X-rays with multiple sources aimed at one sensor. Standard intraoral images flatten three-dimensional anatomy, hiding root fractures and resorption behind overlapping structures. The team imaged an acrylic phantom and a dental quality phantom at 60 and 70 kilovolts, with and without post-processing export, measuring brightness, noise, uniformity, and resolution.

Processed exports were brighter and more uniform, with lower contrast and less noise than unprocessed frames. Spatial resolution reached 9 line pairs per millimeter at 60 kilovolts and 10 at 70, regardless of processing, while contrast resolution favored unprocessed images at either voltage. Dentists get a clear trade-off: post-processing cleans up brightness and noise but costs contrast, while higher voltage improves spatial detail without changing that balance.
pmc-13643671:
Low and Markovic compared in 2026 two imaging routes for dogs that cannot walk after a slipped spinal disc. The dogs were short-legged breeds prone to this injury, where disc material bursts into the spinal canal and needs fast surgery. The standard route is magnetic resonance imaging, but the team tested whether CT myelography, a scan after dye injection, given under set conditions could match it.

Low studied 560 pet dogs, most scanned with MRI and 42 with the CT method during MRI downtime. Recovery of walking was no worse with the CT route in both main analyses, meeting the set non-inferiority margin. Rates of nerve worsening, cord damage, and major problems did not differ either. Total and imaging costs were clearly lower for the CT group. The authors say routine MRI may not be justified when this injury is already highly likely.
pmc-13644371:
Ayaka Ishii-Takahashi and four colleagues present a 2026 systematic review of long-term MRI studies of brain development in children with attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder. Screening 3,385 papers published up to September 2025 left thirty-two longitudinal studies with baseline ages from four to eighteen.

Children with ADHD showed smaller brain and cerebellum volumes and delayed peaks in cortical thickness in frontal, temporal, and occipital areas. Several gaps narrowed with age, while one region, the ventral striatum, shrank atypically. A pooled analysis of gray matter change found no firm group difference. The authors urge standardized multicenter work accounting for sex, other conditions, and medication.
pmc-13644471:
Lin and co-authors argue that hydrogen peroxide deserves a central place in the search for life's chemical origins beyond Earth. Their 2026 perspective gathers recent work showing peroxide feeds several model reactions that mimic early metabolism, and that it forms without life through multiple routes. The molecule has been detected in the atmosphere of Mars and across icy moon surfaces.

Because Earth's geology has erased its earliest chemical record, the authors propose that peroxide-producing worlds may still run prebiotic chemistry today, open to inspection by advanced missions. They offer a guiding slogan to sit alongside astrobiology's traditional follow-the-water rule: where there is water, there is hydrogen peroxide. Testing the idea, they say, needs experiments and theory that model peroxide-rich conditions on Mars and the icy moons directly.
pmc-13645771:
Qiangli Lei and Qing Liu chart research growth on music therapy for cognitive impairment, covering the years 2006 to 2026 in a bibliometric study. Music therapy is a drug-free approach that is easy to deliver, and its use for memory and thinking problems has spread. The pair mined a large citation database and cross-checked findings in a second one. They also gathered randomized trials from a medical database to judge the clinical evidence.

The main database yielded 835 publications, with output rising steadily and peaking in 2025. Leading countries were the United States, China, the United Kingdom, and Australia. Core topics covered dementia, Alzheimer's disease, quality of life, and thinking problems, while newer work turns toward brain plasticity and long-term care. With 250 trials found, the authors say the trial base is growing, though stronger and more uniform trials are still needed.
pmc-13645871:
Perceived autonomy among long-term prostate cancer survivors is studied in a German-language paper led by Peter. Autonomy is a core psychological need in later life, linked closely to quality of life, wellbeing, and everyday functioning. It can be eroded by ageing and by the lasting effects of cancer treatment. Peter and colleagues analysed survey responses from more than two thousand survivors, averaging eighty years old, who had undergone radical prostate removal within a German family prostate-cancer research project.

About eighty-six percent rated themselves as rather autonomous. Lower perceived autonomy tracked with older age, lower education, worse perceived finances, ongoing cancer therapy, lower quality of life, anxiety about progression, and lack of internet use. Peter and colleagues conclude that autonomy largely endures long after prostate cancer, but remains vulnerable to modifiable factors, pointing toward patient-centred follow-up care that protects everyday independence in older survivors.
pmc-13647371:
Lianhua Hou and seven colleagues test a copper-based catalyst for cooking oil out of shale rock inside a sealed reactor, a step toward producing shale oil in place. The target rock is the Chang 7 shale of China's Ordos Basin, rich but stubborn with ordinary methods. Their catalyst joins copper to an amine partner and was dosed at a tiny fraction of the rock's weight. The sealed run held at a fixed high temperature for three hours.

With the catalyst, shale oil yield jumped by about a third over plain heating. The oil also came out cleaner: roughly a third of its sulfur and over half of its nitrogen were stripped away. Quality gains of that size matter for refining costs. The authors say the cheap, low-dose catalyst shows potential for cost-effective in-ground shale production, a route that could unlock reserves that surface mining cannot touch.
pmc-13647571:
Chenyun He and four colleagues compare daily habits against protective routines as predictors of common respiratory infections in Chinese college students after the pandemic. Their survey ran through June 2024 at six universities in the southeast, gathering 1,535 valid replies from students whose first COVID-19 infection was at least a year past. Episodes of upper respiratory infection over the previous year were counted. Models entered habits and protective behaviors in both orders to compare their weight fairly.

Lifestyle factors improved the model far more than protective behaviors did. Daytime sleepiness and heavy sitting tracked with more infections, while sleeping at least seven hours and moderate activity tracked with fewer. Among protective routines, only natural ventilation of rooms held a steady link with fewer episodes; handwashing and distancing showed none. The authors suggest health programs should sell sleep and movement first, with open windows as the one hygiene habit that earned its keep.
pmc-13649471:
Yin Shu and five colleagues report a patient with two distinct stomach cancers at once, one of them a rare liver-like type tied to high levels of a blood marker. The disease at first looked beyond surgery. A team from many fields chose a four-part plan of two chemo drugs, an immune drug, and a drug that chokes tumour blood supply.

Scans showed the tumours shrank, and the blood marker fell back to normal. Surgeons then removed the whole stomach. Lab checks found no live cancer in either tumour bed or in 20 nearby lymph nodes, a full response. The authors warn that one case cannot set a standard, and follow-up was short.
pmc-13649671:
Yongsheng Ruan and four colleagues open a set of 14 papers on child blood diseases, a field they say has entered a precision age. Old tests read cell shape under a lens. New care leans on gene scans, smart math, and immune rescue cures.

The papers sort into four scenes. One set digs into how child leukaemia starts in the genes. One builds models that guess outcomes and side harms. One turns to failed marrow and red cell ills. The last warns of traps in spotting rare cancers. A star case tells of twin babies with the same leukaemia gene swap who stayed clear eight years on cell therapy alone, no donor marrow needed.
pmc-13650471:
Omar Tluli and four colleagues review the role of innate immunity, the body's fast first-line defense system, in driving high blood pressure.
